The decision in this matter is as follows: If a monk, without being commanded by the owners saying, "Take this property and go to such a place," but of his own accord says, "Give me such and such goods, I will carry your goods for you," and while carrying their goods on his head, touches those goods with the intention to steal, he commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). If, without exceeding the aforementioned boundary of the head, he moves it forward or backward while rubbing it from here to there, he commits a grave offense (thullaccaya). At the moment he lowers it to his shoulder, even if the owners have the thought, "Let this monk carry it," because he was not commanded by those owners, he commits an offense of defeat (pārājika). For a monk who moves it even as much as a hair's breadth from the head without lowering it to the shoulder, he commits an offense of defeat (pārājika). In the case of a double load (yamakabhāra) where one part of the prepared burden rests on the head and another part rests on the back, the decision should be understood by way of the two resting places. This decision is stated only by way of a burden solely on the head. This same decision stated regarding a burden on the head should also be understood regarding a burden on the shoulder and so forth.

Deposited goods (upanikkhittabhaṇḍa) refers to goods placed in one's hands by others for the purpose of being well-secured (guarded). It should be connected with the phrase "I do not take it." This statement "I do not take" is a present tense used in the sense of the past, meaning "I did not take it." Although it is a deliberate lie, because it is a preliminary effort (pubbapayoga) of taking what is not given (adinnādāna), he commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). For a monk who says, "What are you saying? This speech is neither suitable for me nor suitable for you," and so forth, he also commits only an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Causing doubt in the owner means causing the owner of the goods to have doubt, thinking, "I deposited the goods in this monk's hand in a secluded place; no one else besides me and the monk knows; will he give it to me or will he not?" Relinquishing the burden (dhuraṃ nikkhipati) means giving up the effort (to get it back) upon seeing the monk's harsh or rude behavior and so forth. In that matter, if this monk still has the effort (intention) to give, thinking, "I will give it only after making this owner exhausted," he is still free (from pārājika). If that monk has no effort to give, but the owner of the goods still has the effort to take it back, he is also still free. If that monk has no effort to give, and the owner of the goods also relinquishes the burden (gives up hope), thinking, "He will not give it to me anymore," thus by the relinquishing of the burden by both, the monk commits an offense of defeat (pārājika). Even if he says with his mouth, "I will give it," but in his mind he does not wish to give, thus by the owner's relinquishing of the burden, the monk commits an offense of defeat (pārājika).

Thinking, "I will take the goods along with the carrier," and crossing the first step means threatening the carrier, blocking his path, and taking one step in the direction of one's own choice. Situated on land (thalaṭṭha) means goods placed on land, whether on the ground or on a stone slab, a mountain surface, and so forth, whether in a concealed or unconcealed place. If he causes it to shake, he commits a grave offense (thullaccaya); this means if a monk...
200:
If he causes it to shake, for every effort of his, there is a grave offense (thullaccaya). In touching with the intention to steal, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa); in causing it to shake, there is a grave offense (thullaccaya). These occur separately for a monk who makes the efforts of touching and shaking with the intention to steal. However, some say, "For one who takes it with a single effort, if it is lifted up, there is only an offense of defeat (pārājika), not wrongdoing or grave offenses."

"From the place" (ṭhānā) means from the place where it is situated. If the goods on dry land are in a heap, the decision should be made according to the decision on [goods] inside a pot, or placed in a vessel, or grasping and cutting with the hand. If it is stuck together with resin and so on, the decision should be made according to the decision on cooked honey or molasses. If it is a heavy load, such as a mass of iron, or a jar of oil or honey, the decision should be made according to the decision on moving [goods] from their place in a pot. The displacement of goods bound with an iron chain should also be noted.

When pulling a spread-out rug (pāvāra), mat, or similar item by holding it straight, if the further edge passes the spot touched by the nearer edge, it is an offense of defeat (pārājika). Likewise, when holding and pushing it forward, if the nearer edge passes the spot touched by the further edge, it is an offense of defeat (pārājika). When moving it to the left or to the right, if the left edge or the right edge passes the spot touched by the right edge or the left edge, it is an offense of defeat (pārājika). When lifting it by rolling it up, for a monk who causes it to reach the air (lift off) even by a hair's breadth, it is an offense of defeat (pārājika).

One's own hand is "one's hand" (sahattha); theft performed by that hand or connected with that hand is "theft by one's own hand" (sāhatthika-avahāra). A command is āṇatti; theft performed by that command is "theft by command" (āṇattika-avahāra). Throwing away is nissagga; standing in a place where customs duties are evaded or in a planned spot and throwing the goods outside is "theft by throwing" (nissaggiya-avahāra). Because it accomplishes the result called the offense of defeat even before the act of theft is completed, it is called "theft that accomplishes the purpose" (atthasādhaka-avahāra). Laying down, abandoning, or reaching a state of no effort regarding the burden, which is the attachment to the responsibility, is "laying down the burden" (dhura-nikkhepa).

Now, wishing to show only the meaning of those terms without paying much attention to the grammar, he said, "Among them, what is called sāhatthika..." and so on. "By one's own hand" (sahatthā) means with one's own hand (sahatthena). Indeed, here the word sahatthā is in the instrumental sense, though it has an ablative ending. In commanding another, "Steal the goods of so-and-so," the offense should be understood at the very moment of the command. If so, what is the difference between this āṇattika and atthasādhaka? Urging to take at that very moment is the effort of āṇattika; urging to take after some time has passed is atthasādhaka. This is the difference between the two. Therefore, it was said, "He commands: Steal the goods of so-and-so when you are able."
201:
Suṅkaghātaparikappitokāsānaṃ refers to the place of evading customs and the planned place. Among those two, evading customs (suṅkaghāta) is a name for a customs office (tax station) designated by signs such as trees, mountains, and so forth. Indeed, because those who carry goods out from that place without paying the tax (suṅka) due to the king are destroying or ruining the king's tax, it is called "suṅkaghāta."

When someone enters another's precinct (pariveṇa) and so forth and sees any desirable object, the place where he plans, at the doorway or the front of the house and so forth, "If they see me in this place, I will act as if I am walking around holding it because I want to look at it; if they do not see me, I will take it away," is called a planned place (parikappitokāsa). "He becomes pārājika at the very moment of commanding" means he becomes pārājika at the very moment of the intention that accomplishes the theft. Even if the thief steals that property after more than sixty years have passed, if the commander dies in the meantime or returns to the lower life (disrobes), or will die or will disrobe, at the very moment the thief steals, the commander becomes pārājika. Oil worth a pāda (pādagghanakatela): in this term, "pāda" is one-fourth of a kahāpaṇa. Oil that is worth that one pāda is called pādagghanakatela. Objects of which sandals (upāhanā) are the first are called upāhanādi. By the word "ādi" (and so forth), fine cloth (dukūla), robes, pieces of leather, and so forth are to be taken. "Pakkhipati" means he puts it in with the intention to steal. Therefore, it is said, "He becomes pārājika as soon as it is released from the hand." If, while another person is pouring ghee or oil into his own jar, he puts in a device for sucking oil with the intention to steal, he becomes pārājika in the manner already stated.

Effort made by body or by speech is the effort of commanding (āṇāpana-payoga). Because it occurs before the commanded person takes the goods, it is called "preliminary effort" (pubbapayoga). Theft that occurs together with the effort of commanding is "simultaneous effort" (sahapayoga). Theft by arranging and consulting together in agreement is "theft by arrangement" (saṃvidhāvahāra); it means theft committed by mutual understanding. Making a recognition by designating a time such as the morning and so forth is an "agreement" (saṅketa). The act of doing so is "act of agreement" (saṅketakamma). The act of making a sign is "sign-making" (nimittakamma); it means the making of some sign for the purpose of creating recognition. Therein, among the five aforementioned types such as preliminary effort and so forth, by way of taking land and so forth by moving stakes (khila) and so forth, the stake, the rope, the fence, or the boundary...
202:
...by moving a wall (pākāra) to seize a field, or by moving a stake, a rope, a fence, a boundary, or a wall to seize a building site. If the land is to be taken by moving two stakes, a thullaccaya offense is incurred for the first stake (plucking or moving it), and a pārājika offense is incurred for the second stake. If it is to be taken by moving three stakes, a dukkaṭa offense is incurred for the first, a thullaccaya for the second, and a pārājika for the third. In this manner, even if there are many stakes, excluding the last two, a dukkaṭa is incurred for the preceding stakes; of the last two, a thullaccaya is incurred for one, and a pārājika for the other. The same method applies to stretching a rope and so forth.

As for the statement in the Samantapāsādikā Commentary, "That [theft] occurs by the owners' relinquishing of responsibility (dhurani-kkhepa)," it should be understood as referring to seizing by means of a lawsuit (abhiyoga), because it was stated in the context of "He brings a lawsuit for a field, there is an offense of dukkaṭa," and so forth.

The word 'saṃvidahitvā' is a synonym for 'saṃmantayitvā'. It means having spoken and consulted with a common desire and a common intention. To prevent confusion regarding this 'saṃvidhā-avahāra' (theft by arrangement), it is said, "When they have gone after arranging thus," and so forth. 'Saṅjānanakamma' (the act of recognition) is the making of a sign by means of a time-limit such as the morning. Therefore, it is said, "If indeed," and so forth.

In this context of 'saṅketakamma', if it is said, "Steal in the morning," and the theft is committed in the morning today, or tomorrow, or in a future year, there is no deviation from the appointment (vi-saṅketa), and both the commander and the thief incur a pārājika offense. However, if it is said, "Steal in the morning today," but the theft is committed tomorrow, it is a theft committed after the fixed appointment of "today" has passed. If it is said, "Steal in the morning tomorrow," but the theft is committed in the morning today, it is a theft committed before reaching the fixed appointment of "tomorrow." When theft is committed in this way, only the thief incurs a pārājika; the commander (mūlaṭṭha) incurs no offense. If it is said, "Steal only in the morning tomorrow," and the person steals on that very day or in the evening tomorrow, he is said to steal before or after that appointment. One who does not act thus but steals only at the designated time should be known as stealing neither before nor after the appointment. This method should also be understood for the evening, night, and day; and for the first watch, middle watch, last watch, the dark fortnight, the bright fortnight, the month, the season, the year, and so forth, regarding the fulfillment of an appointment (saṅketa) or its failure (vi-saṅketa).

Because they are the cause for producing the recognition of the intent to steal another's property, winking and so forth are called signs (nimitta). The making of such signs as winking is called 'akkhinikhana-ādi-nimittakaraṇa'. By the word 'ādi' (etc.), it includes various manners such as raising the eyebrows, nodding the head, raising the hand, clapping the hands, snapping the fingers, craning the neck, coughing, and so forth. The remaining judgment in this 'nimittakamma' is exactly as described in the method for 'saṅketakamma'.
203:
A thief is called 'thena'; the state of that thief is 'theyya' (theft); taking by that state of a thief is 'theyyāvahāra'. Taking by overpowering and force is 'pasayhāvahāra'. Planning by marking clothes, thread, etc., is 'parikappa'; taking by such planning is 'parikappāvahāra'. Taking goods covered with grass, leaves, etc., is 'paṭicchannāvahāra'. Taking by means of a grass-lottery is 'kusāvahāra'.

In the phrase 'kūṭamāna kūṭakahāpaṇādi', fraudulent measurement (kūṭamāna) is of three types: hadayabheda (piercing the heart/interior), sikhābheda (breaking the peak), and rajjubheda (breaking the rope). Among these three, 'hadaya' refers to the interior of measuring vessels such as a nāḷi; piercing that interior with a hole is 'hadayabheda'. This hadayabheda occurs when measuring ghee, oil, and so on. Indeed, a person buying such ghee or oil uses a measure with a hole at the bottom, saying "pour slowly," and takes it after letting much of it leak into his own container. When selling, however, he plugs the hole and gives it after filling it quickly.

Sikhābheda occurs when measuring sesame, rice, and so on. Indeed, a person buying such sesame or rice takes it after slowly letting the peak (the heap) rise. When selling, however, he fills it with great speed and gives it while cutting off the peak.

Rajjubheda occurs when measuring fields and plots of land. Indeed, those who measure fields and so on measure small land making it appear large, and large land making it appear small.

A counterfeit coin made of red copper and so on is called 'kūṭakahāpaṇa'. By the word 'ādi', fraudulent weighing (tulākūṭa), fraudulent gold bowls (kaṃsakūṭa), and deception (vañcana), etc., are included. Therein, fraudulent weighing (tulākūṭa) is of four types: rūpakūṭa (deception by appearance), aṅgakūṭa (deception by limb), gahaṇakūṭa (deception by gripping), and paṭicchannakūṭa (deception by concealment).

Among those four, 'rūpakūṭa' means making two scales of identical appearance and taking with the large scale when buying, and giving with the small scale when selling. 'Aṅgakūṭa' means pressing the back of the scale with the hand when buying, and pressing the front when selling. 'Gahaṇakūṭa' means holding the base of the scale-rope when buying, and holding the tip when selling. 'Paṭicchannakūṭa' means making the beam of the scale hollow and inserting iron filings inside; when buying, one makes those iron filings move to the back, and when selling, one makes them move to the front.

A gold bowl is called 'kaṃsa'; deception with such a gold bowl is 'kaṃsakūṭa'. How is the deception carried out? They make one genuine gold bowl and make two or three other copper bowls have the appearance of gold. Then, going to the countryside and entering a wealthy house, they say, "Please buy these gold bowls," and when asked the price, they intend to give them at a particularly low price...
204:
...and so it is. Then, when those people ask, "How can the genuine gold nature of these bowls be known?", they say, "Buy them after testing," and after rubbing the genuine gold bowl on a stone to show them, they hand over all the bowls and depart.

Deception (vañcana) means deceiving others by various means. Here is an illustrative story: A hunter was coming along bringing a large deer and a small deer. A rogue asked him, "Friend, how much is the large deer, and how much is the small deer?" When told, "The large deer is two kahāpaṇas, and the small one is one," he gave one kahāpaṇa, took the small deer, went a little way, and then turned back, saying, "Friend, I have no need for the small deer; give me the large deer instead." The hunter said, "In that case, give me two kahāpaṇas." The rogue said, "Friend, did I not first give you one kahāpaṇa?" When the hunter said, "Yes, you did," the rogue said, "Take back this small deer; thus, that one kahāpaṇa already given and this small deer worth one kahāpaṇa, these two together will make two kahāpaṇas." That hunter, thinking "He is speaking with sound reason," took back the small deer and gave him the large deer.

"Pasayha" means by overpowering others. Because they destroy villages, they are called "gāmaghātaka"; they are thieves who attack and plunder villages. Such thieves and others are referred to as gāmaghātaka, etc. By the word "ādi", highwaymen (panthaghātaka) and others are to be included. "Pārājika even before lifting" means a pārājika offense occurs because the intention "If there is a robe, I will take it" has arisen, and the robe is actually present in that bag. "Punishment should be given according to the footsteps" is said because the person is testing it without putting it down on the ground. "Bhaṇḍadeyya" means that either the value of the other person's lost property or the property itself must be returned.

"Tassa" refers to the person who plans in this way. This word is connected with the phrase "it is theft (avahāra)."

"Paresaṃ" refers to other people who are playing or entering. Hiding something with dust or leaves, thinking "I will take it later," means thinking, "If I stoop and take it right now, they will know and say 'What is the monk taking?' and will trouble me; I will take it later," and thus covering it with dust or leaves. "Uddhāro natthi" means there is no moving it from its place. "Sāmikā" refers to the owners of the goods who wish to enter the village. "Uddhāre" means in the act of not lifting, or in moving from its place (it should be understood as having this meaning).
205:
In this context, the meaning is: moving from its place should also be understood according to the method previously stated. 'Enters' means entering by way of moving from its place. It means causing it to enter by making the upper edge pass beyond the space touched by the lower edge, even by the tip of a hair.

'Samagghatara' means especially of little value. 'Theft occurs just by lifting' is because the effort to make it one's own property is completed, not by way of achieving the purpose. Because one lifts it with the desire to make it fall into one's own share, one is protected from theft at the very moment of lifting. In the case of making it fall, it should be understood in the same way. Although the meaning that one is not protected in the case of making it fall is clear from the words 'protected only at the moment of lifting', the phrase 'having lifted that property' etc. is said to show the meaning by way of achieving the purpose.

If one makes the lot-stick that has fallen into both shares invisible, and later when the remaining monks have gone, one monk whose lot-stick is missing says, 'Venerable sir, my lot-stick is not seen.' The other says, 'Friend, mine is also not seen.' When asked, 'Venerable sir, which is my share?', he points to his own share saying, 'This is your share.' When that monk takes that share and leaves, whether after disputing or not, if the other monk lifts his [the first monk's] share, a Pārājika offense occurs at the moment of lifting. Even if that monk said, 'I do not give my share to you, you should know and take your own share,' but the other, knowing 'This is not mine,' still takes his share, a Pārājika occurs at the moment of lifting. If the other monk thinks, 'What is the use of disputing whether this is your share or my share? Whether it comes to me or to you, you take the better share,' then it is considered taking what is given, and there is no theft here. If that monk, fearing dispute, is told 'Take what you like,' and he leaves behind the better share that came to him and takes only the inferior one, then there is no theft even if the other takes the remaining share after selection. Thus, by combining these five sets of five, these twenty-five types of theft (avahāra) should be understood. The decision on the word 'ādiyeyya' is finished. Therefore, it is said: 'Thus, the meaning of what was said... is revealed.'

## Rājānoti kiñcāpi avisesena vuttaṃ, aparādhānurūpaṃ pana chejjabhejjanusāsako pamāṇabhūto va idhādhippeto ti āha "rājānoti idaṃ bimbisāraṃyeva sandhāya vutta"nti.

Because King Bimbisāra was a righteous king, he acted only according to tradition. Other kings, however, might cut off a head even for the sake of a single kākaṇika. For a large amount of wealth, they might also remain without doing anything. Therefore, the sentence beginning with 'aññe pana' is said. By the word 'ādi' (etc.), rattan with thorns, rattan without thorns, sticks, spears, etc., are included. In the phrase 'rajjubandhanādīhi', by the word 'ādi', imprisonment, iron shackles, house-arrest, city-confinement, and being guarded by men are included. 'Nīhareyyuṃ' means banishing from the country. In the passage 'corosi thenosi', because the sentence structure is deficient, the word 'paribhāseyyuṃ' (they should revile) should be brought in. Therefore, it is said: 'They should revile with these words.' Since the un-given property starts from one pāda, it is said 'of a pāda or of property worth a pāda'. A quarter of the ancient kahāpaṇa is called a 'pāda'. Property worth a pāda is called 'pādāraha'.
206:
(They) might cut (the thief); for a large amount of wealth, they might also remain without doing anything. Therefore, the sentence beginning with 'aññe pana' is said. To show that 'killing' (hanana) means both beating and cutting, it is said 'even with hands etc.' By the word 'ādi', rattan with thorns, rattan without thorns, a stick of two cubits, a spear, etc., should be taken. In the phrase 'by binding with ropes etc.', by the word 'ādi', imprisonment, iron shackles, house-arrest, city-confinement, and being guarded by men should be taken. 'They should banish' means they should make them leave the country. In this place, 'You are a thief... you are a robber,' because the sentence structure is incomplete, the word 'paribhāseyyuṃ' (they should revile) must be added and read. Therefore, it is said: 'They should revile with these words.' Especially since un-given property starts from one pāda, it is said 'of a pāda or of property worth a pāda'. A quarter of the ancient kahāpaṇa is called a 'pāda'. Property worth a pāda is called 'pādāraha'. (In the taking) of that pāda or that pādāraha. Here, by the word 'pāda', only unallowable goods (akappiyabhaṇḍa) worth a quarter of a kahāpaṇa are shown; by the word 'pādāraha', allowable goods (kappiyabhaṇḍa) worth one-quarter (māt) are shown. It should be understood that by showing this lowest limit, the object sufficient for the second Pārājika in every aspect is shown. 'Ancient' (porāṇakassa) refers to the kahāpaṇa that is produced according to ancient treatises, endowed with marks, and similar to the Nīla-kahāpaṇa. By this statement, coins such as the Rudradāmaka are excluded.

Having thus shown the specific decision not shared with other training rules, now to show the general decision, the passage beginning with 'In Rājagaha' is said. 'Of the king' means of King Bimbisāra. A 'māsaka' is one-twentieth of an ancient kahāpaṇa. That portion is also called 'mañjeṭṭhī' in the world. Now, to show the decision regarding this taking of what is not given (adinnādāna), the passage beginning with 'in all cases' (sabbattha) is said. 'In all cases' means in cases of less than a māsaka, more than a māsaka, or five māsakas. 'By way of deficiency or non-deficiency' means by way of the deficiency or non-deficiency of the value. This is the summary here. The detail should be understood thus: one who wishes to decide on this adinnādāna, when a case arises, should not decide hastily but should examine five points. With reference to those points, the ancient teachers said:

The object, the time, and the place,
The value, and fifthly, the use;
Having weighed these five points,
The wise one should deliver the judgment.

In that verse, 'vatthu' (object) means the goods or property. Even if the thief says, 'I have stolen such and such a property,' without immediately imposing the offense, whether that property has an owner or is ownerless...
207:
Even if one says, "I have stolen this specific property," an offense should not yet be assigned; rather, one should investigate whether that property has an owner or is ownerless. Even if it is owned property, one should investigate whether the owners still have attachment (ālaya) to it or are without attachment (nirālaya). If it was stolen while the owners still had attachment, the property should be valued and an offense assigned accordingly. If it was stolen when there was no attachment, it should not be decided as a pārājika offense. However, if the owners ask for the property back, it must be given. Returning it in this manner is the proper conduct (sāmīci) in this case. Thus should the object (vatthu) be examined.

'Time' (kāla) refers to the time of the theft. This is because the same property may be of low value at one time and high value at another. Therefore, the offense should be assigned based on the value at the exact time the property was stolen. Thus should the time be examined.

'Place' (desa) refers to the place of the theft. The offense should be assigned based on the value at the exact place where the property was stolen. Indeed, property is often of low value in the place where it is produced and of high value elsewhere. Thus should the place be examined.

'Value' (aggha) refers to the price of the property. The value of new property decreases over time as it becomes worn. For example, a newly fired bowl might be worth eight or ten kahāpaṇas, but later, if it is broken, has a hole, or is repaired with a pin or a knot (āṇigaṇṭhikā), its value decreases. Therefore, property should not always be judged by its original value (pakati-aggha). Thus should the value be examined.

'Use' (paribhoga) refers to the usage of the property. Through use, the value of property such as an adze (vāsi) decreases. Therefore, it should be investigated in this way: If someone steals an adze worth a quarter (pāda) belonging to another, the owner of that adze should be asked, "For how much did you buy this adze?" If he says, "For a quarter, venerable sir," he should be further asked, "Did you keep it just as you bought it, or have you used it?" If he says, "One day I used it to cut a tooth-stick, or dye-bark, or wood for firing a bowl, or I sharpened it by grinding," then it should be understood that its original value has fallen. Just like an adze, the value of a collyrium pot, a collyrium pin, a key (kuñcikā), or even straw, chaff, or brick powder decreases even by being rubbed or washed once. By cutting a piece of lead (tipumaṇḍala) with a 'makara-tooth' tool, or even by just kneading it, or by wearing or wrapping a water-strainer cloth just once...
208:
...By the power of use, even by merely placing it on the shoulder or the head; by merely winnowing rice and the like; by removing just one or two grains from it; by taking out and throwing away at least a single pebble or grain of sand; by merely transferring ghee, oil, etc., from one vessel to another; by taking out and throwing away at least a fly or an ant from it; or by merely taking a tiny amount by pricking with a fingernail to know the sweetness of a lump of molasses—the value decreases. Therefore, if any item worth a quarter (pāda) has its value reduced by the owner's own use in the manner described, the monk who steals that item should not be prosecuted with a pārājika offense. Thus should the use be examined.

Having compared these five points in this way,
A wise person should reflect on the facts;
Whether there is an offense or no offense, whether it is grave or light,
One should place it in its appropriate place.

Having thus shown the decision therein, now wishing to show the instances where there is no offense, he said "One who perceives it as his own" (sakasaññissa), and so on. Therein, "one who perceives it as his own" means there is no offense in the taking for one who takes another's property with the perception, "This property is mine." However, the property taken must be returned. If the owners say, "Give it back," and he does not give it, but relinquishes the responsibility to return it (dhura-nikkhepa), he incurs a pārājika offense. In the phrase "taking through trust" (vissāsaggāhe), there is also no offense in taking based on intimacy. The characteristics of taking through trust (vissāsaggāha) should be known by this sutta:

"Monks, I allow you to take the property of one who possesses five qualities through trust: he is a friend one has seen, he is an intimate friend, he is one who has spoken, he is still alive, and one knows, 'When I take it, he will be pleased.'"

Therein, "a friend one has seen" (sandiṭṭho) means a friend known merely by sight. "An intimate friend" (sambhatto) means a firm friend. "One who has spoken" (ālapito) means one who has previously said, "Take whatever you want from my property; there is no need to ask permission before taking." "He is alive" (jīvati) means that as long as the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) is not cut off, he is said to be alive, even if he is lying on a bed from which he cannot rise. "He will be pleased when it is taken" (gahite ca attamano) means having a delighted mind when it is taken. It is allowable to take the property of such a person, knowing "He will be pleased with me when I take it." These five factors are stated in terms of taking everything without remainder. However, taking through trust (vissāsaggāha) is also accomplished with three factors. How? Being a friend one has seen, being alive, and knowing he will be pleased when it is taken. Being an intimate friend, being alive, and knowing he will be pleased when it is taken. Being one who has spoken, being alive, and knowing he will be pleased when it is taken—thus it is accomplished by three factors each.
209:
If one takes the property of a person who is still alive but is not pleased when their property is taken, even if taken out of trust (vissāsa), it must be returned. The monk who returns it should give the property of a deceased person to those who are the owners of that property, whether they are householders or monks. The property of a person who is displeased should be given back to that displeased person only.

If a person first expresses approval by saying, "You have done well by taking my property," either by speech or by a mere thought, and later becomes angry for some reason, they do not have the right to demand it back. Even a person who does not wish to give but remains silent and patient in mind does not have the right to demand it back.

If a person is told, "I have taken your property" or "I have used it," and they reply, "Whether it is taken or used, let it be; however, I had set aside that property for a certain purpose, so it should be restored to its original state," then this person has the right to demand it back.

Regarding "temporary" (tāvakālika): there is no offense for one who takes property for a limited duration, thinking, "I will replace it" or "I will compensate for it." If the owner, whether an individual or a group (gaṇa), allows the taken property, saying, "Let this be yours," then that is good. If they do not allow it and demand it back, it must be given. However, communal property of the Saṅgha must always be returned.

Regarding "possession of a Peta" (petapariggahe): here, those reborn in the realm of Petas, those who have passed away and are reborn in that very state, and deities such as those of the Cātumahārājika realm, all fall under the category of "Peta." There is no offense in taking what is possessed by them. Regarding cloth hung on trees, etc., by those performing offerings dedicated to a deity, there is nothing to be said. If such cloth is not claimed by guardian deities, it is proper to take it; however, if it is claimed, it is not proper to take it.

Regarding "possession of an animal" (tiracchānagatapariggahe): this refers to taking property possessed by animals such as Nāgas and Supaṇṇas. If a deity, a Nāga, or a Supaṇṇa opens a shop in human form, and a monk with divine vision, knowing this, takes something and goes, it is permissible.

Regarding "one who perceives it as refuse-rag" (paṃsukūlasaññissa): there is no offense for a monk who takes property with the perception that "this is ownerless refuse-rag." If, however, that property has an owner and they demand it back, it must be given. Matters concerning the insane and others are as previously described. The first offender in this training rule is the monk Dhaniya.
210:
The monk Dhaniya was the first offender. For thieves such as laundry-thieves and others remaining after Dhaniya, and for the group of six (chabbaggiya) monks and others, it is merely an offense. This Adinnādāna training rule arises from three originations accompanied by the mind; therefore, the author of the Saṅgaha says "Adinnādāna-samuṭṭhāna." The way it is accomplished is: the personal (sāhatthika) effort arises from body and mind. The command (āṇattika) effort arises from speech and mind. The combined personal and command (sāhatthikāṇattika) effort arises from body, speech, and mind. Furthermore, that combined effort is obtained when, after consulting together saying, "This object is heavy; you hold one side, I will hold the other," the object is moved from its place by the exertion of both. The reason for not specifically mentioning "bodily and vocal action" (kāya-vaci-kamma) is that in such a case, body and speech are merely components. The offense should be determined by the power of the intention (cetanā) that produces the effort, whether personal or by command, which primarily achieves the moving of the object from its place. Otherwise, the point that the personal effort is not a component of the command, or the command is not a component of the personal effort, would be contradictory. It is called "release through perception" (saññā-vimokkha) because one is freed from the offense due to the absence of the perception "I will take what is not given." Action done by the body is called bodily action (kāyakamma), meaning it is done through the body-door. The same method should be understood for the term vocal action (vacīkamma). There are three feelings (ti-vedanā) because one falls into that offense whether happy, fearful, or neutral. The rest should be understood in the same way as stated in the first training rule.

## The Explanation of the Second Pārājika is Finished.

## 3. The Explanation of the Third Pārājika

The syllable "saṃ" is a prefix (upasagga) in the sense of "saha" (together). Together with that prefix "saṃ," this word is an expression of exertion; therefore, the author of the Saṅgaha stated the sentence beginning with "sañcetitvā" (intentionally). In this term "ussukka-vacana" (expression of exertion), what is called "ussukka-vacana" is a word for an action occurring in a prior time (pubba-kāla-kiriyā). This usage is a linguistic convention (nirutti-vohāra) for the action occurring in a prior time among actions occurring in prior and subsequent times having the same agent. Now, to clarify the meaning stated briefly by the words "saddhiṃ cetetvā" (having intended together), he stated the words beginning with "pāṇo" (a living being). In that context, "only together with the perception of 'pāṇo'" means without giving up the perception "it is a living being," immediately after the arising of the perception "it is a living being." By doing so, it should be understood that an objection such as "How can a single mind-moment have two objects at once?" has no place. Some teachers, however...
211:
Some teachers say that just as one knows the characteristics of impermanence and so on in a single moment along with the nature of things such as 'form is impermanent'—having attributed the three characteristics through the full understanding of investigation (tīraṇapariññā) to the phenomena whose nature is seen through the full understanding of the known (ñātapariññā)—one knows 'I will kill it' along with the perception 'it is a being'. Other teachers, however, do not say this regarding that word 'pāṇo' (being). Here, the use of the word 'being' instead of 'human' is to show that a monk who kills with the mere perception of 'a being', without knowing 'this is a human', also incurs a Pārājika offense. 'Cetetvā' means having intended. 'Pakappetvā' means having deliberated and made a decision.

Now, to show the human physical form (manussa-attabhāva) from its beginning, the phrase 'manussaviggaha' and so on is stated. In that context, 'starting from the kalala-embryo' means starting from the kalala-form that arises together with the rebirth-linking consciousness. The so-called kalala-form consists of thirty types of matter for women and men, by way of the decads of the body, the physical base, and sex (kāya-vatthu-bhāva-dasaka); for eunuchs, there are twenty, by way of the decads of the body and the physical base. Among these, the kalala-form of women and men is as small as a drop of oil taken up by a single filament of wool and is very clear and translucent. This has been stated in the Commentary:

'Like a drop of sesame oil, or like clear, unclouded clarified butter, a form of such appearance is called "kalala".'

Thus, starting from such a minute basis until the time of death, the physical form that reaches growth in due course during this interval is called 'manussaviggaha' (human being). This is stated generally. This is because humans who are of spontaneous birth (opapātika) or moisture-born (saṃsedaja) are also bases for a Pārājika offense. 'Even at the time of the kalala-embryo' means even in the first week. In that first week, it is possible to deprive the physical form known as kalala, which proceeds by way of continuity, of life. However, it is not possible to deprive the very first moment of the kalala-form of life. This is because thirty karma-born types of matter arise together with the rebirth-linking consciousness. While those karma-born types of matter are still present, sixteen life-continuum (bhavaṅga) consciousnesses arise and cease. During this interval, there is no danger to the child who has taken rebirth or to the mother. This period is called the time when there is no opportunity for death. 'By giving medicine' means by giving medicine that causes abortion. 'Even above that' means also during the periods of abbuda, pesi, and so on. 'Should deprive of life' means one should remove it from the life faculty (jīvitindriya) by way of disrupting the continuity.
212:
## This means the following:

For the purpose of clarifying or manifesting this meaning: "Should intentionally deprive a human being of life," it is said that pāṇātipāta is the swift taking of a being's life, the killing of a being, or the destruction of life. A 'being' (satta) is the continuity of the aggregates (khandha-santāna). The designation 'being' exists in that continuity of aggregates. The 'life faculty' (jīvitindriya) refers to both the physical and mental life faculties. If the physical life faculty is destroyed, the other (mental) life faculty also perishes because of its connection to it.

"By which intention" refers to the intention occurring in either the body-door or the speech-door of one who perceives that being as a 'being'. Taking life (pāṇātipāta) cannot occur through a murderous intention occurring only in the mind-door. That intention is the murderous intention occurring in either the body-door or the speech-door, which originates the effort that cuts off the life faculty. This is what is meant: due to the making of an effort upon the great elements (mahābhūta) which are the support of the life faculty proceeding because of that intention, the subsequent great elements that would have arisen depending on those great elements will not arise. The intention that originates such an effort is called pāṇātipāta. This is because the great elements that have received the impact of the effort are not as clear as other elements and thus cannot be the cause for elements of the same kind.

One who has the act of taking life is called a 'pāṇātipātī' (one who takes life). Here, the suffix 'ī' is used in the sense of association (possession). Therefore, it is said, "a person endowed with the aforementioned intention." One's own hand is 'sahattha'; the effort produced by that hand is 'sāhatthika-payoga'. Throwing is 'nissagga'; that itself is 'nissaggiya'. Similarly, there is 'āṇattika' (by command). The effort consisting of the recitation of mantras is 'vijjāmaya'. The effort consisting of psychic power born of the result of kamma is 'iddhimaya'.

Now, to show the six aforementioned efforts by dividing them, the phrase beginning with "tattha" is stated. There, "tattha" means among those six efforts. In the term 'sāhatthika', the 'hand' is taken by way of synecdoche (upalakkhaṇa), which is why it is said "by the body" and so on. In that context, "by the body" means by the hand, the foot, the fist, the knee, or any major or minor limb. Here, calling a part of the body such as the hand 'the body' is a metaphorical usage of the whole for the part (samudāyopacāra), just as when it is said, "the village is burnt." "By an object connected to the body" means by a weapon such as a sword that is not released from the body. A 'weapon' (paharaṇa) is that which accomplishes the intended purpose through a murderous intention accompanied by bodily intimation. It should be understood by combining them as appropriate: the throwing of spears and so on by the body, or the throwing of arrows, machines, stones, and so on by an object connected to the body.

In that context, "tattha" means among those (efforts).
213:
Among the sāhattika (by one's own hand) [offenses], there are two types: uddissa (specifically) and anuddissa (generally), based on whether the action is directed or undirected. The act of directing is called uddesa; the effort characterized by such directing is called uddesaka. In that uddesaka effort, one is 'bound by the action' (kammabaddha) because of being tied by that kamma; this means pāṇātipāta (taking life). Alternatively, baddha means binding; binding by kamma is kammabaddha, which means the act of pāṇātipāta is accomplished for that person. In both cases—uddesaka and anuddesaka—it is applied as: 'May [the victim] die later from the disease caused by that blow.' Only at the moment of striking, when a blow sufficient to cause death is received, does kammabaddha occur. This means if death will certainly occur from that blow. However, if one strikes with the intention to kill but the victim does not die from that blow, and then strikes again with a different intention, if the victim later dies from the first blow only, then kammabaddha occurs at that moment. If the victim dies from the second blow, there is no pāṇātipāta [for the first intention]. Even if death occurs due to both, kammabaddha occurs only from the first blow. If the victim does not die from either, there is no pāṇātipāta. This same principle applies when many people strike a single person. Among them, kammabaddha occurs only for the person whose blow causes the death. Commanding (āṇāpana) is the fulfillment of the desired objective through the intention to kill, accompanied by vocal intimation (vaci-viññatti).

Now, in order to make known the states of agreement (saṅketa) and breach of agreement (visaṅketa) in this effort of command (āṇattika-payoga), the sixfold limitations are shown, beginning with "Tattha." Therein, "tattha" means in that effort of command. "Āṇattiniyāmaka" refers to the factors that complete the effort of command. Only when these six limitations are not violated does the effort of command [resulting in an offense] occur; it cannot happen otherwise.

"Puggala" (person) refers to the person to be killed. Therefore, the text beginning with "Yaṃ hi" is stated. The commander incurs the offense at the moment of command, while the commanded incurs the offense at the moment of killing. "The commander is released" means that kammabaddha occurs only for the commanded person. Here, due to the specific nature of the object (vatthu), there are distinctions in kamma and distinctions in the offense. If a person commanded to "kill before the meal (purebhatta)" kills before the meal without specifying today or tomorrow, [the commander incurs the offense]. If a person is told to "kill this morning" but kills at noon, in the evening, or the next morning, it is a breach of agreement (visaṅketa), and there is no kammabaddha for the commander. While making an effort to kill in the morning...
214:
Even if death occurs at noon, the same principle applies. By this method, the states of agreement (saṅketa) and breach of agreement (visaṅketa) should be understood in all distinctions of time.

Having thus shown agreement and breach of agreement regarding the object and time, the text beginning with "Iminā nayena" is stated to analogously apply agreement and breach of agreement to location (okāsa) and so forth. In that context, location (okāsa) refers to a village, a forest, or a house door, etc. Weapon (āvudha) refers to a sword, an arrow, or a spear, etc. Posture (iriyāpatha) refers to the walking or sitting, etc., of the person to be killed. Specifics of the action (kiriyā-visesa) refers to piercing, cutting, splitting, or scalping like a conch shell (saṅkhamuṇḍaka), etc. In these matters, in whatever manner the killer is commanded, if he acts according to that manner, the commander incurs the offense; if he acts otherwise, it is a breach of agreement (visaṅketa). Therefore, it is said, "Iminā nayena," etc. Therein, "sabbattha" (in all) refers to the four factors starting with location.

In this regard, there is this summary verse (saṅgaha-gāthā):
'When the commanded person acts exactly according to the command,
The commander incurs the offense; if done otherwise, it is a breach of agreement.'

However, in the matter of command, this distinction should be understood: "adhiṭṭhāya" means having determined [firmly], as found in the Pali text stating, "Pierce thus, strike thus, kill thus."

They fall into this [pit]; therefore, that pit is called a pitfall (opāta). Digging that pit is opātakkhana (pit-digging). "Apassena-saṃvidhāna" means arranging a support. This refers to a couch, a chair, or a leaning-board used regularly, or a leaning-post for one who sits in a day-quarters, or a tree growing there, or a support-tree or support-board for one who stands leaning in a cloister (caṅkama). All these are called "apassena" (support) in the sense of being leaned upon. Arranging a support by placing a weapon—such as a billhook, an axe, a spear, or a needle-pointed stake—in such a way that it pierces or cuts the person who leans on it, is the meaning.

"Upanikkhipana" means depositing nearby. Bringing a pleasant or unpleasant form (rūpa) near or placing it nearby is rūpūpahāra (presenting a form). Alternatively, standing oneself in the guise of a yakkha or a peta is also rūpūpahāra. By the word "ādi" (etc.), presenting sounds (saddūpahāra) and so forth are included. In this matter also...
215:
In perpetual effort (thāvara-payoga) as well, the distinction between specific (uddissa) and non-specific (anuddissa) should be understood. Why? Because in that perpetual effort also, one becomes bound by kamma (kammabaddha) only by the method previously mentioned. This is the distinction: even if the original owner (mūlaṭṭha) gives a pit, etc., to others for a fee or for free, if someone dies because of that pit, the original owner is bound by kamma. Even if that original owner or another person destroys the pit and levels it with the ground, if earth-carriers taking soil or root-diggers digging roots create a hole, or if mud is formed when it rains, and someone falls in or gets stuck and dies there, only the original owner is bound by kamma. However, if the person who received it or another person makes that pit wider or deeper, and someone dies because of that reason, both are bound by kamma. Just as roots intertwine with roots, if that place is made into level ground, one is released from the kamma. Thus, in the preparation of a leaning-board (apassena), etc., as long as those things exist, one should understand the binding of kamma accordingly.

*Vijjā-parijappana* means the recitation of mantras by those proficient in the Atharva Veda and by sorcerers (vijjādharas). *Kamma-vipākajā iddhi* means power born of extraordinary kamma, arising together with kamma-result, or power born as the result of kamma. *Payojana* means causing to happen or performing. It means performing a modification of the power born of kamma-result for the purpose of causing death, just as one might strike the fangs of snakes that have fangs as weapons.

This word 'hāraka' is a *kammasādhana* (objective derivative) by the *bahulavidhāna* method. Since the suffix *ṇvu* is accomplished in that *kammasādhana*, it is said "Alternatively (atha vā)," etc. Because it is spoken of by two alternatives (vikappa) as either a weapon that takes life or a weapon to be placed nearby, it is called 'satthahāraka'. Although it should be said 'hārakasattha', it should be noted that it is said this way by placing the adjective (visesana) at the end. 'Pariyeseyya' means one should seek. By this word 'one should do as one receives', the intended meaning is stated. By this word 'upanikkhipeyya' (should place down), the ultimate meaning (sikhāpattamattha) is stated. Otherwise, this meaning 'upanikkhipeyya' would not be intended for this word 'pariyeseyya'. 'Pariyitthamatteyeva' means only in the mere seeking. If that is so, why is it said in the Pāli, "Or he should seek a weapon-bringer for him, such as a sword, a spear, a javelin, a club, a stone, a knife, poison, or a rope"? It is said in the *padabhājana* (word-analysis) to show the phrasing (byañjana) because it does not reach the meaning by completing it according to the phrasing. 'Assa' is the meaning of this word 'satthahārakaṃ vāssa pariyeseyya'. Completing it according to the phrasing, the meaning...
216:
Because it is not explicitly stated, it is said "without taking the phrasing" (byañjanaṃ anādiyitvā) (meaning without taking the literal meaning). It is called a weapon (sattha) because it harms (sasati), or it is called a weapon because one harms with this weapon. By the word 'ādi' (etc.), the remaining Pāli text such as "or a spear" (sattiṃ vā) is included. In that Pāli, 'lagula' means a mallet (muggara). 'Sattha' refers to any weapon encountered in front that remains after those already mentioned.

"Dies in this way" means dying by bringing a weapon, or by consuming poison, or by hanging with a rope, or by falling into pits, etc., or by other means such as entering fire or entering water. "He obtains wealth," etc.—by this method, it means he obtains wealth, or he obtains fame and retinue, or he goes to heaven, or he gains merit (dhamma). To the question "What should be understood by this?", it says "By this" (etena), etc. There, "by this" refers to this statement: "one should praise the beauty of death." In this Pārājika regarding the human form (manslaughter), one is not released by such (circumlocutory) speech. Therefore, it says "should praise" (saṃvaṇṇeyyā), etc.

In the phrase "bring a weapon" (satthaṃ vā āharā), etc., the word 'ādi' includes all means of death such as "consume poison, die by hanging with a rope, fall into a pit, a *naraka* (chasm), or a precipice." Here, *naraka* refers to a great chasm that arises naturally from the cracking of the ground in various places. Even elephants fall into such great chasms, and thieves also stay there in hiding. *Papāta* (precipice) refers to a cliff that is cut off on one side, either between mountains or between level ground. *Pāpaka* means vile. *Dujjīvita* means living a life of suffering because of much misery. It means "Your death is better than life." Because that person has a mind, it is called *citta*. Likewise, it is called *mano*. The word 'iti' should be understood in the sense of illustration (nidassana), as in "All exists, Kaccāna, this is one extreme; all does not exist, Kaccāna, this is the second extreme," etc. This is because it illustrates death as it occurs in the intellect. Therefore, it says "Your death is better than life," etc.

If one asks, "Since this word 'mano' is also 'citta' in meaning, why is it said?", it says "And here" (ettha ca), etc. It is said to clarify the meaning of *citta*. This word *citta* is not used in the sense of 'variegated' (vicitta), as in "mental intention" (cittasaṅkappa), etc., but is a word denoting consciousness (viññāṇa); it is said to clarify that meaning. By this, it shows the absence of the fault of tautology (punaruttidosa). To the question "How is this known?", it says "Therefore, for him" (tenevassa), etc.
217:
Because there are various and diverse intentions, it is called 'Cittasaṅkappa' (diverse intention). Here, the word 'citta' has the meaning of 'diverse,' as in the Suttas: "Monks, I do not see any other single group so diverse as these animals." Therefore, it is said, "one with diverse intentions." In this term 'Cittasaṅkappa' as well, the word 'iti' should be brought in by way of context. Even if it is not explicitly stated as "iti cittasaṅkappo," it should be understood as stated through authority (adhikāra). Here, the name 'saṅkappa' is not just a name for 'vitakka' (initial thought) alone, as in "takka, vitakka, saṅkappa," but to show that it is also the name for other factors like 'saññā' (perception), the phrase "saṅkappoti ca" is initiated.

'Saṃvidahanamattassa' means the entirety of arranging, which is called perception (saññā), volition (cetanā), and initial thought (vitakka). Here, the word 'matta' has the meaning of 'similarity,' as in examples like "feeding those similar to Brahmins." Therefore, the sentence "that arranging also" is stated. By this sentence, it shows that 'saṃvidahana' here does not mean 'construction.' 'Adhippāya' (intention) is indeed 'vitakka.'

'By various means' (uccāvaca kāraṇa) means by means of great or small methods. In praising the qualities of death, the 'low manner' is known by showing the faults of life, and the 'high manner' is known by speaking of the virtues of death. In inciting (death), the 'high manner' is known by inciting death through punching with fists or striking with knees, etc.; the 'low manner' is known by inciting death by putting poison in fingernails while eating together.

Having thus stated the specific judgment (asādhāraṇa vinicchaya), to show the general judgment (sādhāraṇa vinicchaya), the phrase "Vesāliyaṃ" etc. is stated. In the context of digging a pit, etc., where it says "an offense of wrong-doing (dukkhaṭa) is committed," even if one digs into a clod of earth, because it is a preliminary effort for taking life (pāṇātipāta), an offense of wrong-doing is committed for every effort. A creature such as a Nāga or Garuḍa that has a body like a human is called a 'human-like animal' (tiracchānagata manussoviggaha). Yakkhas, Petas, and human-like animals are called 'Yakkha, Peta, and human-like animals.' Regarding their death, the grave offense (thullaccaya) is indicated by the word "tathā." Now, with the words "by this method," the various offenses in arranging a leaning board, etc., are indicated. "In all places" means in all efforts such as arranging a leaning board.

Now, to show non-offense (anāpatti), the word "asañcicca" (unintentional) etc. is stated. Here, "asañcicca" refers to not noticing the effort that leads to death...
218:
The phrase "for one who does not know" refers to not knowing the instrument (medicine, etc.) that leads to death. The phrase "for one who has no intention to kill" refers to the absence of the intention to kill even if one knows the effort. Therefore, it is said "unintentionally," etc. "Without reflecting" means without noticing, "by mistake."

As in the case of the pestle: "At one time, a certain monk, while spreading seats in the dining hall in a village, took hold of one pestle among the upright pestles. A second pestle fell and struck the head of a certain boy, and that boy died. Remorse arose in that monk... 'Monk, what was your intention?' the Blessed One asked. 'Blessed One, I did it unintentionally,' he replied. 'Monk, there is no offense for you who acted unintentionally,' it was said." It is like this case.

As in the case of the poisoned alms-food: "At one time, a certain monk on alms-round received poisoned alms-food, brought it to the dining hall, and gave it as the first portion to the monks. Those monks died. Remorse arose in that monk... 'Monk, what was your intention?' he was asked. 'Blessed One, I did not know (it was poisoned),' he replied. 'Monk, there is no offense for one who does not know,' it was said." It is like this case.

As in the case of the medicine: "At one time, a certain barren woman said to a monk who frequented her house, 'Venerable sir, please find a medicine so that I may give birth.' 'Very well, sister,' he said and gave her medicine. That woman died. Remorse arose in that monk... 'Monk, there is no Pārājika offense for you, but there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkhaṭa),' it was said." It is like this case. In this (Third Pārājika), the first-doers were monks who deprived each other of life; for those monks, there is no offense. For the remaining monks who praised the qualities of death, etc., there is indeed an offense.

If so, why is it said that there is painful feeling (dukkha vedanā)? Do not kings, upon seeing a thief, say "Go, kill him" even while laughing? True, they say it while laughing, but that laughter belongs to another object; the decisive volition (sanniṭṭhāpaka cetanā) is associated only with painful feeling. This is stated in the Samantapāsādikā: "Even if a king, reclining on a royal couch and enjoying the bliss of sovereignty, says 'Go, kill him' while laughing when told 'Sire, a thief has been brought,' he speaks only with a mind of displeasure (domanassa)." However, because it is mixed with pleasant feeling (sukha vedanā) or because pleasant feeling occurs continuously, it is difficult for worldlings (puthujjana) to know this.

## The Explanation of the Third Pārājika is finished.

## 4 - Explanation of the Fourth Pārājika
"Without knowing" means while not being one who knows (not knowing).
219:
It should be understood that (that monk) speaks. However, because it is mixed with pleasant feeling and because pleasant feeling occurs continuously, it is difficult for worldlings (puthujjanas) to know this kind of speech (speaking to kill while laughing). (For example, it is like a king enjoying royal splendor who says "Kill the thief" while laughing, yet speaks only with a mind of displeasure.)

## The Commentary on the Third Pārājika is Finished.

## 4. Commentary on the Fourth Pārājika

"Anabhijānaṃ" means without knowing (not being one who knows). This is because for whatever person a certain Dhamma is attained and known, that Dhamma is clear to that person; therefore, it is said "in one's own continuity" and so forth. "Uttarimanussānaṃ" means of humans who are especially superior to ordinary humans, or of excellent humans. "Dhammaṃ" refers to the attained and known Dhamma which is of the sublime (mahaggata) and supramundane (lokuttara) levels. Alternatively, it is called uttarimanussadhamma because it is superior to the Dhamma of humans. What is called "human Dhamma" (manussadhamma) is the ten wholesome courses of action (kusalakamma-patha) that are produced by humans naturally without the practice of meditation (bhāvanā) or reflection. Since that Dhamma is accomplished by the mere resolution of the human mind, it exists for those humans as if it were a practiced Dhamma, and thus it is called so (manussadhamma); the term "humans" is used here because it frequently occurs among them. However, states such as jhāna and so forth are far removed from that human Dhamma and are thus superior to it; in this way, it is called uttarimanussadhamma in the sense of a Dhamma superior to the Dhamma of humans. In this context, the meaning should be understood as "to that uttarimanussadhamma". "Samudācaranto" means (a monk) who is speaking or announcing.

Although all mundane and supramundane wisdom can be called "knowledge" (ñāṇa), in this context, only sublime and supramundane wisdom should be understood as knowledge; therefore, it is said: "Sublime and supramundane wisdom is called knowledge in the sense of knowing." Because it is far from defilements and thus pure, it is called ariya (noble); therefore, it is said: "Ariya means pure and excellent." Here, the word ariya is a synonym for visuddha (purity), not a synonym for lokuttara (supramundane). In the phrase "jhānādibhede", the word "ādi" (and so forth) includes these states: liberation (vimokkha), concentration (samādhi), attainment (samāpatti), knowledge and vision (ñāṇadassana), development of the path (maggabhāvanā), realization of the fruition (phalasacchikiriyā), abandoning of defilements (kilesappahāna), the mind's freedom from hindrances (vinīvaraṇatā), and delighting in empty places. The phrase "viññussa manussajātikassa" (to a wise human being) indicates the person to whom the claim is made. This is because a claim is only considered a claim when made to such a human; it is not considered a claim (according to the training rule) when made to devas, brahmas, petas, yakkhas, or animals. "Āroceyya" means one should speak or inform. "Vinā aññāpadesena" means without indirect reference (aññāpadesa), such as saying "That monk who lives in your monastery is an attainer of the first jhāna" and so forth...
220:
...means "excluding". In this very phrase "Thus I know, thus I see," the sentence "Therefore it is said" and so forth is the concluding statement.

"Samanuggāhīyamāno" means being questioned or interrogated. It means being asked by someone regarding the matter that was announced: "What have you attained? How did you attain it? When did you attain it? Where did you attain it? Which defilements have you abandoned? Which states are you an attainer of?" "Asamanuggāhīyamāno" means not being questioned by anyone.

"Remaining in the state of a monk, one is unfit to attain jhāna, etc." is said because transgressing the training rule creates an obstacle. For such a person, the state of being a monk becomes an obstacle to heaven and an obstacle to the Path. Indeed, it was said: "Monkhood poorly handled drags one to hell." In another passage, it was said: "A lax recluse scatters the dust of defilements even more." "The state of a monk" (bhikkhubhāva) here refers to the state of a monk established merely by designation because of claiming "I am a recluse" after committing a Pārājika offense. "Dānādīhi" means through giving, taking refuge, observing the precepts, and so forth.

In the word "ajānam-eva", "eva" is a particle used in the sense of restriction (excluding other meanings). Some also read it as "ajānam-evaṃ". In that case, it should be construed as "without saying: I know thus, I see thus." "Vacanatthavirahato" means because of being devoid of the jhāna and so forth which are the actual meaning of the words "I enter the first jhāna" etc., like an empty vessel devoid of water and so forth. "Musā" (falsehood) is a verbal or physical action that deceives another, preceded by the intention to deceive. Therefore, it is said: "It is called musā because of the intention to deceive." The falsehood and the intention to deceive exist in the moment prior to the lie and at the moment of speaking. Indeed, it was said: "Previously he has the thought: I will speak a lie; while speaking he has the thought: I am speaking a lie." These two are the factors (of the offense); as for the other moments, whether they occur or not is not the cause. "Abhaṇiṃ" means I have made an announcement or informed.

"Aññatra adhimānā" means excluding overestimation (adhimāna), which is the perception "I have attained, I have known," or an excessive estimation, or a stubborn estimation. To whom does this overestimation arise, and to whom does it not? It does not arise in a noble disciple (ariyasāvaka). This is because a noble disciple has great joy through reviewing the Path, Fruition, Nibbāna, the abandoned defilements, and the remaining defilements, and has no doubt in the penetration of the qualities of the noble ones. Therefore, in noble disciples such as stream-enterers, the conceit "I am a once-returner" and so forth does not arise. This overestimation also does not arise in an immoral person (dussīla). This is because such a person is devoid of hope in attaining the qualities of a noble one. It also does not arise in one who, though virtuous, neglects the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) and delights in sleeping and so forth. It arises only in one who possesses perfectly pure virtue.
221:
A noble disciple (ariyasāvaka), through reviewing the path, fruition, nibbāna, the defilements abandoned, and the defilements remaining, possesses great joy and is free from doubt regarding the penetration of the qualities of the noble ones. Therefore, for noble ones such as stream-enterers (sotāpanna), overestimation (adhimāna) in the form of thinking "I am a once-returner (sakadāgāmī)," etc., does not arise. It also does not arise in an immoral person, as such a person has no hope of attaining the qualities of a noble one. Even for a virtuous person, if they have abandoned the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) and are devoted to sleep and such, it does not arise. However, for a person of pure virtue who is diligent in meditation, who has defined mind and matter (nāmarūpa), overcome doubt by grasping the causes, applied the three characteristics, and is contemplating conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra)—that is, one who has initiated insight (āraddhavipassaka)—overestimation can indeed arise. This is why it was said, "yvāyaṃ," and so on.

In that context, "applying the three characteristics" means applying the three characteristics of impermanence and so on by way of comprehension by groups (kalāpasammasana). "One who contemplates" means one who is practicing insight (vipassanā). "One who has initiated insight" means one who is practicing the contemplation of arising and falling (udayabbayānupassanā). "Not yet reached" means a state not yet attained or realized through its arising within one's own continuity. "The overestimation known as the perception of having reached" means the arising of overestimation characterized by the perception, "I have attained a superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma)."

Such overestimation, once arisen, causes either one who has attained pure tranquility (suddhasamathalābhī) or one who has attained pure insight (suddhavipassanālābhī) to stop in the interval (before reaching the path and fruit). Such a person, not seeing the occurrence of defilements for ten, twenty, or even thirty years, thinks, "I am a stream-enterer," "a once-returner," or "a non-returner (anāgāmī)." However, for one who has attained both tranquility and insight, it causes them to stop only at the fruition of arahantship (arahattaphala). Because defilements are suppressed by the power of concentration (samādhi) and conditioned phenomena are well-grasped by the power of insight, defilements do not occur for sixty, eighty, or even a hundred years, and their mental process is like that of an arahant whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava). Not seeing the occurrence of defilements for such a long time, they do not stop in the interval but think, "I am an arahant."

By the phrase "taṃ adhimānaṃ ṭhapetvā," it is shown that in relation to the word "aññatra," the word "adhimānā" is an ablative case (nissakkavacana) used in the sense of the accusative.

"Pāpicchatāya" means because of having evil desires. This refers to the desire to be esteemed for qualities one does not possess, as stated in the method: "Here, someone who is immoral desires, 'May people know me as virtuous,'" and so on. This phrase shows that there is no offense for one who speaks out of dullness or confusion. By the word "pi" in "ayampi," it is shown that not only the previous three cases but also this point is included.
222:
"Asanta" (non-existent) refers to a state that is not real and has never occurred in one's own continuity. "Jhānādidhamma" (states starting with jhāna) refers to the superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) described as: "jhāna, liberation (vimokkha), concentration (samādhi), attainment (samāpatti), knowledge and vision (ñāṇadassana), development of the path (maggabhāvanā), realization of the fruit (phalasacchikiriyā), abandonment of defilements, the mind's freedom from hindrances, and delight in empty places." "Yassa āroceti" (to whom he announces) means announcing to a person who stands within the range of communication, whether through speech or through movements of the limbs such as hand gestures. However, if someone standing beyond the range of communication knows through the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) or hears and knows through the divine ear (dibba-sota), the monk does not incur a Pārājika offense. A person who is in doubt, wondering "What is this monk saying?", or who understands only after a long period of reflection, is also classified as "one who does not understand."

If a person does not know jhāna and so on through their own attainment or through learning and inquiry, but has merely heard the words "jhāna" or "vimokkha," yet understands at least this much when the monk speaks—"He is saying that he attained jhāna"—then they are classified as "one who understands," and the monk incurs a Pārājika offense for speaking to them. All other distinctions regarding whether it is to one, two, or many people, and whether they are specified or unspecified, should be understood according to the method stated in the section on the Renunciation of the Training (Sikkhāpaccakkhānakathā). In the case of speaking indirectly (pariyāya), since the word "I" is not used, it is a grave offense (thullaccaya) even if the listener understands. Because the effort of lying is made with the intent to deceive, it is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) even if the listener does not understand, as stated: "Whoever lives in your monastery... [etc.] ...an offense of wrongdoing." "Anullapanādhippāyassa" refers to a monk who lacks the intent to boast or the intent to announce what is not real. The cases of insane persons and others are the same as the methods stated previously. In this training rule, the monks on the banks of the Vaggumudā river are the original perpetrators (ādikammika), and thus they incur no offense.

## The Explanation of the Fourth Pārājika is Finished.

## Explanation of the Conclusion of the Pārājika Section

"Idha" (here) means in this Bhikkhu Pātimokkha. "Uddiṭṭhapārājikapari-dīpanameva" (the mere illustration of the recited Pārājikas) is the statement that clearly illustrates the four Pārājikas that have been recited. The restriction made by the word "eva" (mere/only) is for the purpose of showing that other Pārājikas are not meant. Therefore, the sentence beginning with "samodhanetvā pana" was said. In that sentence, "samodhanetvā" means collecting, including, and grouping together the Pārājikas that appear in various places into this very Bhikkhu Pātimokkha. "Pāḷiyaṃ āgatāni" means those that appear in the Recitation Pali (uddesa-pāḷi)...
223:
(The Pārājikas) have arrived. The four Pārājikas unique to bhikkhunīs are: Ubbhajaṇumaṇḍalikā (a nun who finds pleasure in being rubbed above the knees), Vajjappaṭicchādikā (a nun who conceals a grave offense), Ukkhittānuvattikā (a nun who follows a monk who has been expelled), and Aṭṭhavatthukā (a nun who fulfills the eight grounds). These four are the unique Pārājikas of the bhikkhunīs that are not shared with the bhikkhus. The state of being unfit (abhabba-bhāva) of the eleven types of persons, such as the paṇḍaka (eunuch), is called Pārājika because it is similar to a Pārājika offense. Therefore, it is said, "ekādasannaṃ" and so forth. The phrase "abhabba-bhāva-saṅkhātehi" means the state of being unfit for the life of a novice or a monk due to the ruin of the basis (vatthu-vipannatā) and so forth.

The three types of persons—the paṇḍaka, animals, and hermaphrodites (ubhatobyañjanaka)—are those whose basis is ruined and who have a rootless rebirth-linking (ahetu-paṭisandhi). For them, heaven is not barred, but the Path (Magga) is barred. They are unfit to attain the Path because their basis is ruined. Since ordination is also forbidden for them, they are also considered Pārājikas. The eight types of persons—the theyyasaṃvāsaka (one who lives by stealth), the titthiyapakkantaka (one who went over to another sect), a matricide, a patricide, a killer of an Arahant, a violator of a bhikkhunī, one who sheds the blood of a Buddha, and a schismatic—are also considered Pārājikas because they have reached an unfit state due to being ruined by their own actions. Among these eight, for the theyyasaṃvāsaka, the titthiyapakkantaka, and the violator of a bhikkhunī, heaven is not barred, but the Path is barred. For the remaining five, both heaven and the Path are barred. They are beings who will be reborn in hell immediately after death.

When a bhikkhunī, desiring to return to the lay life, wears either dyed robes or lay clothes in the manner of a layperson, she is said to have fallen into a Pārājika; thus it is said, "gihi-bhāvaṃ patthayamānāya" and so forth. Even without committing a physical transgression of misconduct, she ceases to be a nun by this much of changing into lay clothes. A monk whose genitals are long and hanging is called a lambī. He does not become a Pārājika by this much alone; however, if, being oppressed by dissatisfaction (anabhirati), he inserts his own genitals into his own mouth or anus, then he becomes a Pārājika. A monk whose back is flexible is called a mudupiṭṭhika; he is endowed with a flexible back that has been prepared. If he, being oppressed by dissatisfaction, inserts his own genitals into either his own mouth or anus, then he becomes a Pārājika. Taking another's genitals with the mouth means a monk who, being oppressed by dissatisfaction, takes the genitals of another person who is asleep or negligent with his mouth. Sitting on another's genitals means a monk who, being oppressed by dissatisfaction, seeing another's genitals fit for the act, sits upon them with his own anus and inserts them into his anus. These four...
224:
Because the conduct of two persons who have reached a similar state by the power of lust is called "methunadhamma" (sexual intercourse), these are called "Anuloma Pārājikas" (Conformable Defeats) because they follow the Pārājika of sexual intercourse by the power of inserting the organ into an organ, even without engaging in sexual intercourse in one particular way.

In this regard, (the sub-commentary teacher) asks: The matricide, the patricide, and the killer of an Arahant fall into the third Pārājika; the violator of a bhikkhunī and the four types such as the lambī fall into the first Pārājika. This being so, how can there be twenty-four? The answer is: The four types such as the matricide are intended here only as laypeople; the four types such as the lambī, although included in the first Pārājika, are mentioned separately because they are those who do not engage in sexual intercourse in one particular way. In the second alternative, for the word "kaccitthā," the word-analysis should be made as "kacci atthā."

## Thus ends the explanation of Pārājika
## in the Līnatthappakāsanī named Vinayatthamañjūsā,
## the commentary on the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Pātimokkha.
225:
## Saṅghādisesa Section

"Piyavacaneana ālapanaṃ" means addressing with endearing words, which is the manner of address used by virtuous people. Indeed, virtuous people address others as "Sirs," "Beloved of the gods," "Good sirs," or "Venerables."

## 1. Sukka-vissaṭṭhi Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

The author of the Saṅgaha stated "saṃvijjati" (it exists) because the prefix "saṃ" has the meaning of existence. "Cetanā" (intention) should be understood as the preliminary intention occurring before the emission through the power of transgression, and the intention of enjoying the emission of semen. "Assa" refers to the emission of semen. Since the meaning of the emission of semen is already expressed by the bahubbīhi compound "sañcetanikā," the author of the Saṅgaha stated that "sañcetanā itself is called sañcetanikā," implying that the suffix "-ika" has no separate meaning. Now, wishing to show that the suffix "-ika" itself can express the meaning of existence, the author of the Saṅgaha stated the sentence beginning with "sañcetanā vā." An existing intention is called "sañcetanā." "Sukkassa" refers to semen. "Vissaṭṭhi" means release or emission.

Now, to explain briefly the time when one causes that semen to be released, the purpose for which it is released, the means by which it is released, and the object of that purpose, and to show that emission in its specific form, the author of the Saṅgaha stated the sentence beginning with "rāgūpatthambhādīsu." In that sentence, the intensity of lust is called "rāgūpatthambha." Alternatively, the stiffness of the male organ due to lust is called "rāgūpatthambha." Because there are factors such as rāgūpatthambha, they are called "rāgūpatthambhādi." Among those "rāgūpatthambhādi," the word "ādi" includes the pressure from feces, the pressure from urine, the pressure from wind, and the pressure from the bite of an insect called uccāliṅga. "Kammaññataṃ patte" means when it has reached a state of readiness for the act of emission, implying it has reached a state fit for making an effort regarding internal forms and so on. "Ārogya" is the state of being free from disease. Because there are factors such as ārogya, they are called "ārogyādi." By the word "ādi," the emission of semen for the sake of pleasure, for medicine, for the merit of giving, for the benefit of sacrifice, for the sake of heaven, for the seed of rebirth, for the sake of testing, and for the sake of fun are included. The form within one's own continuity is called "ajjhatta-rūpa" (internal form). Because there are factors such as internal forms, they are called "ajjhatta-rūpādi." Although this offense is singular, it is called "nikāya" (collection) by way of conventional usage (ruḷhī) or by referring to a part as a whole, similar to expressions like "one aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha)" or "one aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha)."

"Assa" refers to that category of offense. Is it not improper to state, "The Saṅgha is desired for it at the beginning and in the remainder"?
