For the sake of livelihood, by reason of livelihood, if a nun who is not ill requests fine food for her own sake and eats it, there is an offense to be confessed (pāṭidesanīya). For the sake of livelihood, by reason of livelihood, if a monk who is not ill requests curry or rice for his own sake and eats it, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa)."

Thus, by way of Pārājika and so on, six classes of offenses are laid down due to failure in livelihood, excluding dubbhāsita. Due to failure in view (diṭṭhi-vipatti), two classes of offenses, pācittiya and dukkaṭa, are laid down. In the case of not relinquishing a harmful view, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) due to the motion (ñatti), and an offense of expiation (pācittiya) at the end of the formal announcement (kammavācā). Thus...
288:
Due to the cause of failure in view (diṭṭhivipatti), two groups of offenses are prescribed by way of Pācittiya and Dukkaṭa. "Herein" refers to the discussions on failures (vipattikathā).

"Reaching the count" (gaṇanupagata) means the state of entering the count of days. Even if a robe is given into the hands of another with the words, "I give this robe to such-and-such a person," it does not yet enter the count of days as long as it has not reached the [monk's] hand, as stated in the Cammakkhandhaka: "It does not enter the count as long as it does not reach the hand." Therefore, as long as it has not been brought and given, or as long as one has not been informed by a messenger saying, "Venerable sir, a robe has arisen for you," it does not enter the count of days, and it is permissible to keep it without formal determination (anadhiṭṭhita). However, from the time it is brought and given, or from the time one hears that it has "arisen," it enters the count, and must be formally determined within ten days.

It is called "Kathina-origination" (kathinasamuṭṭhāna) because its origin is named after the Kathina. This means there are two origins by way of the third and sixth origins. It is said to originate from body and speech because of the failure to perform the formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna) and assignment (vikappanā) that should be done by body and speech; and from body, speech, and mind if there is intention. It is a "non-action" (akiriya) because the offense is incurred through the non-performance of determination and assignment. It is "not released by perception" (nosannāvimokkha) because one incurs the offense even if unaware. It is a bodily act and a verbal act because of the failure to do what should be done through the bodily door and the verbal door.

## The Explanation of the Kathina Training Rule is Finished.

## 2. Explanation of the Udossita Training Rule

"By the monk" (bhikkhunā) means "of the monk"; here the instrumental case is used in the sense of the possessive (sāmī). Therefore, it is said, "As in the previous training rule," and so on. Why then is the meaning not taken in the instrumental sense but in the possessive sense? To this, it says, "For by way of the instrumental..." and so on. The word "hi" is a particle indicating cause. "One whose obstacles are severed" (chinnapalibodha) means one whose obstacles regarding robes and residence are severed. "One night" (ekarattaṃ) means only one night. "Triple robe" (ticīvaraṃ) is a collective term for the three robes. "With that triple robe" (tena ticīvarena) means with those three robes. Even if one is separated from one robe, it is called being separated from the triple robe, either because it is part of the prohibited set or because the term for the whole is applied to the part. Therefore, it is said, "By the method of determination of the triple robe," and so on.

To define the characteristic of separation (vippavāsa), it says, "A village is of one precinct" (gāmo ekūcāro), and so on. In that context, the name "dwelling" (nivesana) is a name for a specific location not made by way of udossita and so on. It is also called "udavasita." A place where goods such as grain are kept is called an "udossita" (storehouse). An "atta" is a specific building with thick walls made of bricks, four or five stories high, to ward off enemy kings. Some say an "atta" is a house with thick walls and a brick roof without rafters. Others say it is a building constructed in the shape of a court.

A "māḷhikā" is a square mansion with a single peak. Or some say a "māḷhikā" is a building with many corners or a monastery built in a circular shape. A "pāsāda" is a long mansion or any mansion excluding the "aḍḍhayoga" (half-roofed dwelling) and so on. A "hammiya" is a mansion with a truncated roof. Or some say a "hammiya" is a monastery with a balcony. A "nāvā" (boat) refers to both boats on land and boats in water. A "sattha" is a group of caravan traders. A "khala" is a threshing floor. An "ārāma" is a flower garden or an orchard. Some teachers say a "vihāra" refers to all monastery compounds or all houses, whether fenced or unfenced.

Among these fifteen places for keeping robes, "nivesana" and others should be understood as being located outside the village. (Alternatively) Here, fourteen places starting with "nivesana" are taken. If taken by way of "nivesana" and others located within the village, they should be noted as being only within the village precinct (upacāra). Some teachers, however, say that six places starting with "nivesana" are located outside the village.

In the phrase "transgressing the hatthapāsa" (hatthapāsatikkama), a perimeter of three cubits is called a "hatthapāsa." To go beyond that perimeter is to transgress the hatthapāsa. It is proper to stay within the hatthapāsa. If a monk of great psychic power is in the sky beyond that hatthapāsa when dawn rises, the robe is forfeited (nissaggiya).

The decision in this training rule is: if a village is under one king or one village-head and is enclosed by a wall, making it a single precinct, a monk may stay anywhere he likes within the village, depending on the house. If it is not enclosed, he must stay in the house where the robes are kept, or within the hatthapāsa surrounding that house. In the case of a village belonging to many kings or many city-chiefs, such as the cities of Vesālī and Kusinārā, if it is enclosed by a wall, he should stay in the house where the robes are kept or within the hatthapāsa of that house. If the house is on a road, then surrounding that house...
289:
Now, to define the characteristic of vippavāsa (living apart from the robe), the phrase "A village is a single precinct" (gāmo ekūpacāro) and so forth is stated. In that context, nivesana is a name for various types of houses that are not constructed as udosito (sheds or stables) and the like. Udosito refers to a hall (shed) for storing goods such as vehicles. This udosito is also called "udavasito". Aṭṭo is a special type of house with thick walls made of bricks, having four or five stories, built to ward off enemy kings and others. Other teachers say, "Aṭṭo is a house with thick walls where the roof is made only of bricks without using rafters." Some also say, "It is made in the form of a platform." Māḷo is either a square mansion joined by a single peak or a special type of house with many corners joined by a single peak. Other teachers say, "Māḷo is a dwelling made in a circular shape." Pāsādo refers to either a long mansion or any mansion other than aṭṭo, māḷo, and hammiya, including varieties like aḍḍhayoga. Hammiya is a mansion with a flat roof (a top-truncated mansion). Other teachers say, "It is a mansion equipped with a moon-terrace." Nāvā (boat) is of two types: those stationed on land and those stationed in water. Sattho (caravan) is either a group of travelers on foot or a caravan of carts. Dhannyakaraṇa refers to a threshing floor. Ārāmo is either a flower garden or a fruit orchard. Vihāro is an entire dwelling place, whether enclosed or unenclosed. Some teachers say, "A house is also called a vihāro." In this context, nivesana and the like are taken as things situated outside the village. As for those situated inside the village, since they are already included under the name "village", the village regulations apply. Other teachers say, "The items from nivesana to hammiya are situated outside the village enclosure (fence)."

In the term hatthapāsātikkame, hatthapāsa is an area measuring two and a half cubits; exceeding that hatthapāsa is called hatthapāsātikkama. In such an instance of exceeding the hatthapāsa [an offense occurs]. However, staying within the hatthapāsa is allowable. If a monk possessing psychic power causes the dawn to rise while he is in the sky beyond that measure, it is still a nissaggiya (an offense of forfeiture).

The decision in this training rule is as follows: If a village belongs to a single person, whether by the power of a king or a village headman, and it is a single precinct because it is enclosed by walls and so forth, then having placed the robe in such a village, one may stay anywhere one wishes within that village. If it is an unenclosed village, one must stay in the house where the robe is placed, or one must not leave the hatthapāsa around that house.
290:
If the village belongs to various kings or various village headmen, like the cities of Vesālī and Kusinārā, and it is enclosed as described, then in such a village, one must stay in the house where the robe is placed, or one must not leave the hatthapāsa of that house. If there is a house on a certain street, one must stay in the rest house (sabhā) in front of that house on that street, or at the door of the house; one must not leave the hatthapāsa of those rest house doors or house doors. If that village is unenclosed, one must stay in the house where the robe is placed or within its hatthapāsa. Regarding a compound (nivesana), if it belongs to a single family and is enclosed, one may place the robe inside the compound and stay within the compound. If it is unenclosed, one must stay in the room where the robe is placed, or one must not leave the hatthapāsa of that room. If the compound belongs to various families and is enclosed, one must stay in the room where the robe is placed, or one must stay at the common main door or within the hatthapāsa of those room doors. If it is unenclosed, one must stay in the room where the robe is placed, or one must not leave the hatthapāsa of that room. This same method applies to sheds (udosito) and the like.

As for a caravan (sattho), whether it is a group on foot or a caravan of carts: if the caravan belongs to a single group, having placed the robe within the caravan, one must not leave within seven abbhantara from the front or the back, and one must not leave within one abbhantara from the sides. If a traveling caravan stands spanning across a village or a river, being connected with the part that has entered inside and spreading across this bank and the other bank, then only the caravan regulations (satthaparihāra) are obtained. However, if the part that has entered inside is comprised within the village or the river, then both the village regulations and the river regulations are obtained. If [the caravan] stands exceeding the monastery boundary (sīmā) and the robe is within the boundary, one must go to the monastery and stay there. If the robe is outside the boundary, one must stay near the caravan itself. If, while traveling, the caravan is broken in the middle because a cart is broken or an ox is lost, one must stay in the section where the robe is placed. In a field (khetta) as well, if the field belongs to a single family and is enclosed, one may place the robe within the field and stay within the field. If it is unenclosed...
291:
One should not be separated from the robe beyond a forearm's length (hatthapāsa). If it is a field belonging to various families and is fenced, one should place the robe inside the field and stay at the gate of the field or within a forearm's length of that robe. If it is not fenced, one should not be separated from the robe beyond a forearm's length. This method is the same for both threshing floors and enclosures (gardens). Regarding the monastery, the decision is the same as what was said regarding the house (nivesana).

At the foot of a tree, one should place the robe in a place where the shadow falls all around at midday, in a dense area within that shaded space. If one places the robe in a sunny spot of a tree with sparse branches, and at dawn that monk is not within a forearm's length of the robe but is in the shadow of that tree in another spot (not where the robe is), it is a nissaggiya offence. If the tree belongs to various families, one must not be separated from the robe beyond a forearm's length.

In an open space, in forests such as the Viñjhā forest, or on small islands in the middle of the ocean where fishermen do not come, one may place the robe and stay anywhere within seven abbhantaras (sattabbhantara) around that robe. A monk staying beyond these seven abbhantaras is considered to be separated from the robe.

Since this detail is not mentioned in this text but is mentioned in the Samantapāsādikā Commentary, it is said: "Here, this is the summary," and so on. "Here" refers to the phrase "should be separated from the three robes" (ticīvarena vippavaseyya). "Summary" refers to the summary explanation (saṅkhepa-vaṇṇanā). In this Pāḷi text, although the headings are laid down without distinction such as "a village has one precinct or various precincts," the status of having one precinct or various precincts for villages, houses, storehouses (udosita), fields, threshing floors, enclosures, and monasteries is analyzed by way of being fenced or unfenced, such as "a village is called having one precinct if it belongs to a single family and is either fenced or unfenced," and so on. However, for watchtowers, sheds, mansions, flat-roofed houses, boats, caravans (carts), the foot of a tree, and open spaces, it is not said in that way, but rather by way of belonging to one family or various families, such as "it is a watchtower of one family, it is a watchtower of various families," and so on. Finally, it is analyzed as having one precinct or various precincts as: "In an open space, in a forest that is not a village, the area within seven abbhantaras all around is one precinct; beyond that is various precincts." Therefore, in villages and so on, a fenced area is one precinct...
292:
An unfenced village and so on should be understood as 'various precincts' (nānūpacāra). Among watchtowers and so on, if it is the property of one family, it is 'one precinct' (ekūpacāra); if it is the property of various families, it is 'various precincts'. In an open space, it should be understood according to the method already mentioned. Indeed, in phrases like "a village has one precinct or various precincts," the gate is considered the 'precinct' (upacāra). However, in the Pāḷi "an open space is one precinct," other teachers say that the 'precinct' refers to the area measured as seven abbhantaras all around.

'Except by the monk's formal permission' (aññatra bhikkhusammutiyā) means the permission given to a monk by the Saṅgha; it means excluding that permission. Therefore, the author of the Saṅgaha said, "What the Saṅgha..." and so on. 'Gives the permission for non-separation' (avippavāsa-sammutiṃ deti) is the permission for not being separated, or permission for the sake of non-separation; it means giving that permission through a formal act with a motion and a second (ñattidutiya-kammavācā).

In the term 'santaruttarena', 'antara' refers to the undergarment (antaravāsaka), and 'uttara' refers to the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga). The upper robe together with the undergarment is called 'santaruttara'. Therefore, it means with the upper robe together with the undergarment. 'Relinquished within dawn' (anto aruṇe paccuddhaṭe) means that a monk who is unable to return (to where the robes are) and reach them before dawn, stays where he has arrived and relinquishes the determination (of the robes) before dawn. 'Should return' (paccāgantabbaṃ) means that when returning to the place where the robes were kept, one should come in a way that does not aggravate the illness.

In fact, from the moment one starts searching for a companion or makes the resolution "I will go," staying (without relinquishing the robes) is permissible. However, one who gives up the effort (to go), thinking "I will not go now," should relinquish the determination, thinking "This robe will remain as an extra robe (atireka-cīvara)." Therefore, it was said: "One should relinquish the determination while staying in that very place." 'He' (so) refers to the illness for which the permission was given. It means that there is no further need for the act of giving permission; the monk simply possesses the allowed state.

'The state of determined robes' (adhiṭṭhita-cīvaratā) is the state of robes determined according to the method of determining the three robes. 'Separation' (vippavāsa) means, if the robe is within a bound boundary (baddha-sīmā), letting dawn rise outside that boundary. If it is an unbound boundary (abaddha-sīmā), it is letting dawn rise beyond the forearm's length (hatthapāsa) outside the aforementioned villages and so on. In a bound boundary, however, it is permissible to leave the robe anywhere and stay anywhere else within the boundary. In this training rule, not relinquishing the determination is connected as 'non-action' (akiriyā).

## The explanation of the Udosita Training Rule is finished.
293:
## 3. Explanation of the Training Rule on Out-of-Season Robes (Akālacīvara-sikkhāpada)

Just as in the previous Udāsita-sikkhāpada, in this Akālacīvara-sikkhāpada as well, the instrumental case in the word 'bhikkhunā' is used in the possessive sense (sāmī-attha). Therefore, it is stated: 'niṭṭhitacīvarasmiṃ bhikkhunā' (when the robe is finished by the bhikkhu), and so forth. Since it is stated in the Word-for-Word Analysis (Padabhājanīya): 'What is called an out-of-season robe (akālacīvara) is a robe that arises during the eleven months when the kaṭhina has not been spread (from the first day after the full moon of Kattika to the full moon of Assayuja); a robe that arises during the seven months when the kaṭhina has been spread (from the first day after the full moon of Phagguna to the full moon of Assayuja); and even during the robe-season, a robe that is given specifically designating the Saṅgha or an individual—this is called an out-of-season robe' (Pārājika 500), the text says 'yvāyaṃ anatthate kaṭhine' and so forth. This is the explanation concerning the robe-season.

The last month of the rainy season (vassāna) is called the robe-month (cīvara-māsa). During that month, even if the kaṭhina has not yet been spread, it is allowable to keep a robe that has arisen without making a formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna) or an assignment (vikappanā). The 'five months' refer to the last month of Kattika and the four months of winter. 'At other times' (aññadā) means the eleven months if the kaṭhina is not spread, and the seven months if it is spread. 'Even during the season' (kālepi) means that even during the robe-season—which is the robe-month if the kaṭhina is not spread, or the five months if it is spread—it includes robes acquired through various means such as 'I give' or 'I shall give' by way of the 'and so forth' (ādi) method. Although all these robes are called 'out-of-season robes' (akālacīvara), in this training rule, only those robes that arise in the later period (piṭṭhisamaya) are intended as out-of-season robes.

However, a robe given even during the robe-season with the words 'I give this out-of-season robe to the Saṅgha' is mentioned by way of extracting the meaning because it shares the same name 'akālacīvara'. Just as a robe arising in the later period can be shared by those who have completed the rains and other monks present, and is thus called an out-of-season robe, this robe is also similar to an out-of-season robe because it can be shared in the same way. If that is so, why is it said, 'or to an individual, I give this to you,' and so forth? One might ask: is a robe given specifically to an individual not something to be shared by anyone else? This is not a contradiction. It is stated thus to show the benefit that can be obtained because the act of giving by designation is similar. 'By one's own property' means arising from one's own property such as cotton or thread. This should be understood as connected with the word 'uppajjeyya' (should arise). 'Giving in the boundary' (sīmāya deti) and so forth are stated by way of the method of personal designation (puggalādhiṭṭhāna). Here, giving in the boundary is the first heading (mātikā), giving by agreement is the second heading... and giving to an individual is the eighth heading.

By the phrase 'by a place worthy of being fenced,' it is shown that for a monastery that is not yet fenced, the area within the first stone's throw from the regular meeting place and so forth is the precinct boundary (upacāra-sīmā).
294:
Now, to show that the area within the second stone's throw is also within the precinct boundary, the text begins with 'api ca' and so forth. The regular meeting place should also be understood as being within the limits of the boundary. 'If the monastery expands, the boundary expands' means that if the monastery expands without going outside the precinct (upacāra), the boundary is understood to expand. In the Mahāpaccariya, however, it is said: 'Even if the monks increase, the monastery expands.' It is stated in the Samantapāsādikā: 'If monks sitting together in a monastery form a continuous line filling even a hundred yojanas, that hundred yojanas is also the precinct boundary; the gains reach all those monks.' 'Asking about entering the monastery and the lodgings of the bhikkhunīs' means asking permission for entering the monastery and asking about the lodgings for visiting (āgantuka) and departing (gamika) bhikkhunīs. This is true: a visiting bhikkhunī must ask permission to enter the monastery; a departing bhikkhunī must ask permission regarding the ten kinds of communal (saṅghika) lodgings. Here, although it says 'of the bhikkhunīs,' it should be understood that a departing bhikkhu must also ask about the lodgings by the power of this boundary.

'Announcing probation (parivāsa) and penance (mānatta)' means the announcement of probation and penance by monks who are undergoing probation or penance. 'The arrangement of the interruption of the rains, taking dependence (nissaya), and accepting lodgings (senāsana), etc.' means the arrangement for the interruption of the rains, the arrangement for taking dependence, and the arrangement for accepting lodgings. By the word 'ādi' (etc.), it includes the subsidence of dependence, the receiving of gains, and entering the monastery after fulfilling the duties of a visitor, and so forth. 'By the power of this boundary' refers to the precinct boundary; it is stated because all these arrangements can be obtained either inside or outside as appropriate.

A boundary established for the sake of gains is called a boundary for gains (lābha-sīmā). That boundary was neither authorized by the Fully Enlightened Buddha nor established by the Elders who recited the Dhamma; rather, it was established by the donors of gains. Therefore, it is said: 'kings, great ministers of the king, and so forth.' 'Samantā' means around the monastery. 'Yaṃ' refers to things such as grain collected as tax. The remaining text 'establish a boundary' should be added to complete the sense. 'The place where the authority of a single king extends' refers to the territory of the Coḷa king, the territory of the Keraḷa king, and so forth—the place where the authority of each individual king extends. It is called 'dīpa' (island) because the water goes on both sides; if a portion of land not submerged by a flood is itself the boundary, it is called an island boundary (dīpa-sīmā). Therefore, it is said 'samuddantena' (by the edge of the sea) and so forth. Since the universe boundary (cakkavāḷa-sīmā) is delimited only by the Cakkavāḷa mountains, it is said: 'The area within the circumference of a single Cakkavāḷa mountain is called the universe boundary.'
295:
The remaining boundaries (sīmā) refer to khaṇḍasīmā and others. A gift given "to the khaṇḍasīmā" means seeing the Saṅgha assembled for some business in the khaṇḍasīmā and donating with the words, "I donate to the Saṅgha in the khaṇḍasīmā." A monk standing on a tree or a mountain within the khaṇḍasīmā, or even one below in the ground, is to be understood as standing in the khaṇḍasīmā. A gift given "to the samānasaṃvāsasīmā" means donating with the words, "I donate to the samānasaṃvāsasīmā." The same principle applies to the remaining boundaries. The khaṇḍasīmā does not reach monks standing in the sīmantarika (the space between two boundaries), because there is no samānasaṃvāsasīmā in that place. The difference between donations to the samānasaṃvāsasīmā and the avippavāsasīmā is: a gain given with the words "I donate to the avippavāsasīmā" does not reach monks staying in the village (gāma). Why? Because the Buddha said, "excluding the village and its precincts (gāmūpacāra)." However, a gain given with the words "I donate to the samānasaṃvāsasīmā" does reach monks staying in the village.

Donations to the abbhantarasīmā and udakukkhepasīmā mean seeing [the Saṅgha] assembled for the uposatha etc. in those boundaries and donating with the words, "I donate to this abbhantarasīmā," and so on. For janapadasīmā, raṭṭhasīmā, rajjasīmā, dīpasīmā, and cakkavāḷasīmā, the decision is the same as mentioned for gāmasīmā etc., which is why it is said "in the janapadasīmā etc."

"One monk going and being able to collect for all" means one monk can go there, divide according to seniority (vassagga), and bring it back. "One [monk]" means one monk of the same communion (sabhāga); he too is only allowed to take his own share. Therefore it is said, "He takes the share of the sabhāga monks."

Thus, the decision regarding the gift of one who refers to a specific boundary has been stated. Now, to show the decision for one who does not know how to say "in such-and-such a boundary" but only knows the word "boundary" and, coming to the monastery, says "I donate to the boundary" or "I donate to the Saṅgha staying in the boundary," it is said "entering the monastery" and so on. "Which boundary?" means asking which specific boundary is intended. "I do not know this distinction" means not knowing the classification of "such-and-such a boundary." It means the gain should be distributed by the monks within the upacārasīmā (precinct boundary) because the gain is limited by the upacārasīmā. Doing so is to make the gain equal (samānalābhakatikā).

"In which monastery my regular meritorious acts (dhuvakāra) are performed"—the decision here is: in whichever monastery the property of that robe-donor exists as a regular offering (pākavatta) for the Saṅgha; or in whichever monastery he takes responsibility for the monks and always feeds them at his house; or where he has built a dwelling (āvāsa); or where he has constantly donated food-by-tickets (salākabhatta) etc., these...
296:
...are called regular donors (dhuvakāra). For one who has established an entire monastery, there is no need to even mention it (it is very obvious). Therefore, it is said, "In whichever monastery his regular offering (dānavatta) exists." In this context, "pākavatta" means "dānavatta" (regular gift). "Vattati" means it occurs. "Yato" means from which monastery. "Yattha" means in which monastery. "Sabbatha" means in all monasteries.

The method of distribution by setting an agenda (mātikā): If monks are very many in one monastery and very few in another, and there is only one gift, but there are many dhuvakāra places, one should ask "Where should we give?". If there is only one couch (mañca) or chair (pīṭha), one should ask that donor, and for whichever monastery or whichever lodging (senāsana) within a single monastery that donor decides, it should be given there. If he says, "Let such-and-such a monk take it," that is also proper.

If he says, "Give it at my regular donation (dhuvakāra) place" and leaves without specifying, it is proper for the Saṅgha to decide. It should be decided thus: "Give it at the dwelling of the Sangha Elder (Saṅghatthera)." If the lodgings (senāsana) there are complete, it should be given where they are insufficient. If a monk says, "There are no monastery requisites in my dwelling," it should be given at that monk's place.

"I give to the Saṅgha" means donating in this way: "I give these robes to the Saṅgha." Even if [monks] are outside the precinct boundary (upacārasīmā), if they are continuous with the monks who have reached the precinct boundary, they also receive it, because the boundary is considered to have expanded due to the continuity of the assembly (parisā). Therefore, it reaches those who have reached the precinct boundary and those outside who are continuous with them.

If there are residents/disciples (antevāsika) etc. who receive it, they get it. When the monks within the precinct boundary strike the bell to announce the time, those who have entered the precinct boundary even if they haven't reached the place of distribution, or those who are continuous with them and standing at their own monastery gate or inside the monastery, should be given a share. It means they must be given even if the share has already been given to the youngest monk of the Saṅgha. However, in a second distribution, those who arrive after the elders have taken their seats do not receive the first share. They should be given from the second share according to seniority (vassagga).

If they say, "Give to those standing outside the precinct boundary," it should not be given. If the monastery is large and while distributing robes starting from the elders' seats...
297:
When robes are being distributed, if senior elders (Mahātheras) of a lazy nature arrive late, one should not say, "Venerable sirs, the distribution is being made to those with twenty years of seniority (Anutheras); your turn has passed." One should pause that turn, give to those senior elders who arrived later, and only then continue the distribution according to the order of seniority.

Hearing that "many robes have arisen in such-and-such a monastery," monks arrive even from monasteries a league (yojana) away. To those who have arrived, distribution should be made starting from where they stand; this is a summary here. The details should be understood according to the method stated in the commentary on the Cīvarakkhandhaka of the Mahāvagga in the Samantapāsādikā.

After stating the decision regarding robes given after entering a monastery with the words "I give these robes to the Saṅgha," the phrase "Yaṃ pana" etc., is stated to show the decision regarding robes given upon seeing a monk in the vicinity (upacāra) boundary of the monastery with the words "I give to the Saṅgha." "It reaches the continuous assembly" means that even if the assembly is spread out for a league, if it is continuous, it reaches all the monks. Here, continuity should be defined by a distance within twelve cubits. Therefore, "Ye pana" etc., is stated.

"Ubhatosaṅghassa dinnaṃ" means given with the words "I give to both Saṅghas (the Bhikkhu-saṅgha and the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha)." Even if one says "I give to the two groups of Saṅgha, I give to the two kinds of Saṅgha, I give to the Bhikkhu-saṅgha and the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha," it is still considered given to both Saṅghas. "Half is given to the monks, half to the nuns" means making two equal portions, one portion should be given to the monks and one portion to the nuns. It means they are entitled to receive it because the donor included them by the term "both Saṅghas." "Cetiyassa" means to shrines, stupas, etc. Because it is constructed as a repository for relics, etc., and because it is a place of respect for the people, it is called a "Cetiya." Since there is no difference at all, "Idha pana cetiyassa" etc., is stated.

However, if it is said, "I give to both Saṅghas, to you, and to the Cetiya," then twenty-two portions should be made: ten given to the monks, ten to the nuns, one to the individual, and one to the Cetiya. In that case, the individual is entitled to receive again from the Saṅgha's portion according to their seniority (vassagga), but for the Cetiya, there is only one portion. This turn is not stated here because it can be known by the method already mentioned. However, it is indeed stated in the Samantapāsādikā.
298:
Because the donor gave with the words "to the Bhikkhunīs" in an individual sense, it should not be divided in the middle. "The individual does not receive separately" means they do not receive a separate individual portion as before. "Receives only one from the place of arrival" means they receive only one portion from the portion that comes according to their seniority. Why? Because they are included by the term "Bhikkhu-saṅgha." Even if it is said, "To the Bhikkhu-saṅgha, to the Bhikkhunīs, to you, and to the Cetiya," a portion equal to one person is obtained for the Cetiya, but a separate portion is not obtained for the individual. Therefore, after giving one to the Cetiya, the remainder should be divided by counting the monks and the nuns. Therefore, "Cetiyassa cāti vutte pana" etc., is stated.

Mentioning the individual and the Cetiya along with those monks and nuns is just like the preceding method. It means that including the individual and the Cetiya along with those monks and nuns is just like the preceding method. Even if it is said, "To the monks, the nuns, and to you," "To the monks, the nuns, and to the Cetiya," or "To the monks, the nuns, to you, and to the Cetiya," one portion is obtained for the Cetiya, there is no separate portion for the individual, and it means it should be divided only by counting the monks and the nuns. "The individual does not receive separately" means a separate portion is not obtained for the individual, but only one is obtained according to seniority. However, if it is said, "To the Bhikkhu-saṅgha and to the Cetiya," a separate portion is obtained for the Cetiya; thus it says, "Cetiyassa pana labbhati." Even if it is said, "To the Bhikkhu-saṅgha, to you, and to the Cetiya," a separate portion is obtained only for the Cetiya, not for the individual. For the Cetiya, it is indeed obtained. If it is said, "To the monks and to the Cetiya," it means a separate portion is obtained for the Cetiya. Even if it is said, "To the monks, to you, and to the Cetiya," a separate portion is obtained only for the Cetiya, not for the individual. If one starts with the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha, it should be applied in the same way.

Here there is a question: Nowadays, wise people, having established an image with relics or a Cetiya, give offerings to both Saṅghas headed by the Buddha (Buddhappamukha). Having placed the alms-bowl on a stand (bowl-rest) in front of the image or the Cetiya and having given the water of donation (dakkhiṇodaka), they give saying, "We give to the Buddhas." In that case, what should be done with the snacks and food given first? Or if they bring it to the monastery and give alms-food, flowers, incense, etc., saying, "We give this to the Cetiya," how should one proceed with those offered snacks, meals, alms-food, flowers, incense, etc.? The answer is: Flowers, incense, etc., should first be offered to the Cetiya. Banners should be made from the cloths.
299:
Lamps should be lit and offered with oil. As for alms-food, honey, molasses, and so forth, they should be given to the person—whether a monk or a layperson—who constantly looks after and cleans the Cetiya. If there is no constant caretaker, one should not eat the brought alms-food yet; it should be set aside, and after performing the duties at the Cetiya, it is permissible to eat. If the mealtime is near, it is also permissible to eat first and perform the duties later.

Regarding flowers, scents, and so forth, if it is said, "Take this item and make an offering to the Cetiya," it should be taken and offered even if the place is far away. If it is said, "Take it to the Saṅgha of monks," it should also be taken. If, however, one says, "I am on my alms round; there are monks in the refectory, they will take it," and the donor says, "Venerable Sir, I give it only to you," then it is permissible to eat it. Otherwise, if while carrying it with the intention "I will offer it to the Saṅgha," the mealtime draws near on the way, it is permissible to appropriate it for oneself and eat.

To say, "I offer to the Saṅgha who have completed the Rains Retreat," means "I offer these robes to the Saṅgha who have completed the Rains Retreat." These robes also reach the monks who are outside the precinct (upacārasīmā). If the Kathina has been spread, it reaches them until the time the Kathina is withdrawn (uabbhāra). Therefore, it should be given to a monk who has gone to another direction if there is someone to receive it on his behalf. If the Kathina is not spread, it reaches them during the winter; and robes offered in this way also reach the monks who completed the later Rains Retreat (pacchimavassa). "In whichever monasteries" means in any of the monasteries. When saying, "I offer to the Saṅgha who have completed the Rains Retreat," it reaches all monks who are present, because it occurs at a time when the Kathina privileges are absent. If, however, one says, "I offer to the monks currently staying for the Rains," only those staying for the Rains receive it; those who have broken their Vassa do not. During the robe season (cīvaramāsa), if one says, "I offer to the monks staying for the Rains," it reaches only those who entered the later Rains (pacchimikā vassa); it does not reach those who entered the earlier Rains (purimikā vassa) or those who broke their Vassa.

From the robe season until the last day of winter, if one says, "We give the Rains-residence cloth (vassāvāsika)," whether the Kathina is spread or not, it reaches only those who have completed the past Rains. If said from the first day of summer, the schedule (mātikā) should be applied: "Five months of the past Rains-residence have passed; the future one will be in four months. For which Rains-residence do you give?" If one says, "I give to the monks who completed the past Rains," it reaches only those who completed that Rains; fellow monks who have gone to other directions are also entitled to receive it.
300:
If one says, "I will give the Rains-residence cloth in the coming year," that cloth should be kept and distributed on the day of entering the Rains (vassūpanāyika). Then, if a monk says, "The monastery is not secure; there is danger from thieves; it is not possible to keep it or to wander around carrying it," and the donor says, "I give it to the monks who have arrived," then the monks present should distribute and take it. If one says, "Venerable Sir, I did not get to offer the Rains-residence cloth in the third Rains past; I offer that cloth now," it should be assigned to the monks who completed the Rains in that third past year. If those monks have departed to various directions, it should be given if another intimate monk receives it on their behalf. If only one monk remains and the others have passed away, the whole lot belongs to that single monk. If not even one remains, it becomes the property of the Saṅgha (saṅghika) and should be distributed by the monks present.

"Those invited monks who drank the gruel" refers to monks who drank gruel by invitation. Monks who received gruel by going to house doors as part of their alms-round duty, or by entering a house, or those for whom people brought gruel from the refectory after taking their bowls, or those to whom gruel was sent by elders—they are not entitled to those robes (or offerings). If many other monks also come along with the invited monks and sit filling the inside and outside of the house, and the donor says, "Whether invited or not, to all those to whom I have given gruel, let these clothes belong," then all the monks are entitled. Those who received gruel from the hands of elders are not entitled. But if that donor says, "To all the monks who drank my gruel, let it be," then all the monks are entitled. In the phrase "bhattakhajjaka-ādīhi," by the word "ādi" (etc.), robes, dwellings, and medicines should also be included.

"Puggalassa" (to the individual) refers to an individual who is either present or absent. Therefore, it is stated as "this robe," and so forth. If one says, "I offer this robe to you and to your pupils (antevāsika)," it belongs to the elder and the pupils. It also belongs to those who come to learn and those who leave after learning. If one says, "I offer to the monks who constantly wander with you," it belongs to all those who are pupils in study, performing duties and wandering while receiving instructions and inquiries. "Ettha" (herein) refers to the eight schedules (mātikā). This is just a summary; if one wishes to know in detail, it should be understood as stated in the Samantapāsādikā Commentary, in the explanation of the Cīvarakkhandhaka.
301:
“Relatives or friends have sent yarn for the sake of my robe; they will give the robes they have brought.” In this way, it should be understood that there is an expectation (paccāsā) regarding a robe from a relative or a friend. “Kappiya-bhaṇḍena” means with one’s own property such as cotton yarn and the like. “Saṇhaṃ” means delicate or fine. Only after obtaining another expectation-robe (paccāsā-cīvara) that is similar to the fine original robe should it be completed within a month. Such completion within a month occurs only if there is an expectation of receiving the robe. If there is no expectation and the original robe arrives within ten days, it must be determined (adhiṭṭhāna) on that very tenth day. Therefore, the author said, “If one does not obtain it,” and so forth. The statement, “Even the expectation-robe should be determined as a cloth-requisite (parikkhāra-coḷa),” refers to a coarse expectation-robe received before the fine expectation-robe. The word “pi” (also/even) indicates that it is not only the original robe that should be determined.

## The Commentary on the Akāla-cīvara Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 4. Commentary on the Purāṇa-cīvara Sikkhāpada

One who is known as “This nun is indeed our relative” is called “ñāti” (relative). That very nun is called “ñātikā.” A nun who is not known as a relative is called “aññātikā.” Referring to such a nun who is not a relative, the author said, “na ñātikāya” (by one who is not a relative). “Whether from the mother’s side or the father’s side” means from the mother’s lineage or the father’s lineage. “Up to the seventh generation” means up to the extent of the lifespan of the seventh man or the seventh woman. It means the lineage of the paternal grandfather’s side, the paternal grandmother’s side, the maternal grandfather’s side, and the maternal grandmother’s side. Alternatively, “up to the seventh generation” means up to the seventh pair. In this context, the word “yuga” (generation/pair) should be understood by the method of ellipsis (ekasesa) as “yugo ca yugo ca yugā.” Thus, a pair is taken in each instance. “Not related by any means” means not related by any means among brothers, sisters, nephews, sons, grandsons, and so forth. Father, grandfather, his father, and his father—thus up to seven generations; father, grandmother, her father, mother, brother, sister, sons, and daughters—thus up to seven generations upwards and downwards; father, paternal uncles, paternal aunts, cousins, and their succession of sons and daughters—thus up to seven generations; mother, grandmother, her mother, and her mother—thus up to seven generations; mother, grandfather, his father, mother, brother, sister, sons, and daughters—thus up to seven generations upwards and...
302:
...and downwards up to the seventh generation; mother, maternal uncle, maternal aunt, maternal cousins, and their succession of sons and daughters—thus up to seven generations. One who is not related either through the mother’s side or the father’s side in this manner is called “aññātikā” (unrelated).

It is just like the five hundred Sakyan princesses. This is merely an illustration. Therefore, those who, while remaining in the state of a monk, have changed their gender (to female) and become nuns should also be understood as “upasampanna” (ordained) within the pure Bhikkhu Saṅgha in this Dispensation. “Ubhato-saṅghe vā” (or in both Saṅghas) means by a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations (ñatti-catuttha-kamma) in the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha, and by a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations in the Bhikkhu Saṅgha; thus in both Saṅghas. In the term “purāṇa-cīvara” (old robe), “cīvara” refers only to a robe suitable for wearing or wrapping; this is stated by the words “rajitvā” (having dyed) and so forth. “Kappaṃ katvā” means making the prescribed mark (kappa-bindu). Teachers say, “Giving a robe without making this prescribed mark does not become a basis for a Pācittiya offense.” “Paribhoga-sīsena” means primarily through using it by touching it with the body. “Aṃse” means on the shoulder; “matthake” means on the top of the head. However, if one lies down after placing it under a mat, or if one goes along holding it up with the hands like a canopy in the air without it touching the head, this is not called “usage” (paribhoga).

“Kāya-vikāraṃ vā karoti” (or makes a bodily gesture) means making a bodily gesture so that the nun knows, “This monk wants [the robe] washed.” By the words “standing within twelve cubits and throwing it upwards,” it is shown that there is no offense for a monk who, leaving the vicinity (upacāra), throws it from this side. “Or sends it into the hand of another” (aññassa vā hatthe peseti) means sending it into the hand of anyone such as a female probationer (sikkhamānā), a male novice (sāmaṇera), a female novice (sāmaṇerī), a male lay follower (upāsaka), or a woman who is within twelve cubits. “So” (he/that person) refers to the lay follower and the novice. In the phrase “upasampajjitvā dhovati” (washes after being ordained), it should be understood according to the circumstances: a male lay follower changes gender and is ordained among the nuns and then washes; or a male novice changes gender and is ordained among the nuns and then washes. However, if it was given into the hand of a nun and she washes it after changing gender (to male), it is allowable.

In this matter, since there is no requirement to forfeit a single robe three times, for a monk who causes all three actions (washing, dyeing, and beating) to be done, there is one Nissaggiya offense due to one action, and two Dukkaṭa offenses due to the other two. For one who causes two actions to be done, there is one Nissaggiya due to one, and a Dukkaṭa due to the second. Therefore, it was said, “The three [actions] beginning with washing,” and so forth.
303:
The word "vatthunā" is spoken with reference to an action that is completed by first performing it. If it is said, "Having dyed and washed this robe, bring it," and that bhikkhunī washes it first and dyes it later, only a dukkaṭa offense along with nissaggiya is incurred. In this way, the method should be understood in all cases of reversed instructions. If it is said, "Wash it and bring it," and she both washes and dyes it, the offense is incurred only because of the cause of having it washed; there is no offense for the dyeing. This applies in all instances. Therefore, it is said, "If it is said, 'Wash it,'" and so on. For a monk who has a bhikkhunī ordained on one side by the power of the monks wash it, the offense is incurred only according to the object, as stated by "bhikkhunisaṅghavasena," etc.

"Aññassa vā santakaṃ" means having an old robe belonging to another monk washed. "Nisīdanapaccattharaṇaṃ" refers to a sitting cloth or a bedspread, whether it belongs to another or to oneself. Since in this training rule "old robe" is intended only for robes used for wearing or draping, a monk who has his own sitting cloth or bedspread washed incurs only a dukkaṭa, not a nissaggiya. "Avuttā vā dhovati" refers to a bhikkhunī who has come for the purpose of either recitation or instruction, and seeing a soiled robe, takes it from the place where it was kept, or says, "Give it, Venerable Sir, I will wash it," and after having it brought, she washes, dyes, and beats it; this is called "washing without being told." A bhikkhunī who hears the words of a monk ordering a young monk or a novice, "Wash this robe," and says, "Bring it, Venerable Sir, I will wash it," and then washes it, or one who takes it temporarily and gives it back after washing and dyeing, is also called "washing without being told."

"Aññaṃ vā parikkhāraṃ" refers to any requisite such as a sandal bag, an alms-bowl bag, a shoulder strap, a waistband, or a mat spread on a couch or a bench, etc. Because of the phrase "standing in the vicinity (upacāra)," there is no offense even if one sends it to be washed. "Upacāra" refers to the area within twelve cubits.

## The Commentary on the Purāṇacīvara Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 5. Commentary on the Cīvarappaṭiggahaṇa Sikkhāpada

"Channaṃ" means among the six kinds of robes, such as linen (khoma), etc. "Upacāraṃ muñcitvā" means excluding the twelve-cubit vicinity. By the word "pi," if the four assemblies bring robes and various dyed cloths to a monk who is preaching the Dhamma and place them at his feet, or if they stand in the vicinity and throw them over him, "if he accepts them, they are indeed received"—in this passage...
304:
...it shows that there is no need to say anything at all. "Let them throw" means let them throw either by day or by night. "It is indeed received" means that although it is impossible to distinguish, "This robe is for the bhikkhunī, this is for others," yet because it is taken without a discriminating mind, it is indeed received. "Of any non-ordained person" means of any non-ordained person among probationers (sikkhamānā), male novices (sāmaṇera), female novices (sāmaṇerī), laymen (upāsaka), laywomen (upāsikā), and so on. "Placed" means placed by a bhikkhunī. "Determining it as a rag-robe (paṃsukūla)" means giving rise to the perception, "This is ownerless." For an ownerless object is called "paṃsukūla." By this phrase, it is shown that it is not proper to take it with the perception, "It is placed for us," and so on.

"Except by exchange" means that which is to be exchanged is called "parivatta"; that parivatta itself is "pārivattaka," meaning a robe given in exchange; it means except for that robe given in exchange. Therefore, it is said, "even if it is only a piece of gallnut (harīṭaka)," and so on. "Having applied the mind" means repeatedly focusing with the mind. If a bhikkhunī gives a rainy-season robe, it should be known that it is not proper to receive it without following the aforementioned procedure.

"By obtaining" means by receiving. "Tika-pācittiya" means "tika" because it has three measures; it is "tika-pācittiya" because it is both a triad and a pācittiya. It means there are three pācittiyas based on the perception of a non-relative as a relative, being in doubt, and the perception of a non-relative as a non-relative. "Ordained on one side" means one who is ordained in the presence of bhikkhunīs. For receiving a robe from the hand of such a bhikkhunī ordained on one side, except by exchange, a monk incurs a dukkaṭa offense; but if he receives it from the hand of a bhikkhunī ordained in the presence of [both] monks [and nuns], it is a pācittiya. By the phrase "in alms-bowl bags, etc., and in requisites that are not to be determined," it also includes the mattress cover (bhisi-chavi). Although that mattress cover is large, because it is included under lodgings (senāsana), it does not come under the designation of "robe"; therefore, it is neither to be determined (adhiṭṭhāna) nor to be assigned (vikappanā). For it is said in the Samantapāsādikā Commentary: "Even if a mattress cover is the size of a couch, it is indeed allowable." Because of the words "receives a robe from the hand," there is no offense in receiving what is sent by a non-relative bhikkhunī. Because of receiving and because of not making an exchange, [this training rule] is an act of commission and omission (kiriyākirya).

## The Explanation of the Cīvarappaṭiggahaṇa Sikkhāpada is finished.
305:
## 6. Commentary on the Aññātakaviññatti Training Rule

Because he is the master and head of the house, he is called a householder (gahapati). In this training rule, a householder is intended to be any human being who is not ordained. Therefore, it is said, "a human being among those not ordained as monks." The same method applies to the word "housewife" (gahapatānī). Because the word "viññāpeyya" applies to both the sense of the direct agent (requesting oneself) and the causative agent (causing another to request), it is said, "should request or should cause to request." Here, causing another to request should be understood as being for one's own benefit. By doing so, the statement "not by command" (anāṇattika) is established.

In the phrase "except on occasion" (aññatra samayā), it is called "occasion" (samaya) because a being or a natural phenomenon meets with conascent states, or with arising (uppāda), etc., at this time. Although time (kāla) does not truly exist in terms of ultimate reality, because it is merely the occurrence of mental and physical phenomena, it is referred to as the locus or the instrument of the occurrence of phenomena, established merely by conceptualization. It means "setting aside that occasion." Therefore, it is said, "if a monk is one whose robe has been snatched away," and so on. In that context, a monk whose robe has been snatched away by anyone such as kings is called "one whose robe has been snatched away" (acchinnacīvara). As it is said: "One whose robe has been snatched away means a monk's robe is snatched away; it is snatched away by kings, or by thieves, or by rogues, or by anyone at all." A monk whose robe is lost due to any cause such as fire is called "one whose robe has been lost" (naṭṭhacīvara). As it is said: "One whose robe has been lost means a monk's robe is burnt by fire, or carried away by water, or eaten by rats or termites, or worn out through use." Because the word "samayā" is in the ablative case used in the sense of the accusative, looking towards the word "aññatra," it is said "that occasion." "In another" (aññasmiṃ) means at another occasion.

"Three Pācittiyas" (tikapācittiyaṃ) means three Pācittiya offenses by way of perceiving a non-relative as a non-relative, being in doubt, or perceiving a non-relative as a relative. "On occasion" (samaye) means during the aforementioned times when a robe is snatched away or lost. In the phrase "to a monk requesting from a relative or one who has given an invitation," it refers to a monk requesting from relatives or those who have given an invitation, saying, "Please give your robe." Here, from a householder who has given an invitation to the Saṅgha, it is proper to request only according to the measure. However, from a householder who has given a personal invitation, one should request only those specific items that were offered. If someone invites with the four requisites and, reflecting by himself, offers robes and so on, or daily gruel and food at the appropriate times, there is no need to request from him. If someone, though having given an invitation...
306:
...does not give due to foolishness or forgetfulness, he should be requested (reminded). If someone says, "I invite you to my house," one should go to his house and sit or lie down as one pleases, but nothing should be taken. If someone says, "I invite you with whatever is in my house," one should request what is allowable in that house. However, one is not allowed to sit or lie down in that house. "For his sake" (tassevatthāya) means for the sake of that very person, such as Buddharakkhita or Dhammarakkhita, who is referred to as "another." "By one who takes with his own wealth" means purchasing or exchanging using one's own allowable property with allowable terminology.

## The Commentary on the Aññātakaviññatti Training Rule is finished.

## 7. Commentary on the Tatuttari Training Rule

In this training rule, the word "taṃ" expresses the meaning previously mentioned. The word "ce" is merely a particle. Or, the word "ce" has the meaning "if" and should be understood as being connected with the word "pavāreyya." "Pavāreyya ce" means "if he should invite." By saying "abhi is a prefix," it shows that there is no special meaning for that word. Therefore, it was said, "it has the meaning of bringing." Because the word "pavāra" occurs in the sense of desire, it is said, "should cause to desire." One should cause desire for the requisites; it is a synonym for offering. Therefore, it was said starting with "as much as" (yāvattakaṃ). "Nekkhamma" means renunciation (pabbajjā). "Daṭṭhū" means having seen. In this verse, there is the elision of the nasal (anunāsikalopa) for the sake of preserving the meter. "Khemato" means safely. It should be connected as "having brought forward by body or by speech, he should invite." To show the method of bringing forward by body and by speech, the words starting with "having brought near" (upanetvā) were said. "Sa-antaraṃ" means together with the inner robe (antaravāsaka). "Uttaraṃ" means the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga). "Paramaṃ" means the final limit. "Of this robe" (assa cīvarassa) means of this collection of robes to be brought. This bahubbīhi compound "santaruṭṭharaparamam" has a meaning to be understood along with its attributes, like "lambakaṇṇa" (long-eared). Therefore, it was said starting with "by the undergarment" (nivāsanena). By way of the maximum limit, all monks are allowed to take only up to that limit.
308:
## 8. Explanation of the First Upakkhaṭa Sikkhāpada

In the phrase "bhikkhuṃ paneva uddissa", the word "pana" is merely a particle; likewise, the word "eva" is also a particle. Therefore, it is said: "for a monk named so-and-so," and so on. "Apadisitvā" means having spoken or having referred to. "Aññātakassa gahapatissa" means by a householder who is not a relative. Here, the genitive case is used in the sense of the agent (karaṇattha). In the Commentary, however, this was not analyzed, considering it easy to understand.

Robes are bartered or purchased with this item; therefore, it is called "cīvaracetāpanna" (robe-fund). In this term, the letter "na" is an augment (āgama), and it is also read as "cīvaracetāpana". Since that robe-fund is one of the types such as money, it is called "hiraññādikaṃ". In this context, "hirañña" refers to coins (kahāpaṇa). By the word "ādi", gold and so forth should be included. "Upakkhaṭaṃ" means that which is prepared or set aside. Because that robe-fund is collected and prepared in that way, it is said: "Upakkhaṭaṃ hotīti sajjitaṃ hoti" (It is prepared means it is arranged).

"Saṃharitvā ṭhapitaṃ" means placed in a heap. "Parivattana" (bartering/exchange) means having a robe made that has not yet been made, or purchasing one that is already made. Therefore, it is said: "kāretvā vā kiṇitvā vā" (having it made or having it bought). "Acchādessāmi" means "I will cause him to wear/robe himself." Therefore, it is called "vohāravacanametaṃ" (this is a conventional expression). "Vohāravacana" means a metaphorical expression (upacāravacana).

If one asks what the connection of words (padasambandha) is in the phrases beginning with "tatra ce so bhikkhū", the answer is given starting with "yatra so gahapati vā". "Pubbe appavārito" means not having been previously invited with words such as: "I will donate; what kind of robe do you need, Bhante? What kind of robe shall I purchase for you?" "Upasaṅkamitvā" means having gone. In the word-analysis (padabhājanī), it is stated as "gharaṃ gantvā" (having gone to the house) by way of common usage. Here, "pacuravohāravasena" means by way of the way the majority of people speak. Since those who wish to see a householder usually go to his house, it is commonly used in that way.

"Vikappaṃ" means a special arrangement. Here, the prefix "vi" denotes distinction. Therefore, it is said: "visiṭṭhakappaṃ". This explains the grammatical meaning (vacanattha). By the phrase "adhikavidhānaṃ", the intended meaning (adhippāyattha) is shown. "Yathā pana tamāpajjati" means by what manner he reaches that vikappa. To show that manner, the words beginning with "sādhū" are stated.

This word "sādhu" is seen in meanings such as acceptance, rejoicing, goodness, and requesting. Likewise, "Sādhu, Bhante" (It is well, Bhante), that monk [responded] to the Blessed One's...
309:
In passages such as “Having delighted in and appreciated what was said” (M. iii, 86), the word *sādhu* is found in the sense of acceptance (*sampatichana*). In passages such as “Excellent, excellent, Sāriputta” (D. iii, 349; M. i, 340), it is found in the sense of appreciation (*sampahaṃsana*).

In verses such as “Good is the king who delights in the Dhamma; good is the man possessed of wisdom; good is non-treachery towards friends; the non-doing of evil is a source of happiness (goodness)” (Jā. ii, 18, 101), it is found in the sense of excellent (*sundara*). In passages such as “Venerable Sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief” (S. iii, 64-68), it is found in the sense of request (*āyacana*). In this context also, it should be understood only in the sense of request; therefore, it is said, “*Sādhu* is a particle in the sense of request.” Therein, “request” (*āyacana*) means requesting face-to-face, an aspiration. “*Parivitakke*” is connected as a particle in the sense of reflection. “*Ālapati*” means he addresses (*āmanteti*). In the term “*āyatādīsu*,” the word “*ādi*” includes robes that are wide, thick, and smooth.

Since an offense does not reach the peak (*nissaggiya*) merely by reaching this training rule, the phrase “by his words” (*tassa vacanena*) etc., is stated. “*Payoge*” refers to efforts such as searching for thread and so on.

Regarding “requesting a low-priced robe from one who wishes to purchase an expensive robe”: this refers to the intention of a monk who says to a householder wishing to buy and offer a robe worth twenty units, “I have no need for that robe; give me only a robe worth ten or eight units.” “*Evarūpaṃ*” means a group of similar portions; this means equal to this. And that equality is only by way of value, not by way of measurement. For this training rule concerns the increase in value (*agghavaḍḍhanaka*).

## The Explanation of the First Prepared Robe Training Rule is Finished.

## 9. Explanation of the Second Prepared Robe Training Rule
Because it is asked why the meaning should be understood in this way, the phrase “*idañhi*” etc., is stated. The word “*hi*” is a particle in the sense of cause. To show that there is no distinction, the phrase “*kevalaṃ*” etc., is stated.

## The Explanation of the Second Prepared Robe Training Rule is Finished.
310:
## 10. Explanation of the King’s Training Rule

“*Rājato bhoggaṃ*” means wealth obtained from a king. “*Rājabhogga*” refers to a king’s minister. “*Rājato bhoga*” means the authority (power) granted by a king.

By the word “*iminā*” etc., it means: “With this robe-fund, purchase a robe and clothe the monk named so-and-so with that robe.” “*Āgamanasuddhi*” means the purity of the origin (the initial purity of the robe-fund).

If, instead of sending it in this allowable manner, one sends it saying, “Give this robe-fund to the monk named so-and-so,” and that messenger approaches the monk and says, “Venerable Sir, this robe-fund is brought intended for the venerable one; may the venerable one accept this robe-fund,” then, even after refusing, it is not proper for the monk to point out an attendant (*kappiyakāraka*) if questioned. Therefore, it is said, “*Sace hi*” etc. 

“*Akappiyavatthuṃ ārabbha*” means concerning unallowable objects such as gold. “By such words of a messenger” means by the messenger’s words such as “May the venerable one accept the robe-fund.” Because such acceptance is unallowable, it is said “*tasmā*” (therefore).

“*Suvaṇṇa*” means gold. “*Rajata*” means silver. “*Kahāpaṇa*” means a coin made of gold, silver, or an ordinary coin. “*Māsaka*” means whether it be made of copper, wood, or lac; whatever is in use as currency in various regions at various times, including even those made of bone, leather, or the seeds and kernels of fruits, whether they are stamped with a figure or not—all are to be understood here as “*māsaka*.” The decision (*vinicchaya*) that should be stated here, I shall state in the Training Rule on Silver (*Rūpiya Sikkhāpada*).

“*Muttā*” (pearls) refers to the eight kinds of pearls, such as those originating from the frontal bone of an elephant. Indeed, there are eight origins of pearls: the elephant’s frontal bone, a boar’s tusk, a serpent’s head, a cloud, bamboo, a fish’s head, a conch shell, and an oyster. Among those eight, the pearls originating from fish, conch shells, and oysters are from the sea. Some pearls originating from serpents are also from the sea. The remaining pearls are not from the sea. However, because pearls from the sea are most commonly seen in the world, and among those, pearls from oysters are the most frequent while others are only occasional, it is said in the *Sammohavinodanī* Commentary: “*Muttā* means sea-pearls.”

“*Maṇi*” (gems) means, excluding beryl (*veḷuriya*) and so on, everything from high-quality crystal (*jātiphalika*) down to all the various colors such as blue and yellow; all are to be understood as “*maṇi*.” However, only the glass bead (*kācamaṇi*) made by firing (baking) is allowable to be accepted as the price for requisites such as a bowl. “*Veḷuriya*” is a gem the color of bamboo (beryl). “*Saṅkha*” means a conch shell for blowing that has been washed, bored, and inlaid with jewels.
311:
A drinking conch shell mixed with gems is allowable to be accepted for the purpose of medicine such as collyrium, or for the cost of requisites such as alms-bowls. A stone that is washed, pierced, associated with gems, and has the color of a green bean is called a silā stone. However, a stone not mixed with gems is allowable to be accepted for purposes such as a whetstone. In this context, teachers say that "associated with gems" means a stone made by mixing and cooking it with gold. Coral (or amber), whether washed or unwashed, is all called pavāḷa. Lohitanka refers to a red ruby. Masāragalla is a variegated gem, also called marakata (emerald).

The seven kinds of grain, such as hill rice, are called sattadhanya (seven grains). Since secondary grains like nīvāra are included within the primary grains like hill rice, they are referred to as the "seven grains." Among female servants (dāsī), male servants (dāsa), fields, sites, flower gardens, orchards, etc., a dāsī refers to those born in the house, those purchased, those brought from war, and so on. A dāsa is the same. A field (khetta) is a place where grain is grown. A site (vatthu) is a place where various beans are grown. Alternatively, a place where both can be grown is called a field, and a plot of land not yet prepared for such cultivation is called a site. In this context, the terms field and site also include reservoirs, ponds, tanks, and so on. A garden where flowers like jasmine bloom is called a flower garden (pupphārāma). A garden where fruits like mangoes grow is called an orchard (phalārāma). It is not only unallowable to accept [gold and silver] for oneself; even if someone brings gold and silver and says, "I give this to the Saṅgha; please build a monastery, or a stupa, or a dining hall, etc.," it is still not allowable to accept it. It is stated in the Mahāpaccariya that a monk who accepts it for the sake of anyone else commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Therefore, it is said, "It is not allowable to accept it for the sake of a stupa (cetiya), the Saṅgha, a group (gaṇa), or an individual (puggala)."

However, if they do not refer to the Saṅgha, a group, or an individual, but say, "We give this gold and silver for the stupa, for the monastery, or for new construction (navakamma)," it should not be rejected. One should inform the attendants (kappiyakārakas), "These people are saying this." But if they say, "You take and keep it for the stupa, etc.," one must reject it, saying, "It is not allowable for us to take it."

A veyyāvaccakara is one who performs duties. In this context, since it refers to one who performs all duties, it is called a kappiyakāraka. One should point out [the attendant] in his absence, saying, "In such a street, in such a house, the person named so-and-so [is the attendant]." Speaking to that person pointed out in his absence (if one needs clothing), saying, "Friend, I have need of a robe," is an indication of the nature of a request. In that context, "indication of the nature of a request" means...
312:
...it is an indication of the nature of a request by speech. Therefore, [the Buddha] said "If indeed..." (sace hi) and so on. This sentence, "Friend, I have need of a robe," or the meaning of this sentence, may be spoken in any language; this is how it should be understood. However, these words, "Give me a robe," "Bring me a robe," "Exchange a robe for me," "Buy a robe for me," or the meaning of these words, must not be spoken in any language. Therefore, [the Buddha] said "Give me..." (dehi me) and so on. "Should accomplish" (sādheyya) means it should be produced. "This is good" (iccetaṃ kusalaṃ) means that if the robe is produced by requesting up to three times in this manner, it is good, excellent, and proper. Therefore, [the Buddha] said "This is excellent" (etaṃ sundaraṃ).

Since six times is the maximum limit, it is called "six times at most" (chakkhattuparamaṃ). This word is a modifier of the verb "should stand" (ṭhātabbaṃ), meaning one should perform the act of standing for a limit of six times. Therefore, it is said to be an "impersonal neuter usage" (bhāvanapuṃsakavacana). This means that in accomplishing the mere meaning of the root expressed as "should stand" in an abstract sense, it is in the neuter gender and singular number. "Should not sit" means that even if invited, "Venerable sir, please sit here," one should not sit. "Should not accept material things" means that even if entreated with any material thing such as congee or snacks, saying "Venerable sir, please accept," one should not accept. "Dhamma should not be preached" means that even if entreated, "Please preach a discourse on blessings (maṅgala) or a word of appreciation (anumodanā)," nothing should be preached.

"Destroys the standing" means ruining the act of standing. In truth, a monk who has come and is standing to receive a robe should only stand in silence, intending that robe; he should not perform acts such as sitting. However, if this monk performs such acts as sitting, he is said to destroy the standing. Therefore, it is said, "He destroys the reason for his coming." "The reason for coming is indeed the standing; therefore, because he does what is forbidden, such as sitting, he destroys one of the six instances of standing"—this is the intention here. One should stand in silence, intending [the robe], for six times at most. "Nothing else should be done" is the very characteristic of the standing. For this reason, [the Buddha] said "This" (idaṃ) and so on. In that context, "this" refers to the statement: "One should stand in silence, intending [the robe], for four, five, or six times at most." Here, some say, "If one sits or performs other acts, one can no longer receive the robe." Others say, "Two instances of standing are lost." Still others say, "One instance of standing is lost." "Does both" means he both requests and stands.

The phrase "stands in various places" is said in reference only to standing for the sake of the robe in various places, after moving from the place where the requesting monk had been standing. "In this" means in these two places of requesting and standing.
313:
If it is asked whether one should act in this way towards all stewards (kappiyakārakas), the answer is that one should not. In truth, these stewards are of two types in brief: those who are designated (niddiṭṭha) and those who are not designated (aniddiṭṭha). Among those two, the designated ones are of two types: those designated by the monk and those designated by the messenger. The non-designated ones are also of two types: the spontaneous steward (mukhavēvaṭika) and the steward in absence (parammukha). Among them, the one designated by the monk is of four types according to being in the presence (sammukhā) or not in the presence (asammukhā); likewise, the one designated by the messenger is also of four types.

How? In this world, a certain person sends an unallowable object (money) through a messenger for the sake of a monk's robe. That messenger approaches the monk and says, 'Venerable sir, this object has been sent by so-and-so for your robe; please accept it.' The monk refuses, saying, 'This object is not allowable.' The messenger asks, 'Venerable sir, do you have a steward (veyyāvaccakara)?' At that time, there may be certain stewards who have been instructed by merit-seeking lay followers to 'perform services for the monks,' or who are close acquaintances of the monks. If one of them is sitting near the monk at that moment, the monk points him out, saying, 'This person is a steward for the monks.' The messenger hands the unallowable object to that person, says, 'Buy a robe and offer it to the Elder,' and leaves. This person is called one designated by the monk in his presence (sammukhāniddiṭṭha).

If no one is sitting near the monk, but the monk points out, 'In such-and-such a village, so-and-so is a steward for the monks.' The messenger goes, hands the unallowable object to that person, says, 'Buy a robe and offer it to the Elder,' then returns to the monk, informs him, and leaves. This is the first type of one designated by the monk not in his presence (asammukhāniddiṭṭha).

If the messenger does not come and inform the monk himself, but sends someone else to say, 'Venerable sir, I have handed the robe-fund to that person; please accept the robe.' This is the second type designated by the monk not in his presence.

If he does not send anyone else, but while about to leave, he says to the monk, 'I will give the robe-fund to that person; please accept the robe.' This is the third type designated by the monk not in his presence. Thus, there is one designated in the presence and three designated not in the presence; these four are called stewards designated by the monk. Regarding them, one should act according to the method stated in this Rāja Sikkhāpada.
314:
Another monk, when asked by a messenger as in the previous method, says, 'We have no steward,' either because there is none or because he does not wish to investigate. At that moment, a person arrives. The messenger gives the unallowable object (gold or silver) into that person's hand, says, 'Please accept a robe from this person's hand,' and leaves. This person is called one designated by the messenger in the presence (sammukhāniddiṭṭha).

Another messenger enters a village, gives the unallowable object to someone he likes, and then, as in the previous method, either comes and informs the monk, or sends someone else, or says, 'I will give the robe-fund to so-and-so; you should accept the robe,' and leaves. This person is called the third type designated by the messenger not in the presence (asammukhāniddiṭṭha). Thus, with one designated in the presence and three designated not in the presence, these four are called stewards designated by the messenger (dūtena niddiṭṭha-veyyāvaccakara). Regarding them, one should act according to the method stated in the Meṇḍaka Sikkhāpada.

For it has been said:
'Monks, there are people of faith and confidence. They deposit gold in the hands of stewards, saying, "With this, give the monk whatever is allowable." Monks, I allow you to accept what is allowable from that. But, monks, I do not say that gold and silver are to be accepted or sought after in any way whatsoever.'

In this matter, there is no limit to the number of times one may prompt (codanā). For a monk who does not accept the original fund, it is proper to accept the allowable item even if he has to prompt or stand for it a thousand times. If the steward does not give it, he should have it brought even by appointing another steward. If he wishes, he should inform the original donors. If he does not wish, he need not inform them.

Another monk, when asked by a messenger as in the previous method, says, 'We have no steward.' Someone else standing nearby hears this and says, 'Friend, bring it; I will buy a robe for the Venerable one and offer it.' The messenger says, 'Here, friend, please give it,' and hands it to that person, then leaves without informing the monk. This person is called a spontaneous steward (mukhavēvaṭika kappiyakāraka).

Another messenger (Samantapāsādikā Vol. 2, 538-539; Vinayasaṅgaha-aṭṭhakathā 65) gives the unallowable object to a monk's attendant or someone else, says, 'Give a robe to the Elder,' and departs from that place. This person is...
315:
These two, known as the absent steward (parammukhakappiyakāraka) and the unspecified steward (aniddiṭṭhakappiyakāraka), are called unspecified stewards. One should conduct oneself towards them as one would towards those who are not relatives and have not made an invitation.

If they themselves bring and offer a robe, it should be accepted. If they do not offer it, nothing should be said to them. Therefore, it is said, "If..." etc. "Kappiyakārake" refers to the four types of stewards by way of being present or absent. By the words "The donor himself...", the monk is excluded, but not the messenger. Therefore, it is allowable to request as desired from the four types of stewards pointed out by a messenger. One who has opened their mouth and become a steward of their own accord is called a mukhavevaṭikakappiyakāraka. "Evaṃ" (thus) means it is shown in brief in the manner already stated, such as "This indeed..." etc.

"Vuttacodanāṭṭhānaparimāṇato" means from the stated extent of requesting and the stated extent of standing. "Santikaṃ" means near (samīpa). Regarding the word "tattha", one might ask how this sense of proximity (samīpādhāra) is obtained; therefore, it is said, "This locative case (sattami-vibhatti) occurs in the sense of proximity." This means: just as in examples like "Cattle graze at the Ganges" or "The Gaggakūla bank is at the well," because this locative case is used for proximity (samīpādhāra), this meaning is obtained. "One who does not do so" refers to a monk who neither goes himself nor sends a messenger.

"Venerable sir, wait for just this one day" means "Venerable sir, stay for us for this one day, please endure it." "Tikapācittiyaṃ" means the three Pācittiyas occurring by way of a monk who perceives it as more, is doubtful, or perceives it as less, in regard to exceeding the limits of requesting and standing. There is no offense if it is obtained by requesting three times and standing six times, or by requesting less than three times and standing less than six times. "Appitatā" means the state of being established (patiṭṭhāpitatā), the state of having spoken with words such as "I have instructed that person," etc.
