## The Explanation of the Royal Training Rule is finished.
## The First Chapter on Robes.
316:
## 2. Eḷakaloma-vagga
## 1. Commentary on the Silk Training Rule
Kosiyamissaka means silk (kosiya) produced from the cocoons of insects known as "silk-makers" (kosakāraka), and a rug mixed with that silk is kosiyamissaka. Even if mixed with only a small amount of that silk, it is still kosiyamissaka; it cannot be said that this is negligible. Therefore, it is said, "Even with one..." etc. Kosiyāṃsunā means with a thread produced from a cocoon. The words "Even at minimum..." etc., are stated because this training rule is acittaka (without regard to intention), meaning an offense can be committed even without the intention to transgress. A santhata (rug) is something made by spreading out and is non-woven (avāyima). Therefore, it is said, "On a level piece of ground..." etc. "According to the sequence of these words" means according to the words explaining the method of forfeiting this first rug. Sabbasanthata refers to the method of forfeiting the entire rug.

Because there is a dukkaṭa offense if one has it made for the sake of another, it is said "sāṇattika" (one who gives an order) by way of having it made for one's own sake. By the method of finishing what was begun by oneself: "If one finishes by oneself what was begun by oneself, it is a Nissaggiya Pācittiya. If one has others finish what was begun by oneself, it is a Nissaggiya Pācittiya. If one finishes by oneself what was begun by others, it is a Nissaggiya Pācittiya. If one has others finish what was begun by others, it is a Nissaggiya Pācittiya"—this is how it should be understood. There is no offense in making a ceiling, a floor covering, a cloth screen, a curtain, a bolster, or a pillow. Just as in making a ceiling etc., there is no offense in using it with the perception of it being a ceiling etc. Since it is stated as "non-woven" (avāyima), there is no offense for one who makes it by weaving.

## The Explanation of the Silk Training Rule is finished.
## 2. Commentary on the Pure Black Wool Training Rule
Kāḷakānaṃ means sheep's wool that is black either by nature or by dyeing. As the Blessed One said: "Black means there are two kinds of black: naturally black or dyed black." Aññehi amissitānaṃ means black wool unmixed with others such as white wool. Just as it was said in the first training rule, "even with a single silk thread," so too...
317:
In this training rule as well, because [the Buddha] did not directly state 'without mixing with even a single other [hair],' the teachers of the Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā say: 'Even when mixed with other wool, if the non-black form is not apparent, it is called "pure black" (suddhakāḷaka).'

In this training rule, the procedure for forfeiture should be understood by the words: 'Venerable Sir, this rug of mine was made with pure black sheep's wool...' and so forth. The remaining text refers to the dukkaṭa of preliminary effort, the four pācittiyas, and so on. Among the factors, the specific point is 'being pure black.'

## The Explanation of the Suddhakāḷaka Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 3. Explanation of the Dvebhāga Sikkhāpada

'Should be taken' means they should be taken in such a way that the black wool does not exceed [the limit]. Here, it should be understood that apart from black and white wool, the remaining wool is included under 'mottled' (gocariya) wool. In this training rule, 'two parts' is the upper limit (ukkaṭṭhapariccheda) because the training rule was laid down to prohibit taking an excess of black wool. Therefore, exceeding two parts of black wool is not allowable; having less is allowable. Thus, He said 'even a single hair' and so forth. 'Even if there is an excess of a single black hair' means that among the wool that has been weighed, if there is an excess of even a single black hair, even one brought by the force of the wind, [it is nissaggiya]. 'One-third white, one-fourth mottled'—this statement is the lower limit (heṭṭhimapariccheda) because there is no prohibition against taking an excess of those types of wool. Therefore, it is allowable even if they exceed the stated amount.

Here too, the procedure for forfeiture should be understood by this method: 'Venerable Sir, without taking [a new rug before six years], I had this rug made by taking two portions of pure black sheep's wool, one portion of white, and one portion of mottled; it is to be forfeited.' Because of making it by taking the stated limits or making it without taking them, there is the performance of what should not be done and the non-performance of what should be done (kiriyākiriya). The remaining text refers to the dukkaṭa of preliminary effort, the four pācittiyas, and so on. The distinction here is: in making it by taking one portion of white and one portion of mottled, or by taking more white and more mottled...
318:
...in making it, or in making it by taking only pure white or only pure mottled wool, there is no offense.

Among the factors, the first factor should be understood as the state of exceeding two parts of black wool. To show that it is not only unallowable to use these three types of rugs without forfeiting them, He said 'But these...' and so forth. By the words 'they are not allowable to be used,' He shows that if one uses them, a dukkaṭa offense is incurred.

## The Explanation of the Dvebhāga Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 4. Explanation of the Chabbassa Sikkhāpada

'Which gives the rug-permission' is the connection [to the sick monk]. To a sick monk who is not at ease without a rug, or who is unable to travel taking the rug with him—to such a sick monk, the rug-permission (santhata-sammuti) is given. As stated in the Word-Analysis (padabhājana), 'Let the Saṅgha hear me, Venerable Sirs, this monk named so-and-so is sick and unable to travel taking his rug...' and so forth, the rug-permission is given by a formal act consisting of a motion and a second (ñattidutiya-kammavācā).

That permission [is effective]. 'Or if [the illness] has subsided and then recurs' means if that illness subsides and then recurs, it is allowable to make [a rug] annually; there is no need for the business of giving permission again. Not only when that same illness recurs, but even if a different illness occurs, he is allowed to make a rug annually wherever he goes. For this reason, it is said in the Samantapāsādikā: 'If, having recovered, he becomes sick again with the original disease, that same protection [from the permission] applies; there is no other business of permission,' said Elder Phussadeva. However, Elder Upatissa said: 'Whether that same disease recurs or another, once the name "sick" is acquired, it is acquired; there is no further business of permission.' The view of Elder Upatissa is stated last.

In this context, the procedure for forfeiture should be understood by this method: 'Venerable Sir, I had this rug made in less than six years without the permission of the monks; it is to be forfeited.' By the words 'The rest is the same as the first,' the rule regarding making it oneself or having others finish it, etc., is extended. The distinction here is: when six years are completed, or...
319:
There is no offense even when more than six years have passed. However, being within six years is a distinct factor among the components.

## The Commentary on the Chabbassa Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 5. Commentary on the Nisīdana Sikkhāpada

A sitting rug (nisīdana-santhata) refers to a rug with a border or fringe, as it is stated in the Word-for-Word Analysis (Padabhājanī) of this training rule: "Nisīdana means a rug with a border." The use of the name "nisīdana" in this training rule is for the purpose of preventing the perception of it being a robe (cīvara) in relation to the rug. This is because those monks, with the perception that it was a woollen robe, discarded the rug and undertook the ascetic practices (dhutaṅgas). Since a rug has the purpose of being a place for lying and sitting (sayanāsana), it is stated as "what is called an old rug," and so forth.

"Yattha" means in which rug. "Vidatthimatta" means the measure of a span of the Sugata. This measure of one span is the maximum limit. This is because it is stated in the Word-for-Word Analysis: "If one cannot obtain it, there is no offense if one takes a smaller measure and makes it." "Ekadese" means in one part of the new rug that is currently being made. "Vijaṭetvā" means having destroyed or unraveled. "Anādā" is a designation formed by the elision of the letter "ya". Therefore, it means "not taking it even though an old rug exists."

In this training rule, the procedure for forfeiture (nissajjana) should be understood in this manner: "Venerable Sir, this sitting rug of mine, made without taking a Sugata’s span from an old rug, is to be forfeited (nissaggiya)." Seeing the rugs scattered about, the Blessed One thought, "There is no reason for the destruction of gifts given out of faith; I shall show them the method of using them," and thus He laid down the rule in the matter of the disposal of rugs. Since this training rule involves both action and non-action (kiriyā-akiriya)—doing what should not be done and not doing what should be done—it is stated that "the remaining points are the same as the third training rule (Dvebhāga Sikkhāpada)."

The distinction in this training rule is this: there is no offense if one makes it by taking a Sugata’s span from an old rug, or if one cannot obtain that, by taking a smaller measure, or if one cannot obtain it at all, by making it without taking any. Among the components of this training rule, the first component should be understood as not taking a Sugata’s span from an old rug.

## The Commentary on the Nisīdana Sikkhāpada is finished.
320:
## 6. Commentary on the Eḷakaloma Sikkhāpada

"Addhānamagga-paṭipannassa" means one who has set out on a long-distance road. Therefore, it is stated as "known as a long distance (addhāna)," and so forth. Because it is qualified by the word "addhāna," it is called a "long journey." According to the words in the Analysis (Vibhaṅga) of the time of traveling a long distance, "One should eat thinking, 'I will go half a league,'" even half a league (aḍḍhayojana) is considered a long-distance road (addhānamagga). These sheep's wools should not be accepted if they arise elsewhere than on a long-distance road; therefore, referring to the question "addhānamagga-paṭipannassa" etc., He said "sabbañcetaṃ" etc. In that context, "sabbañcetaṃ" refers to all of that, such as "If sheep's wool should arise for a monk who has set out on a long-distance road." "Vatthumattadīpanameva" means it is merely an illustration of the incident, such as "At that time, sheep's wool arose for a certain monk while he was traveling from a district in the Kosala country to Sāvatthī." "Yattha katthaci" means in any place whatsoever without specific designation, other than the long-distance road. "Sahatthā" is in the ablative case in the sense of the instrumental, so it means "with one's own hand." Since this is a characteristic expression (lakkhaṇavacana), it should be understood as carrying with any part of one's body. Therefore, it is said, "The meaning is that they are to be carried by oneself." In the phrase "asante hārake," because the sense of restriction (avadhāraṇa) is inherent within the meaning, the meaning obtained is "only when there is no carrier," and so forth.

In this training rule, the procedure for forfeiture should be understood as: "Venerable Sir, these sheep's wools of mine have been carried beyond three leagues; they are to be forfeited," and so forth. "Tikapācittiyaṃ" means three pācittiya offenses based on the perception of it being more than three leagues when it is more, being in doubt, or the perception of it being less. "Vāsādhippāyena gantvā tato paraṃ haraṇe" means if, having gone to a place with the intention of staying, one carries it further because of not obtaining instruction and interrogation (uddesa-paripucchā) or the four requisites, and then carries it further again, there is no offense even if one carries it for a hundred leagues. "Acchinnaṃ vā nissaṭṭhaṃ vā" means either taken by thieves or forfeited through a disciplinary act. "Katabhaṇḍaṃ" means any finished article such as a blanket, a rug, or a mat, even if it is merely tied with a thread. Therefore, it is said "antamaso" (at the minimum), and so forth. If a monk, for the purpose of protecting from rust, puts wool inside a thin bowl-bag, or between the straps of a carrying-frame, a shoulder-strap, or a waistband, or inside a razor-case for items like a nail-cutter, or finally, even in the ear-hole due to an ailment caused by wind...
321:
If one goes [carrying wool] between the bowl and its bag, or between the āyogapaṭṭa (binding strap), the strap of the bowl-bag (also called a shoulder-slung bag), the waist-belt, etc.; or inside a razor case to prevent a nail-cutter etc. from rusting; or finally, if one goes with wool in the ear-hole due to an earache—for that monk, there is only an offense of nissaggiya (forfeiture). Apart from cases where an offense is committed, I shall mention cases where it is not. Wool that is tied with a thread and placed inside a bag etc. is considered to be in a storage place. If one makes a bundle and carries the wool, this is called carrying it as a bundle for storage, and thus there is only an offense.

Paṭhamappaṭilābha (first acquisition) means the first occurrence of sheep's wool for one's own sake. By this term, wool recovered from thieves or wool that was forfeited through a Vinaya procedure and then regained is excluded. 'Aññassa ajānantassa yāne pakkhipitvā' (placing it in another's vehicle without their knowledge) refers to placing it on a moving carriage etc., or on the back of an elephant etc., without the owner's knowledge, with the intention that 'it will be carried.' The same applies to a vehicle that is not moving. However, if one places it on a stationary carriage or elephant's back etc., and then mounts and drives it oneself, or follows it from below and drives it, or calls out and has it follow, according to the Buddha's words 'having another carry it,' there is no offense. Here, by the phrase 'ajānantassa yāne,' it is shown that if one places wool in the vehicle of an owner who knows, it is considered 'having another carry it.' Aharana-paccāharaṇa (carrying and bringing back) means the absence of carrying it for three yojanas going and three yojanas returning.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Sheep's Wool is finished.

## 7. Explanation of the Training Rule on Having Sheep's Wool Washed

'Sakkesu' (among the Sakyans): Based on the inspired utterance 'Indeed, sirs, the princes are capable,' the region where the princes and princesses named 'Sakya' reside is called 'Sakka' by common usage (ruḷhī), even though it is a single district; it means in that district of the Sakyans. Chabbaggiya (the group of six) refers to the six original teachers such as Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka, and their disciples.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Having Sheep's Wool Washed is finished.

## 8. Explanation of the Training Rule on Gold and Silver

'Rajata' (silver) here does not only mean silver coins stamped with an image (rūpiya), but also refers to the kahāpaṇa (coins) etc. used in trade, as stated by the words 'Moreover' (api ca) etc. In that context, kahāpaṇa means a coin made of gold, a coin made of silver, or a common coin used by ordinary people. Lohamāsaka (copper māsaka) is a māsaka made of copper, iron, etc. Dārumāsaka (wooden māsaka) is a māsaka made by cutting an image on heartwood, or on a bamboo strip, or even on a palmyra leaf.
322:
...or at the very least, a māsaka made by cutting an image on a palmyra leaf. Jatumāsaka (lacquer māsaka) is a māsaka made by forming an image with lac or resin. By the phrase 'whatever things are used in trade,' it includes every object that is used for trade in various districts at various times—at the very least, those made of bone, leather, or fruit seeds/kernels, whether they have a stamped image or not. 'That very thing' (tad eva) refers only to gold and silver. Hirañña means a coin (kahāpaṇa).

By the word 'consents' (sādiyati), the meaning 'desires to take' is clarified. It is not only when it is rejected by body and speech that it is rejected; even when it is rejected by the mind, it is indeed rejected. Thus, it is said 'by body and speech' etc. However, if one does not reject it by body or speech but accepts it in the mind, because the rejection that should be done by body and speech is not done, an offense is committed through the doors of body and speech by way of non-action (akiriyasamuṭṭhāna). In the mind-door, however, there is no such thing as an offense.

A person places a hundred or a thousand coins at [a monk's] feet, saying, 'May this be for you, venerable sir.' The monk rejects it, saying, 'This is not allowable.' The lay follower says, 'I have relinquished it for you,' and leaves. Another person arrives at that place and asks, 'Venerable sir, what is this?' One should explain what was said by that donor and oneself. If that person says, 'Venerable sir, I will look after it; please show me a secure place,' one should go up even to a seven-storied palace and say, 'This is a secure place.' One should not say, 'Place it here.' By doing this much, it remains dependent on what is allowable and what is unallowable. One should live there, closing the door and guarding it. If some trade goods arrive, such as a bowl or a robe, and [the person] asks, 'Venerable sir, will you take this?' one should say, 'Lay follower, we have a need for this; such an object exists, but there is no one to make it allowable (kappiyakāraka).' If that person says, 'I will be the one who makes it allowable; please open the door,' one should open the door and say, 'It is placed in this spot.' One should not say, 'Take this.' By speaking in this way, it remains dependent on what is allowable and what is unallowable. If that person takes that [money] and gives the monk an allowable requisite, it is proper. If he takes more [than the value], he should be told, 'We no longer wish to take your goods; please leave.'
323:
"It should be forfeited only in the midst of the Saṅgha": In this phrase, because gold and silver (rūpiya) are unallowable, the Buddha did not say, "It should be forfeited to the Saṅgha, or to a group, or to an individual." However, because the gold and silver have only been received and no allowable goods (kappiya-bhaṇḍa) have yet been purchased with them, it was said, "It should be forfeited only in the midst of the Saṅgha," for the purpose of showing the use through skillful means. By the word "ādi" (etc.), oil and so forth should be included. "That person" refers to a householder (gahaṭṭha) who is addressed in such a way as, "Lay follower, ghee or oil is allowable." "Obtained through another" means obtained by a monk or a monastery attendant (ārāmika) through their own turn of distribution.

"The shade of a tree produced from that as well" means the shade that stays within the extent of a tree produced from seeds brought with the forfeited object (gold/silver) [is unallowable]; however, the shade that exceeds the extent of the tree is allowable because it is incidental (āgantuka).

"If he does not discard it" means he neither takes it nor discards it, but thinking, "What benefit is there for me in this business?" he goes wherever he wishes. "One endowed with five qualities" refers to a monk endowed with the five qualities as stated: "One who would not go by way of favoritism, would not go by way of hatred, would not go by way of delusion, would not go by way of fear, and would know what is discarded and what is not discarded." "Should be appointed" means he should be appointed by a formal act consisting of a motion and a second (ñattidutiya-kammavācā) as stated in the Word-Analysis (Padabhājana): "Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs. If it is the right time for the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should appoint the monk named so-and-so as the discarder of money (rūpiyachaḍḍaka)."

"It should be discarded like dung without making a sign" means it should be discarded like dung without making a sign by marking the place where it falls. It means that with eyes closed, it should be dropped into a river, or a precipice, or a forest thicket, like dung, without looking back and without attending to the place where it falls. Therefore, it was said, "It should be discarded like dung." "Tika-pācittiya" (the triad of Pācittiya) means there are three Pācittiya offenses by way of: one who perceives it as money, one who is doubtful, and one who perceives it as not money. "One who perceives as money in what is not money" refers to a monk who has the perception of gold, etc., in things like copper plates (kharapatta), etc. "By the method of the Ratana Sikkhāpada" means according to the procedure stated in the rule: "Whether in a monastery or in a dwelling."

## The Explanation of the Jātarūpa Sikkhāpada is finished.
324:
"Should be appointed" means he should be appointed by a formal act consisting of a motion and a second (ñattidutiya-kammavācā) as taught by the Buddha in such a way as: "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me. If the matter of discarding money is appropriate for the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should appoint the monk named so-and-so as the discarder of money." "It should be discarded like dung without making a sign" means it should be discarded like dung without marking the place where the discarded money falls. It means that with eyes closed, it should be discarded into a river, or a precipice, or a dense forest or thicket, like dung, without looking back and without attending to the place where it falls. This is why the commentator said, "It should be discarded like dung."

"Tika-pācittiya" means the three kinds of Pācittiya offenses by way of: perceiving as money, being doubtful, and perceiving as not money. "Perceiving as money in what is not money" refers to a monk who has the perception of gold, etc., in things like copper plates (kharapatta), etc. "According to the method of the Ratana Sikkhāpada" means according to the procedure taught in the training rule: "Whether inside a monastery or inside a dwelling," and so forth. The explanation of the Jātarūpa Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 9. Rūpiyasaṃvohāra Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
"By way of 'made' etc." means by way of made, unmade, or both made and unmade. The four kinds of objects, such as gold, are also included here under the term "rūpiya" (money). Therefore, it is said, "the exchange of gold and silver." This should be understood as being stated by defining the highest limit. Therefore, it is said, "By the previous training rule..." and so forth. "Exchange" means the exchange of money that has been accepted. According to the previous method: "Venerable sirs, I have engaged in various kinds of trading with money. This is to be forfeited by me," and so forth.

Since the act of receiving itself is already prohibited, without looking at the fault in the exchange of what has been received, but looking at the fault in the trading of money, it is said, "in the matter of trading with money (rūpiyasaṃvohāra-vatthu)." "Of that [exchanged object] also" or "of one's own original wealth." Indeed, whether one causes another's money to be purchased with one's own non-money object, or causes another's non-money object to be purchased with one's own money, in both ways, it is considered as having engaged in trading with money (rūpiyasaṃvohāra).

## The Explanation of the Rūpiyasaṃvohāra Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 10. Kayavikkayasikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
Since trading with money is included in the training rule below (previous rule), in this training rule, only allowable goods (kappiya-bhaṇḍa) should be included. Therefore, it is said, "robes and so forth." Among those allowable goods such as robes, it includes all allowable goods without exception, from at least a fringe thread to the four requisites: robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal rejuvenants. "Buying" (kaya) means taking another's goods. "Selling" (vikkaya) means giving one's own goods. Therefore, it is said, "Give this for this," and so forth. "To another" means to someone other than the five classes of co-religionists. In this training rule also, it should be forfeited in this manner: "Venerable sirs, I have engaged in various kinds of buying and selling. This allowable good is to be forfeited by me. I forfeit this allowable good to the Saṅgha," and so forth. Therefore, it is said, "by way of the stated characteristics."

Is it not so that in cases of new work such as washing robes, cutting hair, or clearing the ground, there is no object belonging to another that has come into one's hands to be forfeited? If asked what should be done in such a case, it is said, "If there is no [object], one should simply confess the Pācittiya offense." Just as one confesses a Pācittiya offense when a forfeited object has been used or lost, so too here, the meaning is that one should simply confess. "This is our property" refers to this oil or this ghee that has been formally offered...
325:
In the statement 'This oil or this ghee belongs to us,' it means this oil or ghee that has been formally accepted is in our possession. In the statement 'We have need of this and that,' it means we have need of these things which have not yet been formally accepted, other than the oil and ghee that have already been accepted. By the phrase 'In the same manner as stated in the Rūpiya-saṃvohāra (Trading with Money),' he points out the method: 'In the Tika-pācittiya (Pācittiya involving triads), an offense of Dukkaṭa (wrongdoing) is incurred by a bhikkhu who perceives what is not a purchase or sale as a purchase or sale, or who is in doubt.'

## Commentary on the Kaya-vikkaya Training Rule is finished.

## The Second Chapter, the Eḷakaloma-vagga, is finished.

## 3. Patta-vagga

## 1. Commentary on the Patta Training Rule

'Avikappita' means a bowl that has not been assigned through the method beginning with 'I assign this bowl to you.' 'Takes a half-āḷhaka of boiled rice' means it takes (contains) boiled rice made from two Magadhan nāḷis of raw rice. It is stated in the Andhaka Commentary that 'A Magadhan nāḷi is the measure of twelve and a half palas.' It is stated in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā that 'In the island of Sīhaḷa (Sri Lanka), the natural nāḷi is large, the Tamil nāḷi is small, and the Magadhan nāḷi is of moderate size; one and a half Magadhan nāḷis are equal to one Sīhaḷa nāḷi.' 'Anuttaṇḍula': during cooking, a grain of rice that rises to the top is called uttaṇḍula; anuttaṇḍula refers to that which is not such a grain (i.e., not yet fully cooked). 'Sabbasaṃbhārasaṅkhata' means well-prepared with all ingredients such as cumin (jīraka) and other spices. A portion of curry equal to one-fourth of a mouthful of rice is called a suitable curry (vyañjana) for a mouthful.

Having shown the Ukkaṭṭha (large) bowl in this way, he now spoke the words beginning with 'Ukkaṭṭhato' to show the Majjhima (medium) and Omaka (small) bowls. In this regard, the method is as follows: If, when all the rice made from one nāḷi and so on is put in, it remains level with the lower rim (heṭṭhima-rāji) according to the stated method, this bowl is called a Majjhima (medium) bowl. If it exceeds that lower rim and remains heaped (thūpīkata), this bowl is called a Majjhima-omaka (the small among the medium) bowl. If it does not reach that lower rim and remains only inside, this bowl is called a Majjhima-ukkaṭṭha (the large among the medium) bowl. If, when all the rice and so on is put in the bowl, it remains level with the lower rim, this bowl is called an Omaka (small) bowl. If it exceeds that lower rim and remains heaped, this bowl is called an Omaka-omaka (the small among the small) bowl. If that...

## 2. Ūnapañcabandhanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

'Assa' means 'of this bowl'. 'Tena ūnapañcabandhanena' means 'being marked by that bowl which has fewer than five ties'. In fact, in this training rule, a bowl with fewer than five ties is taken as the mark (lakkhaṇa). Therefore, it is said: 'The instrumental case is applied in the sense of a mark of such a state (itthambhūta)'. In that phrase, 'itthambhūtassa' refers to one who has reached a certain specific state (the state of a monk who possesses a bowl with fewer than five ties). Because it is marked by this bowl, it is called 'lakkhaṇa' (mark); it means the instrumental case (tatiyā vibhatti) is applied in that sense of a mark. 'Pakāra' (mode) refers to a specific distinction that differentiates from the general (sāmañña). This is indeed true; in the phrase 'ūnapañcabandhanena pattena', the state of being a monk is the general (sāmañña), and the state of having a bowl with fewer than five ties is the specific mode (pakāra). The monk has reached that specific mode, and for that monk, the bowl is the mark (lakkhaṇa).

If a bowl with fewer than five ties is called 'ūnapañcabandhana', why does the word-analysis (padabhājanīya) of this term also mention a bowl without ties (abandhana)? To answer this, it says 'Tattha' and so forth. In that context, 'Tattha' is an introduction to the sentence. Whether there is a place for a tie or not, a bowl devoid of ties is called 'abandhana'. A bowl that has places for five ties is called 'pañcabandhanokāsa'. 'Apatta' means it no longer deserves to be called a bowl, meaning it is incapable of being used in its original natural state. This statement is a reason for informing others. Therefore, it is said: 'Therefore, it is proper to ask from another'.

Since a tie exists only when there is a place for it and cannot exist if there is no place, to show its characteristic and the method of tying, it says 'Yasmiṃ pana' and so forth. If one pierces with a bowl-borer near the rim, the bowl-shell tends to break because of its thickness; therefore, it should be pierced only at the bottom. Thus it says 'at the lower edge' and so forth. Or, a small hole should be made and tied; the meaning is that in a small hole, there is no need for patching with lead sheets and so on, but it should be determined (adhiṭṭhāna) by just inserting a thread. It is not only tied with lead, thread, and so on; it also says 'phāṇita' (molasses) and so forth. 'Phāṇitaṃ jhāpetvā pāsāṇacuṇṇena' means boiling molasses with stone powder and (patching) with that boiled stone powder. 'Nissajjitabbo' means it should be forfeited by saying: 'Venerable Sir, this bowl of mine, having been obtained in exchange for a bowl with fewer than five ties, is to be forfeited; I forfeit this bowl to the Saṅgha.' Therefore, it says 'Nissajjantena' and so forth. 'Sammatena' means—

'Venerable Sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. If it is the right time for the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha appoint the monk named so-and-so as the receiver of the bowl. This is...'
329:
The name 'bhesajja' (medicine) is a designation for all suitable medicines. Therefore, it is said: 'Whether they perform the function of medicine or not, they acquire such a designation.' Now, to show ghee and fresh butter, which are objects of forfeiture (nissaggiya) to be used within seven days, it is said 'Sappi nāma gavādīnaṃ' and so forth. By the word 'ādi' (and so forth), she-goats and others should be included. By the phrase 'yeseṃ maṃsaṃ kappati' (those whose meat is allowable), other animals such as deer and elk are also included, besides the well-known cows and she-goats. For whichever creatures have milk, they also have ghee. Whether that milk and ghee are easy or difficult to obtain, this statement is made to avoid confusion. Only honey produced by the three types of flies known as small bees, large bees, and honey-flies is called 'madhu' (honey). Sugarcane juice (ucchurasa) refers to both pure sugarcane juice and sugarcane juice mixed with water. Since it was allowed by referring to it as 'molasses-water is allowed for one who is not ill,' sugarcane juice mixed with water is allowable for one who is not ill. By the phrase 'avavatthukapakka vā,' it is shown that a special sugarcane preparation cooked together with the sugarcane dregs is not allowable. However, in the Mahāpaccariya, the question was raised: 'Is this molasses cooked with the dregs allowable or not?' and it was stated: 'There is no such thing as sugarcane molasses that is not allowable in the afternoon.' It is stated in the Samantapāsādikā that this statement is appropriate. Special sugarcane products (ucchuvikati) refer to the juice, resin, etc., derived from sugarcane. Since the word 'taṃ' refers back to the previously mentioned meanings, only the medicines already mentioned should be taken, and not the raw materials of those medicines; thus it is said 'tāni bhesajjāni' and so forth. 'Not taking the raw materials of those medicines' means not receiving the milk, etc., which are the causes of that ghee, etc.

Fat-oil (vasātela) refers to the oil of the fats allowed as follows: 'Bhikkhus, I allow fats as medicine: bear's fat, fish's fat, porpoise's fat, pork fat, and donkey's fat.' The word 'yāni' refers to those medicines. Because the receiving of fat for the purpose of oil was allowed as follows: 'Bhikkhus, I allow fats as medicine: bear's fat, fish's fat, porpoise's fat, pork fat, and donkey's fat, to be received at the right time, cooked at the right time, and strained at the right time, to be consumed as oil,' therefore 'vasātelaṃ pana' and so forth is said. 'Kāle' (at the right time) means in the morning (before the noon meal). 'Saṃsaṭṭha' means strained. 'Tasmā' means because it is allowed. By the word 'acchavasaṃ,' human fat is excluded, and since the fat of all animals with unallowable meat is allowed, it is said 'excluding human fat.'

'Sāmaṃ pacitvā' means cooking it by oneself only in the morning. 'Nibbattitatelampi' means oil that has been extracted by oneself only in the morning. These three actions are allowable only in the morning. It is also said: 'Bhikkhus, if it is received in the morning, cooked in the morning...'
330:
"...if it is strained in the morning, and if one consumes it, there is no offense." However, in the afternoon, it is not allowable either to receive it or to prepare it. Thus it was also said: "Bhikkhus, if it is received in the afternoon, cooked in the afternoon, and strained in the afternoon, and if one consumes it, there is an offense of three dukkaṭas. Bhikkhus, if it is received in the morning, cooked in the afternoon, and strained in the afternoon, and if one consumes it, there is an offense of two dukkaṭas. Bhikkhus, if it is received in the morning, cooked in the morning, and strained in the afternoon, and if one consumes it, there is an offense of one dukkaṭa" (Mahāvagga, 262). By the statement "It is allowable by consumption free from food-material (nirāmisa) for seven days," it is shown that the consumption of fat-oil received, cooked, and strained in the morning as oil refers to consumption free from food-material.

In this fat, if there is meat, sinew, bone, or blood as fine as dust, it is considered negligible (abbhohārika). If an unordained person (anupasampanna) prepares oil from the fat received by that monk and offers it, how is that? To answer this, "anupasampannena" and so forth is said. "Tadahu" refers to the day it was received. From the afternoon onwards, it is allowable for seven days only if it is free from food-material. Even in the oil cooked by an unordained person, the negligible meat, etc., remain negligible. The connection should be made that it is not allowable to cook the raw material of other yāvakālika (temporary/food) items. In that context, "yāvakālikavatthūnaṃ" refers to ghee, etc., which have yāvakālika materials. "Aññesaṃ" refers to ghee, etc., other than fat-oil. "Vatthu" refers to the yāvakālika material such as milk, etc.; the meaning is that it is not allowable to cook it by oneself.

"Nibbattitasappiṃ vā" refers to ghee that has been extracted from yāvakālika materials like milk. It refers to ghee that has been boiled until the curd or buttermilk is exhausted. "Navanītaṃ vā" means that it is allowable to cook fresh butter that has been well-washed, removing buttermilk drops and curd lumps, because it is not considered "self-cooked" (sāmaṃpāka). If one eats food-material (āmisa) such as alms-food together with the seven-day medicine (sattāhakālika) cooked by oneself, that food-material, when mixed with the self-cooked seven-day medicine, causes its own yāvakālika nature to be affected by the seven-day medicine. In that case, even if the yāvakālika item was not cooked by oneself, it is treated as if it were self-cooked; therefore, it is said: "That item is not allowable to be consumed with food-material even in the morning of the day it was received." Just as fat-oil which is a self-cooked seven-day medicine, and oil from life-long (yāvajīvika) items like mustard seeds roasted by oneself, are not allowable even in the morning of the day they were received if they are with food-material, so also should it be understood for self-cooked fresh butter and ghee. It is also said:
331:
'Items such as the temporary (yāvakālika) cause other items like the period-limited (yāmakālika) that are mixed with them to take on their own nature (i.e., become temporary).' 'A lifelong item (yāvajġvika) cooked only with those temporary items is allowable for seven days if it is without food (nirāmisa); if it is with food (sāmisa), it is not allowable [after noon] because it was cooked by oneself.' Thus spoke the Elder named Dhammasiri in the Khuddasikkhā.

In the word 'milk, etc.' (khġrādito), the word 'etc.' (ādi) includes sesame and such items. 'Even those with food' (sāmisāni pi) means it is not only those without food that are allowable (those mixed with food are also allowable). However, they are certainly not allowable starting from the afternoon (pacchābhatta). Even if seven days have passed, there is no offense because they were accepted along with the substance. For it was said [in the Pārājika], 'Having accepted those substances.' Therefore, it is said, 'Starting from the afternoon,' etc. Ghee and such made from milk accepted in the afternoon should be used for anointing and so on; likewise, ghee made from milk whose acceptance has lapsed in the morning (purebhatta). For both types, there is no offense even if seven days have passed. 'Within seven days' (antosattāhe) means within the period of seven days. In the word 'for anointing, etc.' (abbhañjanādġnaṁ), the word 'etc.' (ādi) includes head-oil, smearing on wounds, and fumigating the house. 'Having determined' (adhiṭṭhahitvā) means having produced the thought: 'Now this substance shall not be for the purpose of consumption (eating) for me; this ghee, oil, or fat shall be for the purpose of head-oil or for anointing; this honey shall be for smearing on wounds, or this molasses shall be for fumigating the house.'

Asking what the difference is between temporary (yāvakālika) and lifelong (yāvajġvika) substances in this training rule, he says, 'Lifelong items,' etc. 'It remains until the rising of the dawn' means if the oil made on the seventh day remains until the dawn rises. In the phrase 'ghee not mentioned in the Pali' (anāgata-sappi), first, the ghee of deer, elk, etc., is called ghee not mentioned in the Pali; likewise, the first oil (cream of oil), and the oil of coconut, neem, koshamba, karamanda, mustard, etc., is called oil not mentioned in the Pali; likewise, the molasses of Madhuka flowers is called molasses not mentioned in the Pali. To show that not all Madhuka flower molasses is of the same nature as [regular] molasses, he says, 'Made with cold water,' etc. 'Made with cold water' refers to molasses made by putting Madhuka flowers in cold water without kneading or crushing them, and when the flower juice has entered the water, taking that water and boiling it. 'It is of the same nature as molasses' by this he shows that this molasses has a period of seven days for which it may be kept; he does not mean it is a matter for forfeiture (nissaggiya). Therefore, it should be understood that for a bhikkhu who lets seven days pass, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṩa). This point was also stated in the Samantapāsādikā Commentary: 'Madhuka flower molasses made with cold water is allowable with food in the morning; starting from the afternoon, it is allowable for seven days only without food; if seven days are exceeded, there is an offense of wrongdoing.'
333: ## 4. Commentary on the Training Rule on the Rainy-Season Cloth "From the first day of the last month" means from the first day of the waning moon of the month of Jeᅩᅩha. "That much" means during a period of that extent. It means during these five months from the first day of the waning moon of Jeᅩᅩha until the full moon day of Kattika. In the phrase "the time for the rainy-season cloth" etc., the word "etc." includes these words: "It is the time for the rainy-season cloth; other people also give rainy-season cloths." In the phrase "Give me a rainy-season cloth" etc., the word "etc." includes these words: "Bring me a rainy-season cloth, exchange a rainy-season cloth for me, have a rainy-season cloth bought for me." To the question of what offense is incurred by a bhikkhu who performs both (requesting and having bought) from those who are not relatives and have not given an invitation, the text says: "In a place of non-relatives and those who have not given an invitation" etc. The statement "An offense of wrongdoing is incurred for a breach of conduct" is said with reference to those who have not previously given rainy-season cloths. For those who have given before, there is no breach of conduct. Indeed, it is stated in the Samantapāsādikā Commentary: "Even if those people who have previously given rainy-season cloths are not relatives and have not given an invitation, there is no breach of conduct because it is permitted to remind them." "An offense of forfeiture and confession is incurred through the training rule on requesting from a non-relative" refers to the forfeiture and confession incurred by this training rule: "Should any bhikkhu request a robe from a householder or a householder's wife who is not a relative, except at the proper time, it is an offense of forfeiture and confession." This offense of forfeiture and confession also applies even to regular donors of rainy-season cloths. In the phrase "From the first day of the last half-month of the summer," this half-month from the first day of the waning moon following the Uposatha of the waning moon of Jeᅩᅩha until the full moon of Āsāᄷhĩ is called the last half-month of summer. "From the first day of that half-month" means from the first day of the waning moon, which is the first day of the half-month. The last day of the month of Kattika is the full moon day of the last month of Kattika. "By this much" means by this calculation: "A bhikkhu should seek a rainy-season cloth thinking 'one month of summer remains,' and should wear it thinking 'half a month of summer remains.'" "The field of seeking" means the period for seeking. Within that month, if the rainy-season cloth has not yet been obtained, it is proper to seek it. "The field of making and wearing also" means the period for making and the period for wearing. By the word "also" (pi)...
334: ...the author summarizes the period for seeking (pariyesanakhetta). In that half-month, seeking, making, and wearing the rainy-season cloth are allowable; only determination (adhiᅩᅩhāna) is not allowable. However, the statement found in some manuscripts of the Samantapāsādikā Commentary: "This half-month from the first day of the waning moon of Jeᅩᅩha until the full moon of Āsāᄷhĩ (kālapakkhuposatha) is called the field of seeking and the field of making. In that interval, if the rainy-season cloth is not yet obtained, it is proper to seek it; if obtained, it is proper to make it; but it is not allowable to wear or determine it," should be regarded as a scribal error (pamādalikhita) because it contradicts the Mātikā. For the Pāᄷi of the Mātikā states: "Thinking 'half a month of summer remains,' it should be worn." "All also" means all of seeking, making, wearing, and determining. By this, it is shown that these four months are the period for all four: seeking, making, wearing, and determining. In those four months, it is proper to seek a rainy-season cloth not yet obtained, and to make, wear, and determine one that has been obtained. "The rains is pulled up (vassaᅃ ukkaᄷᄷhĩyati)" means the year is pulled up, increased, or elevated. It means the first month of the rainy season (Āsāᄷha) is pulled up and made the last month of the summer. "It should be determined on the day of entering the rains" means because ten days have already passed before the rainy season, it must be determined on the day of entering the rains itself. It is not allowable to let that day pass. As for a rainy-season cloth obtained and completed during the rains, it must not be kept for more than ten days from the day it was obtained during that rains; if it is completed after ten days, it must be determined on that very day. If ten days are not sufficient, the robe-season must not be exceeded. This is the remedy (parihāra) for a completed cloth. As for the remedy for an uncompleted cloth, the text says "If" etc. The meaning is that not even a single day can be obtained because there is no other remedy besides this ten-day remedy. From when does that remedy begin? The text says: "Until the first day of the winter." It means from the full moon day of Jeᅩᅩha until the first day of the waning moon of Kattika. "In these seven months of the back-season (piᅩᅩhisamaya)" means in these seven months called piᅩᅩhisamaya, stated in reverse order, beginning from the first day of the waning moon of Kattika and ending with the full moon of Jeᅩᅩha. "By causing mindfulness" means by causing mindfulness in the manner of "It is the time for the rainy-season cloth" etc. "To the one who makes his wish known" means...
335:
For a monk who makes a request in the manner of "Give me a rainy-season robe," etc. (Pārā. 628), although there is no offense under that training rule (regarding requests from non-relatives), there is indeed an offense under this training rule because it is not the proper time. For the teacher, Venerable Buddhadatta, said this:

"Having brought about the production of a rainy-season robe, for a monk who completes it at a time designated as the 'back' (outside the proper period),
"There is an offense of Nissaggiya Pācittiya, whether the request is made to relatives or non-relatives, and likewise for completing it after making a request to those very persons."

In this training rule, the procedure for forfeiture (nissajjana) should be understood in this manner: "Venerable sir, this rainy-season robe of mine, sought when more than one month of the summer remained, and worn when more than half a month of the summer remained, is to be forfeited" (Pārā. 628).

In the matter of seeking a rainy-season robe, it should be understood even in advance. "Tika-pācittiyaṃ" means that for those who perceive it as more, have doubt, or perceive it as less than the period of more than one month and more than half a month, three Pācittiya offenses are incurred through the acts of seeking and wearing. This is a designation by ellipsis (ekasesa-niddesa) or a general designation (sāmañña-niddesa). "Ūnakamāsaddhamāsesu" means in a period less than one month and in a period less than half a month. In the phrase "atirekasaññino, vematikassa vā dukkaṭaṃ," the remaining words "for one who performs the seeking and wearing" should be added to complete the sense. This is what is meant: "If one who perceives it as more or has doubt seeks it when less than one month of the summer remains, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). If one who perceives it as more or has doubt wears it when less than half a month of the summer remains, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)."

By the word "tathā," an offense of wrong-doing is indicated. That wrong-doing should be made to be incurred for every effort (payoga) based on the conclusion of the bath, without counting the number of water drops. Furthermore, this applies only to one bathing with rainwater falling from the sky in an open space, not to one bathing with water poured from jars in a bathroom, a tank, etc. Therefore, it was said: "Satiyā vassikasāṭikāya," etc. The connection should be understood as: "for one bathing naked in a lotus pond, etc., there is no offense." The meaning is that even if a rainy-season robe exists, there is no offense of wrong-doing for one bathing naked in a lotus pond and so forth.
336:
Having thus shown the non-offense for intermediate offenses (dukkaṭa), the phrase "acchinnacīvarassa," etc., is now stated to show the non-offense for the Nissaggiya offense. In that context, "acchinnacīvarassa" refers to a monk whose remaining robes have been snatched away by thieves. For such a monk, there is no offense even if he wears it at an improper time. This same method should be understood for a monk whose robes are lost (naṭṭhacīvara). Just as there is no offense for those monks wearing it at such a time, it should be understood that there is likewise no offense for those seeking it at that time.

However, in this context, the harassment by thieves while one has set aside a costly rainy-season robe and is bathing is called an "emergency" (āpadā); thus it is said, "anivatthaṃ," etc. "Āpadāsu vā nivāsayato" refers to a monk wearing it at an improper time when emergencies exist. As for what is stated in the Samantapāsādikā: "The phrase 'acchinnacīvarassa' is said with reference only to the rainy-season robe. For those who are naked, there is no offense in letting the rain wet their bodies. Here too, the harassment by thieves while one is bathing having worn a costly rainy-season robe is called an 'emergency'"—this showing of non-offense only from the dukkaṭa offense for one bathing naked, without showing the non-offense from the Nissaggiya offense for those whose robes were snatched, etc., does not seem appropriate. This is because in all training rules, the section on non-offense (anāpatti-vāra) is begun for the purpose of showing the non-offense where the root offense (mūlāpatti) would otherwise be incurred, and not for intermediate offenses. Therefore, this point should be investigated. "Sacīvaratā" means being with robes by having the undergarment and the upper robe.

## The Commentary on the Rainy-Season Robe Training Rule is Finished.

## 5. Commentary on the Robe Snatching Training Rule

In the word "datvā" (having given), only giving with the expectation of some benefit is intended here, not giving as an absolute relinquishment; thus it is said, "veyyāvaccādīni," etc. By the word "sakasaññāya" (with the perception of it being one's own), the absence of a Pārājika offense is shown. For even if it was given after relinquishing, there is no Pārājika for one who takes it back with the perception that it is his own. For one who snatches many robes that are not bound together or are placed separately, and for one who causes them to be brought by saying, "Bring the outer robe, bring the upper robe," there are offenses according to the number of objects. Therefore, it is said: "vatthugaṇanāya āpattiyo." Even for one who says, "Bring all that I have given," although it is a single statement, many offenses are incurred. However, if one snatches a single robe or many robes that are bound together, there is only one offense. Regarding the command "Snatch it," the wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is incurred; by the command "Take all that I have given," a single dukkaṭa is incurred. When they have been snatched...
337:
Even if the command is given with a single utterance, many Pācittiya offenses are incurred according to the number of objects taken. Therefore, it is said, "Offenses are incurred according to the count of the objects taken." "Acchinnesu" means regarding the robes taken as commanded by that person. In some manuscripts, the reading is "Acchinnesu yattakāni āṇattāni, tesaṃ gaṇanāya āpattiyo," where "yattakāni āṇattāni" means as many robes as were commanded to be taken. In the Samantapāsādikā Commentary, the statement "If one commands 'Take the robe,' there is one dukkaṭa; if the one commanded takes many, there is one pācittiya" refers to a single bundle. Understanding it this way, there is no contradiction between the Samantapāsādikā and this commentary. If one commands, "Take the saṅghāṭi, take the uttarāsaṅga," a dukkaṭa offense is incurred for each word. However, at the time of taking, offenses are incurred according to the number of objects. In this training rule, the procedure for forfeiture should be understood in this way: "Venerable sir, this robe of mine, having been given by myself to a monk and then taken back, is to be forfeited."

"Tika-pācittiya" refers to the three types of pācittiya offenses based on perceiving [the other] as ordained, being in doubt, or perceiving [the other] as not ordained. "Other requisites" refers to other requisites such as a bowl, even down to a needle. It is not only when taking a novice's robe that a dukkaṭa is incurred, but also when taking other requisites; hence it is said, "And of one not ordained," etc. Therein, "yaṃ kiñci" means anything, whether it be a robe or other requisites such as a bowl. "Tassa vissāsaṃ gaṇhantassa" refers to one who takes through the intimacy of the person who gave it; here, the accusative case carries the meaning of the instrumental case. "Upasampannatā" means being ordained at the time of taking back. Although the Pāḷi and the Mātikā Commentary mention being ordained at both the time of giving and the time of taking, since an offense is incurred if one gives a robe while a novice and takes it back after becoming ordained, it should be understood that being ordained at the time of taking back is the [essential] factor.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Taking Back a Robe is Finished.

## 6. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Requesting Thread

"Six kinds of thread such as linen" refers to the six kinds of thread mentioned as: "Thread means six [kinds of] thread: linen, cotton, silk, wool, hemp, and a mixture of these."
338:
Among those (six kinds of thread), "khoma" is thread made from linen fibers. "Kappāsika" is thread produced from cotton. "Koseyya" is thread made by spinning the filaments (silk thread) of silkworms found in cocoons. "Kambala" is thread mixed with wool. "Sāṇa" is thread made from hemp fibers. Some (teachers) say that "bhaṅga" is just one of the aforementioned types of thread. However, it should be understood that "bhaṅga" is thread made by mixing the five kinds: linen, silk, cotton, wool, and hemp. Threads that are "anuloma" (similar) to those such as linen are the six kinds: dukūla thread, bark thread, thread from the Pattu country, thread from the Somāra country, thread from the Cīna country, thread produced by psychic power, and thread given by devas.

"Turī" is a wooden rod used as a weaving implement, the place where the woven parts are rolled and kept (the cloth beam). "Vema" is a wooden rod used as a weaving implement, used to strike the inserted thread to make it dense and compact (the reed/beater). For all the efforts (payoga) of that weaver, such as preparing the cloth beam and the reed, a monk incurs a dukkaṭa offense. This means that for every single effort of the weaver, a monk incurs a dukkaṭa offense. If the turī (cloth beam) and so on are not available, the same principle applies to all efforts such as seeking, sharpening adzes and axes, and felling trees to make them. Since the threads are one's own property, the woven part is already acquired; therefore, [the author of the Saṅgaha] said, "It becomes nissaggiya upon acquisition." This means it becomes nissaggiya when the minimum robe size suitable for assignment (vikappanā) has been woven. For this reason, [the author of the Saṅgaha] will say later, "When a piece one span in length and one cubit in width has been woven, a Nissaggiya Pācittiya offense is incurred." In this training rule, the procedure for forfeiture should be understood in this way: "Venerable sir, this robe of mine, having been woven by weavers after I myself requested the thread, is to be forfeited."

"Teneva" means only by the weaver who was requested. "Evaṃ idha dukkaṭaṃ" means that here too (when having a non-allowable weaver weave allowable thread), a dukkaṭa offense is incurred when a piece one span in length and one cubit in width has been woven. "Akappiyasuttamaye" means in the portion made with the requested thread. "Itarasmiṃ" refers to the portion made with thread that was not requested (allowable). "Tato ce ūnatara" means even if it is less than the stated size, even down to the size of an eye-socket, [a dukkaṭa is incurred]. Just as it was previously a nissaggiya for a monk who has an allowable weaver weave non-allowable thread, here a dukkaṭa offense is incurred. Therefore, for one who has both allowable and non-allowable thread woven, if the portions of non-allowable thread reach the minimum robe size or are less than that, dukkaṭa offenses are incurred according to the number of those non-allowable thread portions. There is no offense for the portions of allowable thread. Or, whether it is woven with alternating threads, or with the length (warp) being allowable and the width (woof) being non-allowable, a dukkaṭa offense is incurred for every portion that meets the measurement.
339:
If (according to the Pārājika-aṭṭhakathā, Vol. 2, pp. 636-638) there are two weavers, one who is proper (kappiya) and one who is improper (akappiya), and the thread is improper, and they weave in turns: when the improper weaver weaves a portion corresponding to the prescribed measurement, a pācittiya offense is committed for every such portion; for a portion less than that, a dukkaṭa offense is committed. When the other (proper) weaver weaves, a dukkaṭa offense is committed in both cases. If both weave together, holding the shuttle, a pācittiya offense is committed for every portion corresponding to the prescribed measurement.

If the thread is proper and the robe has defined boundaries like a paddy-field (kedārabaddha), a dukkaṭa offense is committed for every portion woven by the improper weaver; if woven by the other weaver, there is no offense. If both weave together, a dukkaṭa offense is committed for every portion corresponding to the prescribed measurement.

If the thread consists of both proper and improper types and they weave in turns: when the improper weaver weaves portions of the minimum robe measurement using improper thread, pācittiya offenses are committed according to the number of portions. A dukkaṭa offense is committed for portions less than that, as well as for portions woven with proper thread. If the proper weaver weaves portions corresponding to the measurement or less using improper thread, only a dukkaṭa offense is committed. For portions woven with proper thread, there is no offense.

Alternatively, if they weave using thread at every other interval, or by using improper thread for the warp (lengthwise) and improper thread for the woof (crosswise), or if both weave together holding the shuttle: in the case of a robe without defined boundaries, a dukkaṭa offense is committed for every portion corresponding to the prescribed measurement. In the case of a robe with defined boundaries, dukkaṭa offenses are committed according to the portions. Therefore, the commentator stated, "By this same method," and so forth.

In this context, regarding the weaver, a weaver obtained by requesting from one who is not a relative and has not offered an invitation is called "improper" (akappiya); the remaining weavers are "proper" (kappiya). Regarding the thread, thread obtained by requesting it oneself is "improper" (akappiya); the remaining thread, and thread obtained through relatives and such, should be understood as "proper" (kappiya). "Triple pācittiya" (tika-pācittiya) means three pācittiya offenses occur based on the perceptions of: one who perceives it as ordered when it is ordered, one who is doubtful, and one who perceives it as not ordered when it is ordered. "Thread requested for the sake of a robe" means thread requested for the sake of a robe either by oneself or by another. Although it is stated in the Pāli text as "having requested the thread oneself," in this commentary, it is not stated as "thread requested by oneself for the sake of a robe," but simply as "thread requested for the sake of a robe" in the factors of the offense; therefore, it should be understood that thread requested by another for the sake of a robe is also included. "Improper requesting" refers to an improper request such as, "Sirs, weave a robe for me."

## The Commentary on the Suttaviññatti Sikkhāpada is finished.
340:
## 7. Mahāpesakāra Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

“Cīvarasāmikehi pubbe appavārito hutvā” means being one who was not previously invited by the owners of the robe, such as: “Venerable sir, what kind of robe do you need? What kind of robe shall I have woven for you? Venerable sir, please say what you wish.” In this training rule, the manner of weaving along with the manner of increasing the thread is shown by the three terms such as āyata (long), etc. By the four terms such as suvita (well-woven), etc., only the manner of weaving is shown, without being mixed with the increase of thread.

The phrase “We will give a small amount of almsfood,” etc., is merely to show the manner of the monk's action and does not show the factor of the offense. This is because, in this training rule, the offense is incurred only by way of increasing the thread. Therefore, it is stated, “Not merely by the monk giving almsfood,” and so forth.

In this training rule, the method of forfeiture should be understood by the following way: “Venerable sirs, this robe of mine, which I caused to be managed by approaching the weaver of a householder who is not a relative and without being previously invited, is to be forfeited (nissaggiya).” “Triple pācittiya” (tika-pācittiya) means three pācittiya offenses occur based on: perceiving a non-relative as a non-relative, being doubtful, and perceiving a non-relative as a relative.

## The Commentary on the Mahāpesakāra Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 8. Accekacīvara Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

“Paṭhamapadassa” refers to the term “dasāhānāgataṃ.” “Purimanayeneva” means by way of the continuous connection (accantasaṃyoga) with the action, just as in the previous method. “Tāni divasāni” means during those days. “Accantameva” means without interruption. It means on any day within those ten days.

“Pavāraṇāmāsassa” refers to the first Kattika month. That month is called the “Pavāraṇā month” here because of its association with the first Pavāraṇā. “Juṇhapakkhapañcamito paṭṭhāya” means starting from the fifth day of the waxing moon. Or, it means starting from the fifth day of the previous waxing moon because it makes the Pavāraṇā month manifest.

In this context, if the text is seen as: “In truth, although this point is already established by the training rule ‘An extra robe may be kept for at most ten days,’ the training rule is established by showing the meaning as if it were new due to a special occasion,” it should be regarded as an erroneous reading (pamādapāṭha) because it contradicts the term “dasāhānāgataṃ.” Furthermore, because it is stated “starting from the fifth day of the waxing moon,” there would even be a contradiction between the preceding and following parts in the commentary itself.
342:
To show both the village (gāma) and the forest (arañña) without confusion by defining the place of theft, it is stated: 'except for the village,' and so forth. In the world, the precinct of a village (gāmūpacāra) is simply called a village. However, in this training rule, according to the Suttanta discourse, the phrase 'at least five hundred [bow-lengths]' refers to a monk living in the forest. Since a monk living in a forest according to the Vinaya discourse is not described in the Suttanta as 'a forest-dweller with a roadside dwelling,' the definition found in that Suttanta should be taken; thus, to show this, it is said: 'by a teacher's bow placed at the furthest points,' and so forth. In that context, 'a teacher's bow' (ācariyadhanu) is nine spans (vidatthi) in length by a normal hand. However, teachers say that when the bowstring is mounted, it is four cubits (hattha) in length. 'Of the village' refers to a fenced village. 'From the indakhīla' means from the threshold. 'From a place worthy of being a precinct' means from the first stone's throw of an average man standing in the precinct of the house situated at the very edge. To the question 'by how much distance should it be measured?', it is said: 'if,' and so forth. In the Middle Commentary (Majjhima-aṭṭhakathā), however, it is said: 'The precinct of the monastery should also be excluded like the precinct of a village, and it should be measured between the two stone's throws.'

'Because of seeing the place where thieves stay' means because of the reason of seeing the place where thieves stay in the monastery or in the monastery precinct. By the word 'ādi' (etc.), the places where they eat, stand, sit, and lie down are included. 'Because of seeing the manner of people being killed, plundered, or beaten by thieves' means because of seeing the manner of killing, plundering, and beating in the monastery or in the monastery precinct.

'He should deposit it in the antaraghara' means either because there are houses in between or because it is in between those houses, it is called 'antaraghara,' which is a village; the meaning is that he should place it there. Therefore, it is said: 'of a forest-dweller,' and so forth. 'And that' refers to the act of depositing. The phrase 'he is one who has performed the Pavāraṇā at the Mahāpavarāṇā' is stated to show the state of having completed the rains-residence without a break, but not as a factor of the Pavāraṇā itself. Therefore, to show the opposite, it is stated in the Samantapāsādikā: 'If he is one who entered the later rains (pacchimikā) or one whose rains-residence was broken, he does not get the right to deposit the robe.' The month of Kattika refers to the 29 days (nights and days) from the first day of the waning moon of the first Kattika until the full moon of the later Kattika. By the word 'eva' (only/just), it shows that it cannot be obtained after the month of Kattika. Let it be that it is not obtained when the measure is less because it does not meet the definition of a forest; why is it not obtained when the measure exceeds a gāvuta? To this, it is said...
343:
In the passage beginning with "Yatra hi," for a monk who has been invited, being able to travel half a league or a league and return to his regular dwelling is not the essential measure. "Sāsaṅka-sappatibhayaṃ eva hoti" means it is both suspicious and dangerous. By the word "eva," it is shown that even a monk living in a dwelling endowed with the factors of being neither suspicious nor dangerous is not allowed to deposit his robe.

By this sequence of words, it refers to a monk who has entered the first vassa, completed it without break, and has finished the vassa. If he makes a certain village his alms-resort and lives in a forest dwelling at least five hundred bow-lengths (dhanu) away, the Buddha allowed him to leave his robe in that village and stay in that same dwelling without that robe throughout the month of Kattika. Now, wishing to allow a monk staying elsewhere than that dwelling to be away from the robe for up to six nights, he said "Siyā ca tassa bhikkhuno" and so forth. It should also be understood in this training rule that only monks who have spread the kathina robe are allowed to travel without taking all three robes; others are not.

In that passage, "that monk should stay away from that robe for at most six nights" means that if a monk, while living in a monastery, has business to go elsewhere and leaves his robe in a village house, that monk should stay away from that robe for at most six nights; he should stay elsewhere than that monastery for six nights. This is what is meant. Indeed, the Venerable Teacher Buddhadatta said:

"If a monk lives in a forest dwelling, making a certain village his alms-resort,
it is allowable to keep that robe in that village for one month.
For a monk staying elsewhere, it is considered allowable for at most six nights;
this is the explanation of the hidden meaning of that monk."

Therefore, he said, "If he should stay away beyond that," meaning if he allows the seventh dawn to rise in that dwelling beyond the six nights. Likewise, "a monk who is unable" means a monk who is unable to return to the dwelling and allow the seventh dawn to rise because of the distance of the place he went to. Such a monk, staying right where he is, should perform the determination (paccuddhor), thinking, "This robe shall remain as an extra robe (atireka-cīvara)." "Vasitvā" means having allowed the dawn to rise. The monk's authorization (bhikkhu-sammuti) has already been mentioned in the Udosittha Training Rule.

"Sesaṃ" refers to the passage beginning with "Apart from the monk's authorization, this is the supplementary regulation in this training rule." In the second training rule of this Cīvara-vagga, there is the fourth factor of being away for a night; the only difference here is that it is being away beyond six nights.

## The Explanation of the Sāsaṅka Training Rule is finished.
344:
## 10. Pariṇata-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā

Is this gain not merely diverted to the Sangha and not yet fully relinquished? If so, how does it belong to the Sangha? (In response to this objection), he said "So hi" and so forth. In that passage, "so" refers to the gain of the four requisites. "Ekena pariyāyena" means by one method, namely the state of being diverted. By the word "labhitabba," he stated the passive sense (kamma-sādhana) of the word "lābha." "Cīvarādi-vatthu" refers to robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicines for the sick, including even bathing powder, tooth-sticks, and fringe-threads. "Pariṇata" means being inclined, sloped, or bent towards the Sangha. To show the reason why the gain is diverted and to show the meaning of that term, he said "Dassāma karissāma" and so forth. "Attano pariṇāmentassa" means to one who, knowing it is diverted to the Sangha, diverts it to himself and takes it, saying "Give this to me." "Payoge" means due to the effort (payoga) of diverting. In this training rule, the procedure for forfeiture should be understood in this way: "Venerable sir, this gain, knowing it to be Sangha-owned and diverted to the Sangha, was diverted by me to myself; it is to be forfeited."

In the word "saṅgha-cetiya-puggalesu," "puggala" (individual) should be understood as any being, down to a dog. "Añña-saṅghādīnaṃ" means to another Sangha, another shrine, or another individual. This is what is meant: "For a monk who diverts a gain diverted to the Sangha to another Sangha, or to a shrine, or to an individual, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). For a monk who diverts a gain diverted to a shrine to another shrine, or to the Sangha, or to an individual, there is an offense of wrongdoing. For a monk who diverts a gain diverted to an individual to another individual, or to the Sangha, or to a shrine, there is an offense of wrongdoing."

Now, to show the section on non-offense (anāpatti), he said "apariṇata-saññino" and so forth. It should be understood as: for a monk who perceives a gain as not diverted, whether it is actually diverted or not (there is no offense). It means there is no offense in both cases, whether it is diverted or not. Thus it was said: "If one diverts it to oneself perceiving a diverted gain as not diverted, there is no offense. If one perceives a gain that is not diverted as not diverted, there is no offense" (Pārājika). "Deyya-dhamma" refers to the four requisites. By the word "ādi," phrases such as "It may be for repair," "It may be for long endurance," or "Give wherever your heart has faith" are included. If the donors...
345:
say, "We wish to provide a Sangha meal, we wish to make an offering to a shrine, or we wish to give requisites to a single monk; we will give according to your preference. Please tell us, where shall we give?" When they have spoken thus, that monk should say, "Give wherever you wish (to the Sangha, shrine, or individual)."

## The Explanation of the Pariṇata Training Rule is finished.

## The Third Chapter, the Bowl Chapter (Patta-vagga), is finished.

## which is the explanation of the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Pātimokkha Commentary,

## the Explanation of the Nissaggiya (Forfeiture) section is finished.
346:
## Pācittiya Section
## 1. Musāvāda Chapter
## 1. Commentary on the Musāvāda Training Rule

In the term *sampajāna-musāvāda*, *musā* refers to a false matter (object). *Vāda* refers to making that false matter known as true. Speaking a lie while knowing it is called *sampajāna-musāvāda* (deliberate lying). This is the meaning in "in that deliberate lying." Therefore, it is said "previously" and so on. That lying occurs to one who knows both in the moment prior to speaking the lie and in the moment of speaking. Because it is stated in the Pācittiya Pali: "First, he has the intention, 'I will speak a lie,' and while speaking, he knows, 'I am speaking a lie,'" it means "to one who knows beforehand and also knows at the moment of speaking." These two (past and present) are the only factors for constituting a lie. Other (future) knowledge, whether it occurs or not, is not a cause. If one asks, "Is it not that only this speaking is known as lying?" it is said "And as for speaking" and so on. *Abhūtassa* means what is untrue.

In the phrase *hatthakaṃ sakyaputtaṃ*, Hatthaka is the name of that elder. He is called *Sakyaputta* because he is a son of the Sakyans. It is said that during the Buddha's time, eighty thousand people from the Sakyan clan ordained, and he was one of them. In the phrase *avajānitvā paṭijānanādivatthusmiṃ*, "denying and then admitting" refers to a situation where, while debating with *titthiyas* (sectarians), seeing a flaw in his own doctrine, he denies it saying, "This is not my doctrine," but later, while continuing to speak and seeing it as flawless, he admits, "This is indeed my doctrine." By the word *ādi* (and so on), it includes admitting and then denying, covering up one thing with another (*aññenanyaṃ paṭicaraṇa*), deliberate lying, and breaking an agreement after making it (*vissambādakarana*). Now, to show the various types of offenses, it is said "for the purpose of announcing a superhuman state" and so on.

*Anupadhāretvā sahasā bhaṇantassa* refers to one who speaks hastily without reflection. It is like saying "I did not see" even though one has seen. "One who says something else while intending to say another" refers to one who, due to dullness or confusion, makes a slip of the tongue, such as saying "*cīra*" instead of "*cīvara*." This is called *aññam bhaṇissāmīti aññam bhaṇati*. When a novice asks, "Venerable sir, did you see my preceptor?" a monk, with a desire to mock, says, "Novice, your preceptor has gone yoking a wood-cart," or hearing the sound of a fox and being asked "Whose sound is this?" he mockingly says, "This is the sound of those who are lifting the wheel of your mother's cart which got stuck in the mud while she was traveling." If one speaks like this (intentionally) without a slip of the tongue, he commits a Pācittiya offense. There is also what is called *pūraṇakathā* (supplementary speech). What is that speech? It is like a monk who, having received a little oil and returning to the monastery, says to a novice, "Where did you go today? The whole village was just oil," or having received a small piece of cake, says, "Today in the village, they were distributing cakes by the basketful." Such supplementary speech is also a lie.
347:
When a novice asks, "Venerable sir, did you see my preceptor?" a monk who wishes to joke or mock says, "Your preceptor has gone yoking a wood-cart." Or when asked, "Whose sound is this?" upon hearing a fox's cry, he says, "This is the sound of those who are lifting the wheel of your mother's cart which got stuck in the mud while she was traveling." If he speaks in this way, not as a slip of the tongue or a mistake, but saying something else (with intent), he indeed commits an offense.

Another type called *pūraṇakathā* (supplementary speech) is when a monk, having received a little oil in the village and returning to the monastery, says to a novice, "Where did you go today? The village was full of nothing but oil," or having received a piece of cake kept in a small basket, says, "Today in the village, they were preparing and distributing cakes with many baskets." This supplementary speech is indeed a lie. *Vissambādana-purekkhāratā* means: because one speaks words devoid of honesty with this mind, it is the prioritizing (giving importance to) the mind that arises with the intent to deceive, which is called *vissambādana*. It means placing the deceptive mind at the forefront.

## The Commentary on the Musāvāda Training Rule is finished.

## 2. Commentary on the Omasavāda Training Rule

*Omasavāda* occurs in speech that is insulting or disparaging. Since that speech is neither pleasant to the ear nor pleasant to the heart, and it pierces the ear and the heart, it is called *ovijjhana-vacana* (piercing speech). It refers to speaking in connection with birth and so on. Therefore, it is said "birth, name," and so on.

Therein, "birth" (*jāti*) refers to high births such as the Brahmin caste and low births such as the Caṇḍāla caste. "Name" (*nāma*) refers to low names such as Avakaṇṇaka and high names such as Buddharakkhita. "Clan" (*gotta*) refers to low clans such as Kosiya and high clans such as Gotama. "Work" (*kamma*) refers to low work such as a scavenger (*pupphachaḍḍaka*) and high work such as farming or trade. "Craft" (*sippa*) refers to low crafts such as basket-weaving and high crafts such as finger-accounting (*muddā*) or arithmetic. "Disease" (*ābādha*) means all diseases are considered low. Alternatively, diabetes (*madhumeha*) is high, and the remaining diseases are low. "Physical appearance" (*linga*) refers to low features such as being excessively tall and high features such as not being excessively tall. "Defilements" (*kilesa*) refers to all defilements such as lust (*rāga*). "Attainment/Offense" (*āpatti*) refers to high attainments such as the path of Stream-entry (*sotāpatti*) and non-high (low) offenses such as *pārājika*. "Insult" (*akkosa*) refers to low insults such as "You are a camel" and high insults such as "You are a wise man."
348:
"Yathā tathā" refers to terms that appear in the Pali text and those that do not, in any manner whatsoever. In this training rule, with the exception of monks, all beings such as bhikkhunīs are considered to be in the status of the unordained (anupasampanna); this is the intended meaning of the phrase "Idha ca" and so forth. "Davakamyatā" refers to the state of desiring to play or to laugh. "Sabbattha" (in all cases) means among monks, laypeople, and novices, as well as in terms that appear or do not appear in the Pali text; it applies to all instances. In the phrase "atthadhamma-anusāsanipurekkharānaṃ," explaining the meaning of the Pali text such as "You are an outcaste (caṇḍāla)" is called prioritizing the meaning (atthapurekkhara).
