Teaching the Pali text is called prioritizing the Dhamma (dhammapurekkhara). Speaking from the position of an instructor, saying "Even now you are an outcaste, do not do evil, do not be one who goes from darkness to darkness," and so forth, is to be understood as prioritizing instruction (anusāsanipurekkhara).

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Insulting Speech (Omasavāda-sikkhāpada) is finished.

## 3. Explanation of the Training Rule on Slander (Pesunña-sikkhāpada)

In the term "bhikkhupesunñe," the meaning is: it is called "pisuṇā" because it crushes and destroys. Speech that causes united beings to break into separate factions is called "pisuṇā." Slanderous speech (pisuṇā) itself is called "pesunña." One endowed with such speech is called "pisuṇo." His action is "pesunña." A monk's slander is "bhikkhupesunña." In this context, "bhikkhupesunña" means slanderous speech heard from one monk and conveyed by a monk to another monk. Therefore, it is said "jātiādīhi" and so forth. Because that slanderous speech is conveyed based on two reasons, it is said "bhikkhuno piyakamyatāya vā" and so forth.

In that context, "bhikkhuno piyakamyatāya" means that for whichever monk one speaks that slanderous speech, it is because of the desire to be dear to him, thinking, "By speaking thus, I will become dear to this monk." "Bhedādhippāyena" means because of the desire to cause division between others, thinking, "By speaking thus, this person will be divided from that person." Alternatively, according to the etymological method (nirutti), it is called "pesunña" because it makes one void of love. The speech by which one speaks to another, making oneself dear to that person's heart while making that person void of love for another, is the speech referred to. The meaning here should be understood in the manner of "bhikkhussa pesunñaṃ bhikkhupesunñaṃ" and so forth. "Vuttanayeneva" means in the same manner already stated, such as "jātiādīhi akkosa-vatthūhi."
349:
"Conveying insults not found in the Pali text" (pāḷimuttaka-akkosūpasaṃhāra) refers to conveying insults such as "You are a thief." Even if it is not a basis for insult, if a monk conveys the actions or words of another monk out of a desire to be liked (piyakamyatā), teachers say that although an offense is not apparent under this training rule on slander, there should be an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). "Speaking out of a desire to blame evil" means seeing one monk insulting and another being patient, and saying "How shameful! He dares to speak thus even to such a patient venerable," speaking solely to blame the evil act without any intent to slander.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Slander (Pesunña-sikkhāpada) is finished.

## 4. Explanation of the Training Rule on Reciting Dhamma Line by Line (Padasodhamma-sikkhāpada)

"Reciting Dhamma line by line" (padaso dhammaṃ vāceyya) means teaching or reciting the Dhamma together line by line or section by section. Since an offense is incurred not only for reciting the Pali text approved in the three Councils line by line, it is said "even Dhamma not included in the three Councils" and so forth. By the word "ādi" (etc.), one should include Sīlūpadesa, Dhutaṅgapañha, Ārammaṇakathā, Buddhikadaṇḍaka, Ñāṇavatthu, Asubhakathā, and so forth. In the Meṇḍaka-Milindapañha, there is no offense for the Elder's own spontaneous inspired answers. However, if he quotes from the Buddha's words to inform the King, and recites them line by line together, there is an offense. Texts such as Vaṇṇapiṭaka, Aṅgulimālapiṭaka, Raṭṭhapālagajjita, Āḷavakagajjita, Gūḷhamagga, Gūḷhavessantara, Gūḷhavinaya, and Vedallapiṭaka are not the Buddha's words.

Since that "line" (pada) is of four types, it is said "pada, anupada, anvakkhara, anubyañjana" to show them. Therein, "pada" means the first line of a verse (gāthā). "Anupada" means the second line. "Anvakkhara" means each individual syllable. "Anubyañjana" means a subsequent articulation similar to the preceding one. Alternatively, any single syllable is "anvakkhara"; a group of syllables is "anubyañjana"; and a group of syllables and articulations is "pada." The first line is "pada," the second is "anupada"; thus the distinction should be understood. If one recites any of these sections together with anyone except a monk or a nun, the connection is that a pācittiya offense is incurred according to the count of lines and so forth.
350:
In this context, regarding the composition of verses (Pācittiya-aṭṭhakathā 45), firstly, for a monk who starts and finishes reciting each individual word together with a novice (sāmaṇera), such as "Manopubbaṅgamā dhammā," a Pācittiya offense is incurred based on the word count (padagaṇanā). When the elder says "Manopubbaṅgamā dhammā," if the monk recites together with the novice at the time when the next phrase "Manoseṭṭhā manomayā" is reached before having reached that [previous] word, a Pācittiya offense is incurred based on the following word count (anupadagaṇanā). When reciting "Rūpaṃ aniccaṃ" etc., for a monk who causes the novice to recite even just the syllable "Rū" together with him, a Pācittiya offense is incurred based on the following syllable count (anvakkharagaṇanā). This method applies similarly to the composition of verses. While teaching this sutta, "Rūpaṃ, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ, vedanā aniccā," if the elder says "Rūpaṃ aniccaṃ" and the novice, being of quick intelligence, utters the sound by reciting this word "vedanā aniccā" together with the elder's word "Rūpaṃ aniccaṃ," it should be understood that the monk who teaches in this manner incurs a Pācittiya offense based on the following phrasing count (anubyañjanagaṇanā).

"Tika-pācittiya" refers to the three types of Pācittiya offenses based on the perception of an unordained person (anupasampanna): perceiving them as unordained, being in doubt, or perceiving them as ordained. In the case of taking a lesson (uddesaggahaṇa) of the Pali text together with an unordained person, it should be connected that there is no offense (anāpatti) for one who recites together. This method also applies to "in the performance of chanting (sajjhāya), and in taking a lesson in his presence." In that regard, this is the decision: An ordained monk and an unordained person sit and request instruction. If the teacher thinks, "I shall recite for those who are sitting," and recites together with them, the offense is incurred by the teacher alone. There is no offense for the monk who is learning together with the unordained person. If both are standing while learning, the same method applies. If a junior monk is sitting and a novice is standing, there is no offense for the one who recites, thinking, "I shall recite for the one who is sitting." If the junior monk is standing and the other (the novice) is sitting, there is no offense for the one who recites, thinking, "I shall recite for the one who is standing." If a novice is sitting in the midst of many monks, a monk who teaches the Dhamma word-by-word while that novice is sitting incurs an acittaka offense (an offense without specific intention). If the novice is standing or sitting outside the precinct (upacāra, 12 cubits), since he is not included among those being taught, it is regarded as "taking a text that has escaped," and thus there is no offense.

"Sajjhāyakaraṇe" means in the performance of chanting together with an unordained person. "Tassa santike uddesaggahaṇe" means in taking a lesson of the Pali text in the presence of an unordained person. "Yebuyyena paguṇaganthaṃ bhaṇantassāti" means if in one verse...
351:
...one foot (pāda) is not mastered but the remaining feet are mastered, this is called a "mostly mastered text" (yebuyyena paguṇagantha). This method should also be understood for the Sutta Pitaka; for one who recites that text, and for one who recites (osārentassa) a sutta in the midst of an assembly, there is no offense.

## The Explanation of the Padasodhamma Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 5. Paṭhamasahasayya Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
In this training rule, because it is stated, "Excepting a monk, the rest are called unordained (anupasampanna)," even an animal is indeed unordained. However, it does not mean every animal, but only an animal that can be the object of an offense of sexual misconduct; thus it is said, "even at minimum (antamaso)," etc. The definition of such an animal should be understood in the same manner as stated in the offense of sexual misconduct. In the phrase "dirattatirattaṃ" (two or three nights), no special meaning is obtained by the word "diratta" (two nights). It should be understood that it is said this way merely for the sake of linguistic smoothness and euphony in worldly usage. The expression "two or three nights" is stated either to show the mere meaning of the words or to show a continuous period of three nights; thus the inclusion of "diratta" should be regarded.

"Sahasayya" means sleeping together. As for "seyyā," it refers to the act of lying down characterized by the stretching out of the body, as in "lying down is seyyā," and it also refers to the sleeping place (dwelling) where they sleep, as in "they sleep here, therefore it is seyyā." In this training rule, both are taken either generally or by the method of eka-sesa (inclusion of both in one term); thus it is said, "fully roofed and fully enclosed (sabbacchannaparicchanna)," etc.

In that regard, a dwelling is "fully roofed" if it is entirely covered from above by the five types of roofing, or by any other means, even at minimum with a cloth. If it is entirely enclosed from the ground up to the roof, whether touching it or not, by a wall at least one and a half cubits (diyaddha-hattha) in height, or by any other means, even at minimum with a cloth, this is called "fully roofed and fully enclosed" (sabbacchannasabbaparicchanna). However, if a dwelling has most of its upper part roofed and a small part unroofed, and most of its surroundings enclosed and a small part unenclosed, this is called "mostly roofed and mostly enclosed" (yebuyyena channaparicchanna). In such a fully roofed and enclosed dwelling, or in a mostly roofed and enclosed dwelling.

"Vidahayya" means one should perform; however, in terms of meaning, it refers to accomplishing or preparing, thus it is said, "sampādeyya." This is the summary of the meaning here: "Having entered the sleeping place known as a dwelling..."
352:
"To perform, arrange, or complete the act of lying down, which is called stretching out the limbs" is the summary meaning in this training rule. One and a half cubits (diyaḍḍhahattha), including the height and the split, should be measured using a carpenter's cubit. "Ekūpacāra" refers to having a single entrance for coming and going. A four-sided rest house with a hundred rooms is also considered a single enclosure (ekūpacāra) if it has only one door. "In that place" means staying in the same monastery where one has stayed on previous days. "In another such place" means staying in another monastery that possesses the aforementioned characteristics but where one has not stayed before. "With that person" means staying with the same person, whether a layperson or a novice, with whom one stayed on previous days. "With another person" means staying with someone other than the person with whom one stayed on previous days. This is the summary explanation. If this is so, how should the detailed explanation be understood? For this reason, [the author] stated, "As for the details..." and so forth.

In the phrase "upaḍḍhacchannaparicchannādīsu" and so forth, by the word "ādi", one should include the intermediate dukkhaṭa offenses mentioned in the Commentary, such as: an offense of dukkhaṭa for a monk who sleeps in a monastery that is completely roofed but only slightly (about one-fourth) walled; a monastery that is mostly roofed but only slightly walled; a monastery that is completely walled but only slightly roofed; or a monastery that is mostly walled but only slightly roofed. "One who leaves before dawn on the third night and stays again" refers to one who leaves before dawn on the third night, lets the dawn rise while outside the monastery, and returns to stay again only after sunset on the fourth day. In the phrase "sabbacchannasabbāparicchannādīsu" and so forth, by the word "ādi", one should include the cases of no offense (anāpattivāra) mentioned in the Pāḷi text, such as: sleeping in a monastery that is completely walled but not roofed at all, or a monastery that is mostly unroofed and mostly unwalled; as well as the cases of no offense mentioned in the Commentary, such as: sleeping in a monastery that is half-roofed and slightly walled, half-walled and slightly roofed, or slightly roofed and slightly walled.

## The Explanation of the First Sahaseyya Training Rule is Finished.

## 6. Explanation of the Second Sahaseyya Training Rule

"With a woman" means with a living human woman. Teachers say, "Although a dead woman can be the basis for a pārājika offense, because she belongs to the category of the non-living (anupādinna), she does not cause a sahaseyya offense arising from sleeping together." There is no offense for a monk who sleeps with a female yakkha (yakkhiṇī) or a female hungry ghost (petī) who are invisible, nor for a monk who sleeps with a female animal, which is not a basis for sexual intercourse. Just as in the first training rule, where the offense is incurred only on the fourth day, in this second training rule, it is not that the offense is incurred only on the fourth day, but rather...
353:
There is no offense in sleeping with a female animal, which is not a basis for sexual intercourse. The phrase "even on the first day" means that, unlike in the first training rule where the offense is incurred only on the fourth day, in this training rule, the offense is incurred even on the first day. By this statement, it is shown that there is no time limit in this training rule. Regarding the factors, it should be noted that there are three factors: a dwelling that is a basis for a pācittiya offense, lying down together with a woman in that dwelling, and the setting of the sun.

## The Explanation of the Second Sahaseyya Training Rule is Finished.

## 7. Explanation of the Dhamma-desanā Training Rule

"With five or six words" means with five or six utterances. How should the limit of words be understood here? For this reason, it was stated, "Beyond five or six words," and so forth. "In all cases" should be understood as in both the Suttas and the Commentaries. If one wishes to preach the Commentary, the Dhammapada, or stories such as the Jātakas, one should preach only about six phrases. A monk preaching together with the Pāḷi should preach without exceeding six phrases, such as one phrase from the Pāḷi and five from the Commentary. "With a man" means a human male. Therefore, it was stated, "Taking the human form," and so forth.

"Tikapācittiya" means that three pācittiya offenses occur based on: perceiving a woman as a woman, being in doubt, and perceiving a woman as not a woman. "Or to another woman" means to another woman who arrives while the monk is sitting and preaching to one woman. In this way, a monk sitting in one place may preach even to a hundred women. Because it is stated, "To a discerning human woman," there is no offense in preaching to a woman who is not discerning. "Absence of change in posture" means the absence of change in the posture of oneself or the woman. "Absence of a kappiyakāraka" means the absence of a discerning attendant, which refers to the absence of a man possessing the characteristics mentioned in the second aniyata training rule. In the phrase "action and non-action," preaching the Dhamma beyond five or six words is called "action" (kiriyā), and not bringing a kappiyakāraka is called "non-action" (akiriyā).

## The Explanation of the Dhamma-desanā Training Rule is Finished.
354:
## 8. Bhūtārocana-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā

"Nippariyāyena" (directly) means speaking straightforwardly in such a way as "he attained the first jhāna," etc. (Pācittiya, 71). "Pariyāyena ārocitaṃ" (announced indirectly) means speaking by referring to another person in such a way as "the monk who lived in your monastery attained, is attaining, or has attained the first jhāna," etc. (Pācittiya, 75).

Whether at the time of approaching Parinibbāna or at other times, an Arahant who is strongly urged until they speak is permitted to announce the existing superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma) to a monk. Even if not strongly urged, if there is a suitable reason, it is indeed permitted to announce it. For this very reason, an elder who was accused by a young monk said, "Friend, do not strive for the sake of the higher paths; you have accused an Arahant." Also, when the elder asked, "Friend, do you have a footing in this Dispensation?", the young monk replied, "Yes, Bhante, I am a Sotāpanna."

Noble Ones (Ariyas) reveal themselves either because they know "this monk is a practitioner" or to inspire and gladden them by showing that the practice (paṭipatti) is not in vain. Therefore, it is said, "to one who announces to a monk when there is such a reason." However, qualities such as learning (suta), scriptural knowledge (pariyatti), and virtue (sīla) may be announced even to unordained persons (laypeople).

As to why the insane (ummattaka) and others are not included in this training rule, it is said, "Yasmā pana," etc. By the word "ādi" (etc.), those with deranged minds and those afflicted by pain are included. "Tasmiṃ sati" means when there is the state of being insane, etc. "Not included here" means they are not included in the Padabhājanīya of this training rule. "Acittaka" (without intention) means it is an offense committed without the mind that recognizes the regulation. The statement "there are two minds: wholesome (kusala) and indeterminate (abyākata)" is said with reference only to Noble Ones as the highest limit. This is because worldlings (puthujjanas) who have attained jhāna but do not know the regulation might also speak with an unwholesome mind due to greed for the object (the jhāna). Alternatively, it should be understood that this is said to be consistent with the term "two feelings" (dvivedana) because of the absence of painful feeling.

## The Commentary on the Bhūtārocana Training Rule is Finished.

## 9. Duṭṭhullārocana-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā

"Of the two classes of offenses" means of the two classes of offenses known as Pārājika and Saṅghādisesa. "For the sake of restraint in the future" means "if spoken thus, that monk, through shame and fear of others..."
355:
"...will arrive at restraint in the future." "Having made a limit of the offenses and the families, or not having made a limit" means speaking by either limiting or not limiting as "this many offenses should be announced, they should be announced to this many families."

"In a non-grave offense" (aduṭṭhullāya) means in a non-grave offense consisting of the remaining five classes of offenses, excluding Pārājika and Saṅghādisesa. "In the remaining six classes of offenses" means in the remaining six classes of offenses excluding Saṅghādisesa. "A grave offense (duṭṭhulla) consisting of the transgression of the first five training rules" refers to the grave offense consisting of the transgression of the first five training rules starting with the abstinence from taking life (pāṇātipāta). "Other non-grave conduct (ācāra)" refers to the other group of five starting with eating at the wrong time (vikālabhojana), and non-grave conduct known as emission of semen (sukka-vissaṭṭhi), bodily contact (kāyasaṃsagga), grave words (duṭṭhullavācā), and desire for one's own benefit (attakāma).

"Mere basis of the offense" (vatthumatta) refers to a monk who announces only the basis/reason as "This monk has reached the emission of semen, speaks grave words, has reached serving through sensual desire for his own benefit, or has reached bodily contact." "Mere offense" (āpattimatta) refers to a monk who announces only the name of the offense as "This monk has reached a Pārājika offense, a Saṅghādisesa, Thullaccaya, Pācittiya, Pāṭidesanīya, Dukkaṭa, or Dubbhāsita offense." "Of a monk with the stated characteristics" means of a monk who has not committed a Pārājika offense. "With the reason" (savatthuko) means it is firmly connected with the basis/reason of the offense.

## The Commentary on the Duṭṭhullārocana Training Rule is Finished.

## 10. Pathavīkhaṇana-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā

In this context of "in stones, pebbles, potsherds, gravel, sand, etc.", stones larger than the size of a fist are to be understood as "pāsāṇa." Stones the size of a fist are "sakkharā." Potsherds are "kathalā." Gravel (or processed stones) are "marumbā." Sand is simply "vālukā." "Is one-third of another thing" means it is a third part. The meaning is: if one brings soil or clay and separates them, and there are two parts of soil or clay and one part of stones etc., this earth is called "mixed earth" (missaka-pathavī). "Ovaṭṭha" refers to earth wetted by rain. "It is said" means it is said in the Padabhājanīya or in the Sihala Commentary (Sīhaḷa-aṭṭhakathā).
356:
## Adhikatarapāsāṇādimissā
This refers to earth mixed with an especially large amount of gravel and so forth. It means earth mixed with gravel, etc., in an amount greater than what was previously mentioned, even if it has not been burnt. The word "vā" (or) has the sense of an unstated alternative; by this word, earth that has been wet by rain for less than four months is included. "Suddhapāsāṇādibhedāya" means that in this earth, there are pure stones unmixed with soil; therefore, that earth is called "suddhapāsāṇa" (earth consisting of pure stones). Because there are various types such as earth consisting of pure stones, it is called "suddhapāsāṇādi." By the word "ādi," earth consisting of pure gravel and so forth should be taken. "Suddhapāsāṇādibhedāya" means in the state of earth having various types such as pure stones. "Suddhapāsāṇādippakārāya" means of that earth which has various types such as pure stones.

In the phrase "digs by oneself," even if one digs with at least a big toe, or breaks the earth while pouring water, or scratches with a big toe, or burns the earth while firing a bowl—all such persons are to be understood as "one who digs." Therefore, it is said, "He destroys it by digging, breaking, scratching, firing, and so forth." A monk wishing to fire a bowl should fire it only in a place previously used for firing. It is not proper to place fire on earth that has not been burnt. However, it is proper to place fire on a potsherd used for firing a bowl. If fire is placed on wood and that fire, while burning the wood, goes on to burn the earth, it is not proper. The same method applies to bricks, stones, and so forth. In those cases too, it is proper to place fire only on top of the bricks and stones. Why? Because those bricks and stones are not fuel (anupādāna). They do not come to be regarded as fuel for the fire. It is also not proper to apply fire to dry stumps or dry trees. However, if one applies it with the thought, "I will extinguish it before it reaches the ground and then leave," it is proper. If one cannot extinguish it later, there is no offense as it is beyond one's power. "Vuttanayeneva" means by the very method already stated: "by digging, breaking, scratching, firing, and so forth." "Niyametvā" means having made a decision. "Itaro" means the one who gives the command.

To say "Dig a pond" is proper. Since it is called a pond only after it has been dug, this is a proper mode of expression (kappiya-vohāra). This method also applies to such words as "Dig a dam, a tank, or a pit." However, it is not proper to say, "Dig this spot," or "Dig a pond at this spot." It is proper to say, "Dig a tuber" or "Dig a root" without specifying the spot. It is not proper to say, "Dig this vine," or "Dig a tuber or a root at this spot." Therefore, it is said, "To one who speaks without specifying the spot..." Dried mud cracked by the heat of the sun may occur; among those pieces of dried mud, it is proper to remove only that which is not connected to the ground below. In this same way...
357:
The same method applies to "gokaṇṭaka" (mud with cow hoofprints). Therefore, it was said, "Because of the sun's heat... not connected to the ground below." In that context, "gokaṇṭaka" refers to mud cut by the hooves of cows. If that mud is connected to the ground at its lower surface, it is not proper to destroy (remove) it. "Bhizzitvā patitanaditaṭa" refers to a riverbank that has broken and fallen near the river, which has been wet by rain for less than four months. However, if it breaks and falls into the water itself, it is proper to destroy it even if it has been wet by rain for more than four months, because it has fallen into the water. "Mahantampi naṅgalacchinnamattikāpiṇဍ" refers to a clod of clay, even if large, that has been cut by a ploughshare in a ploughed area and is not connected to the ground below. By the word "ādi" (and so forth), thin mud suitable for pouring from a water pot and so forth are to be taken.

"To one who breaks the earth by rolling a tree and so forth without intention" means that while rolling stones, logs, etc., or while walking by leaning on a walking stick, the earth might be broken. Such breaking is called "broken without intention" because it was not broken with the intention "I will break it with this." Thus, there is no offense for one who breaks it by rolling a tree and so forth without intention. "To one who scratches with a big toe and so forth without mindfulness" means one who is distracted, talking to someone about something, and stands scratching the earth with a big toe or a walking stick; for such a monk who scratches with a big toe and so forth without mindfulness, there is no offense.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Digging the Earth is finished.

## The First Chapter: The Chapter on Lying.

## 2. The Chapter on Living Plants

## 1. Explanation of the Training Rule on Living Plants

By the word "bhavanti," the author shows young plants that have taken root, turned green, and are growing. By the word "ahesuṃ," he shows large trees, shrubs, and so forth that have already grown and are established. Therefore, he says "jāyanti" and so forth. Here, the explanation of "bhavanti" is "jāyanti vaḍḍhanti" (they are born, they grow), and the explanation of "ahesuṃ" is "jātā vaḍḍhitā" (they were born, they have grown). "Gāma" means a collection or group. "Patiṭṭhitaharitatinarukkhādīnaṃ" means green grass and green trees, etc., established in the earth. By the word "ādi," medicinal plants, shrubs, creepers, and so forth should be understood. The locative case is used in the sense of a cause (nimitta). The complete meaning is stated by the words "bhūtagāmapātabyatāya" and so forth.
358:
Is it not that trees and the like are without life because they lack consciousness? Their lack of consciousness is known through their lack of trembling, their regrowth even when cut, their being of a different class (from sentient beings), and their not being included in the four modes of birth (yoni). Since growth is also found in pearls, crystals, and salt, their growth is not a reason for having life. Their perception of objects, such as the 'sleeping' (folding of leaves) of tamarind trees and the like, is merely a conceptualization, like dreaming. Similarly, longings (dohaḷa) and the like are also merely conceptualizations. If so, why is a Pācittiya offense established for destroying vegetation (bhūtagāma)? It is because it is unbecoming for recluses (samaṇa) and to protect the living beings that depend on that vegetation. Therefore, it was said: 'Indeed, these foolish men have the perception of life in a tree,' and so forth.

'Sāsapabījakasevālam-pi' means moss known as sāsapabījaka, or small moss the size of a mustard seed (sāsapasevāla), or bījakasevāla. Among them, sāsapasevāla is small moss the size of a mustard seed. Bījakasevāla is moss with small leaves above and small roots below.

In the terms 'root-seed' (mūlabīja), 'trunk-seed' (khandhabīja), 'joint-seed' (phallubīja), 'bud-seed' (aggabīja), and 'seed-seed' (bījabīja), the root itself is the seed, thus it is called 'root-seed'. The same applies to the remaining terms. Among them, root-seed refers to turmeric and the like. Trunk-seed refers to the Bodhi tree and the like. Joint-seed refers to sugarcane and the like. Bud-seed refers to ginger and the like. Seed-seed refers to grain crops and the like.

'Bhājanagataṃ' refers to seeds placed in a vessel such as a bowl. If only the root has emerged from that seed, it is called 'nikkhantamūlamatta' (merely the emerged root). By the word 'matta' (merely), the emergence of leaves is excluded. This same principle applies to the term 'nikkhantaṅkuramatta' (merely the emerged sprout). However, if both the root and the leaf have emerged, it falls under the designation of 'bhūtagāma' (vegetation). 'Vidatthimattā pattavaṭṭi niggacchati' means a rolled leaf-bud about a span long, which is not yet dark green, emerges. Therefore, it is said 'nikkhante' and so forth. 'Harito na hoti' means it is not dark green in color. When the leaves of green gram and the like have risen, or when the sprouts of paddy and the like have become green, they are included in the category of bhūtagāma. This same principle should be understood for mango stones and the like.

In the phrase 'bhūtagāma-bījagāme', it should be understood that root-seeds and the like, which have been detached from the vegetation (bhūtagāma) but are still capable of growth, are called 'bījagāma' (seed-group). 'Ubhayattha' means in both bhūtagāma and bījagāma. 'Atathāsaññissa' refers to one who does not perceive them as bhūtagāma or bījagāma. What need is there to speak of an offense for one who does not perceive things that are not bhūtagāma or bījagāma as such? 'Asañcicca' (unintentionally) refers to grass being destroyed when someone rolls stones or trees, pulls a branch, or walks striking the ground with a staff. Since that person did not intentionally think 'I will destroy it,' it is called 'unintentional destruction' (asañcicca-vikopita). There is no offense for one who destroys unintentionally.
359:
'Asatiyā' (through lack of mindfulness) means: a monk who is distracted, talking to someone about something, stands destroying grass or a creeper with his big toe or hand; for such a monk who destroys through lack of mindfulness, there is no offense. 

'Ajānitvā' (unknowingly) means: here, he does not know 'this is bījagāma' or 'this is bhūtagāma', but he does know 'I am destroying it'. For example, when placing a crowbar or a hoe in grass or a heap of straw for safekeeping, or when a person whose hand is burning drops fire; if in doing so, the grass is cut or burnt, for such a monk who destroys unknowingly, there is no offense.

'Yena kenaci agginā' (by any kind of fire) means: by any kind of fire among wood-fire, cow-dung fire, etc., or even by a glowing piece of iron. 'Kappiyaṃ-ti vatvā-va' (only after saying 'kappiya') means: only after saying 'kappiya' (make it allowable) in any language. By the word 'eva' (only/just), it shows that it is not proper to first touch it with fire and then say 'kappiya' afterwards. Teachers say: 'If one first places the fire and, without removing that fire, says "kappiya", it is proper.' This same principle applies to the other methods of making allowable. 

'Tatheva' (in the same way) means it must be done only after saying 'kappiya'. The hooves of horses, buffaloes, pigs, deer, and cattle are very sharp; therefore, it should not be done with them; even if done, it is as if not done. Thus it is said: 'excluding the hooves of cattle, buffaloes, and the like.' Elephant nails, however, are not hooves; therefore, it is proper to use them. 

'Tiraच्छānānaṃ' (of animals) refers to the claws of lions, tigers, leopards, monkeys, and birds. Since the claws of these animals are sharp, it should be done with those claws. By the phrase 'even with a claw that has been cut and brought,' it shows that there is no need to mention that it is proper to do it with claws still attached to the body. 

'Satthe vuttanayeneva' (in the same manner as mentioned regarding the weapon) refers to showing cutting or piercing, and points to the phrase 'only after saying "kappiya"'. Here, although the phrase 'it should be done only after saying "kappiya"' shows the manner in which the monk who makes it allowable should act, it should be understood that only after the monk says 'kappiyaṃ karohi' (make it allowable) should the unordained person (layperson or novice) say 'kappiya' and perform the act of touching with fire, etc. The reason it is not mentioned again here is that it was already stated earlier: 'it should be consumed only after having it made allowable again.' 

'In one... (pe)... when one is made allowable, all are made allowable' means: even if one makes it allowable with the intention 'I will make only one allowable,' because they are connected as one, all...
360:
Even if one makes it allowable (kappiya) with the intention of making only one seed and so forth allowable, it counts as making all the seeds allowable because they are connected to that one seed. In the case of 'piercing wood,' whether knowing or not knowing, piercing it oneself or having another pierce it, it is indeed allowable. The same method applies to 'piercing a grain of cooked rice.' The teachers of the Commentary mean that if one pierces creepers and such, it is not allowable because they are like vessels (bhājana-gatika). The statement 'it should be made allowable by breaking' refers to the shell freed from the seed being allowable because it is like a vessel. Young mango fruits and the like, which lack seeds capable of germinating, are called 'abīja' (seedless). Therefore it was said: 'Whatever fruit is young, that is called seedless.' Fruits like mango and jackfruit, where the seed can be removed and consumed separately, are called 'nibbattabīja.' Therefore it was said: 'It should be consumed after removing the seed.' In such fruits, there is no need for the act of making it allowable; they are meant to be allowable by themselves.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Vegetation (Bhūtagāma Sikkhāpada) is finished.

## 2. Explanation of the Training Rule on Evasive Speech (Aññavādaka Sikkhāpada)

'Yamatthaṃ' refers to any matter such as 'You have reportedly committed a dukkaṭa offense.' 'Tato aññaṃ' means a matter other than the one questioned. 'Aññenaññaṃ paṭicaraṇa' means concealing by using words other than those spoken by the Vinaya-expert monk for the purpose of inquiring into the fault. Because roots have multiple meanings, the word 'cara' also exists in the sense of concealing. 'Vuttaṃ' means what is stated in the Pāḷi.

'Sāvasesaṃ āpattiṃ āpanno': Here, excluding the pārājika offenses, the remaining offenses are called 'sāvasesa' (with a remainder); one has fallen into such an offense. 'Anuyuñjiyamāno' means being questioned: 'Friend, have you fallen into such-and-name offense?' 'Aññena vacanena' means deflecting with other words like: 'Who fell into it? What was fallen into? In what matter was it fallen into? How was it fallen into? Whom are you talking about? What are you saying?' 'Aññaṃ' refers to the questioner's words such as 'Have you fallen into such-and-name offense?' 'Tathā tathā vikkhipati' means deflecting in various ways. The meaning is: When that monk, having been seen committing some transgression, is questioned in the midst of the Saṅgha, 'Friend, you have fallen into an offense,' he says, 'Who fell into it?' Then, when told 'You,' he says, 'What offense have I fallen into?' Then, when told 'A pācittiya or a dukkaṭa,' he asks, 'In what matter did I fall into a pācittiya or a dukkaṭa?' When told 'You fell into it in such-and-such a case,' he asks, 'In what way did I fall into it? By doing what did I fall into it?' When the questioner says, 'You fell into it by doing this,' he says, 'Whom are you talking about?' When told 'We are talking about you,' he says, 'What words are you saying?' or in many such ways, he deflects the conversation.

Alternatively, a monk who has fallen into a sāvasesa offense and, not wishing to disclose it, harasses [the Saṅgha] by remaining silent.
361:
He says, 'I have fallen into an offense.' Then, when told 'In such-and-such a case (you have fallen into an offense),' he asks, 'In what way did I fall into it? By doing what did I fall into it?' When told 'You fell into it by doing this,' he says, 'Whom are you talking about?' When told 'We are talking about you,' he says, 'What words are you saying?' Thus it is meant that he deflects in many various ways.

'The monk who has fallen into a sāvasesa offense and, not wishing to disclose it, harasses [the Saṅgha] by remaining silent'—this is the connection. 'Harasses' means he harasses the Saṅgha by way of making them sit for a long time, speak for a long time, causing back pain, dryness of the throat, and so on; it means he causes exhaustion to those monks. For exhaustion is indeed called 'harassment' (vihēsā). 'Aññavādaka-kamma' is the formal act with a motion and one announcement (ñattidutiya-kamma) that should be performed to charge an evasive monk with the status of being an evasive speaker. The same method applies to 'Vihēsaka-kamma' (the formal act for a harasser). 'When performed by the Saṅgha' means when the Saṅgha has performed that Aññavādaka-kamma and Vihēsaka-kamma with the formal motion and announcement. 'To those who act thus' means to the monks who perform those acts of evasive speech and harassment.

The reason for not stating that 'Vihēsaka' is a supplementary regulation (anupaññatti) here is because it is already evident, as it was stated: 'He becomes one who commits an offense as in the Aññavādaka training rule and others.' This same method applies to the subsequent training rules. 'Three pācittiyas in a valid act' means three pācittiyas occur by way of perceiving a valid act as a valid act, being in doubt, or perceiving a valid act as an invalid act. The same method applies to 'three dukkaṭas in an invalid act.' 'Before being charged' means before being established by the formal act (kammavācā). 'Due to illness' means being unable to speak due to a disease, such as a disease in the mouth. 'There will be quarrels and so on for the Saṅgha' means if it is spoken in the midst of the Saṅgha, because of that speaking, there will be quarrels, strife, contention, disputes, schism in the Saṅgha, or a rift in the Saṅgha—for a monk who does not speak with this intention, [there is no offense]. Here, 'adhammena' (unrighteously) means by way of a false matter.

After pointing out without distinction that 'the origins and so on are similar to theft (adinnādāna),' the phrase 'But this...' and so on is stated to show the distinction. There can be an act of commission (kiriya) for a monk who behaves evasively with other words. There can be an act of omission (akiriya) for a monk who harasses the Saṅgha by remaining silent.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Evasive Speech is finished.
362:
## 3. Ujjhāpanakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

"By whatever word" means by whatever word such as, "So-and-so does this out of favoritism/affection." Therefore, the phrase "out of favoritism" and so forth is stated. In that context, "out of favoritism" (chandāya) means by partiality or bias according to one's desire. As in the phrases "akkharāya vāceti" and so forth, this is merely a change of gender (from masculine to feminine). "Does this" means arranging excellent lodgings for one's acquaintances or directing meals and so forth. In the phrase "the category of lodging-assigner and so forth," the word "and so forth" includes the meal-assigner (bhattuddesaka), the congee-distributor (yāgubhajaka), the fruit-distributor (phalabhajaka), and others. Because roots have many meanings, the word "jhe" also exists in the sense of looking; therefore, it is said, "they make [others] look with contempt." Or, it should be taken only in the sense of thinking; therefore, it is said, "they make [others] think of [him] as inferior." "Saying so" means saying such things as, "So-and-so does this out of favoritism."

"It is said" means it is said in the Pali text. "Complaining" (khiyanaka) is the supplementary regulation (anupaññatti) in this training rule.

"To one not authorized" means to one not authorized by the Sangha through a formal act (kammavācā). It refers to one who is merely assigned a duty by the Sangha saying, "This is your responsibility," or one who takes on the responsibility himself for the comfortable living of the monks, or one who performs such work in a place where only two or three monks reside. "To anyone" means to anyone, whether ordained (upasampanna) or unordained (anupasampanna). Regarding the phrase "whether a novice (sāmaṇera) is authorized or unauthorized," although it is not proper to give the thirteen types of authorization to a novice, the term "authorized" is used in reference to one who received authorization while a monk and later remains in the status of a novice. The term "unauthorized" is used in reference to a skilled novice who has been assigned a duty by the Sangha or by an authorized monk saying, "You do this work."

Since inciting (ujjhāpana) and complaining (khiyana) occur by the power of lying (musāvāda), the first offender (ādikammika) does not incur an offense by this training rule, but it should be understood that he does incur an offense for lying (musāvāda).

## The Commentary on the Ujjhāpanaka Training Rule is Finished.
363:
## 4. Paṭhamasenāsanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

'Mañcaṃ vā' (or a couch) refers to any one of these four types of couches: masāraka, bundikābaddha, kuḷīrapādaka, or āhaccapādaka. The same method applies to the term 'pīṭhaṃ vā' (or a chair). 'Bhisiṃ vā' (or a bolster/mattress) refers to any one of these five types of bolsters: those stuffed with wool (uṇṇa), cloth (coḷa), bark (vāka), grass (tiṇa), or leaves (paṇṇa). Therefore, it is stated as 'mañcādīsu' (on couches, etc.). In that context, by the phrase 'mañcasaṅkhepena' (by summarizing the couch), the inclusion of chairs/stools (pīṭha) is excluded.

'Kappiyacammena' (with allowable skin) refers to deer skin or goat skin. Among these deer skins, only the skins of the following animals are allowable: the eṇī-deer, the 'flying' deer (vātamiiga), the pasada-deer, the kuruṅga-deer, the migamātuka, and the rohita-deer. Others such as:

Monkeys, bears, sarabha-deer, and kadalī-deer,
And whatever fierce beasts (vālamiiga) there are,
The skins of these animals are not allowable.

In this context, 'vālamiiga' (fierce beasts) refers to lions, tigers, bears, and hyenas/panthers. Not only these, but excluding those animals whose skins were said to be allowable, all other animals down to cattle, buffalo, rabbits, cats, and so forth are also to be understood as 'vālamiiga' in this context. The skins of all these animals are not allowable.

'Tālīsapattaṃ' (Tamāla leaf) means that pure Tamāla leaf is not allowable, but if mixed with other leaves, it is allowable. Among bolsters made of grass, bark, or cloth, there is nothing that is not allowable. Because it was asked, 'Is it not allowable to sit or lie on that bolster as if it were a pillow?', it is stated as 'tattha' and so forth.

Furthermore, in saying 'pamāṇaparicchedo'pi cettha natthi' (there is also no limit to the size here), it means there is no fixed regulation for the size of the bolster, such as 'it must be made only this much.' One should consider the suitability for couch-bolsters, chair-bolsters, floor-bolsters, walkway-bolsters, and foot-wiping-bolsters, and make the size according to one's preference. 'Anto saṃvelliitvā baddhaṃ' means it is bound by wrapping it well in the middle so that it becomes narrow in the center.

'Ye aṭṭha māsā' (which eight months) is connected [to the preceding text]. The phrase 'avassikasaṅketā' is an explanation of 'vassānamāsāti evaṃ apaññātā' (not known as the months of the rainy season). 'Apaññātā' means unknown or not well-known. There is also a variant reading 'asaññitā', which means 'aviññātā' (unknown). 'Eight months' refers to the four months of winter and the four months of summer, totaling eight months.

'Ovassakamaṇḍape' (in a rain-leaking shed) refers to any shed made of branches or planks where the rain leaks. 'Yattha' means in whichever districts; 'sabbatha' means in all districts. 'At the foot of a tree where crows and so forth live' refers to the foot of a tree where crows, hawks, and other birds have made nests and live permanently. However, it is allowable [to leave requisites] under a tree where birds merely rest temporarily while foraging. By the word 'kadācipi' (even at any time), it is intended to show that it is not only in the rainy season that it is unallowable to leave them (there are places where it is unallowable in summer and winter too). 'Yattha' means in whatever place; 'yadā' means at whatever time. 'So' (he) refers to the monk who spreads it for himself or the monk for whom it is spread. 'Pakatisanthate' (on a naturally spread bed) means not spreading it oneself and not asking another to spread it. 'Lajjī hoti' means that monk is naturally conscientious, or he is one who fears the destruction of the requisites.
364:
In the countrysides. "Under a tree which is a permanent dwelling of crows, etc." means a place where crows, hawks, or other birds build nests and live permanently; one should not leave [requisites] under any such tree which is a permanent dwelling of crows and so on. However, under a tree where birds searching for food merely rest for a while and then leave, it is allowable to place [requisites]. By the word "sometimes" (*kadācipi*), it is shown that this is not only during the time designated as the rainy season. "Yattha" means in which place. "Yadā" means at which time.

"So" (He) refers to the monk for whose benefit [the bedding] was spread, or the monk who spread it. "On a bedding naturally spread" means a bedding that is spread as it is, which was neither spread by oneself nor ordered to be spread by others. "He is scrupulous" (*lajjī*) means he is of a nature that possesses shame; the meaning is that he is afraid of the destruction of the requisites. Therefore, it is said, "He regards it as his own burden (concern)"; by this statement, it is shown that it is not proper to leave without informing a shameless (*alajjī*) person. "One without expectation" means one who has no expectation such as "I will come back and retrieve it"; by this statement, it is shown that if one goes while still having expectation, no offense is committed. For this very reason, in the section on non-offense (*anāpattivāra*), it is stated (in the Pācittiya Pali), "He goes while leaving it to dry in the sun." "One who goes elsewhere" means one who passes that path and goes to another place. Because he stands outside the clod-throw distance (*leḍḍupāta*), it is said, "The offense is to be incurred by the lifting of the foot"; the meaning is that for one going elsewhere, a *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) is incurred at the lifting of the first foot, and a *pācittiya* (expiation) is incurred at the lifting of the second foot.

The triad of *pācittiya* (*tikapācittiya*) occurs regarding Sangha-owned property (*saṅghika*) through the power of one who perceives it as Sangha-owned, one who is doubtful, and one who perceives it as personal property. In this same way, the triad of *dukkaṭa* should also be understood. The meaning of *cimilikā* (coarse mat) and others was already shown in the second training rule. A "foot-wiper" (*pādapuñchanī*) is an item made of small ropes or rags for the purpose of wiping the feet. A "wooden bench" (*phalakapīṭhaṃ*) is a bench made of wooden planks. It is not only for one who goes away leaving *cimilikā* and such in the open that a *dukkaṭa* is incurred; therefore, it is said, "Or whatever..." and so on. It should be connected as: whatever wooden article, whatever clay article. By the phrase "even down to a bowl-stand," it is shown that there is no need to even mention [the offense regarding] circular fans, square fans, bowl-stands, drinking cups, drinking conch-shells, and so on.

People who are inspired by the perfection of virtue of monks living in leaf-huts in the forest offer couches, benches, and so on, saying, "Please use these as communal property (*saṅghika*)." Regarding what should be done in that case, it is said, "But by a forest-dweller..." and so on. "In the absence of a rain-proof place" means when there is no rain-proof place such as a mountain cleft or a cave. This statement is an illustrative remark (*upalakkhaṇa*).
365:
Because the meaning "in the absence of compatible [monks]" (*sabhāgānaṃ abhāve*) is also desired. When a monk living in the forest, having stayed there, wishes to go elsewhere, he should go only after sending word to the monks in a nearby monastery. If there are no compatible monks, he should go after placing [the items] in a rain-proof place. If there is no rain-proof place, he should go after hanging them on a tree.

To show that it is not only this [hanging on a tree] that should be done before going, it is said, "Or as..." (*yathā vā*) and so on. "Or as it is not eaten by termites" (*yathā vā upacikāhi na khazzati*) means placing it in such a way that termites cannot eat the bedding and furniture; the meaning is that it should be done by placing them on top of stones. This is what is meant: one should place a couch on four stones, then stack the remaining couches and benches on that couch, then make a pile of mattresses and so on on top of them, store away the wooden and clay articles, and having fulfilled the duties of a departing monk (*gamika-vatta*), he should go.

To show that even an open-air dweller (*abbhokāsika*)—thinking, "I am an excellent open-air dweller"—should not sit or lie down in the open at an inappropriate time without even making a robe-tent (*cīvara-kuṭi*), it is said, "By an open-air dweller..." and so on. However, if a tent made with a four-fold robe cannot protect against getting wet, or if there is a seven-day downpour and such, it is allowable [to seek shelter] because it follows the needs of the monk's body. For a tree-root dweller (*rukkhamūlika*), the method is the same.

To show that the property of one with whom there is intimacy (*vissāsa*) becomes like one's own personal property, it is said, "In the case of personal property through intimacy" (*vissāsikapuggalike*). However, if there is no intimacy, a *dukkaṭa* is incurred [if used without permission]. "Non-human" (*amanussa*) refers to a Yakkha or a Peta. "It is obstructed" (*palibuddhaṃ hoti*) means it is disturbed or harassed.

## The Commentary on the First Training Rule on Bedding and Furniture is Finished.

## 5. Commentary on the Second Training Rule on Bedding and Furniture

"Any skin" (*yaṃ kiñci cammaṃ*) means any skin whatsoever, whether allowable or unallowable. Is it not true that in the Khandhaka, the use of lion skins and others was rejected, saying: "Monks, great skins are not to be worn—lion skin, tiger skin, leopard skin; for him who should wear one, there is an offense of wrongdoing (*dukkaṭa*)"? To clarify this [question], it is said, "For lion skins and others..." and so on. The rejection applies only to carrying them as one's own possession (*pariharaṇa*); as one's own...
366:
## 
If one makes it one's own property and brings it to various monasteries, spreading it on couches, chairs, and so forth, the use [of skins such as lion skins] is forbidden. However, if it is made the property of the monastery and used as a floor covering, there is no fault. Therefore, it is said: "In the use of monastery requisites, there is no such thing as unallowable skin."

Because they cover the body with this cloth, it is called pāvāra (cloak). A rug with hair on one side or both sides is called kojava. The remaining bedding is called sesa, which includes bolsters, sitting cloths, grass spreads, and leaf spreads. Among these, a bolster for a couch or a chair is called bhisi. A spread with a border or fringe should be known as nisīdana. A spread made of any kind of grass is called tiṇasanthāra. The same method applies to a leaf spread (paṇṇasanthāra). Here, the bolster is clear as it was mentioned below. The sitting cloth is also clear through the Nisīdana Sikkhāpada. Grass and leaf spreads are well-known in the world. Therefore, it is said: "It is indeed clear."

"One should neither remove it oneself nor have it removed by another" means that one should not remove it oneself and fail to place it in a suitable location, nor should one have another do so. Therefore, it is said: "As it was placed," and so forth. A monk who places that bedding should, as previously mentioned in the section "on four stones," etc., place it in a rain-proof area inside the monastery. If the monastery leaks and grass or bricks have been brought for roofing, he should roof it if he is able. If he is unable, he should place it in a spot that does not leak. If the entire monastery leaks, the able monk should place it in the house of a lay devotee in the village. If those devotees do not accept it, saying, "Venerable sir, property of the Saṅgha is a heavy responsibility; we fear fire and other dangers," then he should place the couch on stones in an open space, place the remaining requisites according to the previous method, and cover them with grass and leaves. For if even a small part remains there, it will be of benefit to other monks who come to that monastery. The precinct (upacāra) is the area within two stone-throws from the very last monastery building.

Regarding this monastery, the decision on whether one must ask permission or not is as follows: Whether it be a long hall or a leaf-roofed hut built on the ground, or a hut built on wooden posts where termites might climb, a monk departing from that monastery must go only after asking permission. For if such a monastery is left without care for even a few days, termite mounds will arise. However, in a monastery built on a stone slab or on stone pillars, a stone cave, or a plastered monastery where there is no fear of termites...
367:
## 
A monk departing from such a monastery may go either after asking permission or without asking. Therefore, it was said: "But where..." etc. If termites climb up even in such a monastery from one side, he must go only after asking permission. Asking permission is a duty; it is the duty of a departing monk (gamikavatta). This is said to show the proper procedure (itikattabyatā), not to show a dukkhaṭa offense for breaking a duty. Some teachers say, "It is to show a dukkhaṭa offense," but that is not appropriate. This is because it is stated in the Vattakkhandhaka Commentary: "In a monastery built on a stone slab or on stone pillars where termites cannot climb, there is no offense for one who goes without asking permission."

When asking permission, if a monk is present, he should ask the monk; if no monk is present, the novice (sāmaṇera); if no novice is present, the monastery attendant (ārāmika); if no attendant is present, the donor who had the monastery built, or anyone from that donor's family.

Regarding the term "upacāre," it is explained as "bahi āsanne," meaning in a place near the outside of the monastery. "Upaṭṭhānasālāya vā" means in the refectory. In the phrase "dukkaṭam eva," for a monk who goes after spreading the ten kinds of bedding mentioned above in a secure place like an inner chamber, a pācittiya offense is stated because both the bedding and the monastery could be destroyed by termites and become mere termite mounds. For a monk who goes after spreading them in the refectory and so forth outside the monastery, only the bedding might be lost due to the lack of security of the place, but the monastery is not destroyed; therefore, a dukkhaṭa offense is stated here. As for couches and chairs, since termites cannot eat them instantly, a dukkhaṭa offense is stated for a monk who goes after spreading them even inside the monastery. If they are spread in the precinct of the monastery, monks wandering through the monastery will see them and put them away.

Regarding the phrase "uddharaṇāni katvā," a monk who goes after removing them should remove all the cords and cane of the couches and chairs, bundle them together, and hang them on a robe-rail before departing. A monk who comes later to stay must also do the same when he departs after spreading and sleeping on the couch or chair. A monk who stays after spreading bedding outside a wall which was originally inside the wall must, at the time of departure, put it back in the place where it was taken. The same method applies to a monk who stays on the lower floor after bringing it down from the upper floor of a mansion (pāsāda). Even if couches and chairs are spread in night quarters or day quarters, they must be put back in the place where they were taken at the time of departure. The same method applies when having another remove them. A monk who goes after asking permission...
368:
Furthermore, as previously stated in the method beginning with "If a monk is present, the monk should be asked," one should depart only after asking permission.

## The Explanation of the Second Senāsana Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 6. Explanation of the Anupakhajja Sikkhāpada

Regarding the word "knowing" (jānanta), where does this specific meaning "knowing that this monk is one who should not be made to get up" come from? It is stated starting with "tenevassā" etc. In the word-by-word analysis (padabhājana), only knowing the seniority etc. is mentioned, not the state of not being made to get up. Addressing this inquiry, it is stated starting with "vuddho hi" etc. "Greatly helpful" (bahūpakārataṃ) means being very beneficial through roles such as being a storekeeper (bhaṇḍāgārika).

To show that it does not mean only this helpfulness, it is stated starting with "guṇavisiṭṭhatañca" etc. Therefore, it shows that a dwelling should not be given if one is helpful but lacks special virtues, or if one has special virtues but is not helpful. Some say, "Having considered the helpfulness of the storekeeper and the special virtues of the Dhamma-preachers (dhammakathika) etc." "For the purpose of permanent residence" (dhuvavāsatthāya) means for the sake of living there constantly. "Having authorized" (sammannitvā) means having authorized through the act of notification (apalokana-kamma). Indeed, in this context, the Saṅgha gives a suitable dwelling even to a sick monk (gilāna). However, it is stated separately to show that even if a sick monk stays in a dwelling not yet given by the Saṅgha after asking, he should not be harassed but should be treated with compassion.

"One and a half cubits all around" refers to the couch or chair (mañcapīṭha) placed in the middle. If a sufficient area is seen on one side, it should be measured from there. "From the foot-washing stone" (pādadhovanapāsāṇato) means starting from the stone for washing feet placed at the doorway. In the phrase "an offense of pācittiya for one who sits or lies down," a pācittiya is incurred by the mere act of sitting or the mere act of lying down. "For one who does so repeatedly" means for one who sits or lies down again and again after getting up.

In a communal dwelling (saṅghika), a triple pācittiya should be understood based on the perception of it being communal, being doubtful, or the perception of it being individual. In an individual dwelling (puggalika), a triple dukkata is incurred based on the perception of it being communal, being doubtful, or the perception of another's individual property. "In the precincts of the monastery" (vihārassa upacāre) means in the nearby area outside of that monastery.

## The Explanation of the Anupakhajja Sikkhāpada is finished.
369:
## 7. Explanation of the Nikkaddhana Sikkhāpada

"Anekakoṭṭhakāni" refers to rest houses having many gateways. Teachers say that if one hears the words "Go out!" and leaves of one's own accord, there is no offense for the monk who ordered it.

"In the expelling of his belongings" (tassa parikkhāranikkaddhane) means pulling out any of his property such as the bowl, robes, water-strainer, water-filter, couch, chair, mattress, pillow, etc., or even at the minimum, a piece of dye-bark. Because of such handling, a dukkata offense is incurred. The same method applies to having someone else pull them out. However, for belongings that are tied up tightly, only a single offense is incurred.

Only a monk who causes quarrels and strife may be expelled from the entire monastery (saṅghārāma). This is because if he gains a faction, he might even cause a schism in the Saṅgha. Shameless monks (alajji) and others, however, should only be expelled from their own living quarters. It is not proper to expel them from the entire monastery. Therefore, it is stated in the commentary starting with "even from the entire monastery" (sakalasaṅghārāmatopi).

## The Explanation of the Nikkaddhana Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 8. Explanation of the Vehāsakuṭi Sikkhāpada

"In an upper-story cell" (uparivehāsakuṭiyā) refers to a cell on the upper floor where the floorboards are not fixed. Therefore, it is stated starting with "on an upper floor with an uncovered surface" etc. Any two-storied or three-storied cell with an uncovered upper floor is called a "vehāsakuṭi". This is the characteristic of a vehāsakuṭi. If so, why is it stated in the word-by-word analysis (padabhājana) as "not hitting the head of a medium-sized man"? It is stated starting with "In the padabhājana, however," etc., to show the specific vehāsakuṭi intended in this training rule.

"Of a medium-sized man" (majjhimassa purisassa) means a man of average height. It is called "asīsaghaṭṭā" because the head does not hit the lowest beams. "Having pierced the members" (aṅge vijjhitvā) means having pierced the frame-ends (aṭani). "With legs inserted" (pavesitapādakaṃ) refers to a couch with legs fitted into the frame. Therefore, the meaning already stated in the passage beginning with "or on the ground" (bhūmatthe vā) is reviewed as the reason. This is stated because the aforementioned meaning applies to couches with legs fitted into the frame, etc.

"Suddenly" (sahasā) means by overpowering or overwhelming. "In a non-upper-story cell" (avehāsakuṭikāya) refers to leaf huts etc. built on the ground; in such places, there is no offense for sitting on a couch. This is because in such a dwelling, it is not possible to harass another...
370:
It is not possible to cause harm. 'Sīsaghaṭṭā' refers to a dwelling that is touched by the head; even in such a dwelling, there is no offense. This is because it is impossible to move about in that lower-level dwelling without stooping; therefore, since it is not a place for walking about, it does not amount to harming others. 'Upari talaṃ vā padarasañcitaṃ' means the upper floor is covered closely with wooden planks without gaps. 'Kiñci gaṇhāti vā' means taking anything such as a robe hung on ivory pegs and so on. In the phrase 'laggati vā', the method is the same. 'Aṇi paṭāṇi' are opposing pegs. It means that when these pegs are fixed, the legs do not fall out even when one sits; such pegs are fixed at the tops of the legs of beds and chairs. Therefore, he said 'pādasīsānaṃ' and so on.

## The Explanation of the Vehāsakuṭi Training Rule is finished.

## 9. Explanation of the Mahallakavihāra Training Rule

'Piṭṭhasaṅghāṭassa' means of the doorframe. 'Sāmantā aḍḍhateyyahattho padeso' refers to a place measuring two and a half cubits around the doorframe, where there is a door in the middle and a high wall above. In a small dwelling, however, it is on two sides. There also, when the door leaf is opened, it strikes a certain wall; that wall may also be one where the surrounding area (upacāra) is incomplete. If there is space for plastering even at the lower part of the door, that place should also be plastered. In the phrase 'aggalaṭṭhapanāya', the word 'aggala' (bolt/bar) implies the doorframe together with the door leaves because of their connection. Therefore, he said 'sakavāṭakassa' and so on. By the phrase 'niccalabhāvatthāya', he shows that such fixing is for the purpose of being without movement in this place. What is the meaning here? He said 'kavāṭဉှိ' and so on. 'Kampati' means it shakes. It means that for the purpose of fixing the door leaves, one should repeatedly plaster it oneself or have others plaster it up to the two-and-a-half-cubit area of the doorframe.

This meaning is stated neither in the Mātikā nor in the Word-Analysis (Padabhājana); if so, from where is it to be known? He said 'tattha' and so on. 'Kiñcāpi' means even if. 'Atthuppattiyam' means in the origin (nidāna) of the training rule. 'Adhikārato' means by way of following in sequence. Because it obstructs light, it is called 'ālokasandhi' (light-junction). Therefore, he said, 'ālokasandhi refers to window shutters.' There, 'vātapānakavāṭakā' means window planks.
371:
Except for the permitted place, it is not proper to repeatedly plaster or have others plaster in any other place. Some teachers say, 'Having finished the work to be done with fine clay, if one plasters a fourth time, a Pācittiya offense is incurred.' Other teachers, however, say, 'Since repeated plastering in places other than the stated measure is merely prohibited and is not declared as a Pācittiya offense, a Dukkaṭa offense is incurred.'

'Adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ' means to be managed. In the word 'appaharite', the word 'appa' has the sense of absence (abhāva), as in 'appiccho' and so on; therefore, it means 'aharite' (in a place without green growth). Early crops such as hill paddy and rice are called 'pubbaṇṇa', and their opposites such as green gram and black gram are called 'aparaṇṇa'. 'Vuttaṃ' means sown. By the statement 'The monk who, standing in that place, manages [the work] incurs a Dukkaṭa,' he intends to show that a dwelling should be built in a place where there are no crops and so on within the stated surrounding perimeter. In a place where they exist, it is not proper to have it built. In the same way, it is [measured] by the edge of the eaves. Standing in that place is because it is a spot where the dwelling about to fall will not fall; the intention is that it should not fall upon that monk. Since the area inside the demarcated space is where the dwelling would fall, one is not allowed to stand and manage there even if there is no green growth. Therefore, it is said, 'Even if there is no green growth inside that [area], one should not stand there.'

'Tato ce uttari' means in the fourth row or layer above the three rows or layers. Therefore, it is said, 'when it is being roofed by a row' and so on. There, 'roofing by a row' (maggena) means roofing straight without circling. 'Pariyāyena' means roofing by circling. Between those two, roofing by a row is obtainable with bricks, stones, and plaster; roofing by circling is obtainable with grass and leaves. Therefore, he said 'iṭṭhakasilāsudhāhi' and so on. Thus, as one wishes, having determined (managed) two rows or two layers, one should give the order for the third row or layer, saying 'Roof it thus,' and then depart. If one does not depart, one should remain silent. All this roofing should be understood as roofing upon roofing. For, thinking that a dwelling roofed layer upon layer will be leak-proof for a long time, they roof it in this way. 'Tiṇamuṭṭhigaṇanāya' means by the count of handfuls of grass.

'Tikapācittiyaṃ' means three Pācittiya offenses by way of perceiving it as more, being doubtful, or perceiving it as less when it exceeds two or three layers. In making white color and so on...
372:
In the making of white color, dark black color, smoothing with red chalk, floral work, creeper work, sea-monster teeth designs, and five-finger marks (it is permissible). In the phrase 'leṇaguhātiṇakuṭikādīsu', 'leṇa' refers to a place fitted with a door. 'Guhā' refers to a mere mountain cave without a door. 'Tiṇakuṭikā' (grass hut) is well-known.

## The Explanation of the Mahallakavihāra Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 10. The Explanation of the Sappāṇaka Sikkhāpada

'Ekassmiṃ ghaṭe ekāva āpatti' means that (when pouring water containing insects) into a single water pot, only one offense is committed. This method is the same for all utensils such as bowls and pots. 'Vicchindantassa' refers to one who pours while breaking the flow of water. 'Ekekaṃ pakkhipantassa' refers to one who throws in grass, leaves, fine clay, or other things such as firewood, cow dung, etc., one by one. 'Pariyādānaṃ' means exhaustion or depletion.

Just as lighting a lamp with a wholesome mind does not involve the intention to kill (vadhaka-cetanā), even if one knows that "small insects like crickets will fall into the lamp and die," similarly, for one who knows before pouring that "insects will die by this pouring" but pours thinking "I am pouring this water," the intention to kill does not arise. Therefore, it is said, "without the intention to kill," and so on. By acting in this way, the point regarding "transgressing the regulation" (paṇṇattivajja) is also established. 'Ticittaṃ' refers to the three types of mind: wholesome (kusala), unwholesome (akusala), and indeterminate (abyākata). This is because for one who pours or causes to pour while disregarding (trampling upon) the regulation, an unwholesome mind arises. For one who pours or causes to pour for the purpose of washing, thinking "I will wash the seat," a wholesome mind arises. For an Arahant who, not knowing the regulation, performs acts such as pouring water, an indeterminate mind arises. Thus, there are three types of mind by way of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.

## The Explanation of the Sappāṇaka Sikkhāpada is finished.

## The Second Chapter: Bhūtagāma Vagga.

## 3. Ovāda Vagga

## 1. The Explanation of the Ovāda Sikkhāpada

'Aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgatassa' refers to one endowed with the eight qualities, such as "being virtuous," and so on. 'Anuññātā' means authorized by the Blessed One in the introduction (origin story) of this training rule.
373:
(The Blessed One) has authorized. The phrase 'vassasatūpasampannāya' etc., is to show the eight Garudhammas (Heavy Rules) which will be mentioned. In that context, 'sāmīcikamma' (proper conduct) refers to suitable duties such as giving way on the path, fanning, and asking about drinking water. By the word 'ādi'—

“A nun must not spend the rains in a residence where there are no monks; every fortnight a nun should desire two things from the Saṅgha of monks: the asking of the date of the Uposatha and the approaching for exhortation; having completed the rains, a nun must invite (pavāraṇā) before both Saṅghas in respect of three matters: what has been seen, heard, or suspected; a nun who has committed a heavy offense (garudhamma/saṅghādisesa) must undergo penance (pakkhamānatta) for a fortnight before both Saṅghas; a female probationer (sikkhamānā) who has trained in the six rules for two years should seek higher ordination (upasampadā) from both Saṅghas; a nun should not revile or scold a monk in any way; from today, the path of speech from nuns to monks is closed, but the path of speech from monks to nuns is not closed” —

these seven rules are to be included. 'Garudhammā' means rules to be respected. They are called 'Garudhammā' because they must be accepted by nuns with great respect.

“Or by another Dhamma” means by any other Dhamma except for the eight Garudhammas. “To one who exhorts a nun who is newly ordained among nuns” means to one who exhorts a newly ordained nun with the Garudhammas, or to one who exhorts a nun who received higher ordination from the monks; in such cases, only the offense (pācittiya) according to the object occurs. In the words 'adhammakamme' etc., the act of giving authorization (sammuti) to exhort a nun should be understood as 'kamma' (legal act); thus it is said “even for one authorized,” and so on. “Three pācittiyas for one who exhorts a divided (vagga) Saṅgha of nuns” means that for one who exhorts a divided Saṅgha of nuns, three pācittiyas occur by way of perceiving it as divided, being doubtful, or perceiving it as unified. “Likewise for one who is doubtful” means that for one who is doubtful about an unlawful act (adhamma-kamma) and exhorts a divided Saṅgha of nuns, three pācittiyas occur. This same method should be understood for the phrase “and for one who perceives it as a lawful act” (dhammakammasaññino ca). Just as there are nine pācittiyas for one who exhorts a divided Saṅgha of nuns, likewise, for one who perceives an unlawful act as an unlawful act and exhorts a unified (samagga) Saṅgha of nuns, three pācittiyas occur by way of perceiving that Saṅgha as divided, being doubtful, or perceiving it as unified; similarly for one who is doubtful and one who perceives it as a lawful act, there are nine pācittiyas. Therefore, it is said, “nine even in a unified Saṅgha of nuns,” and so on. However, in a lawful act (dhamma-kamma), for one who perceives it as an unlawful act and exhorts a divided Saṅgha of nuns, three dukkaṭas (wrongdoings) occur; likewise for one who is doubtful about that lawful act and exhorts a divided Saṅgha of nuns, three dukkaṭas occur; likewise for one who perceives that lawful act as a lawful act and exhorts a divided Saṅgha of nuns, three dukkaṭas occur—thus making nine dukkaṭas. Furthermore, for one who exhorts a unified Saṅgha of nuns, eight dukkaṭas occur. In this way, there are seventeen dukkaṭas. Therefore, it is said, “sace pana,” and so on. “Another Dhamma” refers to a Sutta or Abhidhamma other than the eight Garudhammas. If it is asked whether a dukkaṭa offense occurs for a monk who teaches another Sutta or Abhidhamma, the answer is that the nuns say, “Venerable sir, we are unified,” and they desire the exhortation (the teaching of the eight Garudhammas). Therefore, a dukkaṭa offense occurs for a monk who sets aside the exhortation and teaches another Dhamma. “Without being assigned the exhortation” means “Sister, this is...”
374:
For a monk who exhorts (a group of bhikkhunīs) while perceiving a legal act according to the Dhamma (dhamma-kamma) as a legal act not according to the Dhamma (adhamma-kamma), there are three offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Similarly, for one who exhorts while in doubt, there are three dukkaṭa offenses. For one who exhorts while perceiving it as a legal act according to the Dhamma, there are three dukkaṭa offenses. Thus, there are nine dukkaṭa offenses. For a monk who exhorts a harmonious community of bhikkhunīs, there are eight dukkaṭa offenses. In total, there are seventeen dukkaṭa offenses. Therefore, the author of the Saṅgaha said, "Sace pana..." and so forth.

"Aññaṃ dhammaṃ" (other Dhamma) refers to either a Suttanta or the Abhidhamma other than the eight heavy rules (garudhamma). By the words, "Venerable sir, we are in harmony," they are longing for the exhortation, which is the eight heavy rules. Therefore, an offense of wrong-doing is incurred by a monk who, setting aside the exhortation on the heavy rules, speaks on other Dhamma. "Ovādañca aniyyātetvā" means not saying, "Sister, this is the exhortation on the heavy rules." "Paripucchaṃ deti" means he explains the meaning of that very Pali text of the heavy rules which has been well-studied. "Osārehi" means "recite by raising the voice." "Osāreti" means he recites the eight heavy rules in Pali. "Pañhaṃ puṭṭho" refers to a monk who is asked by a bhikkhunī a question related to the heavy rules or related to the aggregates (khandha) and so forth.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Exhortation is finished.

## 2. The Explanation of the Training Rule on the Setting (of the Sun)

"Ekatoupasampanna" (ordained on one side) refers to one who has just been ordained in the community of bhikkhunīs. From this point forward, wherever the term "ekatoupasampanna" is mentioned, it should be understood in this sense.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on the Setting (of the Sun) is finished.

## 3. The Explanation of the Training Rule on the Bhikkhunīs' Quarters

"Saṃvāsāya" means for the purpose of communion, such as performing the Uposatha and so forth. "Itaraṃ" refers to a bhikkhunī who has attained the status of a nun in both communities (of monks and nuns).

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on the Bhikkhunīs' Quarters is finished.

## 4. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Material Gain

Because robes and other requisites are grasped and touched by craving and wrong view as "my property, my robe," they are called "āmisa" (material things). Since material gain itself is the cause, it is called "āmisa-hetu" (for the sake of material gain). Therefore, the author of the Saṅgaha said, "Cīvarādīnaṃ aññatarahetu" (for the sake of one or another of the robes, etc.). By the word "ādi" (and so forth), alms-food, lodgings, medicinal requisites, honor, respect, reverence, salutation, and offerings are included. "Avaṇṇakāmatāya" means solely because of the desire for a bad reputation (to be spread about the other).
375:
In the phrases beginning with "dhamma-kamme," the act of authorization to exhort bhikkhunīs (bhikkhunovāda-sammuti-kamma) should be understood as "kamma" (legal act). Therein, "tika-pācittiya" (triad of pācittiya) means that in a legal act according to the Dhamma (dhamma-kamma), three offenses to be confessed (pācittiya) occur based on the perceptions of one who perceives it as a legal act according to the Dhamma, one who is in doubt, and one who perceives it as a legal act not according to the Dhamma. Similarly, in a legal act not according to the Dhamma (adhamma-kamma), the three offenses of wrong-doing (tika-dukkaṭa) should be understood based on the perceptions of one who perceives it as a legal act according to the Dhamma, one who is in doubt, and one who perceives it as a legal act not according to the Dhamma.

"Asammata" (unauthorized) refers to an ordained monk (upasampanna) who has been assigned a duty by an authorized monk or by the Saṅgha. One might ask, "Is not the authorization to exhort bhikkhunīs given only to a monk and not to a novice?" Therefore, the text says "tattha" and so forth. Even if assigned by an authorized monk or the Saṅgha, a learned novice (sāmaṇera) should be understood as "asammata" (unauthorized).

"Pakatiyā cīvarādihetu ovadantaṃ pana evaṃ bhaṇantassa" means (a pācittiya is incurred) by a monk who speaks thus with the perception, "This monk exhorts for the sake of robes and so forth," regarding a monk who naturally exhorts for the sake of robes and so forth. For a monk who speaks thus with the perception, "He does not exhort for the sake of robes and so forth," an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is incurred.

"Anāmisantaratā" means the absence of a mind seeking material gain, meaning the absence of the disposition (ajjhāsaya) that "I will exhort for the sake of material gain." In this context, the word "antara" is a synonym for the mind (citta), as in the passage, "Yassantarato na santi kopā" (in whose inner mind there is no anger).

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Material Gain is finished.

## 5. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Giving Robes

The fifth training rule has a clear meaning.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Giving Robes is finished.

## 6. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Sewing Robes
