"Sūciṃ pavesetvā pavesetvā nīharaṇe" means a pācittiya offense is incurred at every stitch (every time the needle is inserted and withdrawn). For a monk who plans and examines, saying "I will sew," or for one who cuts (the cloth), an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is incurred.

"Satakkhattumpi vijjhitvā sakiṃ nīharantassa" refers to a monk who, for the sake of inserting a long thread without withdrawing the entire needle, pierces the cloth even a hundred times and then withdraws it only once. "Sibbā" (sew!) means being told once, "Sew the robe." "Niṭṭhāpeti" means completing all the needlework. "Tassa ārāpathe ārāpathe pācittiyaṃ" means that for the monk who was commanded, a pācittiya offense is incurred for each and every stitch when inserting and withdrawing the needle.
376:
The Elder Udāyi refers to the frivolous Elder Udāyi (Lāḷudāyi). Sewing or causing to sew with the characteristics mentioned refers to sewing or causing to sew with the characteristics mentioned in the manner of "inserting the needle," etc.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Sewing Robes is finished.

## 7. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Arrangement (Saṃvidhāna)

"Having arranged" (saṃvidahitvā) means having consulted by saying either, "Come, let us go to such and such a village," or "I will go tomorrow, you should come too." This consultation is, in essence, the act of making an appointment (saṅketakamma). Therefore, it is said (by the author of the Saṅgaha) that "it means making an appointment at the time of departure."

One who arranges in an improper place (akappiyabhūmi) refers to one who arranges while standing inside a village, at the door of a bhikkhunīs' quarters, on a main road, or at other places such as a four-way intersection, a three-way intersection, an elephant stable, etc. Therefore, it is said, "leaving aside that place," etc.

"Even if it is near" (āsannassāpi) means even if it is very close, even if the distance is only about a cubit, it is considered another village. "Another village" refers to a village other than the one from which he departed. "One who enters that village" refers to one who enters the precinct (upacāra) of that other village. If he wishes to go to a distant place, an offense is committed according to the previous method every time he enters a village precinct. Therefore, it is said, "Thus, Pācittiya offenses are committed according to the count of entering village precincts." However, there is no offense in passing beyond those various villages.

"If there is no village" means there is no village within half a league (yojana). If there is a village within that half-league, Pācittiya offenses are committed only by the count of other villages. "An offense of Pācittiya is committed by the count of half-leagues" means a Pācittiya offense is committed for every half-league. For a monk who passes beyond each half-league, it means that having intended, "I will now pass beyond it," there is a dukkaṭa offense at the first step and a pācittiya offense at the second step. In this method, an offense is committed upon passing beyond, but no offense is committed upon entering.

In the case of a "broken appointment" (visaṅketa), there is no offense only in the case of a mistake in the appointment of time, such as saying "Let us go in the morning" but going in the afternoon, or saying "Let us go today" but going tomorrow. However, even if there is a mistake in the appointment of the exit gate or a mistake in the appointment of the route, an offense is indeed committed.

"In times of danger" (āpadāsu) means when a country is ruined and the inhabitants travel about by mounting a wheel (vehicle); in such times of danger, there is no offense. "Mounting a wheel" means either the wheel of postures (iriyāpathacakka) or the wheel of a cart...
377:
...or mounting (the wheel) is the meaning. "By the training rule concerning women" (mātugāma-sikkhāpadena) refers to the seventh training rule in the Sappāṇaka Chapter (the Mātugāma Training Rule).

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Arrangement is finished.

## 8. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Boarding a Boat

"Intent on play" (kīḷāpurekkhāro) means being focused on amusement and play through worldly enjoyment and friendship. "In that very way" (tatheva) means only by way of such play. "By way of a riverbank without a village" (agāmakatīrapassena) means by way of a riverbank where there are no villages within half a league. Since it is stated in the Pāḷi, "whether a boat going upstream or a boat going downstream," there is no offense even if one goes with the intention of playing in lakes, oceans, etc. Therefore, it was said, "But in the ocean, it is allowable to go as one pleases."

"By a broken appointment" (visaṅketa) means in this training rule also, there is no offense only for a mistake in the appointment of time; however, for a monk who goes with a mistake in the appointment of the landing place or the boat, there is indeed an offense.

"The rest" (sesaṃ) refers to the remaining points along with the origination (samuṭṭhāna), etc. Some teachers say that because of the words "intent on play" and "having arranged," this training rule involves an unwholesome mind and is a worldly fault (lokavajja); therefore, they say that "the rest" refers to the remaining points excluding the two: "prescriptive fault" (paṇṇattivajja) and "having three types of mind" (ticitta). That statement should not be accepted. This is because even if one boards a boat with the intention of playing, upon entering another village or passing beyond half a league, one might gain spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and realize Arahantship, or fall asleep, or go while attending to a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). If so, where could there be the possession of an unwholesome mind that would make this training rule one of an unwholesome mind and a worldly fault?

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Boarding a Boat is finished.

## 9. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Food Cooked (by a Nun)

"Cooked" (paripācitaṃ) means (almsfood) that has been brought to completion in cooking (by a nun), having been prepared and set aside in a way that the monk may receive it. Therefore, the words "not for her," etc., were said. "For her" (tassā) refers to the monk who would consume that almsfood. "By extolling the virtues of the monk" means by making his virtues known, such as "The venerable one is a preacher," "The venerable one is very learned," etc.
378:
Having manifested (the virtues). Piṇḍapāta (almsfood) refers to any one of the five kinds of staple food (bhojana). This word samārambha is said as 'samāraddha' (undertaken) because it completes the sense of an action. Paṭiyādita means (almsfood) that has been prepared. Because almsfood, even if not yet exerted for by relatives or those who have given an invitation for the sake of a monk, is effectively 'well-exerted' (samāraddha) in meaning due to being able to be brought as desired; therefore, it is said, 'whether it belongs to relatives or to those who have given an invitation.'

Ubhayattha (in both cases) occurs in both almsfood arranged by a nun and that not arranged by a nun. Avasese (in the remaining) occurs in all things such as conjee (yāgu), hard food (khajjaka), various fruits (phalāphala), etc., even if arranged by a nun. However, one is not exempt from the offence of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) in the remaining matters through signs, hints, peripheral talk, or intimation (viññatti).

## The Commentary on the Pari-pācita Training Rule is finished.

## 10. Raho-nisajja-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā

Uparī (above) refers to the Acelaka-vagga (Naked Ascetic Chapter). Upanandassa catuttha-sikkhāpadena (by the fourth training rule of Upananda) refers to the training rule concerning sitting in private with a woman in an unshielded place. Because it is the fourth among the training rules laid down concerning the Elder Upananda, it is called 'the fourth training rule of Upananda.' If it is of the same scope, why was it laid down separately? It is said, 'It was laid down separately by way of the origin of the incident (aṭṭhuppatti).' In that context, aṭṭhuppatti-vasena means by way of the arising of the meaning, (that is) by way of the arising of the sitting in private by a nun alone. The intention here is: although the scope is the same, this training rule was laid down separately first because the incident of this training rule occurred before the incident of the fourth training rule.

## The Commentary on the Raho-nisajja Training Rule is finished.

## The Third Chapter: The Chapter on Exhortation (Ovāda-vagga).

## 4. The Chapter on Food (Bhojana-vagga).

## 1. Āvasatha-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā

In this term 'agilāno' (not ill), it refers to a monk who is able to travel at least two gāvutas; therefore, it is said, 'one who is able to travel even half a yojana'.
380:
## 2. Commentary on the Gaṇabhojana Training Rule

Gaṇabhojana (group-meal) occurs because of eating food belonging to a group (gaṇa) that was obtained on account of the group. Therefore, it is said, "in the food of a group." In this context, it is stated "in the food of a group." That "group" is intended in various ways, such as "in some places by two [monks], in some places by three," and so on. If one asks how many are intended here, it is said, "And here," etc. That group-meal arises in two ways: through invitation (nimantana) or through request (viññatti). Therefore, it is said, "through their invitation," and so on. In that statement, "through invitation" refers to an improper invitation. "Of the five [foods] such as cooked rice" refers to the five: cooked rice (odana), confections (kummāsa), flour-cake (sattu), fish (maccha), and meat (maṃsa).

It should be connected thus: one invites by taking the name of one of the five foods, using any synonym or another language, in such a manner as "I invite you with cooked rice; please accept my rice." "Four" refers to four monks situated in one place or in various places. This is a defining statement; therefore, it means four or more monks. "By a synonym" means by using alternative terms such as bhatta or anna. "By another language" means by using other languages such as Andhra or Tamil. "Taking the name of the five foods" means taking the name of any one of the five foods. "I invite you with cooked rice" means "Venerable sirs, I invite you with cooked rice." By the word "etc." (ādi), one should include such phrases as "Please desire, look upon, accept, wait for; I invite you with confections; please accept my confections, please desire, look upon, accept, wait for."

"Together" refers to monks who, upon being seen standing or sitting in one place, are invited together in this way: "Venerable sirs, I invite you with cooked rice," and so on. "Invited separately" means those who are invited separately by going to four different cells (pariveṇa) or monasteries (vihāra). Alternatively, even if they are in the same place, if one monk is invited by the son and another by the father, etc., they are also said to be invited separately. "They accept together" means they accept while situated within each other's vicinity (upacāra) of twelve cubits.

If one asks why it is a group-meal even if eaten separately, it is said, "Here, the acceptance itself is the standard." If that is so, why is it stated in the Pāḷi: "What is called a group-meal is where four monks, invited with any one of the five foods, eat; this is called a group-meal"? That...
381:
...is only for the purpose of defining the acceptance. Since monks do not eat what has not been formally accepted, the word "eat" serves as a term defining the acceptance.

"Having requested together or separately" means that four monks, seeing a lay devotee while standing or sitting together, say, "Give rice for all four of us," or having approached individually, say, "Give me rice, give me rice," thus requesting either together or separately. "To both those kinds of group-meals" refers to the group-meal obtained through invitation and the group-meal obtained through request; it means to both these kinds of group-meals. "In accepting thus" means in accepting together.

"Because of the cracking of the feet" means, at the minimum, because the feet are cracked such that the inner flesh is visible from outside the thick skin (callus). "Unable to walk for alms" means being unable to walk for alms within the village because of the suffering that arises merely from contact with sand or gravel.

"While the robe is being made" means while the robe is being sewn after having obtained the cloth and thread. "Any business concerning the robe" refers to any task to be done for the robe, such as planning, cutting, or tacking with thread; it is intended to mean even as little as threading a needle.

The phrase "even for half a league (yojana)" is stated as the minimum measure. For a monk who wishes to go far, it goes without saying; a monk who is travelling is allowed to eat even within a distance of one gāvuta (a quarter-league) within the half-league; however, once he has arrived, he is allowed for one day. When one wishes to board a boat, is boarding, or is disembarking, this is called the time of boat-boarding (nāvābhiruhana-samaya); therefore, it is said, "The same method applies to the time of boat-boarding." The distinction here is that a monk who has boarded may eat as long as he has not yet disembarked, even if he has reached his desired destination.

"Four monks" is the minimum limit. Where a hundred or a thousand have gathered, it goes without saying. Therefore, at such a time, one should eat after resolving it as a "Great Occasion" (Mahāsamaya). "Any monk" (pabbajita) refers to one of the fellow practitioners or one of the ascetics of other sects.

"Two or three accept together" means that even if two or three monks accept together, having consented to an improper invitation, there is no offense for them [regarding group-meals]. However, teachers say there is indeed an offense under the training rules of Superior Food (Paṇītabhojana) or Requesting Curry and Rice (Sūpodanavinyatti); this statement should be investigated.

"In regular meals, etc." refers to regular meals (niccabhatta), ticket-food (salākabhatta), fortnightly meals (pakkhika), Uposatha-day meals (uposathika), and meals on the day after Uposatha (pāṭipadika). Among these, "regular meal" refers to a permanent meal (dhuvabhatta). "Accept the regular meal"...
382:
The teachers say, "It is also allowable for many monks to accept [food] together." The same method applies to food distributed by tickets (salākabhatta) and so forth.

## The Explanation of the Gaṇabhojana Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 3. Explanation of the Paramparabhojana Sikkhāpada

"Gaṇabhojane vuttanayeneva" means approaching a monk and saying, "Venerable sir, I invite you with rice; please accept my rice," and so forth, using any synonym or another language to name one of the five kinds of food and inviting him, just as previously stated. "Nimantitassa" refers to one who has been invited with an improper invitation. "Avikappetvā" means without performing vikappanā (assignment) in the presence or absence [of the recipient], that is, without relinquishing or giving it away. Indeed, this assignment of a meal (bhatta-vikappanā) is allowable whether in one's presence or absence. Therefore, it is said, "Yo bhikkhu pañcasu sahadhammikesu" and so forth.

"Aññatra nimantanabhojanavatthusmiṃ" means other than the house where one was first invited, due to the reason of eating at another invited house. If there are three supplementary regulations (anupaññatti), why does it say "four supplementary regulations" in the Parivāra? To answer this, it says "Parivāre pana" and so forth. "Vikappanampi gahetvā" means that since the allowance of assignment (vikappanā) is similar to a supplementary regulation, it is taken as a supplementary regulation. "Ekasaṃsaṭṭhānī" refers to foods mixed in one place. The summary of this meaning is: having invited two or three families and having them sit in one place, if they bring food from here and there and pour the rice and pour the curries so that it becomes a single mixture, there is no offense in eating such mixed food.

If the food from the first invitation is at the bottom and the food from the subsequent invitations is on top, an offense is committed by a monk who eats starting from the top. However, if he puts his hand inside, picks up even a single morsel from the first invitation, and eats it, then from that time onwards, no matter how he eats, there is no offense. "Dve tīṇi nimantanāni ekato vါ katvā bhuñjati" means putting two or three invited meals together, mixing them, and eating them as one. In the passages such as "sakalena gāmena vā" (by the whole village), if the whole village has invited together, there is no offense for a monk who eats at any house without distinction. The same method applies to a group (pūga). "Nimantiyamāno vā bhikkhāṃ gahessāmīti vadati" means when being invited with "Please accept the meal (bhatta)," he says "I will accept the alms-food (bhikkhā)."
383:
When being invited, he says, "I have no need for your rice; I will only accept alms-food." In this [training rule], eating the food is called 'kiriya' (action), and not performing assignment (vikappanā) (or eating it oneself without relinquishing it to another) is called 'akiriya' (non-action).

## The Explanation of the Paramparabhojana Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 4. Explanation of the Kāṇamātā Sikkhāpada

'Pahaṇakatthāya' means for the sake of a gift. 'Pātheyyatthāya' means for the sake of provisions for those traveling on a journey. 'Sattu' refers to both lumped flour-cake (baddha-sattu) and loose flour-meal (abaddha-sattu). 'Dvattipattapūre paṭiggahetvā' means having accepted two or three bowlfuls, filled level with the lower line of the bowl's rim. Since this meaning is clear as stated below, "Ettha" and so forth is said to show only what should be done regarding those two or three bowlfuls accepted. 'Sesaṃ' means the bowlfuls other than that one bowlful. It means that if three bowlfuls were accepted, [he should give away] two bowlfuls; if two bowlfuls were accepted, [he should give away] one bowlful.

'Gamane vā paṭippassaddhe' means seeing a danger on the way, or because of a lack of desire [to go], saying "We will not send the gift now; we will not go," and thus when the plan for the journey is cancelled, [it refers to accepting the gift] from those who give it.

## The Explanation of the Kāṇamātā Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 5. Explanation of the Paṭhamapavāraṇā Sikkhāpada

'Bhuttāvī' means one who has finished his meal. 'Sāsapamattampi ajjhoharitaṃ' means having swallowed even a small amount of food, about the size of a mustard seed, whether having chewed it or not. 'Pavārito' means one who has refused. A monk who, while eating, does not desire and refuses the food brought by the server is called 'pavārita' (one who has refused) by that refusal. To show the meaning without emphasizing the literal word, it is said, "It means one who has performed pavāraṇā, one who has performed refusal." That refusal is not merely by refusal alone, but by way of five factors. Therefore, in the word-analysis (padabhājanī) of that term, it is said, "Asanaṃ paññāyati" and so forth.
384:
“The food is evident” means that among the five types of food, one of the foods is clearly seen in the bowl or similar vessels. Therefore, it was said, “If the food is capable of effecting pavāraṇā,” and so forth. “Sāli rice” (sāli) refers to all varieties of sāli rice, starting from wild rice (nīvāra) at the minimum. “Vīhi rice” (vīhi) refers to all varieties of paddy. There is no distinction between barley (yava) and wheat (godhuma). “Millet” (kaṅgu) refers to all varieties of millet, which come in white, red, and brown colors. “Varaka” (varaka) refers to all varieties of white-colored varaka, starting from varaka-coraka at the minimum. “Kudrūsaka” (kudrūsaka) refers to all varieties of grass-grains, including dark kodrava and sāmāka grass-seeds.

In this context, teachers say that wild rice and varaka-coraka are “grain-like” (dhanyānuloma). “Gruel” (yāgu) refers to any kind of gruel, such as sour gruel or milk gruel. Since milk-rice (pāyāsa) is also included under the term “gruel,” it is not separately mentioned as “Let us cook one of the sour milk-rices, etc.” “Effecting pavāraṇā” means completing the refusal which becomes the cause for an offense incurred by eating food that has not been made “leftover” (anatiritta). If the grains (of rice) are not evident, it is classified as gruel and does not effect pavāraṇā. However, from the moment it reaches a thick consistency and is classified as food, it effects pavāraṇā.

“Having poured water, fermented rice-water, milk, etc.” means pouring water, fermented rice-water, milk, etc., and mixing them with the meal without kneading them together. Therefore, it was said, “Take the gruel,” and so forth. If one pours water, fermented rice-water, milk, etc., into the meal, kneads them, and then gives it saying, “Take the gruel,” pavāraṇā does not occur. “Also with gruel” refers to gruel that has been classified as such or any other gruel. However, pure liquid gruel or very watery gruel does not effect pavāraṇā.

Because the state of being a meal in progress by way of any of the five types of food has been interrupted, it is said, “Both have been eaten... [pe]... does not refuse (pavāreti).” For a monk who refuses unallowable meat or unallowable food loathed by the Buddha, pavāraṇā does not occur because it is not a valid basis for pavāraṇā. Thus it is said, “Whichever monk,” and so forth. Pavāraṇā occurs only for a monk who refuses food that is allowable for him to eat. In this case, he refuses the unallowable meat knowing it is unallowable. Even if he does not know, he is refusing what stands in a position that should be refused; therefore, he does not effect pavāraṇā. If, while eating unallowable meat, he refuses allowable meat or food, pavāraṇā occurs. Why? Because it is a valid basis. That food which he refuses is the basis for pavāraṇā. As for the meat he eats...
385:
Even though that meat stands in a position that should be refused, since it does not lose its nature as meat while being eaten, pavāraṇā occurs (he becomes pavārita). What need is there to mention the refusal of allowable food while eating allowable meat? The same method should be understood for one who refuses allowable food while eating unallowable food.

“While food is present” (bhojane sati) means while even one of the five types of food is present. “Other food of the stated characteristics” refers to any one of the five types of food with the stated characteristics other than the food already in the bowl, etc. The phrase “He is without expectation” (nirapekkho hoti) is an explanation of the words “That which is in the bowl, etc.” It is not only the monk who is without expectation who does not effect pavāraṇā; thus it was said, “Or elsewhere,” and so forth. “Even if he refuses, pavāraṇā does not occur” means that if other food is brought in the meantime, even if he refuses that brought food, pavāraṇā does not occur. Why? Because the state of being a meal in progress has been interrupted (or finished).

“He offers” (upanāmeti) shows the act of bringing forward with the body. In the phrase “In the hand or on a support,” the word “or” (vā) has the sense of considering an unstated alternative; by that “or,” one should consider “or on the thighs.” He sends a bowl to a young monk sitting far beyond the hatthapāsa (arm's reach) and says, “Take rice from this bowl.” If the person who took the bowl and went there (or arrived there) stands silently, the same rule (of pavāraṇā not occurring) applies to the monk who refuses that rice. Why? Because the monk who spoke is far away, and the messenger did not actually “offer” it. However, if the monk who took the bowl arrives and says, “Take this rice,” pavāraṇā occurs for the monk who refuses it. “Even when it is said so” means even when it is said, “Take the rice.”

“For one serving while holding a rice basket” refers to one who serves while holding a rice basket with one hand and a ladle with the other. If another person comes and says, “I will hold the basket, you give the rice,” and merely holds it, “It is still considered offered” (abhihaṭāva hoti) means it is considered offered by the server himself. To show that pavāraṇā does not occur for a monk who refuses while that person is holding it, if there is no intention to give on the part of that server, it was said, “But if,” and so forth. “When it is lifted” (udḍhaṭe) refers to the rice that has been ladled out. The intention of the commentator is that the act of bringing forward with the ladle is indeed the act of offering that rice. “While it is being given to the one nearby” means while rice is being distributed to a monk close by. “By a bodily gesture” means [refusing] by using a finger, a hand, a fly-whisk, or the corner of a robe...
386:
(The Blessed One) said: "He shakes his head, or his hand, or a fly-whisk, or the corner of his robe; he makes a sign with his eyebrows; or he looks with anger." By such bodily movements as moving the fingers and so on, [pavāraṇā is established]. In terms of verbal movements such as "Enough, do not give," saying "Enough," or "I do not take it," or "Do not pour," or "Go away"—by any such verbal gesture [pavāraṇā is established].

Furthermore, when food is being brought forward, if a monk, fearing pavāraṇā, removes his hands but says to the person repeatedly pouring rice into the bowl, "Pour, pour, fill it up by pressing it down," pavāraṇā does not occur. This same principle should be understood for a monk who, seeing another monk bringing food, says, "Friend, will you take some more from this? I shall give you some," and the other refuses; in this case also, it should be understood that pavāraṇā does not occur.

Because it is said by mentioning the name of an object that does not cause pavāraṇā, such as "Accept the liquid (rasa)," it is said that there is no pavāraṇā for one who refuses after hearing that. However, regarding the term "maṃsarasa" (meat-broth), it is not understood as only the broth of the meat; rather, "maṃsarasa" is understood as both the meat and the broth by way of a name that causes pavāraṇā. Therefore, for one who refuses it, pavāraṇā indeed occurs; thus [the author of the Compendium] said: "But when 'maṃsarasa' is said, pavāraṇā occurs for the one who refuses." The same principle should be understood in the subsequent passage "fish, meat, curry."

In whatever posture (iriyāpatha) one becomes pavārita, one must eat without changing that posture. According to this, a monk who becomes pavārita while walking must eat while walking. If he reaches mud or water and must stop, he must have the food made 'leftover' (atiritta) while standing. If the river is overflowing in the middle of the journey, he should eat while continuously circling the bushes on the riverbank. If there is a boat or a bridge, he should eat while walking on that boat or bridge; the act of going (the posture) must not be interrupted. This principle applies to other postures as well. A monk who changes his posture must have the food made 'leftover.'

A monk who becomes pavārita while squatting must eat while squatting. A straw stool or some kind of seat should be provided under him. However, a monk who becomes pavārita while sitting on a stool is allowed to eat while turning to the four directions without moving the stool from its place. A monk who becomes pavārita while sitting on a couch (mañca) is not allowed to shift from here to there. But if they carry him along with the couch to another place, it is allowable. A monk who becomes pavārita while lying down must eat while lying down. When turning, he must not exceed the place of the side on which he was lying.

"Alam etaṃ sabbaṃ" (All this is enough) means: all this food is enough, sufficient; this is also in excess for you; you will not receive anything else besides this. "He who makes it leftover" means the monk who...
387:
One should make it 'leftover' (atiritta) by saying "Alam etaṃ sabbaṃ" (All this is enough). By way of the opposite method: "The food that is made allowable is made leftover; the food that has been accepted is made leftover; it is lifted up; it is done within the forearm's length (hatthapāsa); it is done by a monk who has eaten; it is done by a monk who has eaten and is pavārita and has not risen from his seat, saying 'Alam etaṃ sabbaṃ'." By these seven modes of Vinaya procedure, both the leftover made allowable and the leftover of the sick are called 'atiritta.' Thus, it should be understood by the method of the opposite of 'non-leftover' (an-atiritta). In this context, it is said that "Alam etaṃ sabbaṃ" should be said three times; this is said to be the traditional practice (āciṇṇa). However, the Vinaya masters say, "It should be said only once."

To the question "Why can he not perform that Vinaya procedure again?" [the author] said "Yañhi," etc. In that passage, "yañhi akataṃ" means: the food for which the procedure has not yet been done in the vessel where the procedure was first performed, should be done. However, it is not allowed to be done [again] in the first vessel. "Yena ca akataṃ" means: it should also be done by another monk who did not perform it first. "Vuttaṃ" means it is stated in the Sinhalese Commentaries. "Aññasmiṃ pana bhājane" means: in a vessel other than the one where it was first done—such as a bowl, a water-pot, or a basket—placed in front and tilted.

"Aññatra bhuñjanavatthusmiṃ" means: for a reason other than eating after being pavārita. "Tikapācittiyaṃ" means: there are three Pācittiyas regarding non-leftover food by way of the perception of it being non-leftover, being doubtful, or the perception of it being leftover. "Ajjhoharato ca dukkaṭaṃ" means: for every swallow, a dukkaṭa offense is incurred. If, however, they are medicines (yāmakālika, etc.) mixed with food (āmisa), a pācittiya alone is incurred for the monk who accepts and swallows it, whether for the sake of nourishment or for another purpose. "Tesaṃ anuññātapari-bhogavasena" means: by way of the permitted use of yāmakālika and so on; it means yāmakālika is for quenching thirst when there is thirst, and sattāhakālika and yāvajīvika are for the purpose of calming various illnesses when they occur. This training rule is also a bodily action because of swallowing, and a vocal action because of not having someone else say "Venerable sir, make this leftover." Therefore, it is said: "The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so on are the same as the first Kathina training rule." Regarding "Kiriyā-akiriyā" (action and inaction) here: eating after refusing is 'action' (kiriyā), and not making the food leftover is 'inaction' (akiriyā).

## The Explanation of the First Pavāraṇā Training Rule is Finished.
388:
## 6. Commentary on the Second Pavāraṇā Sikkhāpada
"Or having heard" means having heard it reported by another monk or by that [refusing] monk himself. Because it was said, "a pācittiya when eaten," it is stated that a pācittiya offense is incurred at the conclusion of the meal.

## The Explanation of the Second Pavāraṇā Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 7. Commentary on the Vikālabhojana Sikkhāpada
In this [training rule], regarding the term "wrong time" (vikāla), the period from dawn until noon is the designated time (kāla) for eating, as practiced and habitually followed by the Buddhas and other Noble Ones. Any time other than that is "wrong time" (vikāla), meaning "the time that has passed." Therefore, it is said, "when the time has passed," and so on. Even the exact moment of noon is included within the [proper] time. From that point onwards, it is not permissible to chew or eat. Although one might be able to drink quickly, a monk who has remorse should not do so. To know the limitation of time, a sun-dial (kālatthambha) should be set up. The meal business should be completed only within the [proper] time. By the passage "whatever... or snacks (khādanīya)," it is shown that there is no need even to mention snacks made of grains or crops, such as sakkhalimōdaka or kaṭuttha cakes [being forbidden in the wrong time]. Bhojanīya refers to the five types of soft food.

"If there is a cause" means when a reason such as thirst exists. "Of a ruminator" (romaṭṭhaka): food that has been swallowed, then regurgitated and kept in the mouth, not going outside the mouth, but having come out from the food passage (throat), is called "rumination" (romaṭṭha). In this context, it refers to food that has been swallowed, regurgitated, and kept in the mouth. Therefore, it is said, "Monks, [it should] not [be eaten]," and so on. Except for a natural ruminator, for other monks, if they swallow food (regurgitated matter) after holding it in the mouth, they incur an offense. However, if it goes directly back down the throat without being held, it is permissible.

## The Explanation of the Vikālabhojana Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 8. Commentary on the Sannidhikāraka Sikkhāpada
By saying that "kāra, karaṇa, and kiriyā" are identical in meaning, the state of action (bhāva) of the word "kāra" is shown. Proper storing or placing is called sannidhi. "Having received and [keeping it] for one night"...
389: By the words "vītināmitassetaṃ nāma", it shows the uncleanness of this bowl which has been accepted and kept for one night. Although yāmakālika (to be consumed within a watch) is not a snack (khādanīya) or a staple food (bhojanīya), because of the words "storing yāmakālika within the watch and eating it", if the watch is exceeded, an offense of expiation should occur due to the cause of storing (sannidhi). Thus it is said "whether yāvakālika or yāmakālika, any...". Now, to clarify the uncleanness of the bowl, "yaṃ aṅguliyā" etc. is said. In that passage, "lines appear to one rubbing with a finger" means when a washed bowl is rubbed with a finger, if finger marks appear on the bowl, that bowl is unclean. Finger marks appearing on a bowl the color of oil are negligible. "Sneha" means oil. "Sandissati" means clearly visible on top of the rice gruel. "Even in such a bowl" means in a bowl where the acceptance has not been relinquished, and after the food has been removed by oneself or another, if it is not well washed, for a monk eating from it the next day, there is an offense of expiation. This is because there is still something stuck to the bowl for which the acceptance has not lapsed; thus eating on the second day results in an offense of expiation. However, if the bowl was relinquished, there is no offense for eating from it the next day."Yaṃ pana" refers to whatever food. "Apariccattameva hi" means not relinquished, either by giving it away without regard or by giving it to an unordained person without regard (the acceptance does not lapse). "Allowable food" (kappiya-bhojana) means even a single grain of rice is allowable food. "Among unallowable meats" refers to meats other than human flesh, such as elephant, horse, dog, snake, lion, tiger, leopard, bear, and hyena, as well as unexamined meat or meat specifically killed for the monk (uddissakata). In the Pali, it is said "if one accepts sattāhakālika and yāvajīvika for the sake of nutriment, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)", etc. Since swallowing stored sattāhakālika and yāvajīvika for nutriment even in the morning is called a dukkaṭa offense, swallowing yāmakālika for nutriment should also be a separate dukkaṭa offense. Thus it is said "for one swallowing for the sake of nutriment, an offense of expiation along with a dukkaṭa". "In all variations" means in all variations mentioned like "for one eating allowable food", another offense of expiation increases. This means: for allowable food, two offenses of expiation; for human flesh, two offenses of expiation along with a thullaccaya (grave offense); for the remaining unallowable meats, two offenses of expiation along with a dukkaṭa. Regarding yāmakālika, when there is a cause, with a mouth containing food (sāmisa)...
390:
For a monk who swallows with his mouth, two Pācittiya offenses are incurred; however, if he swallows with a mouth free of food particles (nirāmisa), only one is incurred. For a monk who swallows for the sake of nutriment, in both alternatives, it occurs along with a Dukkaṭa.

"Avasesesu" (in the remaining) refers to the Yāvakālika remaining from the Yāmakālika and so forth. "Pācittiyaṃ vaḍḍhatiyeva" means that another Pācittiya offense is simply added. The meaning is this: if he swallows during the wrong time (vikāla), two Pācittiyas are incurred—one due to the reason of storage (sannidhi) and one due to the reason of eating at the wrong time. Among unallowable meats, if it is human flesh, two Pācittiyas are incurred along with a Thullaccaya; in the case of other [unallowable] meats, two Pācittiyas are incurred along with a Dukkaṭa.

Belatthasīsa is the name of a Great Elder who was among the thousand matted-hair ascetics (jaṭilas). "Tika-pācittiya" refers to the three Pācittiyas occurring by way of perceiving stored [food] as stored, being doubtful, or perceiving stored [food] as not stored. "Saṃsaṭṭhāni" refers to foods with mixed flavors. It is only in reference to mixed flavors that it was said, "That which is accepted on that day is allowable during the proper time," and so forth. Therefore, he said "Tasmā" and so on. Here, "Asambhinnarasaṃ" means unmixed flavor. This is said in reference to lumps of ghee and the like received together with cold milk-rice (pāyāsa) and the like. "Sudhotaṃ vā" is said in reference to nutmeg, cloves, and the like received together with almsfood, or ginger and the like added and offered in congee (yāgu) and so forth.

"Tena" refers to the seven-day medicine (sattāhakālika). Because it is accepted on that day, it is called "tadahupaṭiggahita"; it means by that which is accepted on that day. This same method applies to terms such as "dvīhapaṭiggahitena" (accepted for two days). "Tasmā" is because that which is accepted in the morning is also allowable. Regarding the statement "That which is accepted is allowable for seven days," it was said in the Bhesajjakkhandhaka: "Monks, a life-long medicine (yāvajīvika) accepted mixed with a seven-day medicine (sattāhakālika) is allowable for seven days; when seven days have passed, it is no longer allowable." Although keeping [food] in the mouth for a whole night was not explicitly mentioned, because it is called storage (sannidhi) as soon as it is put into the mouth, it is called "mukhasannidhi" (mouth-storage).

"Catasso kappiyabhūmiyo" refers to the four types of allowable grounds (kappiya-kuṭi): Ussāvanantikā, Gonisādikā, Gahapati, and Sammuti. Among these, "Ussāvanantikā" refers to a monastery of the Saṅgha or of a single monk where, while the house was being built, those standing around said, "Let us make a kappiya-kuṭi, let us make a kappiya-kuṭi," or "Kappiya-kuṭi, kappiya-kuṭi," and thus the first auspicious bricks, pillars, and so forth were laid. If a monastery (ārāma) is mostly unfenced and remains as a whole...
391:
...then that monastery is called "Gonisādikā." "Gahapati" refers to a building given by people other than the monk, saying "We give this kappiya-kuṭi," or a building that belongs to them. "Sammuti" refers to one made by announcing with a formal act (kammavācā). As to how the decision regarding these [allowable grounds] should be understood, the author said, "The decision regarding them is stated in the Samantapāsādikā."

## The Explanation of the Sannidhikāraka Sikkhāpada is Finished.

## 9. Paṇītabhojana Sikkhāpada

"Paṇītabhojanāni": This term is indicated by dropping the middle word (saṃsaṭṭha), therefore the author said "Paṇītasaṃsaṭṭhāni" (mixed with superior foods) and so forth. Since the characteristic stated in the Vibhaṅga is "Fish (maccha) refers to aquatic creatures," all aquatic creatures are indeed fish. It means any creature born in water is called a fish.

"Mahānāma-sikkhāpadena" refers to this training rule: "A monk who is not sick may accept an invitation for medicinal requisites for four months, except for a renewed invitation (punapavāraṇā) or a permanent invitation (niccapavāraṇā). If he accepts beyond that, it is a Pācittiya." In this invitation, where an invitation for medicinal requisites for the sick is made by way of the Saṅgha, if a limitation is made by nights or by medicines, such as "Only for this many nights" or "Only this many medicines should be requested," then for one who requests medicine beyond that limit of nights or limit of medicines for a non-medicinal purpose, or who requests another medicine for a different medicinal purpose, a Pācittiya is stated. Therefore, if a monk who is not sick, even if he perceives himself as sick, requests the five medicines, he is one who requests medicine for a non-medicinal purpose; thus it is said, "He should be dealt with according to the Mahānāma Sikkhāpada."

However, if one requests not for the sake of medicine but purely for the sake of one's own consumption, he should be dealt with according to the Supodanavinnatti Sikkhāpada. For it is said in the Samantapāsādikā: "A monk who requests and eats pure ghee and the like [without being sick] does not incur a Pācittiya [under this rule],"
392:
(A monk who requests and eats butter and so forth separately) does not commit an offense; it is stated (in the Pācittiya Aṭṭhakathā 259) that he incurs a dukkaṭa offense of supodanaviññatti (requesting curry or rice) among the sekhiya rules. The phrase "it should be dealt with by supodanaviññatti" means it should be dealt with by the training rule beginning with "A monk who is not ill (shall not request) curry or rice (for his own sake)" (Pācittiya 613); it means he should be made to undergo a dukkaṭa offense. "By this training rule" refers to this paṇītabhojana training rule.

If one asks, "What offense is committed if one says, 'Give me butter-rice'?" the author replies with the passage beginning, "But if one says, 'Give me butter-rice'." It should be understood in connection that only a dukkaṭa offense is incurred due to supodanaviññatti. If one asks why, the author replies with the passage beginning, "Because." If it is asked, "Just as 'superior foods' (paṇītabhojanāni) are understood, why is the meaning of this 'butter-rice' (sappibhatta) not understood in the same way?" it is because the meaning is not singular (it can have various meanings). Indeed, when "superior foods" is said, the meaning "foods mixed with superior ingredients are superior foods" is understood with certainty. However, when "butter-rice" is said, because it can also be understood as "rice made of butter is butter-rice," the meaning "rice mixed with butter is butter-rice" is not understood with certainty. This same principle applies to terms such as "Give me fresh-butter-rice."

"Only by the former method" means by the former method of "Give the rice, make it into butter, and eat it." However, if one says "with butter" but the giver gives any of the remaining items such as fresh butter, it is merely a visanketa (a mismatch of intention). "No offense" means being free from all offenses because it is a visanketa. Some teachers say, "Although there is no offense, because it arose through one's own effort (it is unallowable butter), it should not be eaten." "With allowable butter" means with the butter of an animal whose meat is allowable. In the phrase "with unallowable butter," it should be understood in this same way. Indeed, allowability and unallowability (kappiya and akappiya) are determined only by the nature of the meat, not by the nature of the butter and so forth. Except for human fat (manussavasātela), there is no such thing as "unallowable" among the milk, curd, butter, fresh butter, and fat of all animals.

It should be understood as the intention of the commentator that because it is not intended in this context of superior foods, there is only a dukkaṭa offense even in consumption. If, when unallowable butter is unavailable, one gives unallowable fresh butter etc. according to the former method, saying "make it into butter and eat it," it is considered as having given with unallowable butter. Just as it is a visanketa if one gives unallowable butter when asked for "allowable butter," the same applies here if one gives allowable butter when asked for "unallowable butter." Even if one were to explain each of these one by one in order, this same meaning should be stated. Since that meaning can be understood in brief, the detailed method is omitted and—
393:
—it is stated that the decision in all cases should be understood by this method alone. The summary of the meaning here is: whatever object such as butter is requested, if that object or its value is received, it is considered as having received that specific object. However, if another object is given, whether it is mentioned in the Pāḷi or not, it is a visanketa (mismatch). "Or in various places" (nānāṭṭhāne vā) means in various places, such as butter in that very house and fresh butter in another house.

## The Explanation of the Paṇītabhojana Training Rule is Finished.

## 10. Dantapona Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

"By body" (kāyena) means by any part of the body such as the hand; it should be understood that a monk who takes even with a toe is said to take by the body. The same principle applies to the act of giving (offering). "By what is connected to the body" (kāyappaṭibaddhena) means by any utensil connected to the body, such as an alms-bowl. The same principle applies to giving. If something is given with any utensil such as a ladle, it is considered as given by what is connected to the body. "By any one (of the three)" means by the body, or by what is connected to the body, or by what is released (nissaggiya). There, "by what is released" (nissaggiyena) means a thing that is released from the body or from what is connected to the body and made to fall upon the body or upon what is connected to the body of a monk standing within arm's reach (hatthapāsa); this is called giving by the effort of releasing. "Of that" (tassa) refers to the thing that has been formally received. "By way of the reversal of what was said" means by way of the opposite of the described act of receiving. This is what is meant: while something is being given by any one of the three—the body, what is connected to the body, or what is released—if one takes it with the body or with what is connected to the body, this is called "formally received" (paṭiggahita).

"By what is portable" (saṃhārimena) means by something that can be moved by a man of average strength; by this term, it is shown that receiving upon an immovable plank or stone slab is not valid. "By what is capable of holding" (dhāretuṃ samatthena) means by something suitable for properly supporting; by this term, it is shown that receiving upon delicate and small leaves such as tamarind leaves is not valid. "By a tree leaf not attached to its place of growth" (atatthajātakarukkhapaṇṇena) means by a leaf that has fallen from its place of growth, such as a lotus leaf; by this term, however, it is not allowable to receive upon a lotus leaf or a kimsuka leaf that is still growing on the tree, even if it is large. The reason is that it is shown that such a leaf does not come under the designation of "connected to the body" (kāyappaṭibaddha). Just as...
394:
Just as with things growing on that tree, formal acceptance (paṭiggahaṇa) is not allowable for a couch or similar items tied to a stump. Does the formal acceptance not count for a monk who accepts via a bowl-stand or similar, which is 'connected to a connected object' (paṭibaddhappatibaddha)? If so, why is it said here that acceptance is only through the body or what is connected to the body (kāyappaṭibaddha), and not through what is 'connected to a connected object'? To this, the answer is: 'In this context, there is no such thing as connected to a connected object.' Some teachers, however, say: 'Acceptance via a bowl-stand is not allowable because it is called acceptance through an object connected to what is connected to the body.' That is merely a statement. In actual sense, it is shown that all such instances are simply acceptance through what is connected to the body.

Akallaka means a sick person (gilāna). It refers to one who, being unable to use their hands to consume, accepts with the mouth. Dust falling from a vessel being carried forward is also allowable because it is being 'carried forward.'

'Standing therein' (tasmiṃ ṭhatvā) means standing within such a hatthapāsa (forearm's length). Yaṃ refers to 'whatever load.' A 'middle man' (majjhima purisa) is a man of average strength. An offense of wrongdoing prescribed in the Vinaya is called a vinaya-dukkaṭa. Going to a monastery or a dining hall after collecting alms and giving that alms-food to an unordained person (anupasampanna) is stated in accordance with the prior intention [at the time of receiving]. However, since it does not become that person's property merely by the thought 'I will give this to an unordained person,' it is allowable to accept and consume it oneself without giving it to that person.

In the phrase assukheḷasiṅghāṇikādīsu, assu means tears. Kheḷa means saliva. Siṅghāṇikā refers to the brain-matter from inside the head that has turned into putrid phlegm, descending through the opening in the roof of the palate and filling the nostrils. By the word 'etc.' (ādi), one should include urine, feces, phlegm, tooth-grime, eye-wax, ear-wax, and salt (sweat) produced from the body. If one takes tears and so on from their locations, such as the eye-sockets, while they are in between, what happens? The answer is: 'It becomes uggahitaka (improperly taken).' Uggahitaka means taken badly. Phalinī refers to something that has fruit. It also refers to a fruit-bearing branch growing on that tree. Because one performs an act that has been prohibited with the words 'it should not be done,' one incurs the offense of durupaciṇṇa-dukkaṭa (wrongdoing through bad conduct).

It is called āhāra (nutriment) because it is 'brought forward' (āharīyati). Although it refers to anything that can be swallowed, in this context, the four kālikas (time-limited items) are intended; therefore, it is said 'whatever' (yaṃ kiñci), and so on. In that statement, the word-definition is as follows: Because it is to be consumed from sunrise until noon, it is called yāvakālika (temporary). From sunrise until the end of the last watch [of the night]...
395:
Because it has a time limit for consumption from sunrise until noon, it is called yāvakālika. Because it has a time limit for drinking to quench thirst when there is thirst from sunrise until the end of the three watches of the night, it is called yāmakālika. Because it has a time limit for being stored and consumed for up to seven days, it is called sattāhakālika. Because it is carried and consumed for as long as life lasts, it is called yāvajīvika. Therefore, it is said 'therein' (tattha), and so on.

Among the roots, leaves, flowers, fruits, etc., produced in the forest: 'Root' (mūla) refers to the roots of radish, khāraka, caccuta, tambaka, and so on. It refers to the roots of leafy vegetables used as soup ingredients that serve the purpose of snacks and main meals for people as natural nutriment in various regions. 'Leaf' (patta) refers to the leaves of those same plants like radish, khāraka, etc. 'Flower' (puppha) refers to the flowers of those same plants like radish, khāraka, etc. 'Fruit' (phala) refers to the fruits of jackfruit, wild jackfruit, and so on. It refers to the fruit that serves the purpose of snacks and main meals for people as natural nutriment in various regions. By the word 'etc.' (ādi), tubers, roots, and so on are to be included.

Mango drink (ambapāna) is a drink made from either raw or ripe mangoes. Therein, a monk wishing to make it with raw mangoes should split young mangoes, place them in water, cook them by the heat of the sun (ādiccapāka), strain them, and then mix them with honey, sugar, camphor, etc., which have been formally accepted on that same day. A drink made in this way is allowable only before noon. However, if one receives mango drink made by an unordained person and accepts it before noon, it may be consumed along with food (sāmisa) before noon; in the afternoon, it may be consumed without food (nirāmisa) until sunrise. This method applies to all drinks.

Among those drinks, a drink made from rose-apples is called jambupāna. A drink made from seeded bananas is called cocapāna. A drink made from seedless bananas is called mocapāna. A drink made from the natural juice of madhuka flowers is called madhukapāna. That madhukapāna is allowable only when mixed with water; the pure essence alone is not allowable. A drink made by crushing grapes in water, like mango drink, is called muddikāpāna. A drink made by crushing the tubers of red or blue lotuses is called sālūkapāna. A drink made from phārusaka fruits, like mango drink, is called phārusakapāna. In this same way, drinks made from rattan fruits and so on should be understood. Furthermore, all these drinks are not allowable if they are cooked by fire. Therefore, it is said 'with cold water' (sītodakena), and so on.
396: Regarding the phrase 'avasēthēsu pi anuññātaphala-patta-puppha-rasēsu', this should be understood in the same way for juices of fruits, leaves, and flowers allowed by the Buddha's words such as, 'Monks, I allow all fruit juices except grain juice,' which remain after excluding grain juice, vegetable juice, and fruit juice. 'Khādanīyattha' means the purpose or function to be performed by solid food. 'Neva pharati' means it does not complete or produce the effect. Regarding 'anāhārepi udake āhāra-saññāya', it refers to monks who have doubts, perceiving water (which is not food) as food, due to not being able to properly note the meaning stated in the word-analysis (padabhājana) of the term 'one should bring food (āhāra)', thinking 'it is called food because it is brought'. Regarding 'dantapone ca mukhadvāraṃ āhaṭaṃ idaṃ ti saññāya', it refers to monks who have doubts regarding a tooth-stick that has not yet been brought to the mouth, but perceiving it wrongly as 'this tooth-stick has been brought to the mouth'. 'Yathāsukhaṃ pātuṃ' means to drink as one pleases, whether it has been formally offered or not. 'Dantaponaparibhogena' means by using a tooth-stick, such as cleaning teeth, etc. By this statement, it is shown that it is not proper to swallow the juice of that tooth-stick. 'Cattāri mahāvikaṭāni' refers to excrement, urine, ashes, and clay. They are called 'vikaṭa' (altered/foul things) either because they have an altered appearance due to their source, etc., or because they are not natural food. 'Sati paccaye' means when there is a cause, such as a snake bite, etc. 'Dhūmādi-abbohārikābhāvo' means the absence of negligible things such as smoke, flower scent, or particles worn away by brushing teeth. ## Conclusion of the Commentary on the Tooth-stick Training Rule. ## The Fourth Chapter: Food (Bhojanavagga). ## 5. Acelakavagga ## 1. Commentary on the Acelaka Training Rule 'Acelakassa' refers to anyone who has attained the state of a renunciant but is naked. 'Paribbājakassa' refers to anyone who has attained the state of a renunciant, excluding monks and novices (sāmaṇeras). 'Paribbājikāya' refers to any woman who has attained the state of a renunciant, excluding nuns (bhikkhunīs), female trainees (sikkhamānās), and female novices (sāmaṇerīs). All these are to be understood as external sectarians (aññatitthiya). Therefore, it is said, 'to these sectarians such as the naked ascetics'.
397:
The word "tesaṃ" refers to those of other religions. "Bhājanaṃ nikkhipitvā" means having set down a vessel filled with or containing material food (āmisa). "Bāhirālepaṃ" refers to substances applied externally to the body, such as oil.

In this Acelaka training rule, naked ascetics (acelaka), male wanderers (paribbājaka), and female wanderers (paribbājikā) are considered only as sectarians (titthiyas).
Therefore, the Blessed One made the distinction of the offense regarding those three under the name of 'titthiya'.
Furthermore, it is decided that it is allowable for a monk to give food to a naked person who is not a sectarian, or to a layperson who has the appearance of a sectarian.
In this training rule, it is our view that it is also allowable to give to a person such as a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna) who, though not a sectarian at heart, bears the appearance of a sectarian.

## The Explanation of the Acelaka Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 2. The Explanation of the Uyyojana Sikkhāpada

"Gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā": Here, it should be understood that a city (nagara) is also included by the term 'village' (gāma). "Pavisiassāma": Here, the remaining text "having taken [the monk] and gone [there, then sending him back]" should be added. Alternatively, it means taking the monk and going, saying, "Come, venerable, let us enter the village or town for alms," either without paying attention or without knowing that the woman is present in that village, and then sending him back. "Yaṃ kiñci āmisaṃ" refers to any kind of material food, such as gruel (yāgu). "Uyyojeyya" means sending away or dismissing upon seeing a woman suitable for one's own dalliance.

Therefore, the teacher who made the summary said the words beginning with "mātugāmena saddhiṃ". By the word "ādi" (etc.), it includes transgressions of body and speech other than those already mentioned. "Having said [words] such as 'Go'": This means saying, "Go, venerable, talking or sitting with you is not pleasant for me; talking or sitting alone is pleasant for me."

"Etaṃ anācārameva" refers only to the improper conduct already mentioned, such as laughing. "Na aññaṃ patirūpaṃ kāraṇaṃ" means that the sending away is not done by making another suitable reason or cause, such as the two monks sharing a meal together, excluding the aforementioned improper conduct. "Assa" refers to the monk who sends [the other] away. "So" refers to the monk who is sent away.

"Anupasampanna" refers to a novice (sāmaṇera). Teachers say that in this training rule, only a novice is intended by 'unordained'. "Ubhippampi" refers to both the ordained (monk) and the unordained (novice). In the phrase "kalisāsanāropane", "kali" means anger. "Sāsanaṃ" means a command or instruction. It means in the sense of imposing the instruction of that anger. Being oppressed by such an instruction of anger, if he goes away by another path, he may go; this is meant by the power of anger.
398:
"Kalisāsanaṃ" means the act of imposing the command to speak out of that anger. It refers to speaking unpleasant words out of the power of anger, such as, "May this person go away being thus oppressed," and pointing out faults in their standing, sitting, etc., saying, "Look, sirs, at this person's standing, sitting, looking ahead, and looking aside; he stands like a stump, sits like a dog, and looks here and there like a monkey." There is no fault in speaking thus with a pure mind.

In the phrase "evamādīhi," the word "ādi" includes: sending someone away thinking, "He will feel greed upon seeing expensive goods"; sending someone away thinking, "He will feel dissatisfaction (with the monkhood) upon seeing a woman"; sending someone away saying, "Take congee, a meal, or food for the sick, for those left behind, or for the monastery attendant"; and sending someone away when there is a genuine task to be done, without the desire to practice improper conduct.

## The Explanation of the Uyyojana Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 3. Sabhojana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

"Sabhojane" is an external compound (bāhiratthasamāsa). In the word "ubha," the letter "u" is elided, and it is said as "saha ubhohi janehi" (together with two people). In this context, "two people" refers to a husband and wife. Alternatively, it is called "bhojana" because it is consumed; it is called "sabhojana" because it occurs together with a woman and a man.

"Rāgapariyuṭṭhitassa" refers to the intention of one desiring sexual intercourse. "Sayanigharaṃ" means a sleeping chamber or a dwelling room. "Mahallakassa" means of a large sleeping chamber. "Piṭṭhasaṅghāṭato" means from the doorpost. "Khuddakassa vā" means of a small sleeping chamber made in any way.

"Should sit crossing the middle" means sitting past the ridge-pole (back-beam). A sleeping chamber called "khuddaka" (small) is five cubits in width; the center of that room is only two and a half cubits from the doorpost. Therefore, in such a sleeping chamber, one who sits leaving a distance of one hatthapāsa (two and a half cubits) from the doorpost is said to be sitting past the ridge-pole. Sitting in this manner is called sitting crossing the middle. Therefore, it is stated in the Pali, "He sits crossing the ridge-pole." In this training rule, it should also be understood as having the intention to enter and sit inside.

## The Explanation of the Sabhojana Sikkhāpada is finished.
399:
## 4-5. Rahopaṭicchannarahonisajja Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
Since everything that should be said regarding the fourth and fifth training rules has already been stated in the two Aniyata training rules, it is said, "The rest of the explanation should be understood by the method already stated in the two Aniyata rules."

## The Explanation of the Rahopaṭicchannarahonisajja Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 6. Cāritta Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
"Seeing a monk in the visible vicinity of the inner precinct" means that for a monk standing in a certain place, the thought of visiting families arises; starting from that place, the monk who is going sees another monk either to the side or directly in front within the visible vicinity of the inner precinct. "With natural speech" means with the kind of speech that can be heard by someone standing within twelve cubits (referring to the act of asking permission). There is no task of searching here and there to inform. This is because such a monk to be searched for is simply non-existent. Therefore, He said, "such a one," and so on. "Without asking" means without informing.

Among "antarārāma, bhikkhunupassaya, titthiyasayya, paṭikkamana, and bhattiyaghara": "Antarārāma" is a monastery within a village. "Paṭikkamana" is a sitting hall or rest house. "Bhattiyaghara" is an invited house or the house of those who donate ticket-food, etc. "In dangers" means in dangers to life and dangers to the holy life (brahmacariya) of the Path. In the phrase "action and non-action," the act of wandering among families is to be understood as the action (kiriya), and not asking is to be understood as the non-action (akiriya).

## The Explanation of the Cāritta Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 7. Mahānāma Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
"All this is said by way of the story" means that "A monk who is not sick may accept an invitation for requisites for four months, except for a renewed invitation and except for a permanent invitation." All these words are spoken by way of the story which is the origin of the training rule. In that story, Mahānāma the Sakyan requested, "Venerable Sir, I wish to invite the Saṅgha for medicines for four months," and so on, and with abundant medicines...
401:
At the minimum, it means even a single elephant ridden by one person, or a single man with a bow in his hand. Anuyyutta refers to the kind of army that follows when a king goes to a park or a river. "When there is a suitable cause" means when there is a suitable reason such as "The uncle is sick in the army," and so on. "In times of danger" means when there is danger to life or to the holy life (brahmacariya); there is no offense for one who goes thinking, "If I go here, I will be free from danger."

## The Commentary on the Deployed Army Training Rule is finished.

## 9. Commentary on the Army-Lodging Training Rule

"Blocked by a hostile army" refers to an army that has been blocked by an enemy army so that movement is cut off. "Obstructed by someone" refers to one who is blocked and obstructed by someone, whether by an enemy or by a ruler.

## The Commentary on the Army-Lodging Training Rule is finished.

## 10. Commentary on the Battlefield Training Rule

"Place of combat" means the battlefield. "They know the array of the forces" means they know the divisions of the forces: "There are this many elephants, this many horses, this many chariots, this many infantry." Just as in "I allow, monks, by the group of dwellings (vihāragga)," etc., the word 'agga' here means a division or group. Therefore, it was explained as "the place for counting the forces." "Arranging the army" means the placing of the army, placing them by making groups: "Let the elephants be here, let the horses be here, let the chariots be here, let the infantry be here." Therefore, it was said: "This is the name for the encampment of the army." "An elephant with twelve men" means an elephant with a total of twelve men: four riders and two guards for each of the four legs. "A horse with three men" means a horse with a total of three men: one rider and two leg-guards. "A chariot with four men" means a chariot with a total of four men: one charioteer, one warrior, and two axle-pin guards (āṇirakkhaka).

## The Commentary on the Battlefield Training Rule is finished.

## The Fifth Chapter: The Naked Ascetics is finished.
402:
## 6. Surāpāna Vagga
## 1. Commentary on the Surāpāna Training Rule

Intoxicating liquor made from flour and such is called 'surā'. It means liquor produced from flour, cakes, cooked rice, yeast, and various ingredients (sambhāra). With reference to this, it is said: "There are these five kinds of surā: flour liquor (piṭṭhasurā), cake liquor (pūvasurā), rice liquor (odanasurā), yeast-added liquor (kiṇṇapakkhittā), and ingredient-mixed liquor (sambhārasaṃyuttā)." Among these five, liquor made by putting fine flour into a pot, adding appropriate water, and kneading it is called piṭṭhasurā. The remaining types of liquor should be understood in the same manner. Yeast (kiṇṇā) refers to the 'seed' of that liquor. Liquor made by adding those liquor seeds, also called 'surāmodaka', is known as kiṇṇapakkhittā. Liquor mixed with various ingredients such as gallnuts (harītakī), mustard seeds, and so on, is known as sambhārasaṃyuttā.

Fermented spirit made from flowers and such is called 'meraya'. It means a liquid made from flowers, fruits, honey, molasses, and ingredients, which has been left to ferment for a long time. With reference to this, it is said: "There are these five kinds of meraya: flower-based spirit (pupphāsavo), fruit-based spirit (phalāsavo), honey-based spirit (madhvāsavo), molasses-based spirit (guḷāsavo), and ingredient-mixed spirit (sambhārasaṃyutto)." Among these five, the juice of flowers such as madhuka, palmyra, and coconut, which has been left to ferment for a long time, is called pupphāsavo. The juice of fruits such as jackfruit, which has been fermented, is called phalāsavo. The juice of grapes (muddikā) which has been fermented is called madhvāsavo. However, in the Samantapāsādikā Commentary, it is stated: "Phalāsavo is the spirit made by kneading fruits such as grapes and using their juice. Madhvāsavo is the spirit made from the pure juice of grapes; teachers also say it is made from bee honey." Spirit made from sugarcane juice is called guḷāsavo. The juice of various ingredients such as gallnuts, emblic myrobalan (āmalaka), and pungent substances, which has been left to ferment for a long time, is called sambhārasaṃyutto. In this context, although the ingredients (sambhāra) of surā and meraya may be similar, the distinction between the two should be understood thus: that which is made by kneading is surā, while that which is formed merely by long fermentation is meraya. "Starting from the seed" means starting from the time the ingredients are prepared and put into the pot, or starting from the time the fresh flower juice of palmyra, coconut, etc., is collected.

Loṇasovīraka (salted medicinal liquid) and sutta (sour gruel) are special types of fermented spirits prepared with many medicines. "To take the scent" means to make it have a fragrant smell. In this training rule, because of not knowing the object (vatthu), it should be understood as 'acittaka' (unintentional). Because it is drunk only with unwholesome consciousness, it is called 'lokavajja' (a worldly fault). Everything that should be said regarding this training rule should be understood according to the method stated in the commentary on the first Pārājika.

## The Commentary on the Surāpāna Training Rule is finished.
404:
Whether with the intention, "May it vanish or may it be destroyed," or because of not wishing to learn that regulation, one acts disrespectfully; this is called showing disrespect towards the Dhamma. Therefore, it is said starting with "Tasmā" (Therefore).

In the phrase, "This does not lead to effacement (sallēkha)," it is called "sallēkha" because it thoroughly scrapes away (likhati) the defilements (kilesa); it refers to fewness of wishes (appicchatā). The meaning is that this [action] does not lead to that fewness of wishes. By the word "ādi" (etc.), it includes the statements: "This does not lead to shaking off (dhuta) defilements, it does not lead to being inspiring (pāsādikatā), it does not lead to the elimination (apacaya) of defilements, and it does not lead to the arousing of energy (vīriyārambha)." "Apanyattena" refers to what is stated by the regulations appearing in the Suttas or the Abhidhamma. "Paveṇi-āgata" refers to the doctrine handed down through the lineage of teachers starting from the time of the Council, such as the Venerable Mahākassapa and others. If one adopts a blameworthy teacher's view, such as: "Since sugarcane juice is a seven-day medicinal (sattāhakālika) substance and its fiber is a life-long (yāvajīvika) substance, it is proper to eat the sugarcane stalk in the afternoon, just like eating gallnuts with molasses," and says, "This is the learning and inquiry of our teachers," it is indeed an offence.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Disrespect is finished.

## 5. Explanation of the Training Rule on Frightening.

"Rūpādīni" refers to frightening sights, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles. "Bhayānakakathaṃ" refers to talk related to the danger of thieves, the danger of wild beasts in the wilderness, or the danger of demons in the wilderness.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Frightening is finished.

## 6. Explanation of the Training Rule on Fire.

"Agilāno" (not ill) in this training rule refers to one who can live comfortably without fire. "Joti" refers to fire.

"Bhaggesu" means in the country of that name. The entire country, which was the residence of the princes of the country named Bhagga, is called "Bhagga" by way of common usage (ruḷhī). Therefore, it is said, "Bhaggesu means in the country of that name." Likewise, it means that for a monk who picks up a burning brand that has fallen down, there is similarly a dukkaṭa offence.
405:
By the word "Tañca," the Buddha refers to the dukkaṭa offence. "Avijjhāta" refers to a firebrand that is not yet extinguished. The meaning is that there is no offence for a monk who lights a fire for the purpose of lighting a lamp, firing a bowl, using a sweat-house (jantāghara), etc., or in a fire-hall (aggisālā). Similarly, there is no offence if one lights a fire for other such reasons besides lighting lamps, etc., or in times of danger (āpadā) from fierce wild beasts and non-human beings (demons).

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Fire is finished.

## 7. Explanation of the Training Rule on Bathing.

"The remaining month and a half of the summer and the first month of the rainy season"—this two-and-a-half-month period is known as the hot season (uṇhasamaya) and the feverish season (pariḷāhasamaya). The meaning is that, in sequence, the remaining month and a half of summer is the hot season, and the first month of the rainy season is the feverish season. Therefore, it is stated in the Padabhājanīya: "The remaining month and a half of summer is called uṇhasamaya; the first month of the rainy season is called pariḷāhasamaya." The time when one cannot be comfortable without bathing is called the time of illness (gilānasamaya). Since the time of illness is already determined when a sick person is defined in the Padabhājanīya, it is said: "One who cannot be comfortable without bathing should be considered as being in the gilānasamaya and may bathe." It also refers to at least sweeping the monastery grounds.

"Digging the sand" means digging the sand in a dry river (to find water). By the word "pi" (also) in the phrase "even in pits," it shows that there is no need to mention [bathing] in a river (if there is water). "In times of danger" refers to occasions such as being chased by large bees (or wasps) and the like.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Bathing is finished.

## 8. Explanation of the Training Rule on Discoloring.

This word "lābha" is used in the passive sense (kammasādhana), as in "What gain (lābha) has been obtained by the venerable?" Since that word here denotes the past tense, the commentator says "alabbhi" (it was obtained).
406:
“Labha” means “obtained.” By this phrase “labha eva lābha,” it is shown that the suffix ‘ṇa’ is applied in the sense of its own meaning (kamma). “Kiṃ alabbhi” means “what was obtained?” “Nava” means “very new.” Through this sequence of words, because it is both new and a robe, it is “navacīvara.” Because of obtaining that new robe, the compound (samāsa) “navacīvaralābha” should be understood here. If that is so, why is it said “navaṃ cīvaralābhena”? It is said “iti navacīvaralābhena” and so forth.

In this training rule, because “vikappanupagaṃ pacchimaṃ” is not stated, “cīvara” should be understood as only that which is capable of being worn or draped; thus it is said “nivāsanapārupanupagaṃ cīvaraṃ.” “Dubbaṇṇakaraṇaṃ ādātabbaṃ” (discoloring should be applied) refers to the kappabindu (the smudge mark). It does not mean discoloring the entire robe with dark blue or other colors. A monk wishing to make this kappabindu, after dyeing the robe, should apply it on the four corners, or three, or two, or one corner, the size of a peacock’s eye-circle or a bedbug’s back; thus it is said “tassa” and so forth.

“Kaṃsanīlena” means with the dark color used by leather workers. In the Mahāpaccariya, however, it is said “iron rust and copper rust are called kaṃsanīla.” “Pattanīlena” means with any kind of dark green leaf-juice. “Kappabinduṃ ādiyitvā” means taking one circular kappabindu.

Pāḷikappa, kaṇṇikakappa, and so forth are forbidden in all commentaries. Regarding patches (aggaḷa) and so forth added later to a robe that has already had the kappabindu made, there is no need to make another kappabindu; thus it is said “pacchā āropitesu” and so forth. “Aggaḷanuvātapari-bhaṇḍesu” refers to patches, top-borders, and side-borders applied after removing worn edges. “Kiriyākiriyam” (action and non-action): it is action (kiriya) due to wearing and draping, and non-action (akiriya) due to not taking the dubbaṇṇakaraṇa called kappabindu.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Discoloring (Dubbaṇṇakaraṇa) is finished.

## 9. Explanation of the Training Rule on Assignment (Vikappana)

Assignment in the presence [of the recipient] is sammukhavikappanā. Assignment in the absence [of the recipient] is parammukhavikappanā. “Sannihitāsannihitabhāva” refers to the state of being near or far. The manner of being near or far should be understood exactly as stated in the section on determination (adhiṭṭhāna).

“Mitto” means a firm friend. “Sandiṭṭho” means an acquaintance, one seen but not a very firm friend. “Akatapaccuddhāraṃ” means that for which the withdrawal (paccuddhāra) has not yet been made, such as by saying “Use my property or dispose of it,” and so forth. “Yena vinayakammaṃ kataṃ” means the monk with whom the Vinaya act of assignment was performed.
407:
By using [the robe], a bodily act is committed; by not causing the withdrawal (paccuddhāra) to be made, a verbal act is committed; with this intention, the author said, “The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are just like the first Kathina training rule.” Here, “action and non-action” (kiriyākiriya) means: using is action (kiriya), and not causing the withdrawal to be made is non-action (akiriya).

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Assignment (Vikappana) is finished.

## 10. Explanation of the Training Rule on Hiding (Apanidhāna)

“Adhiṭṭhānupaga” refers to iron bowls and clay bowls suitable for determination. “Sūkarantaka” is a waistband (belt) made by hollowing out the inside like a keyhole and then striking and weaving it.

“Other requisites” refers to bowl-bags and so forth that are not directly mentioned in the Pāḷi text. “Having given a Dhamma talk” means there is no offense for a monk who, after giving a Dhamma talk saying “One called a monk should not be one who has unkept requisites,” puts it away with the intention “I will give it back later.”

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Hiding (Apanidhāna) is finished.

## The Sixth Chapter, the Chapter on Drinking Fermented Liquor (Surāpāna Vagga), is finished.

## 7. The Chapter on Living Beings (Sappāṇaka Vagga)

## 1. Explanation of the Training Rule on Intentionally [Killing] (Sañcicca)

“Pācittiya” means: at the minimum, a monk cleaning a bed or chair, even if it is a bedbug egg, if he perceives it as a living being and, out of lack of compassion, destroys and removes it, he incurs a pācittiya offense. Therefore, it was said, “even that small thing,” and so forth. “Because the effort (payoga) is great, the unwholesome [act] is great” means: because the effort is great due to the power of the concluding volition (sanniṭṭhāpaka-cetanā) which has the repetition-condition (āsevana-paccaya) obtained through many occurring impulsion-moments (javana), the unwholesome act is great and the fault is heavy.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Intentionally [Killing] (Sañcicca) is finished.
408:
## 2. Explanation of the Training Rule on [Water] Containing Living Beings (Sappāṇaka)

In this Sappāṇaka training rule, just as it should be known that there is a fault according to the regulation when lighting a lamp with a pure mind even though knowing moths might fall into it, so too it should be known that there is a fault according to the regulation because of using water with the perception of water even though knowing there are living beings in it.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on [Water] Containing Living Beings (Sappāṇaka) is finished.

## 3. Explanation of the Training Rule on Reopening (Ukkoṭana)

“Tassa tassa bhikkhuno” means: by whichever monk [the legal issue] was settled, of that monk who settled the issue. “One who says ‘the act was not done’ and so forth” means one who says, “The act was not done, the act was badly done, the act must be done again, it was not settled, it was badly settled, it must be settled again.” To show the manner in which those agitating monks behave, it was said, “He should not give the opportunity to remain in a stable state.” Therefore, it was said, “A legal issue that is settled according to the Dhamma is indeed well-settled.”

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Reopening (Ukkoṭana) is finished.

## 4. Explanation of the Training Rule on Grave Offenses (Duṭṭhullā)
