The four pārajika offenses have been shown in the word-analysis (padabhājanīya) by way of extracting the meaning; therefore, it is said, “Duṭṭhullā refers to the saṅghādisesa.” “By any means” (yena kenaci upāyena) means by any of the methods mentioned: “knowing it oneself, others informing him, or that monk himself informing him.” The meaning is that the pācittiya offense is incurred as soon as the burden [of concealment] is taken up. Even if he informs later, he is not freed from the offense because of having taken up the burden. Therefore, it was said “sacepi” and so forth. “Even a hundred monks incur [the offense]” means that even if a hundred monks hear of it and conceal it, they all incur a pācittiya offense. “Yena assa ārocitaṃ” means that which was told by a second monk to a third monk. “Tassa eva” means only to that second monk. “Āroceti” means saying “Do not tell anyone” only for the purpose of concealment. “Koṭichinnā hoti” means that only after incurring the offense due to the cause of concealment...
409:
The second monk has informed the third monk; because of that informing, there is no longer a basis for that second monk to incur an offense due to concealment, thus it is said that the 'edge' of the offense is cut.

'Ādipade' refers to the first phrase 'one who perceives it as a grave offense conceals it' among the three: 'perceiving as grave,' 'doubtful,' and 'perceiving as non-grave.' 'Itaresu dvīsu' refers to the phrases 'one who is doubtful conceals it' and 'one who perceives it as non-grave conceals it.' 'Aduṭṭhullāyā' refers to the remaining five groups of offenses. 'Anupasampannassa duṭṭhulle vā aduṭṭhulle vā ajjhācāre' refers to the transgression of the first five precepts by an unordained person (a novice), whether it be grave conduct or otherwise. The statement in the Samantapāsādikā Commentary that 'the emission of semen and physical contact by an unordained person is called grave conduct' does not agree with the Commentary on the Duṭṭhullārocana Sikkhāpada. Furthermore, it is not appropriate to say 'one type of grave conduct for an unordained person is intended in the case of informing, and another in the case of concealing,' because no specific reason for such a distinction is found. Therefore, this statement should be carefully examined.

## The Explanation of the Duṭṭhulla Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 5. Explanation of the Ūnavīsativassa Sikkhāpada

Even one who has reached twenty years including the period spent in the mother's womb is counted as 'one who has completed twenty years,' as stated by 'starting from the taking of conception,' etc. In that context, 'starting from the taking of conception' means starting from the first mind that arose in the mother's womb, from the first consciousness that became manifest. 'So' refers to that person who was ordained before reaching twenty years of age. 'Aññaṃ upasampādeti' means acting as the preceptor (upajjhāya) or the teacher of the formal act (kammavācācariya) to ordain another person. 'Taṃ' refers to that person who is under twenty years of age. 'Sīmaṃ vā sammannati' means marking out a new boundary (sīmā).

## The Explanation of the Ūnavīsativassa Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 6. Explanation of the Theyyasattha Sikkhāpada

'Rājānaṃ vā vañcetvā' means having defrauded the king, having taken something belonging to the king, and thinking 'now we will not give it to that king,' [this refers to] thieves who have set out on a journey but have not yet committed the theft...
410:
...it means thieves who have not yet committed the theft and thieves who have already committed the theft. In the case of 'those wishing to evade tax,' it should be understood in this same way.

'Kālavisaṅketena' means breaking the appointment of time, or postponing the day. However, for a monk who travels by deviating from the path or by deviating through the forest, an offense is indeed incurred.

## The Explanation of the Theyyasattha Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 7. Explanation of the Saṃvidhāna Sikkhāpada

'Mātugāmena' means together with a woman. Even these three types—a nun (bhikkhunī) ordained by one side, a female trainee (sikkhamānā), and a female novice (sāmaṇerī)—are included here. However, for these three types, the designated time (for traveling) protects them from an offense. It should be understood that this protection by the designated time is the distinction between these three types and a laywoman.

## The Explanation of the Saṃvidhāna Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 8. Explanation of the Ariṭṭha Sikkhāpada

Because it arises in the midst of the continuity of beings by way of obstructing various attainments (prosperity), it is called 'antarāya' (obstacle). It is simply the lack of benefit occurring in the present life and so on. They are called 'antarāyika' (obstructive) because they are associated with that obstacle in the sense of being insurmountable, or because they deserve the result known as an obstacle, or because they tend to create an obstacle. Therefore, it is said: 'They are called obstructive because they create an obstacle to heaven and liberation.'

Those obstructive things are of five kinds: by way of action (kamma), defilement (kilesa), result (vipāka), reproach (upavāda), and transgression of regulations (paññattivītikkama). Among these five, the five actions with immediate result (pañcānantariya-kamma) are called 'kammantarāyika.' Likewise, the act of violating a nun is also an obstructive action. However, that act of violating a nun only creates an obstacle to liberation, not to heaven. Fixed wrong views (niyatamicchādiṭṭhi) are called 'kilesantarāyika.' The rebirth-linking of eunuchs (paṇḍaka), animals (tiracchāna), and hermaphrodites (ubhatovyañjanaka) are called 'vipākantarāyika.' Disparaging the Noble Ones (ariyūpavāda) is called 'upavādantarāyika.' However, these are obstacles only as long as they do not ask for forgiveness from the Noble Ones; after asking for forgiveness, they are no longer obstacles. Offenses committed intentionally are called 'paññattivītikkamantarāyika.' These too are obstacles only as long as one still claims to be a monk, or has not emerged from the offense, or has not confessed the offense; after such claiming, emerging, or informing, they are no longer obstacles.
411:
Among those five obstructive things, this monk Ariṭṭha was a very learned person (bahussuta) and a Dhamma preacher (dhammakathika). He knew the obstructive things other than the obstacle of violating the Vinaya regulations. However, because he was not skilled in the Vinaya, he did not know the obstacle of violating the Vinaya regulations. Therefore, when he was in seclusion, he thought: "These laypeople enjoy the five strands of sensual pleasure and yet become Stream-enterers (Sotāpanna), Once-returners (Sakadāgāmi), and Non-returners (Anāgāmi). Monks also see pleasant forms cognizable by the eye... (as mentioned)... touch tangible objects cognizable by the body. They use soft rugs, coverings, and so forth. All this is allowable. Why is it that only the forms of women... (as mentioned)... and the touch of women are not allowable? These things must also be allowable." Thus, comparing one pleasant taste with another, and making the enjoyment with desire and lust the same as enjoyment without desire and lust—like joining a very fine thread with coarse fibers, or like comparing a mustard seed with Mount Sineru—he gave rise to a wicked wrong view. He challenged the Omniscient Knowledge, saying, "Why did the Blessed One, with great effort as if damming the great ocean, prescribe the first Pārājika training rule? There is no fault in this." By cutting off the hopes of those capable of realization, he struck a blow against the Wheel of Authority (āṇācakka) of the Conqueror. Therefore, it is said, "tesu" (among them), and so forth.

In that passage, "tesu" means among the aforementioned obstacles. In the phrase "aṭṭhikaṅkalūpamā kāmā" (sensual pleasures are like a skeleton), "aṭṭhikaṅkala" refers to a chest bone, a backbone, or a skull bone. Because that bone is fleshless, it is called "kaṅkala". The term "kaṅkala" is well-known for a fleshless skeleton or even a single fleshless bone. The meaning is that sensual pleasures are like that fleshless bone because they provide little gratification. By the word "ādi" (and so forth), one should take these phrases: "sensual pleasures are like a piece of meat, like a grass torch, like a pit of glowing coals, like a dream, like borrowed goods, like the fruit of a tree, like a butcher's block, like a sword and stake, like a snake's head."

Among those similes, sensual pleasures are like a piece of meat because they are common to many. They are like a grass torch because they burn. They are like a pit of glowing coals because they cause great affliction. They are like a dream because they appear only for a moment. They are like borrowed goods because they are possessed only temporarily. They are like the fruit of a tree because they cause the destruction of all limbs, large and small. They are like a butcher's block because they are a place of cutting. They are like a sword and stake because they pierce. They are like a snake's head because they are suspicious and fearful.
412:
"In the same way" (tatheva) refers to the prohibition by saying, "Do not, venerable sir," and so forth. "To other monks" (itaresam) means to the other monks who heard those words when that person (Ariṭṭha) was brought into the midst of the Saṅgha and addressed with "Do not, venerable sir," and so forth. "By a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations" (ñatticatutthakamma) refers to the formal act as explained in the Word-Analysis (padabhājaniya): "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. Such and such a monk has given rise to such a wicked wrong view," and so forth.

## The Explanation of the Ariṭṭha Training Rule is finished.

## 9. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Associating with an Expelled Monk (Ukkhittasambhoga)

"With a monk who has not acted according to the rule" (akatanudhammena) refers to a monk who has been expelled (suspended) and has not yet been restored to the Saṅgha. Therefore, it is said, "anudhamma is mentioned," and so forth. Here, "anudhamma" should be connected to mean "restoration" (osāraṇā). Alternatively, it is called "anudhamma" because it is a practice that conforms to the act of suspension (ukkhepanīyakamma) and should be practiced thereafter. "Having seen the conforming duties" (anulomavattaṃ disvā) means having seen the eighteen types of duties such as "ordination should not be given, dependence (nissaya) should not be given," and so forth, and seeing that he is practicing those eighteen conforming duties. In the phrase "material association or Dhamma association" (āmisasambhogaṃ vā dhammasambhogaṃ vā), the giving and receiving of any material thing is called material association. The reciting or teaching of the Dhamma is called Dhamma association. "Should associate" (saṃvaseyya) means performing the three types of association mentioned in the Word-Analysis: "Uposatha, Pavāraṇā, or a formal act of the Saṅgha (Saṅghakamma)." However, since Uposatha and Pavāraṇā must also be performed by the Saṅgha, they are indeed formal acts of the Saṅgha. Therefore, it is said, "should perform Saṅghakamma such as Uposatha." "With every effort" (payoge payoge) means with every act of giving and every act of receiving.

It is said "with three types of consciousness" (ticitta) because even an Arahant who does not know the regulation can fall into an offense with a functional indeterminate consciousness (kiriyābyākata-citta).

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Associating with an Expelled Monk is finished.

## 10. The Explanation of the Kaṇṭaka Training Rule

"Pire" is an indeclinable particle used in the sense of addressing (vocative), and it is said to have the same meaning as the word "para". Therefore, it means "a stranger (novice) who is not one of our own." It means one who is not internal to us.
415:
## 3. Mohanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā
"Tasmiṃ anācāre" means in that practiced bad conduct. "Mokkho natthi" means there is no escape from that offense. "Tassa te" means of that you. "Alābhā" means that all the benefits and essences of the present and future lives, which should be desired and obtained by paying careful attention (making it a matter of concern) when the Pātimokkha is being recited by others, are not obtained by you. "Dulladdhaṃ" means that even the human life obtained through exceptional merit is badly obtained (i.e., it is in vain). "Sādhukaṃ" means well. "Aṭṭhiṃ katvā" means having made oneself one who is interested (being attentive). "Ñattidutiyena kammena" means by the formal act with a motion as the second, which is the imposition of [the charge of] delusion (mohāropanaka) as described in the Word Analysis (Padabhājaniya) starting with "Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs."

In the word "adhammakamme," it refers to the formal act of imposing [the charge of] delusion.

## The Commentary on the Mohana Training Rule is finished.

## 4. Pahārasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā
"Pahāraṃ dadeyya" means giving a blow with any of the things connected to the body or things that can be released (thrown), starting from at least a lotus leaf. In giving such a blow, whether a hand, foot, or head is broken, or if death occurs, it is only a Pācittiya offense. Therefore, it is said "with the desire to strike," etc.

"Anupasampanne" refers to a layperson, a monk [of another order], a woman, a man, or even at least an animal. However, if one strikes a woman with a lustful mind (ratta-citta), it is a Saṅghādisesa offense. "Keñci viheṭhiyamānassa" means being harassed by a human or an animal. "Mokkhādhippāyassa" means for a monk who desires his own escape from that harasser [there is no offense]. If one sees a thief or an enemy on the road who wishes to harass him and says, "Layman, stay right there, do not come," and if they do not heed the words and advance, and the monk strikes them with a club (muggara) or a small knife while saying, "Hey, fool, go away," and if that person dies from that blow, it is an Anāpatti (no offense). The same method should be understood regarding fierce wild animals.

## The Commentary on the Pahāra Training Rule is finished.
416:
## 5. Talasattikasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā
"Talasattika" means the surface of the palm itself. Some teachers say it is called "sattika" (weapon-like) because of its ability to strike. "Uccāreyya" means should raise up. In the phrase "it is a Dukkaṭa because it was given without the desire to strike (only to threaten)," if one strikes with the desire to strike, it is a Pācittiya by the previous training rule. If one merely raises the hand with the desire to raise it [to threaten], it is a Pācittiya by this training rule. However, if this monk strikes by accident [while threatening], it is a Dukkaṭa offense due to that accident. In this training rule, teachers say that if one raises a hand in anger upon seeing animals defecating, etc., it is merely the desire for release (to drive the animal away).

## The Commentary on the Talasattika Training Rule is finished.

## 6. Amūlakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā
The sixth training rule is clear in its meaning.

## The Commentary on the Amūlaka Training Rule is finished.

## 7. Sañciccasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā
"Kukkuccaṃ uppādantassa" means to a monk who causes remorse (anxiety). Whether the other person actually feels remorse or not, that person's remorse or lack thereof is not the criterion. "Maññe" means "I suppose" or "I think." By the word "ādi" (etc.), one should include phrases such as "I suppose you ate at the wrong time (vikāla)," "I suppose you drank intoxicants," "I suppose you sat in a secluded place with a woman." "Anupasampanna" refers to a novice (sāmaṇera).

## The Commentary on the Sañcicca Training Rule is finished.

## 8. Upassutisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā
Because it is heard, sound is called "suti." The vicinity of hearing is called "upassuti." Therefore, the author of the Saṅgaha says "suti-samīpa" (near hearing). It means near the sound. A monk standing in a place where he can hear the sound...
417:
The phrase "Yattha ṭhatvā" etc. is stated with the intention that one who stands in that place to hear the sound is said to be standing near the sound. Alternatively, it is called "upassuti" (eavesdropping) because one approaches and hears the sound there; it is a place (ṭhāna). The meaning in this training rule should be understood as standing in a place where one who has approached can hear the sound of those speaking. "Turitagamanepi" means even in going quickly for the purpose of hearing the sound of those going in front by one going behind. "Ohīyamānepi" means even in lagging behind for the purpose of hearing the words of those coming behind by one going in front, an offense is incurred.

"Vūpasamissāmi" means "I will attain peace; I will not engage in a quarrel." "Attānaṃ parimocessāmi" means "I will free myself by stating my non-involvement." "Siya kiriyaṃ" means it may be an action (offense) if it arises due to the cause of going with the desire to hear at some time. "Siya akiriyaṃ" means it may be a non-action (offense) if it arises due to the cause of not letting those who come to the place where one is and consult know of one's presence.

## The Explanation of the Upassuti Training Rule is Finished.

## 9. The Explanation of the Kammap-paṭibāhana Training Rule

"Dhammikānaṃ" means those that are righteous/legal because they are performed according to the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher's instruction. "Kammānaṃ" refers to the four types of Saṅgha acts (saṅghakamma). Therefore, "dhammena" etc. is said. Therein, "dhammena" means by way of a true matter. "Vinayena" means by way of accusation (codanā) and reminding (sāraṇā). "Satthusāsanena" means by way of the completeness of the motion (ñatti) and the completeness of the proclamation (anussāvana). "Samaggassa saṅghassa" means for the Saṅgha that is united in body and mind because the act is performed after clearing the Saṅgha within the boundary (sīmā) and bringing the consent (chanda) of those entitled to give it. "Taṃ taṃ vatthuṃ" refers to various matters such as speaking dispraise.

"Osārenti" means it is called "osāraṇā" because one is brought into the midst of the Saṅgha by this apalokana act. "Nissārenti" means it is called "nissāraṇā" because one is expelled from the Saṅgha by this apalokana act. "Bhaṇḍukammaṃ" means making the head bald, which means asking for the shaving of the hair. "Kammalakkhaṇa" means the act itself is the characteristic (lakkhaṇa). It means "kammalakkhaṇa" because, unlike osāraṇā etc., it does not receive another name while being an act, but is characterized as being only an act. Here, saying "osāraṇā nissāraṇā" is for the sake of the smoothness of the phrasing. In reality, expulsion (nissāraṇā) occurs first, and reinstatement (osāraṇā) occurs later.
418:
"Tattha kaṇṭakasāmaṇerassa" etc. is said. Regarding "nissāraṇā" like the expulsion of the novice Kaṇṭaka: just as the expulsion by punishment of the novice Kaṇṭaka is called "nissāraṇā," so it is for any other novice who speaks dispraise of the Buddha, the Dhamma, or the Saṅgha, who points out what is unallowable as "allowable," who holds wrong views, or who is possessed of a view that holds to an end—

"Venerable Sir, I ask the Saṅgha: This novice named so-and-so is a speaker of dispraise of the Buddha, the Dhamma, or the Saṅgha, and holds wrong views. Other novices receive shared sleeping (sahaseyya) with monks for two or three nights; for his deprivation of that, is expulsion (nissāraṇā) pleasing to the Saṅgha? A second time... A third time, Venerable Sir, I ask the Saṅgha: This novice named so-and-so... is it pleasing to the Saṅgha? Go away, you wretch, be destroyed!"—such an expulsion performed is called "nissāraṇā."

Seeing that same expelled novice behaving properly and bringing him back is called "osāraṇā." Seeing that same novice at a later time confessing and asking for forgiveness, saying, "Venerable Sir, I did this because of foolishness, ignorance, and lack of merit; I now ask the Saṅgha for forgiveness," and having him ask up to three times—

"Venerable Sir, I ask the Saṅgha: This novice named so-and-so was a speaker of dispraise of the Buddha, the Dhamma, or the Saṅgha, and held wrong views; although other novices receive shared sleeping with monks for two or three nights, he was expelled to deprive him of that sahaseyya. That expelled novice is now devoted to merit, humble in his way of life, has entered upon the state of shame, stands in moral shame and moral dread (hiri-ottappa), has performed the penalty, and confesses his fault. Is the giving of unity in physical association (kāyasambhogasāmaggī) to this novice as before pleasing to the Saṅgha? A second time... A third time, Venerable Sir, I ask the Saṅgha... is it pleasing to the Saṅgha?"—such a bringing back is called "osāraṇā."

"Kေသစ္ဆေဒနာပုစ္ဆန" (Asking for the shaving of the hair) means having the monks within the boundary assemble, bringing the candidate for novicehood there, and saying, "Venerable Sir, I ask the Saṅgha for the shaving of the head (bhaṇḍukamma) of this boy."
419:
The word "I inform" (āpucchāmi) should be said three times, twice, or once. In this context of the announcement (apalokana) for tonsure, it is also appropriate to say, "I inform [the Saṅgha] of the tonsure of this boy," or "I inform of the making of this boy into a recluse," or "I inform of the going forth of this boy," or "This boy wishes to become a recluse," or "This boy wishes to go forth."

"Mukhara" means one who is harsh with the mouth. "An act not to be saluted is permitted" is connected with the following cases. "In cases such as exposing the thigh, etc." means:

"At that time, the group of six bhikkhus splashed muddy water on the bhikkhunīs with the intention, 'Perhaps they might fall in love with us'; they exposed their bodies to the bhikkhunīs, exposed their thighs to the bhikkhunīs, exposed their genitals to the bhikkhunīs, mocked the bhikkhunīs, and matched the bhikkhunīs [with others], with the intention, 'Perhaps they might fall in love with us'"—this refers to these cases.

"To those whose robes were stolen, etc." refers to those whose robes were stolen, those with worn-out robes, those who lost their robes, sick bhikkhus, learned bhikkhus, and those who bear the burden of the Saṅgha, etc. "Robes, etc." refers to robes, medicine, and lodgings, etc. "To be used" refers to roots, bark, leaves, shoots, flowers, and fruits, etc., that are to be used. "Things to be removed" refers to shade trees, fruit trees, etc., that are to be removed for the purpose of building a monastery, etc. "By those who make such a righteous agreement (dhammika-katika)" refers to bhikkhus who make such an agreement or other righteous agreements, such as repairing the monastery using materials donated for robes and alms-food.

"The Sutta does not come" means the Mātikā does not come to mind (is not memorized). "The Sutta Vibhaṅga also does not come" means the Vinaya has not been mastered through repeated study. "Obstructing the meaning with the shadow of the letter" means rejecting the meaning by taking only the literal words. Seeing a Vinaya-expert bhikkhu punishing an offense in matters such as accepting gold, silver, fields, or property, one might say, "Why do you punish these bhikkhus with an offense? Is it not taught in the Sutta merely as 'He is one who abstains from accepting gold and silver'? There is no offense here in accepting gold and silver." Another Dhamma-preacher, because he has [only a superficial] grasp of the Sutta, when an offense is being charged against bhikkhus who wear their robes hanging down, might say, "Why do you charge these bhikkhus with an offense? Is it not taught that the training rule should be practiced as 'I will wear the robe all around'?"
420:
"Thus, only the undertaking of the training rule is taught; there is no offense here," he says. "Ubbāhikā-decision" refers to the decision made by selecting two or three bhikkhus endowed with the ten qualities, such as "He is virtuous," as taught in the Samatha-khandhaka regarding the Ubbāhikā-decision.

"Pavāraṇappaccukkaḍḍhanā" means pulling the Pavāraṇā upwards (postponing it). "The all-inclusive motion (ñatti) in the Tinavatthāraka-samatha" refers to the very first all-inclusive motion made in the Tinavatthāraka-samatha (Settlement by Covering with Grass), such as: "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me. Regarding our disputes... (pe) ...excluding those connected with the laity."

"Alābhāya parisakkanādikehi" means by making efforts for the non-gain of the four requisites, etc. By the word "etc." (ādi), the remaining seven factors are included: "striving for non-benefit, striving for non-residence, reviling and threatening, causing division among bhikkhus, speaking in dispraise of the Buddha, speaking in dispraise of the Dhamma, and speaking in dispraise of the Saṅgha." "Aṭṭhahaṅgehi samannāgatassa" refers to one endowed with the eight factors collectively or with any one of the factors. "Asambhogakaraṇatthaṃ" means for the purpose of not accepting the gifts offered by that lay devotee. "Pattanikkujjanavasena" means by way of turning over the alms-bowl through a formal act (kammavācā), not by way of physically turning it upside down by hand. In the case of "Pattukkujjanavasena" (turning the bowl upright), the same method should be understood. "Tasseva" refers to that same lay devotee who was excommunicated by turning over the bowl. "Sammāvattantassa" refers to one who [now] conducts himself properly, being endowed with the qualities for which the bowl is turned upright. "Sā" refers to the aforementioned excommunication (nissāraṇā) and reinstatement (osāraṇā).

"Appamattakavissajjaka" is one who distributes minor items such as needles to the bhikkhus who need them. "Sāṭiyaggāဟာပကော" is the bhikkhu who causes the rainy-season cloths to be received. The authorization given for the purpose of directing monastery attendants who perform work is called "Ārāmika-pesaka-sammuti." The same method applies to "Sāmaṇera-pesaka-sammuti" (Authorization of the sender of novices).

"Tajjaniyakammādīnaṃ sattannaṃ" refers to the seven acts: Tajjaniya-kamma, Niyasa-kamma, Pabbājaniya-kamma, Paṭisāraṇiya-kamma, and the three types of Ukkhepaniya-kamma. "Aṭṭhayāvatatiyakā" refers to the eight Saṅghādisesas: four regarding bhikkhus and four regarding bhikkhunīs [that involve formal admonition up to the third time].
421:
"By way of ñattikamma, etc." means by way of ñattikamma, ñattidutiyakamma, and ñatticatutthakamma. Some teachers say, "If an apalokanakamma is performed as a ñattikamma, etc., it becomes especially firm; therefore, it should be done so." However, because doing so can lead to a confusion of legal acts (kammasaṅkara), the commentators have rejected it, stating that an apalokanakamma should not be performed as a ñattikamma, etc. If there is a deficiency in syllables, a deficiency in words, or if it is poorly recited, it is proper to repeat it for the purpose of correcting that error. Such repetition makes a valid act (akuppakamma) firmer, but in the case of an invalid act (kuppakamma), it remains as a legal act. "By the complete characteristics" means only after reciting the motion (ñatti) and the four proclamations (kammavācā). "Not by way of the remaining acts" means it should not be performed by way of the remaining acts such as apalokanakamma.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Preventing Legal Acts is Finished.

## 10. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Leaving Without Giving Consent

"The reported matter is undecided" means the reported case has not yet been decided as to whether it constitutes an offense. In this context, the accuser monk and the accused monk have finished their statements, and the Vinaya expert has been appointed; by this much, the matter should be understood as reported. "Should leave the seat without giving consent" means leaving the seat without giving consent with the intention: "How might this act be made invalid? How might it be made discordant? How might I act so that this act cannot be performed?" Therefore, it is said, "Whatever monk," and so on. In the phrase "action and non-action," going is the action (kiriya), and not giving consent is the non-action (akiriya).

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Leaving Without Giving Consent is Finished.

## 11. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Weak [Friendship]

"According to acquaintance" means according to one's friends. Therefore, it is said, "Whoever," and so on. In that context, "by way of friends, acquaintances, and intimates" means by the power of friends, acquaintances, and intimates. Among those three, "friends" (mittā) are simply beloved friends. "Acquaintances" (sandiṭṭhā) are those seen only by meeting here and there, not very firm friends. "Intimates" (sambhattā) should be understood as those well-served, affectionate, and firm friends.

"Five heavy items" means there are five types of heavy items by way of groups, but by way of individual items, there are many. Therefore, it is said, "Five heavy items are mentioned by way of groups."
422:
"Park" (ārāma) means a flower garden or a fruit orchard. "Park-site" (ārāmavatthu) means the space demarcated for making those parks, or the former ground of those parks when they have been destroyed. "Dwelling" (vihāra) means any kind of lodging such as a mansion (pāsāda), etc. "Dwelling-site" (vihāravatthu) means the place where that dwelling stands. "Couch" (mañca) is any one of the four types of couches mentioned previously: the masāraka couch, the bundikābaddha couch, the kuḷīrapādaka couch, and the āhaccapādaka couch. "Chair" (pīṭha) is any one of the four types of chairs such as the masāraka, etc. "Bolster" (bhisi) is any one of the five types of bolsters such as the wool bolster, etc. "Pillow" (bibbohana) is a pillow stuffed with any one of tree-cotton, creeper-cotton, or poṭaki-grass-cotton. "Metal pot" (lohakumbhī) is a pot made of iron, copper, or any kind of metal. The same method applies to metal jars (lohabhāṇaka), etc. Here, bhāṇaka means a large water jar. Vāraka means a drinking-water pot. Kaṭāha means a cauldron. Regarding tools such as axes and materials such as creepers, there is nothing difficult to understand. Thus:

##
There are two groups of two, the third is a group of four,
The fourth has nine divisions, and the fifth has eight varieties.
Thus, the Lord, who possesses the five stainless eyes,
Has declared the twenty-five kinds of heavy items in five groups.

"It is not proper to give away or to divide" means it is not proper to give away or to divide by way of permanent alienation. However, there is no offense in giving away or dividing by way of exchange. Therefore, it is said, "With a permanent item..." and so on. In that context, "a permanent item for a permanent item" means exchanging a park, a park-site, a dwelling, or a dwelling-site for a park, a park-site, a dwelling, or a dwelling-site. "With another item" means exchanging with non-permanent items from the last three groups. "With an unallowable item" means exchanging with a couch made of gold, etc., or with unallowable bolsters and pillows. "With a valuable allowable item" means exchanging with a couch made of ivory, etc., or with covers, rugs, etc. "To exchange another item by an allowable exchange" means to exchange in an allowable way so that it does not become unallowable.

In this regard, the method of exchange is as follows: A coconut grove belonging to the Saṅgha is in a distant place, and the monastery attendants (kappiyakāraka) consume most of it; the coconuts they do not consume...
423:
When those coconuts are brought after paying the cartage, only a small amount is obtained. If laypeople living in a village not far from that monastery have a garden near the monastery, and those people approach the Saṅgha and request to exchange their own garden for that garden belonging to the Saṅgha, it should be accepted after announcing, "Is it pleasing to the Saṅgha?"

Even if the monks' garden has a thousand trees and the laypeople's has only five hundred, one should not say, "Your garden is too small." Although this [lay garden] is small, it may yield more income than the other. Even if it yields an equal amount, it should still be accepted because it can be used at any desired moment. If the laypeople's garden has more trees, one should say, "Do you not have more trees?" If they say, "May we gain extra merit; we give it to the Saṅgha," it is proper to accept after informing [the Saṅgha].

If the monks' trees are bearing fruit and the laypeople's trees are not yet bearing fruit, it should still be accepted, considering that although they do not bear fruit now, they will bear fruit before long. If the laypeople's trees are bearing fruit and the monks' trees are not yet bearing fruit, one should say, "Do you not see that your trees are bearing fruit?" If they give it saying, "Please accept, Bhante, it will be for our merit," it is proper to accept after informing [the Saṅgha].

In this way, a garden should be exchanged for a garden. By this same method, garden land (ārāmavatthu), a monastery (vihāra), or monastery land (vihāravatthu) should also be exchanged for a garden. Whether large or small, a garden, garden land, a monastery, or monastery land should be exchanged for garden land.

How is a monastery exchanged for a monastery? If the Saṅgha owns a house within a village and laypeople own a mansion (pāsāda) in the middle of the monastery grounds, and both are equal in value, if the laypeople request to exchange that mansion for that house, it is proper to accept. If the monks' house is more valuable, when it is said, "Our house is more valuable," and they reply, "Although it is more valuable, it is unsuitable for renunciants; it is not possible for renunciants to live there, but this [mansion] is suitable; please accept it," then it is also proper to accept. If the laypeople's house is more valuable, one should say, "Is your house not more valuable?" If they say, "Let it be, Bhante, it will be for our merit; please accept it," then it is proper to accept. In this way, a monastery is exchanged for a monastery. By this same method, monastery land, a garden, or garden land should be exchanged for a monastery. Whether it is of high value or low value, with monastery land...
424:
...or a monastery, monastery land, a garden, or garden land are exchanged [for monastery land]. Thus, first, the exchange of permanent property (thāvara) for permanent property should be understood.

Furthermore, in the exchange of non-permanent property (athāvara) for non-permanent property, whether a couch (mañca) or a stool (pīṭha) is large or small—even a couch with legs only four finger-breadths high made by village children playing at building sand-houses—from the moment it is given to the Saṅgha, it becomes heavy property (garubhaṇḍa). If a king or a great royal minister and so forth gives a hundred or a thousand couches at once, all allowable couches should be accepted. After accepting them, they should be given according to seniority, saying, "Use these as communal property (saṅghika-paribhoga)"; they should not be given for personal use. It is also proper to use surplus couches by laying them out in storehouses and the like to place bowls and robes upon.

A couch given outside the boundary (sīmā) with the words "We give to the Saṅgha" should be placed in the residence of the Sanghatthera. If there are already many couches there and there is no need for a couch, it should be given to whatever monk's residence has a need for it, saying, "Use it as communal property"; it should not be given for personal use.

If one can obtain a hundred other couches in exchange for one couch that is very valuable or worth a hundred or a thousand, it should be taken in exchange. Not only couch for couch; it is also proper to exchange them for a garden, garden land, a monastery, monastery land, a stool, a mattress (bhisi), or a pillow (bibbohana). This same method applies to stools, mattresses, and pillows.

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of protecting noble lodgings (vara-senāsana) and so forth": if there is a famine and monks cannot subsist on alms-food, or if there are dangers from kings, diseases, or thieves in this place, and the monasteries of those going elsewhere fall into ruin, or if [people] destroy palmyra and coconut trees and so forth—if it is possible to subsist by relying on the lodging-requisites, then in such a time, it is for the sake of protecting noble lodgings [that inferior items are discarded]. "To discard inferior items" means to discard them starting from the most inferior grade. It is proper to use the gruel, rice, robes, and so forth obtained from discarding them.

Regarding "iron, copper, bronze (kaṃsaloha), and waṭṭaloha": here, bronze and waṭṭaloha are artificial alloys (kittimaloha). There are three artificial alloys: bronze (kaṃsaloha), waṭṭaloha, and brass (ārakūṭa). Among them, bronze is made by mixing tin and copper. Waṭṭaloha is made by mixing lead (sīta) and copper. Brass is made by mixing calamine (rasaka) and copper. Therefore, it is said, "Bronze and waṭṭaloha are artificial alloys." "Tato atirekaṃ" means having a capacity greater than that [one pāda].
425:
A saraka (small bowl) is a type of vessel made by forming a bud-like shape in the center, widening the rim, and curving it towards the back of the bowl. It is also called a 'sarāva'. By the word 'ādi' (etc.), lay utensils such as gold bowls should be included. Even if small, these gold bowls and similar items are garubhaṇḍa (communal property) because they are lay utensils. By the word 'pi' (even), it is shown that there is no need to mention that large utensils are garubhaṇḍa. These pitchers (karā) and so forth, however, are bhājanīya (distributable) items because they are requisites for monks.

Just like those pitchers and so forth, a kuṇḍikā (water pot) is also a distributable item. It will be stated (in the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Aṭṭhakathā): "Just as a kuṇḍikā among earthenware belongs to the distributable portion, so also among metalware, a kuṇḍikā belongs only to the distributable portion." "Saṅghika-paribhoga" means by giving it to visiting senior monks for their use. "Gihi-vikaṭa" refers to items prepared by laypeople, or items made to look different by treating them as one's own property. "Not allowable for personal use (puggalika-paribhoga)" means it is not allowable to take and use them as one's own property without giving them to visiting monks. Pipphalika refers to scissors. Ārakaṇṭaka refers to an awl or needle-piercer. Tāḷa refers to a mechanical lock. Kattarayaṭṭhi-vedhaka refers to a metal ring for a walking stick. "Solid metal" refers to metal made into solids such as rods, balls, lumps, or circular discs. "Khīrapāsāṇamaya" refers to items made of soft, milk-colored stone.

(Bowls made of gold, silver, brass, or pure crystal) are not allowable even if made by laypeople because they are anāmāsa (items not to be handled). By the word 'pi' (even), it is shown that there is no need to mention that they are not allowable for communal or personal use. Monastery requisites (senāsana-paribhoga), however, are entirely allowable. Therefore, all monastery accessories made of gold and so forth are āmāsa (items that can be handled). Thus, it was said, "Senāsana-paribhoga pana," and so forth.

"Sesa" refers to a billhook larger than that one. "Yā pana" refers to a large knife (machete). A hoe (kudāla) is garubhaṇḍa even if it is at least four finger-breadths in size. Whether a chisel (nikhādana) has a square edge, a trough-shaped edge, is curved, or is straight—even a small awl for piercing broom handles—if it is fitted with a handle, it is garubhaṇḍa. Therefore, it is said, "There is no such thing as a hoe or a handled chisel that is not garubhaṇḍa." Sipāṭikā refers to a razor case. Since a small awl (sikhara) is similar to a handled chisel, it is said, "The small awl is also included under chisels." If that awl is just the blade without a handle, it is a bhājanīya (distributable) item. Upakkhara refers to accessories such as billhooks.

Pattabandhaka refers to one who makes repairs such as knots for an alms-bowl. It is also said to be "one who makes bowls from gold for images, etc." This also includes knives for cutting lead (tin) and knives for cutting gold.
426:
These three types of small knives, such as the small knife for cutting treated leather, are included in the category of nail scissors (pipphalika); therefore, it was said, "This is the distinction," and so on. "The others" refers to large scissors and such.

"Half-cubit length" (according to Sāratthadīpanī Ṭīkā, Cūḷavagga, 321) means the length from the elbow to the shoulder, which is one span and four finger-breadths. "Grown in that place" refers to creepers grown on communal (saṅghika) land. Because it is protected by providing a guard, and because it is secured to prevent destruction just as one would place it in a box, it is called "guarded and secured" (rakkhita-gopita). A creeper grown on communal land that is not guarded is not garubhaṇḍa. By the words "if done for the sake of the Saṅgha or for the sake of a shrine (cetiya)," it is shown that it is allowable to use communal property to protect or exchange for shrine property. "Thread" (sutta) refers to both twisted and untwisted thread.

"An eight-finger stylus handle" means at least eight finger-breadths in length and the thickness of a Sri Lankan stylus handle. "In this place" refers to bamboo items. Those whose houses have burned are called "fire victims." "Should not be forbidden" means one should not prohibit them by saying, "Do not take it and go." When they reach another place, they must leave it at a communal residence in the monastery they have reached.

"Remaining thatch grass" refers to all types of thatch grass remaining after munja and pabbaja grasses. In places where there is no grass, they roof with leaves. Therefore, since leaves are also included in the category of grass, it was said, "Among those included in the summary of thatch grass," and so forth. "Eight finger-breadths in length" refers to the width being eight finger-breadths. A written manuscript (book), however, is not garubhaṇḍa.

"The measurement stated for bamboo" is the same measurement stated for bamboo items as "an eight-finger stylus handle." "Whether donated to the Saṅgha" refers to wood donated to the Saṅgha in places where wood is scarce. After stating the determination of wooden items according to the order in the Kurundī Commentary, the phrase "Furthermore" (api ca) and so forth was said to state it according to the order in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā. In the context of "āsandika and so forth," āsandika refers to a square stool. According to the Buddha's word, "A high one is also called an āsandika," only a long bench with eight-finger legs is allowable. A square āsandika (high stool) should be understood as allowable even if it exceeds the size limits. By the word 'ādi' (etc.), the sattaṅga (seven-limbed chair), bhaddapīṭha (cane chair), eḷakapādakapīṭha (ram-footed stool), āmalakavaṭṭakapīṭha (myrobalan-shaped stool), phalaka (plank), and koccha (brush/mat) are included.
427:
It should be understood that these items called "Palālapīṭhaka" (straw bench) are also to be taken. Therefore, it is said, "even at the minimum," and so forth. "Paṇṇehi vā" refers to a bench made of banana leaves and the like. A kocchaka (rug/mat) covered with tiger skin, surrounded by figures of wild beasts, or sewn with jewels is also a garubhaṇḍa (heavy article).

Ghaṭṭanaphalaka (beating board) is a board on which dyed robes are placed and beaten by hand. Ghaṭṭanamuggara (beating mallet) is said to be a mallet used for beating the borders (of robes) and so forth. Daṇḍamuggara (stick mallet) is a stick mallet used for beating dyed robes. Ambana is a water vessel made of wooden boards like a pond. Rajanadoṇī (dyeing trough) is a vessel for pouring and keeping boiled dye.

Akappiyacamma (unallowable skin) refers to the skins of lions and such animals. The statement "It is allowable to spread it on the ground" is said with reference to akappiyacamma. By the phrase "paccattharaṇagatika," it is shown that it is also allowable to spread it on couches and benches. Some say that an upper covering such as a woolen garment (pāvāra) and the like is also a garubhaṇḍa. Others say it is not. It should be taken after investigation. Kappiyacamma (allowable skin) refers to the skins of deer and such animals.

Sabbaṃ cakkayuttayānaṃ refers to all wheeled vehicles such as chariots and carts. However, a vehicle with its wheels removed is a bhājanīyabhaṇḍa (distributable article). Anuññātavāsi (permitted adze) refers to an adze that can be carried by putting it in a bag (sipāṭikā). Muṭṭhipaṇṇa is a palmyra leaf. Because they carry that palmyra leaf by grasping it with the fist (muṭṭhi), it is called "muṭṭhipaṇṇa." Some say muṭṭhipaṇṇa is just an umbrella leaf. Araṇisahita means a pair of fire-sticks, the upper fire-stick and the lower fire-stick.

Phātikammaṃ katvā means having performed an act of permanent increase (compensation), even at minimum with sand equal to the value of that garubhaṇḍa. A monk who takes it without performing phātikamma (act of increase) should use it only in that monastery. When leaving, he should leave it in the saṅghika (communal) dwelling and go. If he takes it away by forgetfulness, he should send it back. If he has gone to another place, he should leave it in the saṅghika dwelling of the monastery he has reached. "Here" (ettha) refers to clay articles. Kuṇḍikā (pitcher) refers to both iron pitchers and copper/bronze pitchers. Bhājanīyakoṭṭhāsameva bhajati means it belongs only to the class of distributable items and is not a garubhaṇḍa. However, a kuṇḍikā made of gold is intended to be a garubhaṇḍa. The other (itara) is a garubhaṇḍa.

## The Commentary on the Dubbala Training Rule is finished.
428:
## 12. Commentary on the Pariṇāmana Training Rule
In this twelfth training rule, there is nothing special to be said.

## The Commentary on the Pariṇāmana Training Rule is finished.

## The Eighth Chapter, the Sahadhammika Vagga, is finished.

## 9. Ratana Vagga

## 1. Commentary on the Antepura Training Rule
In the Pali "anikkhantarājake aniggataratanake," the remaining substantive "sayanighare" (in the bedchamber) should be understood; thus it is said, "when the king has not yet departed from this bedchamber," and so forth. In that phrase, "from here" means from the bedchamber. "Sayanighare" means in the house for sleeping. It refers to the place where the king's bed is prepared, even if it is at least surrounded by a curtain-wall. Although elephants and so forth are called "jewels" (ratana) because they produce delight, in this training rule, the Chief Queen is intended as the jewel; thus it is said, "The Chief Queen is called a jewel."

"In both" (ubhosu) means in both the king and the queen. In the phrase "action and non-action" (kiriyākiriyam), crossing the threshold (indakhīla) is considered "action" (kiriya), and not giving prior notice is considered "non-action" (akiriya).

## The Commentary on the Antepura Training Rule is finished.

## 2. Commentary on the Ratana Training Rule
The ten kinds of jewels—pearl, gem, beryl, conch, crystal, coral, silver, gold, ruby, and emerald/cat's eye—are called "muttādidasavidha." "Ajjhāvasathe" means in the house. Therefore, it is said, "of the enclosed house," and so forth; the meaning is "of the enclosed dwelling." In this context, "āvasatha" refers to a house situated inside a village. A house situated inside a monastery is already included by the term "ajjhārāma" (inside the monastery). Some teachers say, "In this training rule, āvasatha refers to one's own dwelling place, whether it be inside a monastery or elsewhere."

"It is only a dukkaṭa offense for the benefit of all" means that for a monk who picks up (a jewel) himself or causes another to pick it up, whether for his own benefit or for the benefit of the Saṅgha and so forth, it is only a dukkaṭa offense. However, if it is the property of his parents and is a kappiya (allowable) object that must be kept without fail...
429:
Regarding the phrase "Tādisaṃ pana" etc., it is said with the meaning that if there is an allowable item (kappiya-bhaṇḍa) that should be stored, one should take it for oneself and store it. "Tādisaṃ" refers to the kind of allowable property belonging to parents that must definitely be stored. "Chandenapi bhayenapi" means out of affection for carpenters and the like, or out of fear of those who are favorites of the king.

"Tādise ṭhāne" refers to being within a walled enclosure of a large monastery like the Mahāvihāra. "Saññāṇaṃ katvā" means marking and defining, either by the number such as "this many kahāpaṇas" or by a sign such as a seal. "Patirūpānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ hatthe" means in the hands of monks who are conscientious (lajjī) and scrupulous (kukkuccaka) regarding the Vinaya. Indeed, it should not be placed in the hands of monks who are of a confused or unreliable nature. "Neva pakkamati" means not departing from that monastery to another place. By the phrase "Thāvaraṃ senāsanaṃ vā" etc., it is shown that one should not use the funds intended for one's robes and so forth for permanent lodgings. In showing this, it is done by pointing out, "Lay follower, this permanent lodging etc. has been made with your property." "Samādapetvā" means either by encouraging another person or by begging according to the method stated as: "The Noble Ones stand with an objective; this standing is the begging of the Noble Ones."

"Anuññātaṭṭhāne" means within the monastery precincts or within a house. "Āmāsaṃ" refers to items such as clothing that are to be handled and stored.

## The Explanation of the Ratana Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 3. Vikālagāmappavesana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

"Cāritte" refers to the Cāritta Sikkhāpada. "Upacāraṃ" refers to the distance of a second stone's throw. For monks going to another village, if they continue without relaxing their effort, there is no need to ask permission again. It means that even if there are a hundred villages, there is no need to ask permission again. Therefore, it is said "Sace pana" etc. "Ussāhaṃ" refers to the effort to enter the village. In places such as intermediate monasteries (antarārāma), there is no offense not only for one who goes without asking permission, but also for one who goes without fastening the waist-band or without wearing the outer robe (saṅghāṭi). "Āpadāsū" refers to when a lion or a tiger comes, or when it rains, or when any other danger...
430:
...arises, there is no offense. In such dangers, it is proper to enter the village from outside the village.

## The Explanation of the Vikālagāmappavesana Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 4. Sūcighara Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
That needle case belongs to that monk. Since it must be broken first and then confessed later, the 'breaking' (bhedanaka) of that needle case exists in that Pācittiya offense.

'Araṇike' refers to the fire-drill. 'Vidhe' refers to the buckle of the waist-band. 'Vāsijaṭe' refers also to the handle of an adze.

## The Explanation of the Sūcighara Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 5. Mañcapīṭha Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
'Aṭṭhaṅgulapādakaṃ' is a neuter designation indicating the meaning. By the statement "The chedanaka (cutting) is just like the bhedanaka (breaking)," it points to this meaning: the cutting itself is called chedanaka, and because that cutting exists in that Pācittiya offense, it is called chedanaka.

If one does not wish to cut it, one should bury it in the ground so that only the allowed measurement appears above the ground; or 'Aṭṭakaṃ vā bandhitvā' means lifting it up and placing it on the beams and rafters to make a scaffold.

## The Explanation of the Mañcapīṭha Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 6. Tūlonaddha Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
'Cimilikaṃ pattharitvā tūlaṃ pakkhipitvā' means spreading a piece of cloth over the bed or chair and putting cotton on top of it. 'Upari cimilikāya' means on the upper part of the cloth.
431:
A pillow of head-size refers to a pillow on which the entire head is placed, starting from the throat. To show that the maximum limit of that pillow is a cubit-and-a-fist (muṭṭhiratana) in width and two cubits in length, it is said "Yassa vitthārato tīsu koṇesu" etc. When measuring the distance between two corners, it is one span (viddatthi) and four finger-breadths. The center of the pillow is a cubit-and-a-fist in width. This is the maximum limit of a head-sized pillow. A pillow exceeding that limit is not allowable; one smaller than that is allowable. For a monk who is not ill, only two types are allowable: a head-pillow and a foot-pillow. For a sick monk (gilāna), however, it is allowable even to spread pillows and then lay a bedsheet over them to sleep.

## The Explanation of the Tūlonaddha Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 7. Nisīdana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
The seventh training rule is clear in its meaning.

## The Explanation of the Nisīdana Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 8. Kaṇḍuppaṭicchādi Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
It means below the navel and above the knee-caps. In the phrase "Kaṇḍupīḷaka-assāva-thullakacchābādhānaṃ," "kaṇḍu" refers to scabies (kacchu). "Pīḷakā" refers to small boils or pustules containing blood. "Assāvo" refers to the discharge of impure fluids due to hemorrhoids, fistulas, or diabetes. "Thullakacchābādho" refers to a large sore or ulcer.

## The Explanation of the Kaṇḍuppaṭicchādi Sikkhāpada is finished.
432:
## 9-10. Explanation of the Vassikasāṭika Sikkhāpada and Nanda Sikkhāpada

The ninth, the Vassikasāṭika Sikkhāpada, and the tenth, the Nanda Sikkhāpada, are both clear in their meaning.

## The Explanation of the Vassikasāṭika Sikkhāpada and Nanda Sikkhāpada is finished.

## The ninth chapter, the Ratana Vagga, is finished.

## Thus, in the explanation of the Pātimokkha called Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī,

## in the New Sub-commentary (Ṭīkā) Līnatthappakāsanī, which explains the meanings in the Vinayatthamañjūsā,

## the Explanation of the Pācittiya is finished.
433:
## Pāṭidesanīya Section

## 1. Commentary on the First Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule
'Antaragharaṃ paviṭṭhāya' means having entered a carriage road, a cul-de-sac (alley), a short path, a junction, or a house. 'Asappāyaṃ' means that which is not beneficial and is unsuitable for heaven, the Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna. In this training rule, it should be understood that an offense is incurred through the action of a bhikkhunī who stands within the village and gives; however, the standing place of the monk is not the determining factor. Therefore, the words 'Antaragharaṃ paviṭṭhāya' and so forth were said. 'Antarārāmādīsu' means inside the monastery, the bhikkhunīs' quarters, the quarters of non-Buddhist ascetics (titthiya), and the dining hall. Among the terms 'rathiyā-byūha-siṅghāṭaka-gharānaṃ', 'rathiyā' means a road or a carriage path. 'Byūha' means a road that does not lead through to the other side, where one must return by the same way (a cul-de-sac). 'Siṅghāṭaka' means a place where roads meet, whether in a square or triangular shape. 'Ghara' means the house of a family. Just as an offense is incurred by a monk who receives food while standing in places such as roads, it should be understood that an offense is also incurred by a monk who receives food while standing in places such as elephant stables and so forth.

'A dukkaṭa offense is incurred both in receiving and in swallowing yāmakālika and so forth'—this statement is made with reference to yāmakālika and such items that are not mixed with food (khādanīya or bhojanīya). However, if they are mixed with food and become of one essence, only a pāṭidesanīya offense is incurred for both receiving and swallowing. 'Ekato upasampannāya' refers to a bhikkhunī who has been ordained only in the presence of bhikkhunīs. Regarding the yāvakālika of a bhikkhunī ordained in the presence of bhikkhus, only a pāṭidesanīya offense is incurred according to the object.

'Ñātikāya vā dāpentiyā' refers to a bhikkhunī who does not give herself but causes another bhikkhunī who is a relative to give; the meaning is that there is no offense if she causes a non-relative to give. 'Upanikkhipitvā vā dadamānāya' refers to a bhikkhunī who gives by placing the food on the ground and saying, 'Venerable, I give this to you.' After receiving food given in this way and saying, 'Good, sister,' it is allowable to eat this food only after having that bhikkhunī or someone else offer it again.

## The Commentary on the First Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule is Finished.

## 2. Commentary on the Second Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule
The connection should be understood as 'Whichever monk receives and eats.' In the phrase 'attanō vā bhattaṃ dāpentiyā,' if a bhikkhunī gives her own alms-food to a monk, even so, there is no offense for that monk by this training rule, but an offense is incurred by the previous training rule. In the phrase 'aññesaṃ vā bhattaṃ dentiyā'...
434:
In this case, if she causes [another's alms-food] to be given, an offense would be incurred by this training rule. For a bhikkhunī who gives [her own alms-food], no offense is incurred by this training rule nor by the previous one.

## The Commentary on the Second Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule is Finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Third Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule
'Laddha-sekhasammutikāni' refers to families that have received the Sekha designation (Learner's designation) through a formal act with a motion as the second (ñattidutiya-kamma). When a family increases in faith but decreases in wealth, the Sekha designation is given to such a family by a formal act with a motion as the second; this statement is made with reference to such a family.

'Gharato nīharitvā' means having brought it from the house to the dining hall or to the monastery. Therefore, it is said, 'āsanasālādīsu vā.' This phrase is connected with the word 'denti.' 'Dvāramūle vā ṭhapitaṃ denti' refers to giving food placed near the door of the house to a monk who arrives later. However, it is not allowable to see a monk and then bring food out from inside the house to give. 'Niccabhattake' refers to alms-food that is given constantly. 'Salākabhatte' refers to alms-food given by having someone draw a ticket made of heartwood, or a strip made of bamboo, palm leaf, etc., on which the words 'The ticket-food of such-and-such a family' are written. 'Pakkhike' refers to alms-food given on one day within a fortnight. 'Uposathike' refers to alms-food given on the Uposatha day. 'Pāṭipadike' refers to alms-food given on the first day of the lunar fortnight (the day after the Uposatha).

## The Commentary on the Third Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule is Finished.

## 4. Commentary on the Fourth Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule
'Tassa parivāraṃ katvā, aññaṃ vā tena saddhiṃ bahukampi' means having previously announced gruel (yāgu) and then making an accompaniment for that hard food or soft food, or bringing many other things along with that [announced] food, in such a way as: 'What is the use of giving plain gruel? We will give snacks, rice, etc., as an accompaniment to this gruel.' 'Khādanīyaṃ' (hard food) is just an example, as 'bhojanīyaṃ' (soft food) is also intended. 'Tena saddhiṃ āharantu' means 'Let them bring their own offerings along with that food.'
435:
"Having made it an accompaniment to gruel and having notified [the monks] by saying 'We will offer [this],' if they bring snacks or almsfood, such snacks and almsfood brought [even without specific notification for them] are allowable." Thus it was stated by the teachers in the Kurundī.

Regarding the term "paṭisaṃviditāgilānāvasesakaṃ": it means the leftovers of food that was notified and the leftovers of a sick monk; the meaning is the leftovers of notified food and the leftovers of a sick monk. Leftovers of food brought after notification for one monk are allowable for another monk to consume. If food is brought for many monks after notifying four or five, and they wish to give it to other monks as well, this is also considered notified leftovers and is allowable for all monks. If there is still a surplus, food kept in a way that avoids the offense of storing up (sannidhi) is allowable even on the second day. The same method applies to leftovers brought for a sick monk. Food brought without prior notification should be sent back outside the monastery grounds to be notified before being brought back in. Alternatively, monks may go outside the monastery and receive it on the way. Food brought from the forest and offered by those passing through the monastery or by forest-dwellers, etc., should also be notified according to the previous method. In some palm-leaf manuscripts, the reading "paṭisaṃviditaṃ katvā āhaṭaṃ vā gilānāvasesakaṃ vā" is found, but that reading should not be accepted. "Tatthajātakam-eva" refers to things growing naturally within the monastery grounds. There is no offense for a monk who consumes roots, fruits, bark, leaves, etc., that have been made allowable (kappiya) and offered by another person (kappiya-kāraka). However, if those items are taken to a village, cooked, and then brought back, they are not allowable. Notification must be made.

## The explanation of the fourth Paṭidesanīya training rule is finished.
## Thus, in the Vinayatthamañjūsā Līnatthappakāsanī,
## which is an explanation of the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Pātimokkha,
## the explanation of the Paṭidesanīya is finished.
436:
## Section on Sekhiya
## 1. Explanation of the Parimaṇḍala Training Rule
Because it is not specifically stated as "in the village" (antaraghare), it is said inclusively as "everywhere, both in the monastery and in the village." "In the monastery" refers to times such as when attending upon the Buddha.

Just as a delimitation is made in various places by saying "These four Pārājika rules come into the recitation," why is no delimitation made here by saying "These seventy-five Sekhiya rules come into the recitation"? It is said, "In this Dispensation..." and so on. The duties taught in the Vattakkhandhaka include: duties for incoming monks (āgantuka-vatta), resident monks (āvāsika-vatta), departing monks (gamika-vatta), the duty of giving thanks (anumodana-vatta), dining hall duties (bhattagga-vatta), alms-round duties (piṇḍacārika-vatta), forest-dwelling duties (āraññaka-vatta), lodging duties (senāsana-vatta), sauna duties (jantāghara-vatta), toilet duties (vaccakuṭi-vatta), duties toward a preceptor (upajjhāya-vatta), duties toward a teacher (ācariya-vatta), duties toward a co-resident (saddhivihārika-vatta), and duties toward a pupil (antevāsika-vatta). This is merely an illustration; it is intended that other Khandhaka duties be included here as well.

The meaning here is: by mentioning "Sekhiya," the duties mentioned in the Vattakkhandhaka etc. are also to be included. They are desired as "Sekhiya" in the sense that they must be trained in (sikkhitabba). Therefore, unlike the Pārājikas in the Mātikā, no delimitation was made for the Sekhiyas. Not only to include the duties from the Vattakkhandhaka, but it is also said "for the purpose of showing the Vinaya of conduct (cāritta-vinaya)." Here too, it should be understood that no delimitation is made. Although "dukkaṭa" (wrongdoing) is not mentioned in the Mātikā, how is it known to be a dukkaṭa offense here? It is said, "Whoever..." and so on.

"About eight finger-breadths" means about eight finger-breadths of an ordinary person. However, for one with thin shanks or very large calves, it is allowable to wear the robe lower than eight finger-breadths for the sake of propriety.

"Pāsanta" means the edge of the belt-loop, the base of the fringe.

Regarding "I will wear it unevenly," this refers to wearing it sagging either in front or in back without [wrongful] intention. Although there is no offense for one who does not know how to wear it evenly, the duty of dressing must be well-learned. Since not learning it intentionally would constitute disrespect, it is said, "The duty of dressing should be learned."

## The explanation of the Parimaṇḍala training rule is finished.
437:
## 2. Commentary on the Second Parimaṇḍala Training Rule

"Paṭikkhittaṃ gihīpārutaṃ" refers to the wearing of robes in the manner of laypeople, which was prohibited by the Blessed One in the Khuddakavatthu-khandhaka of the Cullavagga. Now, in order to explain in detail the meaning that was briefly taught with the words "Na, bhikkhave" and so forth, he said "Tattha" and so forth. The connection should be understood as "wearing in any other unspecified manner." Because wearing white cloth and so forth is known as the laypeople's way of wearing, it is said "tasmā" (therefore). The word "setapaṭā" is merely an explanation of that.

"Aḍḍhapālaka-nigaṇṭha" means they are called "Aḍḍhapālaka" because they protect half of the body; they are both Aḍḍhapālaka and Nigaṇṭhas (Jains), hence they are called "Aḍḍhapālaka-nigaṇṭhas." They cover the upper part of the body by tucking a single white cloth under the armpits, but the lower part is naked, thus protecting only half of the body. "Paribbājakas" are those who have gone forth into the ascetic life, having abandoned the bonds of laypeople. "Opening the chest" means exposing the middle of the chest. "Just the size of the pupil of the eye" means just the eye. The phrase "In the monastery" is said with reference to times such as attending to the Buddha. "In the inhabited area" (antaraghare) refers to a village named "Antaraghara" because houses are situated here and there, or because houses are located within that village.

## The Commentary on the Second Parimaṇḍala Training Rule is finished.

## 3-4. Commentary on the Suppaṭicchanna Training Rule

"Well-covered" means being covered by covering the places that should be covered, without exposing the neck or the chest; it does not mean covering by wrapping the head. Therefore, he said "fastening the button" and so forth. In that phrase, "fastening the button" means fastening the button into the loop. "In the inhabited area" means in the village for alms-round. It is written in the Gaṇṭhipada that it is allowable to go as one pleases to the presence of a monk who has arrived to stay for even one day; what then to say of monks who have stayed having determined to stay for four or five days?

"One who has arrived to stay" means there is no offense if a monk who has arrived to stay for the night sits with his body uncovered during the night or during the day.

## The Commentary on the Suppaṭicchanna Training Rule is finished.
438:
## 5-6. Commentary on the Susaṃvuta Training Rule

"Susaṃvuta" means well-restrained. To show in what manner one is well-restrained in this training rule, the words "either the hand" and so forth were said.

## The Commentary on the Susaṃvuta Training Rule is finished.

## 7-8. Commentary on the Okkhittacakkhu Training Rule

To what extent is one called "one with downcast eyes" when the eyes are lowered? He said, "looking at the ground about a yoke's length." Indeed, a well-trained thoroughbred horse harnessed to a yoke looks at a distance of a yoke's length, which means looking at the ground for a distance of four cubits (hattha) ahead; in this manner, a monk should also go looking at the ground for this distance of four cubits. If any monk, out of disrespect, goes looking here and there at mansions, gabled houses, or the street, he commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). 

"Absence of danger from elephants, horses, etc.": Danger (parissaya) is so called because it dwells all around, or because it overcomes, or because it oppresses. Since elephants, horses, etc., are themselves dangers, they are called "elephant and horse dangers"; the absence of such dangers means the absence of the peril of being oppressed by elephants, horses, and so forth. The authors of the Sāratthadīpanī say: "Just as one standing in one place is allowed to look for the absence of danger, so too a monk while walking is allowed to look for the absence of danger; likewise, a monk receiving offerings in a village is allowed to look."

## The Commentary on the Okkhittacakkhu Training Rule is finished.

## 9-10. Commentary on the Ukkhittakāya Training Rule

"Starting from within the doorpost" means starting from within the threshold of a walled village, or starting from the distance of a second stone's throw in an unwalled village, one should not go with the robes hitched up.

## The Commentary on the Ukkhittakāya Training Rule is finished.

## 11-12. Commentary on the Ujjagghika Training Rule

In the phrase "in a matter of laughter," the locative case is used in the sense of cause (nimitta); it means because of a matter that is a cause for laughter.

## The Commentary on the Ujjagghika Training Rule is finished.
439:
## 13-14. Commentary on the Uccasadda Training Rule

By asking to what extent the sound is considered low, the author of the Saṅgahakāra said "Ayaṃ panettha" and so forth. "He hears only the sound" means hearing only the sound with indistinct, unclear, and blurred syllables. Therefore, the author of the Saṅgahakāra said "How does he not determine?"

## The Commentary on the Uccasadda Training Rule is finished.

## 15-20. Commentary on the Kāyappacālakādi Training Rules

The phrase "keeping them still and straight" is just an explanation of the term "holding the body and so forth." "One should go and one should sit" means one should go and sit with a composed posture. This is a group of six training rules associated with swaying the body and so forth.

## The Commentary on the Kāyappacālakādi Training Rules is finished.

## 26. Commentary on the Pallatthika Training Rule

In this training rule "Dussapallatthikāya," sitting with knees up and encircling them with a cloth or with a binding strap (āyogapaṭṭa) is also called "Dussapallatthikā."

## The Commentary on the Pallatthika Training Rule is finished.

## The Commentary on the Twenty-six Sāruppa Training Rules is finished.

## 27. Commentary on the Sakkaccapaṭiggahaṇa Training Rule

"Establishing mindfulness" means not being like one who wants to throw away the almsfood, but keeping mindfulness on the almsfood, and generating the thought "I will receive the almsfood."

## The Commentary on the Sakkaccapaṭiggahaṇa Training Rule is finished.
440:
## 28. Pattasaññīpaṭiggahaṇa-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā
'Upanibaddhasaññī hutvā' means having a perception associated with mental attention (manasikāra) on the bowl, without looking here and there due to disrespect when a donor is offering almsfood.

## End of the Commentary on the Training Rule on Receiving with Attention to the Bowl.

## 29. Samasūpakapaṭiggahaṇa-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā
'Samasūpakaṃ' means making it with a suitable amount of curry; this term 'samasūpakaṃ' is an adverbial use (bhāvanā-napuṃsaka-niddesa). To show only the meaning without taking the literal sound (vyañjana), it is said 'samasūpako nāma' etc. 'Sabbāpi sūpeyyabyañjanavikati' refers to all various kinds of curries such as salted curry, vegetable curry, fish or meat broth, and so forth.

## End of the Commentary on the Training Rule on Receiving with an Equal Amount of Curry.

## 30-32. Samatittikādi-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā
'Samatittikaṃ' is an adverbial use, meaning filling it evenly with the rim of the bowl. The meaning should be understood similarly in other such places. 'Samapuṇṇaṃ' (according to Sāratthadīpanī-ṭīkā, Pācittiya, 3.605) means filling evenly with the inner rim-line of the bowl. In the term 'samabharitaṃ', the method is the same. Such filling evenly with the rim applies only to a bowl that has been determined (adhiṭṭhānupaga), not to others. Therefore, it is said 'adhiṭṭhānupagapattassa' etc.

'Racitaṃ' means made, placed, or filled. 'Yaṃ kiñci yāvakālikaṃ' refers to any kind of material food (āmisa) such as gruel, rice, large or small fruits, etc. 'Yattha katthaci' means in any bowl, whether it is a determined bowl or an undetermined bowl.

'Thūpīkatāni' means made like a stupa, meaning made to overflow beyond the inner rim-line of a determined bowl. This term 'thūpīkatāni' is said in relation to periodical (yāmakālika) items, etc. Regarding temporary (yāvakālika) items, by changing the grammatical number, it should be connected as 'thūpīkatampi vaṭṭati' (it is allowable even if made into a heap). By the word 'pi', it shows that there is no dispute regarding the allowability of periodical items etc. that are not heaped. 'Heṭṭhā orohati' means because there is empty space around, when moved, it [falls] down...
442:
## 38. Ujjhānasaññīsikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā
Because one criticizes with this mind, it is called "ujjhāna", which is the mind. The perception that arises in that mind which is the cause of criticism is called "ujjhānasaññā". Therefore, it is said "ujjhānasaññī" etc. "Olokentassa" refers to one who looks at the bowls of others.

## End of the Commentary on the Training Rule on Perceiving with Criticism.

## 39. Kabaḷasikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā
Because of the statement "a peacock's egg is too large," a morsel of food the size of a peacock's egg is also not allowable. Some teachers say, "Only what is larger than a peacock's egg is not allowable, not what is the size of a peacock's egg"; that statement should not be accepted. In the case of "a hen's egg is too small," the same method applies. However, for a sick (gilāna) monk, there is no offense even if he makes a very small morsel.

## End of the Commentary on the Training Rule on Morsels.

## 41-42. Anāhaṭasikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā
"Sakalaṃ hatthaṃ" means all the fingers. In this training rule, the word "hattha" (hand) should be understood as the fingers, which are parts of the hand, as in the term "hatthamuddā" etc. By doing so, the word "sabba" (all) becomes accomplished. Otherwise, if it were the whole hand instead of the fingers, the word "sabba" would not be accomplished because one is unable to put the whole hand into the mouth. Since a term used for the whole is also used for its parts, it is not allowable to put even one finger or a part of it into the mouth.

## End of the Commentary on the Training Rule on Not Bringing to the Mouth.

## 43. Sakabaḷasikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā
"Tattake sati vaṭṭati" means it is allowable to speak while such a morsel is in the mouth.

## End of the Commentary on the Training Rule with a Morsel in the Mouth.
443:

## 57. Chattapāṇi-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā
"Any kind of umbrella" refers to any umbrella among white umbrellas, reed umbrellas, or leaf umbrellas. ## 60. Āvudhapāṇi-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā
"All kinds of bows" refers to all varieties of bows such as the *cāpa* bow and the *kodaṇḍa* bow. A *cāpa* bow is a type of bow that is curved in the middle and resembles a carrying pole (yoke). A *kodaṇḍa* bow is a type of bow with a rounded bow-staff. "Equipped with" (*paṭimukka*) means inserted, attached, or slung. "As long as one does not yet hold it by hand" means as long as it is not held with the hand; or this is simply the original reading. "For that long it is allowable" means that as long as it is not held in that manner, it is allowable to preach the Dhamma.
