445:
Although it is of one kind in the sense of being a legal issue (adhikaraṇa), the Blessed One used the plural form "adhikaraṇāni" because it becomes various kinds based on the grounds (vatthu). Now, to show and explain its various divisions, the phrase beginning with "vivādādhikaraṇa" was stated. A dispute itself being a legal issue is called a dispute-legal issue (vivādādhikaraṇa). This method should be understood for the remaining terms as well. The term samatthattha means for the purpose of settlement (appeasement).

Because it is settled in the presence of the legal issue (destroying the absence), it is called sammukhāvinaya (verdict in the presence). The disciplinary act given only to an Arahant who has attained abundance of mindfulness, like the Elder Dabba Mallaputta, is called sativinaya (verdict of mindfulness). The disciplinary act given to a monk who is insane, like the monk Gagga who was severely deluded, is called amūḷhavinaya (verdict of past insanity). Acting by means of an acknowledgement which serves as the instrument is called paṭiññātakaraṇa (acting in accordance with the acknowledgement). Alternatively, the action performed when one acknowledges having committed an offense, or the verbal act proceeding by way of giving parivāsa (probation) etc., saying "Restrain yourself in the future," is called paṭiññātakaraṇa. In a settlement where the speakers of Dhamma (dhammavādī) are particularly numerous, that act is called yebhuyyasikā (decision by majority). Where there is a person who is depraved due to the abundance of evil unwholesome deeds, the settlement performed for such a person like the monk Upavāḷa is called tassapāpiyasikā (verdict of further misconduct). This term is an aluttasamāsa (un-elided compound). Because it is like covering over with grass, it is called tiṇavatthāraka (covering over with grass). How so? If excrement or urine is stirred, it causes distress with a foul smell. However, if it is well-covered with grass, that smell no longer causes distress. In the same way, if a certain legal issue is settled by tracing it to its very root, it might lead to harshness, violence, or schism; but when that legal issue is settled by this formal act (kammavācā), it becomes well-settled like excrement covered with grass. Therefore, it is said, "Because it is like covering over with grass, it is called tiṇavatthāraka."

The word "tatra" means among those seven adhikaraṇasamathas. The phrase "by eighteen grounds" is an indicative statement (upalakkhaṇa), like the statement "If a disease should afflict me, this medicine should be given." Therefore, monks who dispute by any one of those eighteen grounds are said to "dispute by eighteen grounds." Vivāda means contradictory speech. Upavadanā means abuse. Codanā means interrogation or investigation. "Dve" (two) refers to the two offenses: thullaccaya (grave offense) and dubbhāsita (wrong speech). "Performing the four formal acts" means performing any one of the four formal acts (kamma). Having shown the legal issues in this way, now to show that "this legal issue is settled by this many settlements," the phrase beginning with "tattha" was stated. In whichever monastery...
446:
The connection should be understood as: it arises in a certain monastery, or it is settled in that very monastery. This applies to the remaining terms as well. In that context, 'yassmiṃ vihāre uppannaṃ' (arisen in whichever monastery) refers to a dispute-legal issue arising concerning requisites such as alms-bowls and robes, in the manner of "This monk took my bowl, he took my robe," etc. 'Tassmiṃyeva vā sammati' (or is settled in that very monastery) means that the resident monks gather in that very monastery and, saying "Enough, friends," they make the monks who are opposing each other's interests understand, and settle it by a decision that is free from the Pāḷi text (pāḷimuttaka). If, however, the resident monks are unable to settle that legal issue, and another monk who is an expert in Vinaya (vinayadhara) arrives and asks, "Friends, why are the uposatha or pavāraṇā suspended in this monastery?" and when those monks explain the reason, he settles that legal issue by deciding according to the Khandhaka, Parivāra, and Sutta. Such a settlement is also to be regarded as "settled in that very monastery."

Settlement "on the way" for those going to settle it elsewhere means: monks who set out thinking, "We cannot abide by this monk's decision; he is not skilled in Vinaya. In such-and-such a village, there are elder monks who are experts in Vinaya; we will go there and have it decided," notice the cause while on the way and settle it by making each other understand, or by being persuaded by other monks. However, it is not settled merely by mutual understanding or by the persuasion of fellow monks (sabhāga); rather, a vinayadhara coming from the opposite direction sees them and asks, "Friends, where are you going?" and when told, "To such-and-such a village for such-and-such a reason," he says, "Enough, friends, what is the use of going there?" and settles that legal issue right there according to the Dhamma and Vinaya. Such a settlement is called "settlement on the way."

"Going to a place and handing it over to the Saṅgha, and it is settled by the Saṅgha there" means: even if told "Enough, friends, what is the use of going there?", they disregard the words of the vinayadhara and go, saying "We will go to that very place to get a decision." When they hand over the legal issue to the Saṅgha of fellow monks, that Saṅgha says, "Enough, friends, the gathering of the Saṅgha is a serious matter," and sitting right there, they decide and settle it. However, it is not settled merely by the persuasion of fellow monks; rather, after convening the Saṅgha and making an announcement, the experts in Vinaya settle it in the midst of the Saṅgha. Such a settlement is called "settled by the Saṅgha there."
447:
"Decided by persons appointed by the ubbāhikā method" means a decision made either by requesting or by persons appointed through the ñattidutiya-kammavācā (a formal act with one motion and one announcement) as taught by the Blessed One in the Samatha-kkhandhaka of the Cullavagga, sitting separately from the assembly of the Saṅgha, having informed the assembly that "no one other than the appointed persons should say anything." This is the aforementioned fourfold sammukhatā (presence).

"Kāraka-saṅghassa" refers to the acting Saṅgha that has assembled to settle (the legal issue). Presence by way of saṅgha-sāmaggī (unity of the Saṅgha) means presence by way of the unity of the Saṅgha as stated: "As many monks as are entitled to the act have come, the consent of those who should give consent has been brought, and those present do not protest." By this statement, it is shown that the mere presence of the principal acting persons does not constitute saṅgha-sammukhatā (presence of the Saṅgha). Bhūtatā means the state of being true (tacchata). Here, the word "dhamma" is a synonym for truth (sacca), as in terms like "dhamma-vādī" (one who speaks the truth). It is called Vinaya because it disciplines through this procedure. The procedure taught by the Blessed One to settle various legal issues is the Vinaya, and the presence of that Vinaya is called vinaya-sammukhatā. Therefore, it is said: "As that... vinaya-sammukhatā." "Yena" means "with which person." "Attha-paccatthikānaṃ" refers to those who are opponents in the matter known as the ground for dispute (vivāda-vatthu). Since the settlement is made only by the appointed persons, the saṅgha-sammukhatā is diminished.

"Naṃ" refers to the vivāda-adhikaraṇa (legal issue of dispute). "Endowment with five factors" means being endowed with the five factors stated as: "He does not go to a wrong course through favoritism, he does not go to a wrong course through malice, he does not go to a wrong course through delusion, he does not go to a wrong course through fear, and he knows what is taken and what is not taken (of the voting tickets)." "In the three types of taking voting tickets, namely gūḷhaka, vivaṭaka, and sakaṇṇajappaka" refers to the three types of taking voting tickets taught in the Samatha-kkhandhaka: "Monks, I allow three ways of taking voting tickets to inform those monks: the secret (gūḷhaka), the open (vivaṭaka), and the whispering (sakaṇṇajappaka)." "Having caused the voting tickets to be taken" means having placed marks on the voting tickets of those who speak according to the Dhamma and those who do not, placing them within the folds of the robe, and having them taken according to the method taught in the Samatha-kkhandhaka. Thus it is stated in that Samatha-kkhandhaka:

"And how, monks, is the secret taking of voting tickets? That monk who causes the voting tickets to be taken, having made the voting tickets of various colors, approaches each monk and speaks thus..."
448:
...should say this: 'This is the ticket for the one who speaks thus; this is the ticket for the one who speaks thus. Take whichever you desire.' After it is taken, he should say, 'Do not show it to anyone.' If he knows that those who speak against the Dhamma are more numerous, it should be withdrawn, saying, 'It is badly taken (wrongly taken).' If he knows that those who speak according to the Dhamma are more numerous, he should announce, 'It is well taken.' Thus, bhikkhus, is the secret taking of voting tickets (gūḷhaka-salāka-ggāha).

"And how, bhikkhus, is the open taking of voting tickets (vivaṭaka-salāka-ggāha)? If he knows that those who speak according to the Dhamma are more numerous, it should be caused to be taken openly and clearly. Thus, bhikkhus, is the open taking of voting tickets.

"And how, bhikkhus, is the whispering taking of voting tickets (sakaṇṇajappaka-salāka-ggāha)? That bhikkhu who causes the voting tickets to be taken should inform each bhikkhu in his ear: 'This is the ticket for the one who speaks thus; this is the ticket for the one who speaks thus. Take whichever you desire.' After it is taken, he should say, 'Do not tell anyone.' If he knows that those who speak against the Dhamma are more numerous, it should be withdrawn, saying, 'It is badly taken.' If he knows that those who speak according to the Dhamma are more numerous, he should announce, 'It is well taken.' Thus, bhikkhus, is the whispering taking of voting tickets."

In this context, it should be understood that the secret taking of voting tickets should be performed in an assembly where shameless (alajjī) bhikkhus are in the majority; the open taking of voting tickets should be performed in an assembly where conscientious (lajjī) bhikkhus are in the majority; and the whispering taking of voting tickets should be performed in an assembly where foolish (bāla) bhikkhus are in the majority. "The majority of those who speak according to the Dhamma" means that even if there is one more person who speaks according to the Dhamma, it is a majority; what need is there to mention if there are two or three more?

"It is settled by four samathas" is said by way of encompassing everything; however, in that (anuvādādhikaraṇa), settlement should be understood to occur by only two samathas. "Thus it is decided" means if there is no offense, (it is decided) by making both parties ask for forgiveness; if there is an offense, it is decided by way of pointing out the offense and presenting it (ropana). As for the remedy (paṭikamma), it will be understood in the āpattādhikaraṇa-samatha that comes later. If there is a transgression or violation in that matter which is unbecoming of a recluse, an act of non-recluses, and which should not be done by recluses (then an offense is incurred).
449:
An offense near Pārājika refers to a dukkaṭa (wrongdoing) or a thullaccaya (grave offense). Indeed, in the case of sexual intercourse (methunadhamma), the offense near Pārājika is a dukkaṭa; in cases like theft (adinnādāna) and others, it is a thullaccaya. 'Paṭicarato' means one who conceals. 'Acchinnamūlo bhavissati' means one will not reach the state of Pārājika, meaning one will remain virtuous. 'Sammā vattitvā' means having fully fulfilled the duties. 'Osāraṇaṃ labhissati' means one will obtain the cessation of the legal act (the cessation of the nissaraṇa act).

'Tassa' refers to that āpattādhikaraṇa (legal issue regarding an offense). Settlement cannot occur through sammukhāvinaya (verdict in the presence) alone without an admission (paṭiññā) or without appropriate forbearance (or affection), because it cannot be settled otherwise. 'Ya pana paṭiññā' is the connection.

'Ettha' refers to the confession of the offense. 'Siyā' means it must certainly be. 'Kakkhaḷattāya vāḷattāya' means due to being harsh and due to being fierce. 'Thullavajjaṃ' refers to Pārājika and Saṅghādisesa offenses. 'Gihippatisaṃyuttaṃ' refers to offenses involving base insults, disparagement, or formal promises made to laypeople.

'Yathānurūpaṃ' means as appropriate, according to the method stated as "by two samathas, by three, by four, or by one." 'Ettha' means in this section on samatha. 'Viniccayanayo' is merely the method of decision. Therefore, it says "as for the details," etc. 'Assa' refers to those details. 'Samantapāsādikāyaṃ vutto' means it has been stated in the Vinaya commentary named Samantapāsādikā. Therefore, it should be understood according to the method stated in that commentary.

'Ettakaṃ' means this much is the limit; there is no more than this.

## 5. Ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

'Ubbhakapparaṃ' means above the elbow, which is the second major joint. 'Ito cito ca sañcaraṇaṃ' means the movement of the hand or the body to and fro crosswise.

'Ekato-avassute' means when there is an oozing (of lustful fluid) in the nun, when there is the state of oozing through lust for bodily contact in the nun. The state of oozing from one side should be taken only in terms of the nun. This matter has been stated in the Samantapāsādikā commentary:
452:
“In the term 'ekato-avassute', although 'ekato' (from one side) is stated generally without specification, it should be understood that this division of offense is mentioned only when the nun herself has the oozing (delight) through a lustful mind.”

The body of a man means any part of a man's body. “Even if there is oozing from both” means even if both the nun and the man have the state of oozing through lust for bodily contact (the offense is still incurred). “With the body” means with one's own body as defined. “An object connected to the body” means an object connected to the man's body. “With the rest of the body” means with the body remaining from the defined parts, namely the body above the two collarbones, below the two kneecaps, and below the elbows. “His body” means any part of the body of that man who has the oozing of lust. In this training rule, just as a thullaccaya is incurred if she touches him herself, it should be understood that a thullaccaya is also incurred if she consents to his touching. “A man has no lust for bodily contact” means the man has sexual lust, or household affection, or a pure mind. “In the remaining area” means in the area remaining from the Pārājika field. In all cases such as “touching an object connected to the body with an object connected to the body,” a dukkaṭa offense is incurred. In terms like “unintentionally,” there is no offense (anāpatti) even if there is touching for a nun who touches by mistake, or a nun whose mind is elsewhere, or a nun who does not know “is this a man or a woman?”, or a nun who does not delight in the touch even though she is touched by him.

## Ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā Niṭṭhitā.

## 6. Vajjappaṭicchādikāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

“Transgressing a Pārājika Dhamma” means transgressing any one of the eight Pārājikas—the four common to monks and the four uncommon (specific to nuns). Although this Pārājika training rule was prescribed later, it should be understood that the Great Teachers who conducted the Council placed it in this position, pairing it with the previous training rule. Because of the words “any one of the eight Pārājikas,” it should be noted that a nun who conceals a fault is indeed a Vajjappaṭicchādikā (one who conceals a fault). Although concealing a fault occurs due to affection,
453:
However, because the mind that transgresses the training rule is only accompanied by displeasure (domanassa), it is associated with painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā). Thus, it is said: "In that case, there is an offense of Pācittiya... the rest is just the same."

## The Explanation of the Vajjappaṭicchādikā Training Rule is finished.

## 7. The Explanation of the Ukkhittānuvattikā Training Rule

"Satthusāsana" (by the Teacher's instruction) means by the accomplishment of the motion (ñatti) and by the accomplishment of the proclamation (kammavācā) [referring to the act of suspension]. In this training rule, however, it is intended to show that only the motion and proclamation preceded by an accusation and reminding of the fault are called "Satthusāsana"; therefore, the words beginning with "Idhāpi" were said. "Karaṇa" means the placing of the motion and the reciting of the proclamation. "Anādara" means the lack of respect for both the person and the Dhamma. Therefore, the words beginning with "Yena" were said. In that context, "pariyāpannagaṇe vā" means in the group consisting of many individuals included in that Saṅgha [performing the act]. By the meaning "one who does not practice proper conduct," the intended sense is stated. "Ekakammādike" is because of having the same formal act, the same recitation, and the same training. "Saha ayanabhāvena" means with the state of occurring together. Because those monks have a common communion, they are called "samānasaṃvāsaka" (those of common communion).

Now, the communion by which those monks are called "samānasaṃvāsaka" does not exist for that suspended monk together with those [who suspended him]. Because there is no communion with that suspended monk, those monks are no longer his companions. Therefore, that monk is called "one without companions (akatasahāya)." To show this meaning, the words beginning with "Yassa pana" were said. Having thus explained the words, to show the brief meaning, it is said: "one who has not reached the state of common communion." Since someone might have a doubt, "What is that following (anuvattana)?", to show it by its nature, the words beginning with "That monk has such a view" were said. In that context, "so" (he) refers to the suspended monk.

## The Explanation of the Ukkhittānuvattikā Training Rule is finished.

## 8. The Explanation of the Aṭṭhavatthukā Training Rule

"Lokassādamittasanthavavasena" means by the power of forming friendship which is called worldly enjoyment. To the question "What is that?", it was said: "with lust for physical contact." In this training rule, only a nun who is "oozing" (avassutā) with lust for physical contact is called "avassutā." A nun who is "oozing" with lust for sexual intercourse is not called "avassutā." To make this point known, the words beginning with "Ayameva hi" were said. The reason why only a nun oozing with lust for physical contact is intended in this training rule is analyzed and investigated in the Samantapāsādikā.
455:
## Saṅghādisesa Section
## 1. Explanation of the Ussayavādikā Training Rule
The Recensionist Elders stated the phrase 'by way of accumulation of conceit, by way of accumulation of anger' (mānussayavasena kodhūssayavasena) according to the method of the majority. Because it was stated according to the method of the majority, the Recensionist Elders will later say 'three minds, three feelings'. In the term 'aḍḍakaraṇatthāya', 'aḍḍa' refers to the judgment of judicial officers (vohārika). It means for the purpose of making a judgment, which monks also call 'adhikaraṇa' (legal issue); that is, for the purpose of the judgment of judicial officers. The phrase 'vītikkamakkhaṇeyyeva' means that the offense is incurred only at the moment of committing the act (vatthujjhācāra); the commentator means that the offense is not incurred only when the third formal warning (samanubhāsana) is completed. 'Expels the bhikkhunī from the Saṅgha' (bhikkhuniṃ saṅghato nissāreti) means expelling an offending bhikkhunī from the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha. Here, the name 'nissāraṇīya' (entailing expulsion) is used as an agent in the sense of cause. This is because the Blessed One called the offense 'nissāraṇīya' as it is the cause of expulsion.

'Standing where' (yattha ṭhitāya) refers to the place where the bhikkhunī is standing, such as in the monastery or on the alms-round path. 'Going from there' (tato paṭṭhāya gacchantiyā) refers to the bhikkhunī going from that place to the judicial officers. 'In the second' (dutiye) refers to the second time of reporting. 'By him' (tena) refers to that lay follower (upāsaka). 'Being thus spoken to' (evaṃ vuttāya) refers to the bhikkhunī who was told, 'Speak only your own words and my words yourself.' 'Causes another to speak' (aññena kathāpeti) means causing a lay attendant (kappiyakāraka) to speak. 'In whatever way it is reported' (yathā vā tathā vā hi ārociyamāne) means whether the lay attendant speaks the bhikkhunī's words first, or another speaks their own words first, or the lay attendant speaks the words of both, or another speaks the words of both—if it is reported in any of these ways. 'Having heard the words of both' (ubhinnampi pana kathaṃ sutvā) means after hearing the words of both the bhikkhunī and the lay donor reported in any of those ways.

'Goes being summoned' (ākaḍḍhiyamānā gacchati) means the bhikkhunī goes to the judicial officers when summoned; this sentence should be understood in connection with the sentence 'there is no offense for her' (tassā anāpatti). The remaining sentences should be understood in the same way. 'Requests protection' (rakkhaṃ yācati) means requesting righteous protection. To show how the requested protection is righteous, the Recensionist Elders said, 'Reporting improper conduct done by others in the monastery without specifying the person.' In that regard, there is reporting by specifying the person regarding what was done in the past, and there is reporting without specifying the person. There is also reporting by specifying the person regarding what will happen in the future, and there is reporting without specifying the person.
456:
How is reporting by specifying the person regarding the past? If village boys or rogues and so forth commit improper conduct in the bhikkhunīs' monastery, or cut trees, or take fruits, or seize requisites, the bhikkhunī approaches the judicial officers and says, 'Such an act was done in our monastery.' When asked 'Who did it?', she says, 'So-and-so and so-and-so did it.' This is reporting by specifying the person regarding the past; such reporting is not allowable. If the judicial officers hear those words and punish them, the entire punishment becomes the bhikkhunī's liability (gīvā). Even if she only intends 'they will be punished', she is still liable. If she actually says to them 'Punish them' and a value of five māsakas is taken, it is a Pārājika offense. When asked by them 'Who did it?', it is not allowable for us to say 'So-and-so'; one should say, 'You yourselves will know. We only request protection; please give us that protection and also have the stolen goods returned.' This is reporting without specifying; such reporting is allowable. If the judicial officers then search for the perpetrators and punish them, or even seize all their property, the bhikkhunī is not liable and there is no offense.

Seeing someone taking requisites and shouting 'Thief! Thief!' with the wish for their harm is also not allowable. Any punishment imposed on them because of such shouting makes the bhikkhunī liable. However, it is allowable to say to one who follows one's words, 'This person has taken my requisites; please bring those requisites back, but do not punish him.' If they engage in legal proceedings (aḍḍa) for the sake of male or female slaves and so forth, this is called 'unallowable legal proceeding' (akappiya-aḍḍa); it is not allowable. How is reporting by specifying the person regarding the future? In the same manner as mentioned, if others commit improper conduct and so forth, the bhikkhunī says to the judicial officer, 'They do such and such in our monastery; please give us protection so they cannot do it in the future.' When asked 'Who does this?', she says 'So-and-so and so-and-so.' This is reporting by specifying the person regarding the future; this is also not allowable. If they are punished, the entire punishment becomes the bhikkhunī's liability as in the previous method. The rest is the same as stated before.
457:
If judicial officers, while punishing those who commit such misconduct in a nunnery, proclaim by beat of drum, "We shall impose such-and-such a penalty," and then search for and punish those who do not submit to the authority, there is no liability for compensation (gīvā) nor an offense for the bhikkhunī.

This method described for bhikkhunīs is the same for monks. For monks as well, it is improper to speak by specifically pointing out (someone). If they are punished because of such specific pointing out, the monk is liable for all compensation. According to the method already mentioned, a monk who causes a penalty to be accepted in this way commits an offense of Pārājika. However, if he speaks without specifically pointing out, even knowing that "they will be punished," and the officers search for and punish them, there is no fault.

It is improper to take the billhooks, axes, etc., of those who cut trees within the monastery precincts and strike them against stones. If the blade is damaged, it must be repaired before being returned. One should also not run after them to seize their requisites. This is because the mind changes quickly; if an intention to steal arises, it could lead to the uprooting of the spiritual life (Pārājika).

## The Commentary on the Ussayavādikā Training Rule is finished.

## 2. Corivuṭṭhāpikā-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā

Regarding the terms such as Mallagaṇa and Bhaṭiputtagaṇa: the Mallagaṇa refers to a group of devotees of Nārāyaṇa who perform meritorious deeds such as providing drinking water stands and digging ponds in various places. The Bhaṭiputtagaṇa refers to a group of devotees of Kumāra. The Dhammagaṇa refers to a group of devotees of the Sāsana who perform many kinds of meritorious deeds. The Gandhikaseṇī refers to a guild that produces various kinds of perfumes. The Dussikaseṇī refers to a group of cloth merchants, meaning a guild of weavers.

"Ordaining" (vuṭṭhāpeန္တိယာ) means acting as a preceptor to grant higher ordination (upasampadā). If a bhikkhunī ordains someone together with her own group of followers at the place where she is sitting, without going to the boundary (sīmā) while other bhikkhunīs have left for some business, the offense arises through speech and mind. For a bhikkhunī who goes to another boundary or a river to ordain someone, the offense arises through body, speech, and mind; thus it is called "the origination of ordaining a female thief" (corivuṭṭhāpana-samuṭṭhāna). This training rule concerns action and non-action (kiriākiriā) resulting from ordaining without asking permission. It is said to have three types of consciousness (ticitta) either because even Ariyas (Noble Ones) who are unaware of the regulation might grant ordination, or because at the moment of the offense at the conclusion of the formal act (kammavācā), one is endowed with resultant (vipāka) or indeterminate (abyākata) consciousness.

## The Commentary on the Corivuṭṭhāpikā Training Rule is finished.
458:
## 3. Ekagāmantaragamana-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā

Another village is called "gāmantara". "Nadīpāra" refers to the opposite bank of a river. Because it is said, "should she go to another village" (Pācittiya 687, 691), the offense occurs only in the other village, not in one's own village; thus (the author of the Saṅgaha) said, "First from one's own village..." and so on. "When crossing the enclosure or the precinct" means when crossing the enclosure of a fenced village, or the area suitable for an enclosure in an unfenced village. "Merely by crossing with the second step" means when the second foot has just crossed the enclosure or the precinct of the other village.

In some texts, the reading appears as: "If one crosses the enclosure of another village with one foot, or enters the precinct, it is a Thullaccaya offense; merely by crossing with the second step, or merely by entering, it is a Saṅghādisesa offense." However, in that reading, the two terms "enters" (okkante) and "merely by entering" (okkantamatte) contradict the original Pali. This is because the Pali states: "For a bhikkhunī who crosses the precinct of an unfenced village." Likewise, they also contradict the Samantapāsādikā Commentary. For in that commentary it is said:

"If one crosses the area suitable for an enclosure with one foot, it is a Thullaccaya. Merely by crossing with the second step, it is a Saṅghādisesa. Moreover, in this training rule... (omission)... merely by crossing the enclosure or the precinct of another village with one foot, it is a Thullaccaya; merely by crossing with the second step, it is a Saṅghādisesa."

Because of the words "For a bhikkhunī who crosses with the first step," etc., it is intended here only to mean traveling on foot; thus it was said, "The offense occurs for a bhikkhunī who enters on foot." By this, it is shown that if she enters by means of an elephant's back, etc., or by psychic power (iddhi), it is permissible (no offense). This is a summary of the matter; the detail is stated in the Samantapāsādikā Commentary.

Regarding the river with the characteristics mentioned in "going to the other side of a river": "A river is that where, when crossing at any point, the inner robe (antaravāsaka) becomes wet, covering the three circles (the knees and waist area)." This refers to the river with the characteristics described in the Nadīpāragamana-vibhaṅga. This is because the Nadīpāragamana-vibhaṅga is referred to here by the term "Nadīpāragamana." Furthermore, the phrase "or when crossing back to this bank" was said because she descended (into the water) with the intention of going to the other bank. For the other (returning) bhikkhunī, however, since she is situated at the place of departure, no offense occurs when she goes to that bank. If...
459:
While chanting, practicing meditation, or performing any other task, if a bhikkhunī thinks, "I will go to the companion bhikkhunī before dawn," but dawn breaks while she is unaware, there is no offense. This is stated starting with "Pure aruṇeyyeva." However, if she thinks, "I will stay in this place until dawn," or even without such a thought, stays in a part of the monastery and does not come within the hatthapāsa (reach) of the companion bhikkhunī, she commits a saṅghādisesa offense at dawn. In this context, the hatthapāsa is the standard. If she exceeds the hatthapāsa, even being within the same room cannot protect her from the offense. Therefore, it is said, "Ekagabbhe... pe... āpatti."

In the phrase "dassanūpacāraṃ vā savanūpacāraṃ vā," dassanūpacāra refers to a place where the companion bhikkhunī can see the bhikkhunī who is standing there. Savanūpacāra refers to a place where the bhikkhunī standing there can hear the voice of the companion calling out "Lady!" similar to the sound of someone lost on a path or the sound of an announcement for a Dhamma talk. Therefore, staying behind (ohīyana) is defined as such because it involves leaving either the visual range (dassanūpacāra) or the hearing range (savanūpacāra). Within a village, however, staying behind is permissible; thus it is said, "Indakhīlātikkamato paṭṭhāya" and so on. In that context, "indakhīlātikkamato" means from the moment of crossing the threshold. "Bahigāme" means in the area outside the village. Because those lost on a path tend to make loud noises, it is said, "maggamūḷhasaddena viya." Teachers also say it is like the sound of someone calling out to a person lost on a path. "Saddāyantiyā" refers to the bhikkhunī who is making the sound. By the phrase "saddassavanātikkame āpattiyeva," it is shown that once such a hearing range is left, the visual range cannot protect her, and the mere act of leaving results in a saṅghādisesa offense.

"Maggaṃ gacchanti" means traveling on the same path. If the bhikkhunīs in front go by another path, it is called "departed" (pakkanta), and there is no offense. Among two traveling bhikkhunīs, if one stays behind thinking, "Let the Lady go ahead," because she cannot keep up, and the other goes on thinking, "Let this Lady stay behind," both commit an offense. However, if among the traveling bhikkhunīs, the one in front takes another path and the one behind also takes another path, since each stands in a place where the other has departed, both are free from offense.

The question "Saṅghādisesā caturo" refers to a bhikkhunī who, at dawn, reaches the other side of a river that belongs to another village. Having departed from her own village at the time of early dawn, at the moment of dawn, by merely reaching the other side of the river as described, she simultaneously incurs four saṅghādisesa offenses characterized by rattivippavāsa, gāmantaragamana, nadīpāragamana, and gaṇa-ohīyana.

## 6. Bhojanappaṭiggahana Dutiya Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
Offenses beginning with dukkaṭa and ending with saṅghādisesa occur only for the nun who incites or urges (uyyojikā) by means of this training rule. Regarding the different offenses of the other nun (the one who is suspended, ukkhittaka), the author of the Compendium (Saṅgaha) stated, "She, by thus inciting..." (sā evaṃ uyyojanena) and so forth, that they occur through the first training rule.

"Kulānuddayatāya" means because of being one who compassionately favors families, or by the state of being one who compassionately favors families.

## The Commentary on the Second Training Rule on Receiving Food is Finished.

## 7-13. Sañcarittādi Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
The seventh and subsequent training rules have meanings that are quite clear.

## The Commentary on the Training Rules starting with Sañcaritta is Finished.

## 14-17. Saṅghabhedakādi Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
A nun cannot cause a schism in the Saṅgha. The reason is that a schism in the Saṅgha occurs through two factors: the four formal acts (kamma) and the five recitations (uddesa); since such a schism does not exist in connection with a nun, a nun cannot cause a schism in the Saṅgha. The author of the Compendium stated, "Even due to the factor of concealing..." (chādanapaccayāpi) and so forth, to show that it is not merely the absence of probation (parivāsa). In this statement, the text "chādanapaccayāpi na dukkaṭaṃ āpajjati" should be accepted, meaning that even due to the factor of concealing, she does not fall into a dukkaṭa offense. In this regard—

"She falls into a heavy offense that is with a remainder,
She conceals it based on disrespect,
She is not a nun, nor would she touch the fault,
This question has been considered by those skilled in the Vinaya."

In this verse, the prohibition regarding the nun is appropriate and sufficient.

In some palm-leaf manuscripts, if the text is found as "chādanapaccayā pana dukkaṭaṃ āpajjati" without the word "na," it should be understood as a text written incorrectly due to negligence. "Tasmā" means because there is no such thing as probation, therefore (it is so). The phrase "Having cleared her own boundary or the bound boundary (baddha-sīmā) of the monastery" refers to the monastery...
462:
It is said with reference only to the established bound boundary (baddha-sīmā). "Sodhetuṃ asakkontīhi" means by those nuns who are unable to clear the bound boundary established in the monastery.

"Mukhamattanidassanaṃ" means showing merely the means or method of entry. Here, an objector asks: "In the explanation of the monks' mānatta (penance), it is said, 'beyond two stone-throws from the enclosure of a fenced monastery, or from a place suitable for an enclosure of an unfenced monastery'; why is it not said so here, but instead said, 'beyond two stone-throws from the precincts (upacāra) of the village and from the precincts of the nuns' monastery'?" Regarding that question, some teachers say, "For monks, after passing the aforementioned place, it is allowable to perform that act of mānatta even in a village; for nuns, however, it is not allowable in a village, therefore it is stated thus." Other teachers, however, say, "For monks also, it is not allowable to perform that act in a village. This is because a monks' monastery is already situated beyond the village precincts; therefore, in the explanation of the monks' mānatta below, the village was not mentioned, only the monastery precincts. But a nuns' monastery is situated only within the village and not outside; therefore, both the village precincts and the monastery precincts are shown here. Thus, in both cases, there is no difference in meaning." One should investigate these views and accept what is appropriate.

"Tato paṭṭhāya" means starting from the time of notification.

## The Commentary on the Training Rules starting with Schism in the Saṅgha is Finished.

## 1. Patta-sannicaya Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
The first training rule, the Patta-sannicaya Sikkhāpada, is very clear in its meaning.

## 2. Akālacívara Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
"Yaṃ attanā laddhaṃ, taṃ nissaggiyaṃ hoti" means that whatever robe she receives for herself due to the reason of having it distributed becomes a forfeiture (nissaggiya). Even after performing the Vinaya procedure (vinaya-kamma), she cannot keep it for herself. Therefore, the phrase "nissaṭṭhaṃ" and so forth is stated. In that context, "nissaṭṭhaṃ paṭilabhitvāpi" means even if she receives back the robe that was forfeited with the words "I give this to the lady." As stated in "yathādāneyeva upanetabbaṃ," it must be brought forward exactly as it was given by the donors; it means it must be placed only on the side of out-of-season robes (akālacívara).

## The Commentary on the Training Rule on Out-of-season Robes is Finished.
## 3. Cīvaraparivattana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
"Metaṃ" should be resolved as "me etaṃ" (this of mine). Because it was taken with the perception that it was her own property, the Buddha declared it a pācittiya and a dukkaṭa. Otherwise, if taken with a different perception, it must be dealt with according to the value of the goods.

## The Commentary on the Training Rule on Exchanging Robes is Finished.
## 4. Aññaviññāpana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
"Paṭilābhena" means by the acquisition of something else that is even less than what was first requested.

"Tasmiṃ appahontante puna taññeva" means if the item first requested is insufficient because it is too little, it refers to the nun who requests that same item again. Even with another (material object)...
464:
The phrase "Atthe sati" (when there is a need) refers to needing a material other than the one initially requested. "Tena saddhiṃ aññañca" (along with that, another) refers to another material along with the one first requested. What does this mean? If ghee was initially requested, but because the doctor said, "It should be cooked with both ghee and oil," oil is also needed. In that case, it refers to a bhikkhunī who requests other oil by saying, "I also have a need for oil," and so on. "Showing the benefit" means saying, "If ghee worth one kahāpaṇa is brought, twice as much oil can be obtained for this price, and the task can be accomplished with oil; therefore, bring oil."

## The Explanation of the Aññaviññāpana Training Rule is finished.

## 5. Explanation of the Aññacetāpana Training Rule

This means having something else bought that was not specified, other than the item that was first ordered to be bought.

## The Explanation of the Aññacetāpana Training Rule is finished.

## 6. Explanation of the First Saṅghikacetāpana Training Rule

This means with the requisites donated for the benefit of a material other than the one she has bought. The word "Aññuddisikena" (intended for another) is merely an explanation of the meaning of the preceding phrase.

"Seseakaṃ upanentiyā" (bringing the remainder) refers to a bhikkhunī who, after having bought the requisite for which the donation was given, brings the remaining value for the sake of another requisite, such as an alms-bowl. "Sāmike apaloketvā" means after asking the donors. "In such dangers" means for bhikkhunīs who bring [the funds] for the sake of any kind of danger in the face of such calamities.

## The Explanation of the First Saṅghikacetāpana Training Rule is finished.
465:
## 7. Explanation of the Second Saṅghikacetāpana Training Rule

Because it is not only with that requisite [donated for the Saṅgha] without mixing, the author of the Saṅgaha says, "also with the requisite requested by oneself." For this was said by the Elder Upāli in the Bhikkhunī Pācittiya Pali: "The bhikkhunīs, having had medicine bought both with that [donated] requisite and by requesting it themselves, consumed it." However, in the Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha Mātikā, the Buddha did not use the word "pi" (also) because the conjunctive sense can be understood. Indeed, it is appropriate to use words as one pleases, excluding the use of a word whose meaning is already understood.

## The Explanation of the Second Saṅghikacetāpana Training Rule is finished.

The eighth, ninth, and tenth training rules have clear meanings.

Because requesting is not prohibited in a place where one has been invited, it should be understood that the Blessed One showed the limit—that when one is told, "Noble ladies, speak of what you need," by way of a formal invitation, a heavy wrap (garupāvuraṇa) worth at most four kaṃsas may be requested. ## The Section on Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)

## 1. The Chapter on Garlic (Lasuṇavagga)

## 1. Explanation of the Lasuṇa Training Rule
Although "Lasuṇa" (garlic) is mentioned generally without distinction, in this training rule, only garlic grown in the Magadha country is intended. Furthermore, it refers only to multi-cloved garlic (bhaṇḍikalasuṇa), as stated in the phrase "grown in the Magadha country," and so on.

Bhaṇḍikalasuṇa means bundle-like garlic (poṭṭalikalasuṇa); this is a designation for garlic with a full set of cloves. Therefore, it is said, "It is not garlic with only one or two cloves." In the phrase "at every swallow," if one chews and swallows two or three cloves together, it constitutes one pācittiya offense. However, for a bhikkhunī who eats them clove by clove after peeling them, there are as many pācittiya offenses as there are efforts (payoga).

The distinction among palaṇḍuka (onion) and others should be known by color or by cloves. By color: palaṇḍuka is pale yellow, bhañjanaka is red, and haritaka is the color of green leaves. By cloves: palaṇḍuka has one clove (layer), bhañjanaka has two, and haritaka has three. Cāpalasuṇa has no cloves; it has only sprouts. However, in the Mahāpaccari and other texts, it is said: "Palaṇḍuka has three cloves, bhañjanaka has two, and haritaka has one." These onions and similar plants are allowable by their very nature. In cooking and so on, even Magadhan garlic is allowable. Indeed, it is allowable if it is added anywhere—even in gruel or rice—when cooking mung bean soup and the like, or in fish and meat preparations, or in oil, or in jujube jam and the like, or in sour vegetables and the like, or in appetizers. Badarasāḷava is a special kind of edible made by drying and powdering jujube fruits.

## The Explanation of the Lasuṇa Training Rule is finished.
468:
## 2. Sambādhaloma-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā
For the purpose of showing the distinction of this general term "paṭicchannokāse" (in a concealed place), the author of the Compendium stated the meaning as "in the armpits and in the private parts."

"Ābādhapaccayā" (due to illness) means that there is no offense for a bhikkhunī who has hair removed due to the cause of an illness such as an itch or scabies. The ancient teachers said, "For a monk, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkhaṭa) in this matter and also regarding garlic."

## The Commentary on the Training Rule regarding Hair in the Private Area is finished.

## 3. Talaghātaka-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā
"Talaghātaka" (striking with the palm) occurs because of giving a blow to the top. Regarding the surface of that striking, because it is stated in the Word-Analysis (Padabhājanīya) as "gives a blow to the private parts," it is understood as "of the private parts"; therefore, the author of the Compendium stated, "in the striking of the private parts with the palm." In the same manner as the previous method, "sāṇattikaṃ" means that for a bhikkhunī who commands another for her own benefit, an offense occurs along with the command.

## The Commentary on the Training Rule regarding Striking with the Palm is finished.

## 4. Jatumaṭṭhaka-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā
"Vatthuvasena etaṃ vuttaṃ" means that the author of the Compendium stated this word "jatumaṭṭhaka" (a lacquered stick) only by the power of the incident (vatthu) that arose by way of the origin story. In fact, there is an offense for a bhikkhunī who inserts any kind of stick. Therefore, the words beginning with "kāmarāgena pana" (but with sensual desire) were stated.

## The Commentary on the Training Rule regarding the Lacquered Stick is finished.

## 5. Udakasuddhika-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā
"Ādātabbaṃ" means it should be inserted or caused to enter. "Aggapabbaṃ" refers even to the tip of a finger-joint the size of a hair-tip. "Tatiyaṃ pabbaṃ paveseti" means the insertion of the third joint, even if it is only the size of a hair-tip. Indeed, in the Samantapāsādikā Commentary, the author of the Compendium stated, "In terms of depth, for a bhikkhunī who inserts even a hair-tip's length above two joints, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya)."
469:
In the case of an extremely deep water-cleansing incident (udakasuddhika-vatthu) caused by the act of inserting too far into the birth canal to wash with water: even if there is enjoyment of the touch due to the reason of cleansing with water, there is no offense if the washing is within the aforementioned limit.

## The Commentary on the Training Rule regarding Water-Cleansing is finished.

## 6. Upatiṭṭhana-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā
"Takkādīsu vā aññatarena" means with any one of buttermilk, curd, whey, milk, and so forth. "Yāya kāyaci bījaniyā" means with any kind of fan, beginning at minimum with the corner of a robe.

"Imaṃ pivatha" means "Drink this drinking water or this soup, etc." "Imini bījatha" means "Fan with this palm-leaf fan." "Dāpentiyā" refers to a bhikkhunī who causes another person to give both the food and the fanning.

## The Commentary on the Training Rule regarding Standing Near is finished.

## 7. Āmakadhañña-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā
"Tasmā" (therefore) is said because the requesting and the eating of raw grain (āmakadhañña) are the essential measures. In this training rule, an offense of wrong-doing (dukkhaṭa) does not occur only because of receiving raw grain; but also in bringing it from the field after receiving it, in drying it, in preparing the hearth for roasting on a cloudy day, in preparing the roasting pan, in preparing the ladle, in taking firewood and lighting a fire, in putting the grain into the roasting pan, in stirring with the ladle, in preparing the mortar and pestle, etc., for pounding, in pounding, winnowing, washing, and so forth—up to the point of chewing with the teeth for the purpose of swallowing after placing it in the mouth—in all such preliminary efforts (payoga), offenses of wrong-doing occur. Therefore, the teacher of the Compendium stated, "From the time of receiving until the chewing with the teeth, offenses of wrong-doing occur in the preliminary efforts."

## The Commentary on the Training Rule regarding Raw Grain is finished.
471:
Whether it be the "dancing of a peacock," singing (gīta) refers to the singing of performers and the like, or the celebratory singing of the virtuous associated with the virtues of the Triple Gem at the time of the Parinibbāna of the Noble Ones (Ariyas), or at the very least, making a sound in the beginning with the intention of "singing with the teeth" (whistling). All of this is indeed singing (gīta).

Therefore, it was said, "Singing (gīta) includes, at the very least, the singing of Dhamma-reciters (Dhamma-bhāṇakas)." In that context, the singing of a Dhamma-reciter refers to unrestrained monks who break the specific duty of reciting verses and recite the Dhamma with a song-like tone, making it excessively long. Such recitation of Dhamma with a song-like tone is allowable neither for monks nor for nuns.

That it is not allowable is stated in the Khuddakapāṭha Commentary named Paramatthajotikā: "Singing associated with the Dhamma is allowable, but Dhamma associated with singing is not." Therefore, one who recites the Dhamma should make the syllables and phrases clear and well-rounded, using a graceful and balanced (caturassa) manner without destroying the specific traditions of reciting Jātaka verses and so on.

Instrumental music (vādita) refers to the sound of musical instruments such as stringed instruments, or the sound of a pot-drum, or at the very least, the sound of a water-drum. All of this is indeed instrumental music (vādita). Therefore, it was said, "Instrumental music (vādita) includes, at the very least, the sound of a water-drum."

However, there is no offense in snapping the fingers or clapping the hands when spitting or when standing in a suspicious place.

In this context, by the word "seeing" (dassana), "hearing" (savana) is also included by the method of Virūpekasesa. Alternatively, because the five consciousnesses have the nature of contemplating, and the act of hearing can be included within seeing, it was said only "for the purpose of seeing." Therefore, it was said, "to a nun who goes for the purpose of seeing any of these [dances, etc.]." "Standing in which place" means going and standing in such a location.

One might ask, "Since the Pāḷi text does not mention a Pācittiya offense for dancing oneself and so on, why should it be accepted?" The answer given is, "It is stated in all the Commentaries." By this, it is shown that even if it is not directly stated in the Pāḷi text, it should be accepted based on the authority of the Commentaries. The statement that the origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so on are similar to the Eḷakaloma-sikkhāpada was made only in terms of the Pācittiya offense mentioned in the Mātikā. In all respects, however, it should be understood as having six origins.

"Standing within the monastery" is merely an example. This is because it is intended that there be no offense for a nun who watches while in other postures (sitting or lying down). Otherwise, it would mean that watching while sitting is also not permitted. For a nun who goes from one monastery to another with the intention "I will watch," there is indeed an offense. If she watches while sitting in the refectory, there is no offense. If she gets up and goes with the intention "I will watch," there is an offense. For a nun who stands on the street and turns her neck to watch, there is also an offense. The same principle applies to a monk, though there is a difference in the category of offense.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Dancing and Singing is finished.
## The First Chapter on Garlic (Lasuṇavagga) is finished.
472:
## 2. Rattandhakāra-vagga

## 1. Explanation of the Rattandhakāra Training Rule

"Arahopekkhāya" means not out of regard for delighting in privacy. "Aññavihitāya" means being occupied with an object other than delighting in privacy, such as a nun who asks about her relatives, or who consults regarding giving or making offerings (in these cases, there is no offense).

## The Explanation of the Rattandhakāra Training Rule is finished.

## 2-3. Explanation of the Paṭicchannokāsa and Ajjhokāsa-sallapana Training Rules

The second and third training rules have meanings that are clear and obvious.

## The Explanation of the Paṭicchannokāsa and Ajjhokāsa-sallapana Training Rules is finished.

## 4. Explanation of the Dutiyika-uyyojana Training Rule

By the words "only according to the previous method," this method is shown: in the phrase "if she should stand," a Pācittiya offense is incurred merely by standing within a forearm's length (hatthapāsa) of a man. In the phrase "if she should speak," a Pācittiya offense is also incurred by a nun who stands there and speaks words concerning the household life. In the phrase "if she should whisper in the ear," a Pācittiya offense is also incurred by a nun who whispers in the ear.

## The Explanation of the Dutiyika-uyyojana Training Rule is finished.

## 5. Explanation of the Anāpucchā-pakkamana Training Rule

People sit here, therefore this place is called "āsana." Thus, it is said, "in the place that is the seat." It means in the place where one sits cross-legged. "Anovassakaṃ" refers to the eaves. "The precinct in the open" (ajjhokāse upacāra) refers to a place measuring twelve cubits while sitting in the open. "Gilānāya" refers to a nun who is unable to ask permission due to such an illness. "In times of danger" (āpadāsu) means if a fire breaks out in the house, or there is danger from thieves; if she departs without asking permission when such a calamity occurs, there is no offense.

## The Explanation of the Anāpucchā-pakkamana Training Rule is finished.

## 1-2. Ārāmapavisana-ādi-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā

## 5. Kulamaccharinī-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā
In the term "kula maccharo kulamaccharo," the suffix 'inī' is added in the sense of its own meaning (sakkattha) to the preceding part. It means a bhikkhunī who speaks of the lack of virtue or the lack of reputation of a family, saying that the family has no faith or is not devoted. "For a bhikkhunī who speaks dispraise of bhikkhunīs" means a bhikkhunī who speaks of the lack of virtue or the lack of reputation of bhikkhunīs, saying, "Bhikkhunīs are immoral, they are of evil conduct."

## 10. Ananuññāta-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā

"Without knowing that they exist" means without knowing that those guardians, such as the mother and so forth, exist (referring to the preceptor who ordains). "Ananuññātasamuṭṭhāna" (origination of the rule on lack of permission) means that training rule which arises from speech, from body and speech, from speech and mind, or from body, speech, and mind. How? A bhikkhunī sitting in a small boundary (khaṇḍasīmā) for some business such as an Abbhāna act says, "Call the probationer, I will ordain her right here," and ordains her; thus it arises from speech. For a bhikkhunī who says, "I will ordain her after leaving the convent," and goes to the small boundary, it arises from body and speech. For a bhikkhunī who, knowing the regulation in both places, transgresses it, it arises from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind. Because of ordaining without getting permission from the guardians, it is an action and non-action (kiriyākirya).

## Ananuññāta-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā Niṭṭhitā.

## Asādhāraṇa-samuṭṭhāna-vaṇṇanā
"Acittaka (non-intentional) training rules" (according to Sāratthadīpanī Ṭīkā, Pācittiya 3.1214) are those where an offense can occur for a nun who watches dancing and so forth without knowing the nature of the action; thus, they are acittaka because the offense is incurred with a mind that does not know the object (vatthu).

"Lokavajja (worldly fault) training rules" are those where an offense is incurred only with an unwholesome mind by a nun who watches and so forth while knowing it is dancing and so forth. Therefore, the author of the commentary said, "This is the intention here," and so on.

"Sacittaka (intentional) training rules" are those where an offense can occur only when one performs the act while knowing the object, such as knowing someone is a "thief."

Because acts like higher ordination (upasampadā) and so forth cannot be performed with an exclusively unwholesome mind, they are "paṇṇattivajja" (prescribed faults). It is said by the teachers: "In this context of unique origins (asādhāraṇa-samuṭṭhāna), the state of being sacittaka or acittaka should be taken not by the knowledge or ignorance of the regulation (paṇṇatti), but by the knowledge or ignorance of the object (vatthu)."

## The Commentary on the Unique Origins is finished.

## 1. Parimaṇḍalādi-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā
"Sekhiyāni ceva" refers to the seventy-five Sekhiya rules themselves. By the statement, "They should be understood in the same manner as stated in the Bhikkhu Pātimokkha-vaṇṇanā," it is shown that because the wise say the legal determination of the meaning here in the Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha is exactly the same, a separate commentary on their meaning is not given. Whatever commentary was stated there in the Bhikkhu Pātimokkha is considered as having been stated here as well.

## The Commentary on the Training Rules concerning the Parimaṇḍala, etc., is finished.

## Thus, in the exposition of the Pātimokkha called Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī,

## in the work called Vinayatthamañjūsā, which is the Līnatthappakāsanī,

## the Commentary on the Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha is finished.

## Anigamana-kathā-vaṇṇanā
"The commentary on the Pātimokkha which was begun" is the connection (sambandha). The term "Mahāvihāravāsīnaṃ" should be connected with the preceding and following words, such as "with the ancient commentaries of the Mahāvihāra dwellers," and so forth. "Pāḷiyatthañca kevalaṃ" means the entire meaning of the Pāḷi and both Vibhaṅgas (Bhikkhu and Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga). "Ettha" means in this work, the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī.
487:
The word "Yasmā" is connected with the phrase "na hi atthi". "Yaṃ" is simply the word "yaṃ". "Sīhaḷaṭṭhakathānayaṃ" refers to the method of the Sinhalese Mātikā Commentary. "Aṭṭhakathāsāraṃ" refers to either the essence of the meaning in the Sinhalese Mātikā Commentary or the essence of the meaning in the Vinaya Commentaries. By saying this, it is shown that the teacher who composed this Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Commentary, while taking the essence of the meaning from the Sinhalese Mātikā Commentary, also took the essence of the meaning from the Vinaya Commentaries suitable for making decisions in this work.

Now, wishing to share his own merit for the attainment of supreme happiness by the world including the devas, he spoke the two verses beginning with "Yathā ca niṭṭhaṃ sampattā". "Kalyāṇanissitā" refers to those who rely on wholesome merit. "Sabbasattānaṃ" refers to all beings of various types, such as those of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara).

## The Explanation of the Concluding Remarks is finished.

## Concluding Remarks

With this sequence of words—

The famous King named Parakkamabāhu, who conquered enemy kings, who ruled the island of Laṅkā, and whose arms were valorous, made the island of Sīhaḷa, which was divided into three parts, into a single kingdom under one rule; likewise, he made the community of the Saṅgha (which was divided into three sects) united.

In the noble city of Pulatthi, which is superior to all cities, in the midst of cities that are the source of various jewels, delightful with the weight of infinite prosperity, delightful with excellent houses as high as great mountains.

In that city which has unbreakable walls and excellent gates, which is crowded with many undisturbed households, which is the dwelling place of the sacred Tooth Relic of the Lord of Munis (the Buddha), and which brings joy to the eyes of beholders.
488:
(In the city of Pulatthi) which is extremely delightful with lakes having cool, clear, and pleasant water with well-bloomed lotuses, and with trees such as the well-flowered Kadamba, Jambu, Punnāga, and Nāga; which is endowed with rows of walls and gates that are white with plaster and heart-delighting, and with stone pavements as beautiful as scattered pearls. Having built great monasteries such as Jetavana, which have more than a thousand delightful palaces and bring joy in various places, he donated them to the well-restrained monks. That King, who had faith in virtues, constantly provided the pleasant four requisites to those monks like a great flood of river water, and encouraged them in the study of scriptures (gantha) and the development of insight (vipassanā). 

That famous King built monasteries, among which is the beautiful and delightful monastery named Pacchimārāma, adorned with flower gardens and the like. I, the Elder Buddhanāga, who dwells in a beautiful palace near the residence of the Cola lineage in that monastery, being motivated by compassion; being the disciple of the Great Elder Mahāsāmi Sāriputta, who possessed pure conduct like the rays of the moon and great wisdom; being requested by the Elder Sumedha, who is endowed with a multitude of wise virtues, has a pure livelihood, and desires the stability of the Vinaya; [I] who greatly promotes the welfare of the energetic monks residing in the Mahāvihāra, in accordance with the tradition (samaya)...
489:
...have composed this excellent explanatory commentary (saṃvaṇṇanā) of the Mātikāṭṭhakathā, which is like a casket for storing the meanings found in the Vinaya and which clarifies obscure meanings.

May this commentary, which is praised by the wise, easy to understand, and approximately seven thousand [units] in extent, shine forth by dispelling delusion in the Vinaya, just as the moon traveling in the sky shines by dispelling darkness.

Desiring the welfare sought by others, I have accumulated much merit by well-composing this commentary which has noble essence and good decisions.

Through that accumulated merit, as well as the various types of merit such as generosity (dāna) and virtue (sīla) accumulated in the past, may all beings be free from suffering, be happy, be free from enmity, and reach a good destination (sugati) and the peaceful Nibbāna.

Just as this Līnatthapadīpanī text has reached completion free from dangers and obstacles, likewise, may the righteous desires of all people always reach fulfillment.

May the clouds always rain at the proper time; may the kings rule the earth righteously; may beings have faith in the Triple Gem and delight in meritorious deeds such as generosity.

## The Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī New Sub-commentary named Vinayatthamañjūsā Līnatthappakāsanī is finished.

(Conclusion of the Nissaya Teacher) Thus, this new Nissaya that we have endeavored to produce was safely completed in the year 1345 [Burmese Era]. Through this noble merit and past merits, may the wise reach Nibbāna, the deathless. May I always have a loyal audience and an audience that desires to hear the Dhamma; may suffering caused by the audience never occur. May I have pure virtue and blameless livelihood in every life, and may my audience be like me. In every life, may I see, hear, and associate with the virtuous.

The famous Saṅgha exists because of certain wisdom; that wisdom is also famous because of that Venerable One; because of that wise Saṅgha, the Mahāvissutārāma Monastery is famous. Because extraordinary sons of the Buddha (monks) appeared in a certain sect (nikāya), this sect is called the Mahāvissutārāmika Nikāya.
